articles.text: At the start of the 2021 calendar year, Piedmont school campuses were largely empty, aside from a sprinkling of teachers using classrooms to broadcast distance learning, and a handful of SPED, Millennium and TK students. From January through March, Piedmont students were brought back slowly and part time, starting from the youngest. Schedules remained in a hybrid format (online and in-person) until the school year finished in June 2021. Determined not to be tied down to a computer for another school year, parents insisted on a guarantee for in-person learning. As of August, all grades in Piedmont were back with in-person instruction. Campus life returned, masks were worn by all, and mental health concerns lessened. The school board took an aggressive stance in requiring Covid-19 vaccination for all retuning students and then for all teachers and anyone on campus. Aside from a couple of class quarantines in August, Piedmont classes have stayed open.

articles.text: This time of year, when Hallmark is running on all cylinders and images of happy families around the fireplace abound, it is easy to forget that many find this time of year difficult, to say the least. In response, congregations all over the country are embracing what some call “Blue Christmas” services. Others refer to these services as “Longest Night” services because they are timed to occur at that point in the lunar cycle when the night is longer than any other time in the year. Faith communities are waking up to the realization that their role is not simply to create opportunities for the joyful observance of Christmas, but also to offer an opportunity for those who are facing loss of one kind or another to find a place where that grief can be named, welcomed and processed with others. And here is something that should not be missed. Even though nativity scenes are found on lawns all over our county, while families sleep in the warmth of their homes, the nativity story itself is about being on the outside, uninvited and living as strangers in a strange land. The story of Mary and Joseph is a story about a family in distress. Even though the story has been romanticized over the centuries, the simple fact is that this couple found themselves pregnant out of wedlock, no doubt rejected by many in their community, on the road in a strange land with no place to lay their heads. This is a story about how light arrives at the darkest moment, how birth occurs when darkness abounds. On behalf of all the congregations sponsoring Blue Christmas, or Longest Night services

articles.text: On January 1, 2022, a new California law, Senate Bill 1383, goes into effect requiring that compostable materials (“organics”) be kept out of landfills – including food scraps, paper, cardboard, and plant trimmings – to prevent the production of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Under the law edible food currently thrown away must be recovered and donated for people to eat; the remaining organics must be collected for composting; and recyclables must also be kept out of the landfills. In Alameda County, the law is being implemented under the Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance in a partnership with local jurisdictions, garbage service providers, StopWaste, and the Alameda County Environmental Health Department. The new law affects all organic waste and pertains to residents in single-family homes, apartments, and condos; businesses, institutions, and nonprofit organizations; multifamily property owners; schools (public and private); and government agencies. Piedmont residents are already provided with curbside recycling and organics/compost collection bins. Anyone not having them should contact Republic Services at 800-320-8077. Additionally, Piedmont residents can request a free 1.5-gallon kitchen scrap pail by contacting awensley@piedmont.ca.gov. Under the law, residents must sort recyclable materials (cardboard, paper, bottles, cans) and compostable materials (food scraps, compostable paper, plant waste) into the appropriate containers (blue container for recycling, green container for composting, and black container for garbage). Businesses, institutions, nonprofits, and multifamily property owners/managers must subscribe to compost/organics and recycling collection service. In addition, sites must set up labeled and color-coded recycling and compost bins and educate employees, contractors, and tenants about the law. Certain food-generating businesses must also donate surplus edible food. The State law aims to reduce methane emissions, which are emitted into the atmosphere when compostable materials like food, paper, and yard waste are buried in landfills instead of composted or recycled. When food scraps and yard trimmings are sent to a composting facility instead of a landfill, they are turned into compost, a valuable resource farmers and gardeners use to build healthy soil and grow healthy food. The State law aims to reduce organics going to the landfill by 75% by 2025. The law also sets targets to recover and donate edible food. That’s because much of the food currently thrown away in California is perfectly good to eat and could feed people instead of going to waste or even composting. Setting up systems to make this high-quality food available for people to eat will not only cut greenhouse gas emissions, but also alleviate food insecurity in our communities. If you don’t already have service, contact Republic Services at 800- 320-8077. For more information and free resources, visit www. StopWaste.org/Rules. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov. “Investment bankers don’t network at bowling alleys.”

articles.text: Council member Tim Rood announced his intent to resign from Piedmont City Council at the December 20 meeting. Rood’s resignation becomes effective December 31. Rood explained to his council members that he is resigning because he is in the process of purchasing a home in the Laurel District of Oakland and will no longer be a resident of Piedmont. His term on the council was set to expire in November 2022. He was named by the council as Vice Mayor for the past year. Rood has served as a member of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, and as City Council liaison to the Park Commission, Planning Commission, and Recreation Commission. During his tenure, twice with the responsibility of being your Councilmember,” said Rood. “Even as a private citizen in Oakland, I’ll be cheering Piedmont’s progress in doing its part to address the state and region’s housing crisis, creating opportunities for greater diversity of households and incomes in its housing stock, and acknowledging and trying to make amends to those hurt by the shameful injustices in Piedmont’s past, including the descendants of Sidney Dearing and others excluded from Piedmont by racial prejudice.” Piedmont’s City Charter requires that Council members appoint a successor within 60 days after the effective date of resignation. The City Council will hold a meeting early in January to determine the process for appointment of a successor. The new law affects all organic waste and pertains to residents in single-family homes, apartments, and condos; businesses, institutions, and nonprofit organizations; multifamily property owners; schools (public and private); and government agencies. Piedmont residents are already provided with curbside recycling and organics/compost collection bins. Anyone not having them should contact Republic Services at 800-320-8077. Additionally, Piedmont residents can request a free 1.5-gallon kitchen scrap pail by contacting awensley@piedmont.ca.gov. Under the law, residents must sort recyclable materials (cardboard, paper, bottles, cans) and compostable materials (food scraps, compostable paper, plant waste) into the appropriate containers (blue container for recycling, green container for composting, and black container for garbage). Businesses, institutions, nonprofits, and multifamily property owners/managers must subscribe to compost/organics and recycling collection service. In addition, sites must set up labeled and color-coded recycling and compost bins and educate employees, contractors, and tenants about the law. Certain food-generating businesses must also donate surplus edible food. The State law aims to reduce methane emissions, which are emitted into the atmosphere when compostable materials like food, paper, and yard waste are buried in landfills instead of composted or recycled. When food scraps and yard trimmings are sent to a composting facility instead of a landfill, they are turned into compost, a valuable resource farmers and gardeners use to build healthy soil and grow healthy food. The State law aims to reduce organics going to the landfill by 75% by 2025. The law also sets targets to recover and donate edible food. That’s because much of the food currently thrown away in California is perfectly good to eat and could feed people instead of going to waste or even composting. Setting up systems to make this high-quality food available for people to eat will not only cut greenhouse gas emissions, but also alleviate food insecurity in our communities. If you don’t already have service, contact Republic Services at 800- 320-8077. For more information and free resources, visit www. StopWaste.org/Rules. articles.text: As the Post celebrates its 24th year of publication, it may bring a smile to the faces of our readers as they see a list of the top newspapers in the country. 1. The Wall Street Journal is read by the people who run the country. 2. The Washington Post is read by people who think they run the country. 3. The New York Times is read by people who think they should run the country and who are very good at crossword puzzles. 4. USA Today is read by people who think they ought to run the country, but don't really understand The New York Times. They do, however, like their statistics shown in pie charts. 5. 6. The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn't mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn't have to leave Southern California to do it. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. The New York Daily News is read by people who aren't too sure who's running the country and don't really care as long as they can get a seat on the subway. The New York Post is read by people who don't care who is running the country as long as they do something really scandalous, preferably while intoxicated. The Miami Herald is read by people who are running another country but need the baseball scores. The San Francisco Chronicle is read by people who aren't sure if there is a country, or that anyone is running it; but If so, they oppose all that they stand for. There are occasional exceptions, such as if the leaders are handicapped minority feminist atheist dwarfs who also happen to be illegal aliens from any other country, or galaxy, provided, of course, that they are not Republicans. The National Enquirer is read by people trapped in line at the grocery store. The Piedmont Post is read by people who quietly run everything but the country, and prefer a smaller newspaper for Where In the World Are We photo ops when they travel. Scan to book your estimate!

articles.text: 15 miles. 10 boys. 4 adults. 39 thousand steps. A ferry ride and 2 bay area cities. The statistics alone should raise some interest for pandemic weary readers itching to travel. An intrepid group of urban explorers assembled at Corpus Christi School at 8 a.m. on Saturday, December 11, for a hike from the school in Piedmont to San Francisco’s Ocean Beach. The group assembled on a cold morning at the school parking lot and made their way to Jack London Square to catch the ferry. Everyone was appropriately dressed for the weather, especially Jack Gros in his standard t-shirt and athletic pants – but it was a Troop 6 shirt. On the way Scoutmaster Bill Bruin imparted his building and engineering knowledge to the young Scouts, pointing out buildings that were retrofitted or almost collapsed due to the Loma Prieta earthquake im 1989. The Scouts walked by Oakland landmarks Lake Merritt, Children’s Fairyland, and Frank Ogawa Plaza while traveling down Broadway to Jack London square to await the ferry. We took a short ferry ride to the Ferry Building, where the Saturday Farmers Market was in full swing. The Scouts had a chance to check out the different stalls. The Chalaquilles and Key Lime pie offerings were rated top notch. From there, we saw the leaning Millennium tower, walked around the beautiful Salesforce park, looked at the murals at the Old Post Office, and stopped in Chinatown for a quick dim sum lunch before going on to Union Square where we ran into the participants of the city-wide Santa Pub Crawl. Who knew? We continued on to the Civic Center via Market Street and on to the famous Victorian houses called the Painted Ladies at Alamo Square. At this point we had done about 10 miles of hiking and everyone was tired but in Troop 6 Scouts and advisors prepare to leave Oakland on their journey to Ocean Beach on December 11. Piedmont Scouts at the entrance to San Francisco’s Chinatown. Troop 6 Scouts Alex Mante (left), Jack Gros, Anson Co, Peter Ichimaru, Vincent Doubrava, Brett Batcheller, Sammie Do, RJ Grace, and Matthew Goldweber in front of the “Painted Ladies” Victorian homes in San Francisco. very good spirits. The final leg of the trek included walking around the University of San Francisco campus and its beautiful St. Ignatius Church. This was the jumping off point to the eastern edge of Golden Gate Park and the final leg of the hike to the beach. Entering the park we walked by the Conservatory of Flowers, watched a few rollerbladers, saw the de Young Museum, Japanese Tea Garden and Botanical Garden. The Scouts purchased some well deserved snacks at the local hot dog stand, including ice cream, then embarked on the final push, walking by Stow Lake, the Polo Fields, the Bison Paddock, Dutch Windmills and finally to the final destination of Ocean Beach in time for the sunset at 4:50 p.m. We took some final photos on the beach before being picked up by Troop 6 parents for a ride back to Oakland. Thanks to hike master Jack Throne and Troop 6 Senior Patrol Leader Sammie Do for leading the hike. I can safely say that a good time was had by all. Aristotle Aquino is an Eagle Scout parent with Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 6. RJ Grace (left), Vincent Doubrava, Jack Throne, and Alex Mante take a well-deserved break in Golden Gate Park. Jack Throne, Mr. Aquino, Brett Batcheller, Matthew Goldweber, and Bill Bruin celebrate arriving at Ocean Beach. Troop 6 Scouts view the shimmering winter sunset at Ocean Beach.
articles.title: Troop 6 Scouts – from Corpus Christi to Ocean Beach in SF

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, December 29, 2021 SchOOLs Thinking Outside The Classroom Questions about questions By Katie Pengilly Questioning is a common technique used by most parents hoping to encourage their children to talk and have conversations. Sometimes this technique works, and sometimes it does not. Let’s consider why. Not all questions are created equal when it comes to enhancing language and extending conversations. For example, questions based on the child’s interests and experiences encourage conversation and stimulate vocabulary development. Take the time to follow the child’s lead to discover what he/she may want to talk about. On the other hand, overuse of questions that are not based on the child’s interest may be interpreted as “testing questions” and tend to discourage conversation. These questions are often aimed at showing us if the child knows something or not, for example “what color is that?” or “what does a lion say?” Another consideration is the level of difficulty of the questions posed. If the questions are all very easy for the child to answer, and do not require much thought, they will not encourage language or thinking skills. Alternatively, if your Practice engaging your children in conversation by asking them questions. questions are all very challenging the child may lose interest in interacting with you. We can aim for questions that are just one step ahead of the child’s level, and make sure that the child understands the question and has the vocabulary needed to answer them. Some questions are naturally answered with one word, and others encourage a longer response. If your child is primarily answering with one word, it could be that you are relying on “closed ended” questions such as “yes/no” questions (“is that your hat?”), “what” or “who” questions (“what is that?”), or “do questions” (“do you like dinosaurs?”) “Open ended” questions require longer answers and encourage children to think and express more. This question type often requires the child to give their opinion (“what do you think about the fireman we saw?”) or an explanation which requires the child to think beyond the here and now (“what are we going to do at the birthday party?”) “Why” and “how” questions can promote expanded responses (“why do you think she is crying?”, or “how should we build the snowman?”) Research shows that there are other ways that are just as (or even more) effective in terms of helping children to participate in conversations and encouraging children to talk. One such technique is to reduce the number of adult questions in favor of adult comments. For example, instead of asking the child “what is the bear doing?”, you could comment “oh no, the bear got hurt” and wait for your child to add their own comment. A balance of adult driven questions and comments can promote more sincere and interactive communication. Another language enhancing alternative to questioning is wait time. With this technique, after the parent says or does something, they wait (without saying anything!) while looking expectantly at the child. In my practice, when coaching parents, I notice that this may feel uncomfortable at first. But if the parent waits long enough the child will often say something. We often jump in with questions, in an attempt to keep the conversation going, but perhaps we would benefit from questioning all of the questioning? Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. February 24: A Piedmont parent “Reopening Advocacy” online group presents the school board with a survey containing data from 406 Piedmont families imploring the district to commit to in-person learning in fall 2021. February 25: All K-6 grades are back in-person on a hybrid learning schedule. And estimated 25% of students choose to remain entirely in distance learning. March 1: Piedmont Makers donates $420,000 to the high school to outfit its Fabrication Lab in the new STEAM classroom building. March 1: Amid chaotic Covid-19 vaccine rollout, Gov. Newsom designates that 10% of doses per week (75,000) doses to go to school employees. March 2: Covid-19 case rates in Alameda County go below 7 new cases per day per 100,000 population, clearing way for PMS and PHS to reopen. March 9: The Reopening Advocacy group distributes over 400 lawn signs reading “OPEN OUR SCHOOLS.” March 16: 7-10th graders return to campus part time in a hybrid model. Middle schoolers receive 2.5 hours of instruction in person per week. March 23: 11-12th graders return to campus part time in a hybrid model. High schoolers with a full schedule receive an average of 4 hours 22 minutes of class time per week. March 25: A commitment to full-time in-person instruction for the fall of 2021 is made by the school district, school board and teachers’ union in a signed joint statement. April 5: The city’s Recreation Department waives childcare fees for teachers who are teaching in person. April 15: Individuals age 16 and older are now eligible for the Covid-19 vaccine. April 27. All PHS, MHS and PMS student are given more class time and will be on the same schedule. A full course load warrants 8 hours and 45 minutes per See Schools in Review on page 8 Staff photos PHS Principal Adam Littlefield addresses the crowd at the start of the 2021 graduation ceremony. E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Jay Russell Chabot Space and Science Center: NYE Balloon Drop Chabotspace.org Friday, December 31, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. Ring in the new year without staying up past bedtime. When it’s noon in Oakland, it will be 2022 somewhere on the planet. Chabot will be celebrating the stroke of midnight around the world with multiple balloon drops throughout the day. Continuing a 21-year Bay Area tradition, the party will feature hundreds of colorful, biodegradable balloons raining down from above starting at 11 a.m., then at 12:00, 1:00, 2:00, 3:00 and 4:00 p.m. Bring the kids to watch the stunning stream of cascading balloons. Little Ice Rink at Alameda Point Littleicerink.com 1951 Monarch St, Alameda, 993-0939 The Little Ice Rink is the only ice rink in the inner East Bay, The Little Ice Rink has partnered with Off the Grid which means a rotating selection of delicious food trucks and libations. Adding to the fun, local musicians and DJs will perform on an indoor stage. Housed in a historic airplane hangar The Little Ice Rink offers an outdoor feel with protection from the elements. The 5,000-square-foot location offers bay views and is open through the holidays weekdays and weekends everyday. Oakland Zoo – Glowfari Oaklandzoo.org 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 Lit up Lantern show The Oakland Zoo’s nighttime Glowfari event remains open through February 6, due to immense popularity. Glowfari will entertain every member of the family young and old with the hundreds of brilliantly lit and life sized animal lanterns all different from last year. Take the milelong illuminated stroll through the Zoo and don’t forget to ride the gondola to the land of bugs featuring a 65-foot Queen Ant Tunnel. Finish the evening with a ride on the Express Train through the Winter Wonderland. Bay Area Discovery Museum – New Year’s Eve Bayareadiscoverymuseum.org/visit/first-time-visit/events/ noon-years-eve 557 McReynolds Road, Sausalito December 31, 2021, 9:00 am to 2:00 pm Ring in the new year without keeping your family up past bedtime. Celebrate the start of 2022 at Bay Area Discovery Museum with this popular annual event. This kidfriendly celebration includes a ball drop at noon, so you can enjoy the countdown without the midnight meltdown. Enjoy a live DJ and join in a dance party. COLLEGE NEWS 3 from Piedmont receive Dean’s Award at Colgate Piedmont residents Colin Dixon, Charlotte Prendergast, and Tucke Backer were named to the Dean’s List with Distinction at Colgate University for the 2021 Spring semester. To be eligible, students must achieve a grade point average of 3.6 or higher while completing at least three courses. Dixon, a 2016 graduate of Piedmont High School, is a Physics major. Prendergast, a graduate of Carondelet High School ,is a Sociology undeclared major. Backer, a graduate of Head-Royce School, is a Political Science major. Located in Hamilton, New York, Colgate is a leading university for students who want classes with rigor, faculty with passion, and confidence in knowing they will learn how to thrive in work and life. Colgate offers 56 majors and supports 25 Division I athletic teams with an undergraduate enrollment of 3,000 students. Meuller named to Oregon State Honor Roll Sebastian Mueller, a senior majoring in Environmental Science, was named to the Honor Roll at Oregon State University in Corvallis for the Fall semester. A total of 8,043 students earned a letter grade of B plus (3.50) or better to make the listing. Students on the Honor Roll must carry at least 12 graded hours of course work.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: The holidays gave the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir much to celebrate, with a return to live concerts and performances in the community. The Performing Department Choirs shared the light of the season with Luminescence, their 40th annual Candlelight Concert, on Saturday, December 4 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. “Heralded as a welcome home to choir, this performance featured a diverse array of music that reminds us what it is to be human, exploring experiences of love, loss, and renewal through the power of shared song,” according to Artistic Director Eric Tuan. Due to Covid 19 protocols, ticketing was limited to singers’ families and performances were done at reduced capacity. Ensemble shared selections from Rautavaara’s Lapsimessu (A Children’s Mass) and a lively arrangement of a Hindu devotional song, Bolo Bolo Sab Mil Bolo, arranged by Eric Tuan. They previewed their performance at Yoshi’s with David Benoit’s A Charlie Brown Christmas with the holiday favorite Christmas Time is Here. Concert Choir embodied the sounds and coziness of the season with Henry Purcell’s Sound The Trumpet and Miklós Kocsár’s Cozy Cat Nap. Conductor Andrew Brown lifted the spirits of everyone with a rousing and joyful welcome, followed by a call to a better world with Jim Papoulis’s Give Us Hope. In the second performance, Ancora and Ecco returned live with nuanced renditions of diverse musical styles. Ancora’s selections spanned traditional carols, an arrangement of the spiritual Deep River, to selections by Dublanc, Karai and Tuan. Robert Geary, the choir’s founding Artistic Director, led PEBCC’s premiere women’s ensemble, who delivered ethereal tone, beautiful vocal lines, and energized harmonies. Rounding out the evening, Ecco set toes tapping with TāReKiTa by Reena Esmail, in addition to selections from Estonia and Herbert Howells. They brought the soul of the season into Moses Hogan’s arrangement of Music Down in My Soul with Tuan at the piano. “I was truly amazed at what [PEBCC has] achieved with these kids, given the crazy new world we live in. If anything, the choir sounds even better than before – Singers in Ancora masks or not,” commented choir parent Anastasia Edel. The following weekend PEBCC’s younger singers in the Training Department presented a recital at First Presbyterian Church of Oakland on December 11. For more than half of the singers, it was their first live concert performance with the choirs. Their excitement and beautiful singing shone brightly. Offerings ranged from the Hebrew song Al Shosha D’Varim, selections from Oscar Hammerstein’s The King and I, to folk songs and One Foot/Lead With Love written by Oakland choral activist Melanie de More. The masks could not contain the singers’ energy and excitement to be performing for live audiences again. Community performances finished out the holiday season with Ensemble performing with David Benoit at Yoshi’s and with the Oakland Ballet for Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker at the Paramount Theatre. Because seating for these December performances was limited, PEBCC will offer a filmed version of all the choirs as its Winter Concert in multiple screenings on the afternoon of Saturday, January 22 at the New Parkway Theatre in Oakland. Tickets and more details on this special event are available at https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ event-calendar. Artistic Director Eric Tuan conducts Ecco in a concert in Berkeley. articles.text: Staff Photo One year ago sports were still on the horizon for Piedmont. Instead of the typical Fall, Winter, and Spring seasons, the Covid pandemic forced reduced seasons earlier this year from late February until early June. Reflecting on the days one year ago leading into 2021, we’re able to put in the rear-view mirror a time when Alameda County was still waging the Covid color-coded tier system. Prep sports in California were still looking for clearance from the state, and the California Interscholastic Federation made the decision to compress 9 months of sports into four months from late February until the first week of June this year. Now a full semester into the school year, Piedmont’s teams are grateful to have a full season of activity, a renewed chance at postseason play, and the possibility of earning banners and annual awards. Our annual sports recap of the year includes highlights of the most outstanding achievements. Although the 2020-2021 school year did not provide the opportunity for traditional sports schedules and seasons and competitions, we’re able to sing their praises, and look toward more success in 2022. Here are our top moments from 2021: • The saga of clearance for prep sports Talking about sports in 2021 cannot be done without starting with the progression of events in California. It wasn’t until late February before schools were permitted to have interscholastic competition. The CIF and North Coast Section boards were scrambling for answers up until January. The state differentiated on sports based on contact and possible level of transmission. In the Purple tier was Cross Country, Golf, Skiing/Snowboarding, Swimming & Diving, Tennis, and Track & Field. The Orange tier featured Football, Boys Lacrosse, Badminton, Volleyball, Soccer, Water Polo. The Yellow tier, considered the most restrictive based on contact level, was just boys’ and girls’ basketball. But on February 19, Gov. Gavin Newsome loosened restrictions to permit outdoor contact sports (football, lacrosse, baseball, softball, soccer, and water polo) to begin competition starting on February 26. It put each sport on course for a mid-March starts, with soccer not starting The boys’ water polo team set school history this fall by winning its their first WACC championship. until April. The largest hurdle came with basketball. Former Piedmont High and current Miramonte boys’ basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis spearheaded the sports’ return to action with the Bay Area Basketball Coaches Alliance. The change came with findings provided from the Golden State High School Football Coaches coalition, which successfully initiated an agreement to bring back football to California in late January. They found that transmission level for student-athletes for indoor sports showed favorable data compared to their outdoor counterparts. Lavdiotis’ Bay Area Basketball Coaches Alliance eventually finalized a late-April return for basketball. Piedmont High boys’ and girls’ programs then got the green light to have an 18-game season. The 2021 school year during the pandemic also came with several protocol changes. There was no postseason play for North Coast Section teams and no league championships, other than boys’ and girls’ tennis and water polo. Schools were forced to play only schools nearby, meaning Piedmont couldn’t play against schools from Marin, Sonoma, Napa, or Solano counties. Now the North Coast Section and league (WACC) have returned to traditional schedules with full seasons and post-season championships. • Boys’ Water Polo first league title Piedmont’s Boys’ water polo team finished with a 19-6 overall record in the recent fall season, setting school history by winning the program’s first-ever Western Alameda County Conference Championship on October 30 with a 12-8 win over No. 1 seeded Berkeley. The championship banner required at least 15 years of effort by the school. Senior captain Antonio Rivera logged five goals and three assists, while junior goalie Dariush Kashani had nine saves and one steal. The Highlanders went into the Division 2 NCS playoffs as the No. 3 seed and defeated Terra Coach John Savage and his team celebrate after defeating Berkeley 12-8 for the league title on October 30 this fall. Linda 18-13 in the quarterfinals. They fell to No. 2 Marin Academy 7-4 in the semifinals on November 10. The squad earned six AllLeague selections, including firstteam honors for Antonio Rivera and Dariush Kashani. Second-team honors were awarded to Murray Davis, Peter Krumins, and Shane Miller, while Declan Linnane and George Stein were given Honorable Mentions. • Jack Stein’s record year In the recent cross country season, senior Jack Stein helped lead Piedmont to the State Meet in Fresno on November 27 for its first reappearance since 2017. At the Woodward Park course, Stein clocked a time of 15:43.4 to finish Jack Stein made history this fall with a time of 15:29.4 at the NCS Cross-Country Finals on November 20 at Hayward High for a course record. He also clocked a 15:43.4 at the CIF State Championship in Fresno, the second fastest in Piedmont history.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Phil Witte, a former attorney, is the cartoonist whose FLIP has appeared in the Piedmont Post since 2008. His cartoons have been published in dozens of publications in the U.S. and U.K., including The Wall Street Journal, Reader’s Digest, San Francisco Chronicle, New Statesman, and Private Eye, as well as in books, calendars, and greeting cards. His humor book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and the sequel on turning 60 have sold over 170,000 copies. Phil also co-writes the Anatomy of a Cartoon blog for CartoonStock, founded by Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker. Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in group shows in San Francisco, Minneapolis, London, and Galway, Ireland. He has been a cartoonist-in-residence at the Charles Schulz Museum and the San Francisco Cartoon Art Museum. Phil is a member of the National Cartoonists Society. See www.philwitte.com. The cartoons shown below represent our favorite picks from 2021. Self-drawn sketch of cartoonist Phil Witte. “Wait—zoom was a word before it was a thing?” “As a harbinger of doom, you’re a little late.” “I got Pfizer, I got Moderna, I got AstraZeneca.” “How’s the remote learning going” “That’s a mammoth. I told you to bring home a mastodon.”

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Pace Gallery teamLab: Sketch Ocean, 2020–present, by teamLab (Japanese, est. 2001). Interactive digital installation. Sound by Hideaki Takahashi. San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now displaying an immersive art exhibition entitled “teamLab: Continuity.” The art experience immerses patrons in a “wondrous ecosystem of lush imagery drawn from nature and East Asian art that dynamically evolves around you.” Rich hues are displayed dramatically via light-work onto the museum’s walls, in sumptuous images of crows, flowers, butterflies, fish, and more imagery. The Tokyo-based artist-collective teamLab is known for producing interactive, interconnected digital artworks that marry art and technology. “Everything exists in a long, fragile, yet miraculous borderless continuity of life,” teamLab founder Toshiyuki Inoko said. The exhibition is designed to be an immersive experience – not about the digital realm, but instead about the natural world. Tickets are available at: https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/teamlab-continuity.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum exhibiting teamLab: Continuity

articles.text: Twelfth Night, a contemporary musical adaption of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery, is now playing at SF Playhouse. It was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. In Shakespeare’s story, Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a Duke. Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role and finds her true love in the process. San Francisco Playhouse’s production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk score by Shania Taub. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Maria (Cathleen Riddley) bids Toby (Michael Gene Sullivan) good night after they have hatched a plot with Andrew (Caleb Haven Draper) in “Twelfth Night.” Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/upcoming-plays/ for play times and to purchase tickets. The box office phone is (415) 677-9596. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required to attend the production. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street.
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s Twelfth Night runs through Jan. 15

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre will fully reopen on January 21, 2022 since its closure in March 2020 due to the Covid- 19 pandemic. The company will produce Freestyle Love Supreme, created by Thomas Kail, Lin-Manuel Miranda, and Anthony Venezaile, and directed by Kail. The show will be performed from January 21 through February 13. Through a donation and matching funds from Salesforce ACT will offer 15,000 tickets for as little as $5. Launching its American tour at the Geary Theater in San Francisco, Freestyle Love Supreme pays tribute to John Coltrane’s improvisational musical genius, taking the audience on a freestyle music and comedy ride. The cast includes Andrew Bancroft, Jay C. Ellis, Aneesa Folds, Kaila Mullady, Morgan Reilly, and Chris Sullivan. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatso n / 2 0 2 0 212 2 - s e a s o n /f r e e - style-love-supreme/, or call the box office at (415) 749-2228. articles.text: UC Berkeley’s Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive currently is presenting an art exhibition. Titled New Time: Art and Feminisms in the 21st Century, the exhibit it on view now through January 30. The exhibition explores the values, strategies, and ways of life and culture in current feminist art. Artworks made in 2000 and beyond are the primary focus, but many installations on view span several generations, mediums, and geographies. The exhibition is organized around eight themes: hysteria; the gaze; revisiting historical subjects through a feminist lens; the fragmented female body; gender fluidity; labor, domesticity, and activism; female anger; and feminist utopias. New Time is inspired by Bay Area poet Leslie Scalapino’s feminist poem of the same name. Many female artists, groups, musicians, and activists are featured, including Judy Chicago, Laura Aguilar, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Nicole Eisenman, Kiki Smith, and Amy Sillman. To learn more, visit https:// bampfa.org/program/new-timeart-and-feminisms-21st-century. Poster for Art and Feminisms at BAMPFA. ®
articles.title: Art and Feminisms exhibit at Berkeley Art Museum through Jan. 30

articles.text: Ronn Guidi with the founding of Oakland Ballet put Oakland on the map, much like the Oakland Symphony’s conductor Gerhard Samuel, back when Oakland had no professional performing arts profile evident on any level. Guidi turned the Oakland Ballet into an habile touring ensemble performing in major venues, taught ballet students, and lectured to kids entering dance, telling them fairy tales leaving them wide-eyed with wonder. I followed his new ballet enterprise from 1964 on. Overlooked in many tributes since his passing on Thanksgiving Day, November 25, were three of his great professional accomplishments: He brought two earlier choreographic greats, and Leonid Massine of the pre-World War II renowned Ballet Russe, and Eugene Loring (Billy the Kid) in residence to Oakland, to restage their works. In addition, he created a soft-focus white ballet by moonlight to go with Eric Satie’s Gymnopedies music, performed on tour in New York state. It was Choreographer Ronn Guidi (left) guiding Oakland A’s Manager Tony LaRussa for his guest appearance with Oakland Ballet in The Nutcracker. savaged by the New York press for stealing the idea from Sir Frederic Ashton and the Royal Ballet. (It took a yellowing Oakland Tribune clipping I’d written around 1965 to force retraction of the misinformed critique.) Along the way, he was a consistently diplomatic arts leader here, running his troupe and school, a sparkplug to the cultural growth of Oakland. Shortly before his accidental death on Thanksgiving Day, the 85-yearold native Oaklander was still teaching evolving East Bay dancers, active to the end. Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy, an active music critic, was the music and dance critic for the Oakland Tribune from 1964-1979, and later for the San Jose Mercury News.
articles.title: Reminiscences of an unforgettable dance director, Ronn Guidi

articles.text: In lieu of a tired Xmas letter, here is a highly inspiring “Silent Night” story that has not so much to do with religion, as with rising to the occasion, far beyond one’s everyday meager talents. I ferret it out a few years ago, but it bears retelling during the Twelve Days of Christmas. Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers two centuries ago, the answer is an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ broke down, with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices – equally straightforward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, and eventually was attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818 they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we could still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We could create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith, and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Paul Hertelendy is a music reviewer whose reviews of classical music may be viewed on the website sfarts.org.

articles.text: this year I cannot offer my annual “The Best and the Rest” as a For more than two decades I have reviewed movies for the Piedmont Post. I’ve sat in dark rooms (preferably on the aisle), and watched, sometimes in complete wonder, as a story unfolds on a large screen, a display of remarkable technology that blends images, sound, and music together so seamlessly that the world beyond fades away. Good or bad, a larger than life narrative appears, asking only that we suspend our disbelief and embrace a drama, a comedy, or perhaps a chilling dystopian/futuristic story. And the key word is “story.” From the time that our antecedents sat around campfires and listened to an elder fashion a tale, we have entered the world of imagination, driven by, well, storytelling magic. Today, remarkably, if screenwriters and filmmakers can visualize it (with the aid of CGI), they can create it. At this moment we find ourselves on the cusp of the third year of the COVID-19 pandemic (and its variants). It often haunts our days – inviasible, everywhere but nowhere – and we continue to hide behind totemic masks, trying to remember to keep our distance from one another while avoiding enclosed spaces. Since January of 2020 I have not entered a movie theater, and I wait, along with the global community, for this malignant virus to be finally behind us, hopefully equated with the seasonal flu. But review of the year past. I have no movies to offer, and I wonder with a hint of dread if the movie industry will ever fully recover. Meanwhile I have spent the last two years suggesting to readers of the Post that they revisit previously reviewed films. On occasion I’ve written reviews of new films streamed on a variety of platforms such as HBO. My favorites were the wonderful, yet deeply sad, Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close; the remarkable Book of Henry; the surprising News of the World; and I followed weekly The Undoing, Mare of Easttown, plus the recent American Rust. Also, a new experience was binge watching Billions and The Affair. One final comment: I watched some of the above films more than once, and realized that though we assume that movies are a one and done experience, I’ve come to believe that it is impossible to catch all of the dialogue, images, plot intricacies and performances in just one viewing. I’ve concluded that movies were not made to be seen only once. Those that are extraordinary – films we can accurately describe as works of art – are intended to be analyzed, pondered, and enjoyed. It’s been a revelation. Postscript, so to speak: Happy New Year to all of our readers. May newspapers and journalism continue to thrive, the tenacious Piedmont Post being a fine example.

articles.text: Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position. 1. 2. 3. long. 4. 5.

A hole was found in the nudist camp wall, but the police are looking into it. Music vs. musical terms By Joseph Gold Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position. A matching game for music lovers We are celebrating the 251st birthday of one of Classical Music’s greatest composers, Ludwig van Beethoven, born on a winter night in Bonn, Germany on December 16, 1770. Despite the success of his works, not all of them were universally appreciated when they were first performed. To test the knowledge of our readers, match the bad review with the Beethoven masterpiece shown below. 1. Beethoven’s ____ is generally regarded as an incomprehensible production, the depths of which (if they really were depths) it was impossible to fathom 5. The general impression it left on me was that of a concert made up of Indian war whoops and angry wildcats. A. Symphony #2 B. Fidelio Overture C. Symphony #6 D. Missa Solemnis E. “Ode to Joy” Celebrating Beethoven’s 250th Birthday Answers:1A, 2B, 3C, 4D, 5E

articles.text: • 2018 Jim Barry Cover Drive Cabernet Sauvignon, $15 (Best Value) The Coonawara region of South Australia is known for its high-quality Cabernet Sauvignon vineyards. articles.text: Great Value Aussie wines invade the U.S. My taste in wine has changed over the years. I remember when I first started out imbibing in the early 80’s it was all about bigger is better. I wanted wines that punched me in the mouth. I remember adoring huge Australian Chardonnays that had so much wood a koala could live in them. Likewise with red it was either teeth staining Petite Sirah or giant Aussie Shiraz that drank like someone had dumped a wheelbarrow of blueberry jam in your mouth. Nowadays nothing thrills me more than an ethereal, light as a feather French Burgundy or a crisp, ephemeral Riesling from the Mosel. It turns out in the intervening years Australian wine has changed, too. They have diversified greatly and now produce wines in every style imaginable. Quality, too, has risen – at least in the fine wine producers. (OK lets be upfront about the Yellow Tail problem. Australia’s best-known wine, shipped in the billions of gallons around the world. is what many people think of when they hear the term Australian wine. To be clear, Yellow Tail is an abomination. It is not wine ….it is fruit punch with a kick.) So, many quality Aussie wineries have to try extra hard to get folks to take them seriously. One winery that has proven its place in the high-quality group from Australia is Jim Barry. The Barry family founded their winery in South Australia’s Clare Valley in 1959 and helped make the region one of Australia’s most noted winegrowing areas. They specialized in Riesling and Shiraz and later added Cabernet Sauvignon from vineyards purchased in the Coonawara region. Today the winery is run by the founders’ grandchildren who are carrying forward the legacy.

articles.text: On an autumn Sunday evening this year Piedmont resident Laura Maestrelli walked down the front stairs of her home on Oakland Avenue to see a man staring at her house. She introduced herself, and it was the start of a unique Piedmont tale of strangers united by one home. A well-dressed gentleman in a fedora stood on the opposite sidewalk in the dusk with a friendly smile. Scott Kilner had taken a stroll down memory lane to admire a beautiful home special to his memory. “Excuse me, but do you live here?” he asked. “My grandparents owned this home from the 1930s to the 1960s. Some of my happiest memories from my childhood took place here,” he said. Maestrelli recalled her reaction. “Of course I had to invite him in for a tour, even though the house was a total disaster with toys strewn everywhere.” Kilner was invited into a home he hadn’t stepped inside since 1960. He took the tour wide-eyed and smiling as long-ago memories surfaced. Maestrelli then invited Scott and brother Brian to a brunch to share tales about the home along with the most recent former owners of the house, Barry and Jane Horn and their daughter Jane Essner. A month later, on an October afternoon, three generations of residents came together to share their memories of the Piedmont home they all shared. Old pictures were brought out, and stories shared as Maestrelli displayed the 100-year-old floor plans found in the attic. The Horns had a surprise for the others. In the basement was a Frederick Ackerman, Scott and Brian’s grandfather, bought the home on Oakland Avenue in 1930, seven years after it was built by noted architect Houghton Sawyer. Brian (left) and Scott Kilner hold up a picture of their grandparents who owned the home from the 1930s to 60s. New friends brought together by the history of one Piedmont home share stories over brunch in September 2021. hidden button that when pressed produces an electric buzzing sound. With the home’s original circuitry intact, the button popped open a little chamber on the other wall, which likely was used to store alcohol during prohibition. The next big surprise for the Kilners was the transformation of their grandfather’s office. “My grandfather, Frederick Ackerman, had a strong personality and was a pretty serious business executive as Chairman for the Greyhound Corporation. His office upstairs had a big desk and was a sanctuary of sorts. Now that room is painted with a rainbow on the wall and was filled with children’s toys. It could not be more different than the way it was used decades ago; that made me laugh,” said Scott Kilner. Maestrelli and husband Dustin Frazier were in for more history lessons courtesy of their backyard. Vic Bergeron, of Trader Vic’s restaurant fame and inventor of the Mai Tai, was a frequent guest of the Ackermans. A brick fireplace in the backyard, which Maestrelli doesn’t use, was where Bergeron would smoke ducks, a popular specialty for many years at Trader Vic’s restaurant. Tales of a pond in the backyard, now long gone, offered insight into Piedmont history. “We learned there used to be an annual autumnal faire at Havens in which kids would win prizes like goldfish. It was well-known that if you won a goldfish, kids could come up to the Horn’s house and dump it in their fish pond. Because of the deciduous trees over it, no one had to feed them and the goldfish got huge in this pond,” Maestrelli recounted. Summing up the remarkable visit of three generations of homeowners, Maestrelli said, “I think we all left the gathering feeling a special kind of kinship with each other, and an appreciation for how quickly strangers can become friends when a wellloved 100-year-old house plays matchmaker.” In 1958 Brian Kilner (left) and brother Scott are shown on the front steps of their grandparents’ home on Oakland Avenue. Brian Kilner shares old photos with Jane and Barry Horn who owned the home for 36 years until 2014.
articles.title: When the walls talk, 100 years of a home’s history revealed

articles.text: Construction is set to begin on the Montclair Village Plaza and Antioch Court Streetscape Improvement. The highly anticipated and hard-fought capital improvement campaign now has a contractor in place, Beliveau Contractors of Oakland, having won the bidding process that began in the Fall of 2020. The goal has been to break ground in February of 2022. The long-awaited roadway replacement and traffic safety infrastructure upgrade to Antioch Court at the intersection of Mountain Blvd. will also incorporate a “Village Plaza” into the redesign allowing the quaint side street to be closed for special events, al fresco dining, and cultural and educational programming. Antioch Court will remain open to vehicle traffic but can be easily closed to host an event like a summer concert series or dine out. The project will help implement a safe, more walk-able space for everyday use as well as having the ability to host community gatherings and celebrations, highlighting the talented artists and small businesses of the area. Over 700 individuals have purchased commemorative bricks to be displayed in the new Plaza. They will include dedications, graphics created from artwork or photographs, logos, and positive messages to be etched in stone for posterity. These visuals will bring a lifetime of inspiration for all to see! Funds raised will go towards the final enhancements of the streetscape and to creating a full events calendar for all to enjoy. The deadline to have a custom engraved granite paver or standard brick is January 8. To order a brick, visit MontclairVillage. com. Gifts of any amount or the purchase of a donor brick (starting at $125) can be made at MontclairBricks.com. “This will be a transformative project and an economic engine for this small business community, as well as a public venue able to connect the residents of Montclair and neighboring Piedmont to artists, performers, and nonprofits, especially youth and schools.” said Daniel Swafford, The streetscape project is adjacent to Peet’s Coffee, Sophie’s Tea Shop, and Kakui Sushi, centered around a number of eateries and cafes, and anchored by Montclair’s newest commercial development, the F & M Bank Building (constructed in 2019). In addition to Antioch Court, La Salle Ave. and Merced Ave. will be repaved in February 2022 as part of the City of Oakland’s 3-year paving plan. Daniel Swafford is Executive Director of Montclair Village Association.

articles.text: Charles “Sandy” A. McPhee Jr., a second generation and longtime Piedmont resident, died on the afternoon of December 16, 2021 at home with his wife by his side. Born on January 15, 1945 in San Francisco, he was the oldest son of Margaret and Charles McPhee of Piedmont. He moved to Piedmont from Los Angeles and attended Piedmont High School where he graduated in 1963. He attended the University of Oregon and was a member of the Beta Theta Pi Fraternity. He transferred to the University of California in Berkeley and graduated with a degree in economics. Following graduation, he married Sue Mulford at St. Leo’s Church in Oakland on July 1, 1967. He then entered the Naval Officer Candidate School and served in the Navy, living in Rhode Island, Japan, Hawaii, San Diego, and Santa Cruz, picking up lots of friends and fun memories along the way. After an Honorable Discharge from the United States Navy, he moved back to the Bay Area and attended Hastings Law School in 1970. Sandy practiced law in the Bay Area for 50 years and was a member of the California Bar Association since December of 1973. He was a member of the Pioneers of California and a longtime member of Claremont Country Club. Sandy enjoyed spending time tions with people. Known as “the Sarge” by his children's friends, he was a well known face in Piedmont. Charles Albert McPhee Jr. is survived by his wife Suellen Mulford McPhee, and three children, Charles A. McPhee III and his wife Alison of Lake Oswego, OR, Mollie McPhee Callahan and her husband Patrick of Pleasant Hill, CA, and Robert McPhee and his wife Jodie of Centennial, CO. He is also survived by seven grandchildren, Charlie and Kelly McPhee of Lake Oswego, Katie, Abigail and Jake Callahan of Pleasant Hill, and Jordan and Rachael McPhee of Centennial. He is also survived by his sisters Patrice Barlow, and husband Scott, Margaret “Missy” Nelson and husband Fred, Marcy Potter and husband Adam, and two brothers, Dean McPhee and wife Anne Marie, and David McPhee, along with a large extended family. Sandy meant a lot to many people, and he will be greatly missed by his entire family and his many friends. A Catholic Mass will be held at Corpus Christi Church, 322 St. James Drive, Piedmont, CA at 1:00 p.m. on Saturday, January 8, 2022. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations be made to the “Tunnel to Towers Foundation” at 2381 Hylan Blvd., Staten Island, NY 10306, tel. (718)-987-1931. He was beloved by his family and friends and loved entertaining. Most of all he cherished the time he spent with Sue, his wife of 54 years. He adored his wife, children and grandchildren. articles.text: But 2021 also marked a return to a more familiar Piedmont, beginning with the long-standing tradition of the Piedmont July 4 parade, albeit in a much scaleddown fashion. After 15 months of sheltering-in-place, and with obsessive hygienic practices and isolation now behind us, the city celebrated Independence Day modestly with a small parade and many block parties. Even though the summer saw the elimination of most public health orders, the city was cautious in allowing a large parade. Piedmont’s July 4 parade this year was a small, “sample-size” version, with a small convoy of vehicles driving through neighborhoods throughout the city. The quaint parade was truly a “wonderful day in the neighborhood, just like it has been year after year,” said Parade Committee Chair Carla Betts. “It exceeded our expectations, and it was incredible what [the committee] and community was able to achieve this year,” she said. On July 6, all fully-vaccinated city staff members were welcomed back to the workplace. A report was provided to City Council by the city’s new Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, who noted that Piedmont was the first and only city in the county to reach 100% of the available population over the age of 12 to receive their first vaccine. By July about 86% of Piedmont residents were fully vaccinated. “We believe this is a more upbeat report on COVID than [we] have received in the past year and a half. By all accounts, we are coming out on the other side of the pandemic,” Special Officer Tyler Petit expanded the Piedmont Police Department’s annual car show to 80 vehicles this year. The line for the Curative COVID-19 mobile testing site in front of Piedmont City Hall stretched around the corner on Sunday, December 26.
articles.title: Year in Review

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, December 29, 2021 Year in Review Continued from page 1 But 2021 also marked a return to a more familiar Piedmont, beginning with the long-standing tradition of the Piedmont July 4 parade, albeit in a much scaleddown fashion. After 15 months of sheltering-in-place, and with obsessive hygienic practices and isolation now behind us, the city celebrated Independence Day modestly with a small parade and many block parties. Even though the summer saw the elimination of most public health orders, the city was cautious in allowing a large parade. Piedmont’s July 4 parade this year was a small, “sample-size” version, with a small convoy of vehicles driving through neighborhoods throughout the city. The quaint parade was truly a “wonderful day in the neighborhood, just like it has been year after year,” said Parade Committee Chair Carla Betts. “It exceeded our expectations, and it was incredible what [the committee] and community was able to achieve this year,” she said. On July 6, all fully-vaccinated city staff members were welcomed back to the workplace. A report was provided to City Council by the city’s new Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, who noted that Piedmont was the first and only city in the county to reach 100% of the available population over the age of 12 to receive their first vaccine. By July about 86% of Piedmont residents were fully vaccinated. “We believe this is a more upbeat report on COVID than [we] have received in the past year and a half. By all accounts, we are coming out on the other side of the pandemic,” Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit said regarding the Fire Chief’s report. And by mid-2021, it certainly did appear that we were coming out on the other side of the pandemic. Music and arts venues everywhere began opening their doors to performers and patrons once again. The Piedmont Center for the Arts launched a summer series of events in a hybrid, indoor-outdoor fashion. Showing even more promise and perhaps a community urge to socialize, the Piedmont Police Department saw a record number of entries for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, September 6. The first car show featured 44 cars. Officer Tyler Petit arranged for over 80 vehicles to be on display this year. The three-hour event was packed with Piedmont residents, kids and car enthusiasts. Then on September 19, Piedmont’s 23rd annual Harvest Festival returned to nearly its full form and drew large crowds. Although the festival was held almost entirely outdoors, the majority of festival-goers donned masks, and activities were modified to encourage minimal physical contact. On Thanksgiving morning, over 2,200 runners ran in the annual Turkey Trot, another large local event. Registered runners hailed from all over the Bay Area and beyond - winners across all divisions included residents of Oakland, Berkeley, El Sobrante, Lafayette, Brentwood, Emeryville, and Fairfax Station. This year’s annual tree lighting ceremony, held on December 1, also drew a record large Staff Photos Officer Tyler Petit expanded the Piedmont Police Department’s annual car show to 80 vehicles this year. Staff photo The line for the Curative COVID-19 mobile testing site in front of Piedmont City Hall stretched around the corner on Sunday, December 26. Zach Murphy and younger daughter Ella by their handmade sign, which was installed by their home in September 2020, two months prior to the national election. crowd. Mayor King touted the healthy attendance as “evidence that Piedmont is back.” A few days later, it was announced that residents were once again welcome to attend public meetings in-person, beginning with a City Council meeting on December 6. The last time residents were welcomed to City Hall chambers was March 2020. The Federal Drug Administration (FDA) on December 22 authorized two pills to treat symptoms caused by the COVID- 19 virus and its variants, a breakthrough beyond vaccinations in our years-long fight against the pandemic. But as the general population began easing the habits acquired from last year’s virus hysteria, a new and more infectious variant emerged and plagued the holiday season: Omicron. And so, the year has ended the way it began, with collective anxiety over COVID. Despite the Bay Area’s, and specifically Piedmont’s, higher-than-average vaccination status, breakthrough cases of COVID have sprouted periodically. Lines for the mobile Curative clinic in front of Piedmont City Hall stretched around the corner on both Sunday and Monday, December 26 and 27, so much so that walk-ups without an appointment were no longer granted. Multiple public health agencies, including the Alameda County Public Health Department, are now strongly urging residents to “get boosted.” A number of San Francisco restaurants are now requiring proof of vaccine booster shots in addition to the already-mandated proof of vaccination set by the county. It is unclear at this point if other eateries, or industries, will follow suit. Touting a return to normalcy Photos courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department A member of the Inyo Hot Shots Crew that Piedmont Fire Department was assisting at the Dixie forest fire. may now be asinine, as the world, the country, the state, and Piedmont seem to have gravitated to a “new normal.” The idiom “new normal” became increasingly overused throughout the pandemic, but the phrase can be first attributed to Henry Wood Wise in December 1918, who penned an article in the National Electric Light Association Bulletin following the end of World War I. “Some contend that we should envisage the new normal, and carve the measures of transition to suit its requirements,” Wise wrote. “Others believe that we should cautiously feel our way through the period of transition, and arrive at what the new normal shall be by the road of experience.” And now, we cautiously step into 2022 – the new normal, return to normal, or perhaps no longer normal – but now following the road of experience that 21 months of a pandemic has paved us. The first wave of runners sprint away from the starting line during the 2021 Turkey Trot.

By March 19, four proposals for project manager were received, and all were reviewed independently by city staff and Howard Fuchs – an independent private sector. April The City began seeking volunteers to serve on the Pool Advisory Committee on April 20. May Five residents were appointed to the Pool Advisory Committee on May 29. The roster includes David del Villar Fernandez, Sarah Olsen Meyjes, Carolyn Pan, Steve Roland, and Lynne Wright; Councilmember Betsy Andersen serves as City Council Liaison, and Chelle Putzer serves as staff liaison in her capacity as Recreation Director. June City Council unanimously approved an agreement with Griffin Structures for project management services for the Piedmont Pool Project, or Measure UU, at a June 7 meeting. An overall budget of $612,700, which includes a 10% contingency, was awarded for the contract. “Of the four firms [that submitted proposals], it was the unanimous opinion of the reviewers that Griffin Structures stood out. They seemed the most capable of meeting everything we’ve addressed in the RFP. Unlike the other firms, they have extensive experience in managing public aquatic design and construction,” Benoit said. July The ad-hoc Pool Advisory Committee held its first meeting on July 12. At its first meeting, the committee was joined by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman, and Benoit. August City Council reviewed and approved the first reading of Ordinance 762 N.S on August 16, authorizing the borrowing of money via issuances of general obligation bonds in the amount of $19.5 million. September The city received the green light from Alameda County to begin draining the Piedmont Community Pool’s main pool. The process of draining the 154,000-gallon pool began on Tuesday morning, September 14, Photo courtesy of EL Olympic medalist Dana Vollmer and ELS CEO Clarence Mamuyac post banners around town in anticipation of a series of community workshops. Photo courtesy of ELS Residents weigh in on design details at the second community workshop hosted by the City and ELS Concept C – Lower Deck at 12-Lane Competition Pool Photo courtesy of ELS An early design schematic from ELS shows the lower deck of the proposed aquatic facility. and was handled by the Piedmont Fire Department. October On October 18, Piedmont City Council unanimously selected ELS Architecture and Urban Design as the architect for the Piedmont Community Pool Project. ELS was one of eight firms which submitted proposals to design the new Pool. ELS President and longtime Piedmont resident Clarence Mamuyac is leading the core design team. “With ELS designing our Community Pool, under the skill and leadership of Clarence Mamuyac, I am incredibly excited and look forward to the design of this amazing project” said Mayor Teddy Gray King of the selection. In addition, a Bond Oversight Committee was established by City Council, with a focus on reviewing and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds as required by Measure UU. November ELS launched a series of community workshops beginning November 2, and provided three early-design concepts for residents to provide comment on: Concept A, B, and C. Residents weighed in on three design concepts provided by ELS Architects, the design firm chosen by City Council for the Community Pool project, during a workshop held on November 16. Attendees were invited to join a table-top design team for a 20-minute charrette. Each team consisted of approximately ten people who looked over the three concepts, joined by an ELS firm representative. All eight teams were unanimous in their choice of Concept C. December By December 8, all Measure UU general obligation bonds issued were sold. The city concurrently received an ‘AAA’ long-term rating from Standard & Poor’s (S&P) Global Ratings, the highest possible rating issued by the credit rating agency. Cities that receive this rating are considered to have the highest degree of safety regarding timely servicing of financial obligations and carry the lowest credit risk. The rating allowed the city to sell the bonds at lower interest rates. The bonds were issued as a single series bearing a tax-exempt rate of 5%, resulting in an issue premium of $5.8 million. The total bond proceeds will be $25,329,463. The bond proceeds are not the same as the design and construction budget for the pool. The project budget is currently under development. ELS Architects is estimating costs at roughly $21 million. At the final event in the community workshop series hosted by the City and ELS Architecture and Urban Design, refinements were presented to the consensus concept “C.” A video unveiled that night, December 14, presented the firm’s direction, and can be viewed by visiting https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=D_-ffD7LbI8. A final design and direction was revealed before the end of 2021. Against the Matadors on March 2, Breber was among the few wins with a straight-set 6-3, 6-1 win at No. 3. • Pro Sports: Mackie McDonald The ATP Tour officially honored tennis pro Mackenzie McDonald, originally from Piedmont, with the 2021 Comeback Player of the Year award on December 14 after he compiled his strongest season since recovering from a torn hamstring tendon in 2019. McDonald ascended to his career high of No. 54 in the world Staff Photo Pro tennis player Mackie McDonald was named Comeback Player of the Year by the ATP Tour. in November after falling all the way to No. 272 in 2020. The 26-year old pro will return appear in the Australian Open on January 17-30. ATP 250 events like the Antalya Open from Jan. 4-11, or the Murray River Open (To Be Determined) are typical preparatory trials ahead of the Grand Slam in Australia. • Hiking with Jon When recollecting back to the beginning of the year, it’s uncanny that “Hiking with Jon” had spanned nearly 200 miles of trails from January 2020 until March of 2021. Now with sports schedules in full swing, our hiking sticks are a bit less used these days. At the start of 2021, we ventured down some of The Posts’ favorites since revamping our outdoors content. articles.text: County confirms cases of Omicron variant The Alameda County Public Health Department and the City of Berkeley released a joint statement on December 3 confirming five cases of the Omicron COVID variant in the county. The cases were identified by public health officials as “mildly symptomatic,” and are among 12 local COVID cases linked to a November 27 wedding in Wisconsin. One of the infected individuals attended the wedding upon return from international travel, the press release confirmed. A state-run lab used genomic sequencing to identify the five infected with the COVID-19 Omicron variant, which is now being detected around the world. Alameda County and the City of Berkeley Public Health Departments are investigating these cases with the assistance of the California Department of Public Health. All infected individuals and close contacts are being notified and provided with isolation and quarantine guidance; infected individuals range between the ages of 18 and 49. One is a resident of Berkeley, and the remaining twelve are Alameda County residents. All 12 individuals were vaccinated, and most had received booster shots. No one has been hospitalized as a result of their symptoms. “Public health officials continue to be vigilant and are monitoring evidence of this variant’s transmissibility and the severity of illness resulting from infection,” said ACPHD Public Information Officer Neetu Balram. “We don’t yet know how Omicron will impact a highly vaccinated region like the Bay Area. We remind residents that vaccination continues to provide the best protection against severe illness from COVID-19 that could result in hospitalization and death.” travel, whether international or domestic. State mask mandate reimposed As of today, December 15, the State of California will reimpose indoor mask mandates for all residents regardless of vaccination status in public settings. The mask requirement will be in place through January 15. The announcement was made by Health and Human Services Secretary Dr. Mark Ghaly on Monday, December 13. The news comes as Omicron variants have been detected throughout the state, with 18 cases reported statewide as of December 10. “This is a critical time. We have a tool we know has worked and can work,” Dr. Ghaly said. “We are proactively putting this tool of universal indoor masking in place [now] to ensure we get through a time of joy and hope without a darker cloud of despair. Californians have done this before, and we believe we can do it again.” In addition, the state will require those who attend “megaevents” of 1,000 or more people to show vaccination or proof of negative test taken within one day of arrival; the previous allowable window for testing before attending an event was 72 hours. The state is also recommending that travelers who return to California test three to five days after arrival. Dr. Ghaly confirmed that COVID case rates statewide have jumped 47% since the Thanksgiving holiday. Neetu Balram, Alameda County Public Health Dept. Both public health agencies are urging residents to continue to utilize known strategies that stop the spread of COVID. These include staying home if sick, washing hands diligently, wearing a mask indoors, and getting tested if symptomatic. Curative operates a rapid test COVID clinic, stationed in front of Piedmont City Hall this Sunday and Monday between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. Public Health agencies are reminding residents to get tested before and after anticipated
