articles.text: Editor: We write to express our deep appreciation for the outpouring of love and support we have received since we lost our beloved Mitch. From meals to cards to flowers to texts to the donations made in Mitch’s honor: we are grateful beyond measure. In the coming weeks we will reach out to everyone personally, but in the interim please know how much your kindness and generosity mean to us. It a testament to the number of people Mitch touched in his too-short life and also a reminder of how much good there is in our community and beyond. In gratitude and profound sadness. –Vern, Kathleen, and Elizabeth Winters

articles.text: “Until the day dawns and the morning star rests in your hearts.” (II Peter 1:16-21) In the church of my youth much attention was paid to the second coming of Jesus. While no one, at least as far as I remember, was of the “I know the exact date it will occur so until then don’t count on me for anything” school of thought. Much attention was paid to world events, especially the establishment of the Nation of Israel in 1948, as clear signs that Jesus would soon physically return. Of course, we were not the first, or the last, to live with the expectation that the second coming was near at hand. Many, if not most, of the first followers of Jesus, expected that he would return while they were still alive. This belief made them courageous but it also meant that their ethics could be greatly influenced by a “it doesn’t matter because we are not long for this world” outlook. Throughout the centuries the belief that Jesus would soon return has waxed and waned. There were times when it was fervently anticipated and times when the attitude was “maybe we should reconsider what we mean by the second coming of Jesus.” While the writer of the second letter of Peter (likely the last of the books of the New Testament to be written) is intent on upholding the belief that Jesus would soon physically return, even he recognized that Jesus’ return could also be a spiritual promise – a matter of the heart. articles.text: Residents gathered at the Veteran’s Hall on Tuesday, December 14, for the last workshop in the 3-part community workshop series hosted by ELS Architecture and Urban Design. At last night’s meeting, participants were given a brief presentation of ELS’ programming and design effort over the past four weeks. A final draft program, which outlined potential features and a preferred conceptual direction, was presented by ELS President and CEO Clarence Mamuyac. Following the presentation, everyone was again invited to join a table-top design team, where residents were invited to comment on, critique, and evaluate the preferred concept. Following last night’s meeting, ELS and city staff will use data gathered to create a final concept that reflects all community workshops. The preferred direction will be presented to City Council early next year for approval. There will be more opportunities for engagement in the following weeks, including a Pool Advisory Committee meeting scheduled for tomorrow, December 16. articles.text: For many a highlight of the holiday season is food. From turkey and mashed potatoes, to ham and stuffing, and latkes and challah, food can bring communities together and unify us with friends and family. However, the holiday season is often a time in which there is an excess of food wasted. According to CalRecycle’s waste characterization study in 2018, food waste comprised 13 percent of what we dispose annually. In fact, every year, Californians throw away 5-6 million tons of food waste. During the last edition of the Piedmont Post, the Climate Corner highlighted gifting ideas for “greening” the holidays across the three “R’s”: Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle. This week, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks to further green the holiday season by reducing food waste and a family’s carbon footprint. From purchasing to cooking, donating, and composting, there are significant ways to reduce the carbon footprint of your food both during and after the holiday season. Resources like the United Nations World Food Programme and #StopTheWaste campaign highlight how the food we purchase can significantly impact the carbon footprint. According to the UN, “food system” refers to the activities involved in producing, processing, transporting, and consuming food. Food systems touch every aspect of human existence. One aspect to consider is “food miles”, the distance travelled by your food before it reaches your plate, and the mode of transportation that transports your food. For instance, flying one ton of food is nearly 70 times more carbon intensive than transporting that same weight by rough other methods like a cargo ship. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce these food miles, and as a result, its carbon footprint. Consider supporting a nearby farmers market, where you can not only support local businesses, but have a conversation about where your food came from and how it was prepared. In addition to food miles, food preparation can impact your carbon footprint and your health. Did you know using a gas range stove releases pollutants into our homes and can produce unsafe levels of indoor air pollution? While most residential appliances vent pollution outside (think gas-powered furnaces and water heaters), your stove may be the one gas appliance that is likely unvented. Common pollutants from gas stoves include carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and formaldehyde. Some ways to reduce these pollutants include opening windows, running exhaust fans and range hoods, using a HEPA air purifier with a carbon filter, and cooking using an electric induction cooktop rather than a gas range stove. Annie Wensley is the City of Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: “Greening” the Holidays: Food Edition

At last night’s meeting, participants were given a brief presentation of ELS’ programming and design effort over the past four weeks. A final draft program, which outlined potential features and a preferred conceptual direction, was presented by ELS President and CEO Clarence Mamuyac. Following the presentation, everyone was again invited to join a table-top design team, where residents were invited to comment on, critique, and evaluate the preferred concept. Following last night’s meeting, ELS and city staff will use data gathered to create a final concept that reflects all community workshops. The preferred direction will be presented to City Council early next year for approval. There will be more opportunities for engagement in the following weeks, including a Pool Advisory Committee meeting scheduled for tomorrow, December 16. From turkey and mashed potatoes, to ham and stuffing, and latkes and challah, food can bring communities together and unify us with friends and family. However, the holiday season is often a time in which there is an excess of food wasted. According to CalRecycle’s waste characterization study in 2018, food waste comprised 13 percent of what we dispose annually. In fact, every year, Californians throw away 5-6 million tons of food waste. During the last edition of the Piedmont Post, the Climate Corner highlighted gifting ideas for “greening” the holidays across the three “R’s”: Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle. This week, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks to further green the holiday season by reducing food waste and a family’s carbon footprint. From purchasing to cooking, donating, and composting, there are significant ways to reduce the carbon footprint of your food both during and after the holiday season. Resources like the United Nations World Food Programme and #StopTheWaste campaign highlight how the food we purchase can significantly impact the carbon footprint. According to the UN, “food system” refers to the activities involved in producing, processing, transporting, and consuming food. Food systems touch every aspect of human existence. One aspect to consider is “food miles”, the distance travelled by your food before it reaches your plate, and the mode of transportation that transports your food. For instance, flying one ton of food is nearly 70 times more carbon intensive than transporting that same weight by rough other methods like a cargo ship. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce these food miles, and as a result, its carbon footprint. Consider supporting a nearby farmers market, where you can not only support local businesses, but have a conversation about where your food came from and how it was prepared. In addition to food miles, food preparation can impact your carbon footprint and your health. Did you know using a gas range stove releases pollutants into our homes and can produce unsafe levels of indoor air pollution? While most residential appliances vent pollution outside (think gas-powered furnaces and water heaters), your stove may be the one gas appliance that is likely unvented. Common pollutants from gas stoves include carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and formaldehyde. Some ways to reduce these pollutants include opening windows, running exhaust fans and range hoods, using a HEPA air purifier with a carbon filter, and cooking using an electric induction cooktop rather than a gas range stove. pages.text: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 5 SchOOLs INSIDE THE CLASSROOM By Jay Russell Piedmont High School English teacher and department head Beth Black invited the Post to her AP Literature on Friday, December 10 for a lively discussion on mortality and death courtesy of metaphysical poet John Donne. This reporter was included on the discussion some 17 years after attending the class as a member of the PHS class of 2004. Black’s passion for the subject matter at hand, John Donne’s 1633 poem “Death be not Proud,” was returned by her class with thoughtful responses. Black focused first on the structure of the work, which is a Petrarchan sonnet with an octave and a sestet. The famous poem finishes without rhyme: One short sleep past, we wake eternally And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die. (For the full text, see: Poetryfoundation.org/poems/44107/holysonnets-death-be-not-proud.) Donne was known for his tense syntax and abrupt openings in sharp comparison to the smoothness of Elizabethan poems which were favored at the time. He was born a Catholic in a country that had just become Protestant in the 16th Century. Donne had lofty ambitions of disruption with his poems about love, sexuality, religion, and death in 17th Century England. articles.text: During November and December Piedmont Middle School’s Student Body government led highly successful food drives to benefit the Alameda County Food Bank, and a toy drive in support of the national Toys for Tots campaign. The food drive, held between November 1-19 generated $10,000 for the food bank. The ASB class, led by Advisor Jamie Van Kleeck, organized a schoolwide competition to see which counselor group could raise the most money for the food bank. Ms. Balaban’s students raised the most money overall. For their efforts, ASB rewarded all participants with hot chocolate on December 10 on campus. The toy drive took place in December and was won by the 8th grade which filled two barrels with toys. Seventh graders filled half a barrel and sixth graders filled one and a half barrels. ASB member Preston Kwei puts a toy into the collection bin for Toys for Tots in front of Piedmont Middle School. articles.text: We get asked this question a lot by high school students: “When am I ever going to use Algebra or history in real life?” The short answer is that you probably won’t, but we need you to show that you can tackle high school before we want you building bridges or performing brain surgery. The long answer is that high school is about developing thinking skills, so when it comes time to do things as an adult, students are ready to use their mind to solve problems and achieve success. The Practicality of an Impractical Education In grammar school, we learned essential skills: reading, writing, and arithmetic. But it is harder to see the point of high school classes like Algebra, English Literature, Ancient History or Physics. So, if students are never going to actually use cosine, recite the causes of World War I, or write a 5-paragraph essay as an adult, what is the point? When my students ask why they have to learn what they are learning, I often ask them, “if your friends were accepted into medical school right now, do you think they would become very good doctors?” Generally, the answer is “no”. Most students recognize that they themselves and their peers are not really ready to tackle adult tasks. Their brains are not ready yet. Their ability to learn, think, comprehend, or problem-solve are not developed enough. That is why we teach what we teach in high school. We are working to develop these underlying cognitive skills that are required in our society. What are the “Skills” It’s possible to just memorize their way through school, but that will leave a student only able to follow instructions. What other skills can students develop in each class? Math and Science: To actually solve a problem (not just repeat memorized steps) someone must comprehend difficult concepts, solve logically, and use rigid, linear thinking. All of these cognitive abilities are essential to succeed in a business world in which we are forced to tackle problems for which there is no answer key or teacher’s notes. English and History: We disseminate information through the written word. When students are reading The Joy Luck Club or a history textbook, it is important that they develop the ability to thoroughly understand what they are reading. This skill is probably more important than the actual facts or themes in the reading. That’s not to say that learning history or understanding literature isn’t important – it is. But from a practical standpoint, it is more important that students learn to read for content than the content itself. The same goes for an essay. Is it really important that the world knows their opinion on the Industrial Revolution? Probably not, but one day every student will have a message they want to get out there, and when that happens, the ability to express oneself through the written word will be essential. Next month we can go over ways to develop these skills in each class. Paul the Tutor (aka Paul Osborne) runs Paul the Tutor’s Education Services online and on Piedmont Avenue. articles.text: This year’s Giving Campaign has raised the highest total ever to date, and the number of families donating is still growing. The team hopes to conclude the campaign by raising a total of $3.5 million for Piedmonts schools. “We really appreciate the generosity of the Piedmont families who have donated to the Giving Campaign. Over 1,000 families have contributed this year, and the gifts are still coming in. The success of this campaign is a tribute to our community’s commitment to our excellent public schools,” said Giving Campaign Co-Chairs Colleen Allan and Christine Wente von Metzsch. In the district-wide gradelevel competition, kindergarten and first grade are still tied for first place, with 69% of the families from each grade donating. TK, 3rd, and 5th grades are close behind, each with 63% of families participating. The winning grade will be awarded a family taco truck party in Piedmont Park in early 2022. Families making a donation by December 31 will be able to take advantage of 2021 tax deductions, and will have their names included in the Giving Campaign donor lists published in local papers. Many companies offer end-of-year corporate matching, which can increase donor impact. To participate in the Giving Campaign and help fund our students and schools, visit www. piedmontedfoundation.org/ donate/

articles.text: There are many volunteer opportunities available to adults and youth this holiday season. Here are just a few. San Francisco SPCA The San Francisco SPCA, the largest animal welfare organization on the West coast, is seeking volunteers to commit to six months. Volunteers gain valuable work experience and will develop animal handling skills, as well as receive extensive training and guidance from staff. Most volunteer positions are for individuals 18 years or older, and you must attend a volunteer info session to start. Visit https://www.sfspca.org/get-involved/ volunteer/ for more information. Alameda County Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank is in need of volunteers this holiday season to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites. All employees must be fully vaccinated to apply. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, and to inquire about the food bank’s needs this Christmas, email volunteer@accfd.org, or visit https://www.accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer/. Donations are also welcome. Children’s Fairyland Children’s Fairyland in Oakland is always seeking volunteers, especially during the holidays. Volunteers of various ages can help with painting and restoration projects, gardening, animal care, and office work. You can still sign up to volunteer to prepare for Fairy Winterland, one of the major events of the year. Register to volunteer by visiting https://www.volgistics.com/ex/ portal.dll/ap?ap=115816441. Project Open Hand Project Open Hand, located near San Francisco City Hall, produces 2,500 nutritious meals to those in need every day. Volunteers are an essential component of Project Open Hand and assist in both preparing and packaging meals. Volunteers also help deliver meals by walking or by car. You can volunteer as a group or individually. Visit https://www.openhand.org/volunteer/ individual-volunteer/volunteer-our-kitchen to learn more. Habitat for Humanity Volunteers are always welcome at Habitat for Humanity. No carpentry or construction experience is needed. The organization’s mission is to create successful homeownership opportunities for families with limited incomes. Founded in 1988, Habitat for Humanity East Bay is an independent affiliate of Habitat for Humanity International and serves residents of Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Sign up online at www.habitateb.org, or contact Eliza Schissel, Volunteer Coordinator, at 510-251-6304, ext. 360, or email eschissel@habitateb.org. Do you know of a volunteer opportunity that you would like to highlight this holiday season? Please send your suggestions to City Editor Allyson Aleksey at allysonaaleksey@gmail.com

Volunteers gain valuable work experience and will develop animal handling skills, as well as receive extensive training and guidance from staff. Alameda County Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank is in need of volunteers this holiday season to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites. All employees must be fully vaccinated to apply. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, and to inquire about the food bank’s needs this Christmas, email volunteer@accfd.org, or visit https://www.accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer/. Donations are also welcome. Children’s Fairyland Children’s Fairyland in Oakland is always seeking volunteers, especially during the holidays. Volunteers of various ages can help with painting and restoration projects, gardening, animal care, and office work. You can still sign up to volunteer to prepare for Fairy Winterland, one of the major events of the year. Register to volunteer by visiting https://www.volgistics.com/ex/ portal.dll/ap?ap=115816441. Project Open Hand Project Open Hand, located near San Francisco City Hall, produces 2,500 nutritious meals to those in need every day. Volunteers are an essential component of Project Open Hand and assist in both preparing and packaging meals. Volunteers also help deliver meals by walking or by car. You can volunteer as a group or individually. Visit https://www.openhand.org/volunteer/ individual-volunteer/volunteer-our-kitchen to learn more. Habitat for Humanity Volunteers are always welcome at Habitat for Humanity. No carpentry or construction experience is needed. Founded in 1988, Habitat for Humanity East Bay is an independent affiliate of Habitat for Humanity International and serves residents of Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Please send your suggestions to City Editor Allyson Aleksey at allysonaaleksey@gmail.com Thinking Outside The Classroom What do students get out of a high school education? By Paul Osborn We get asked this question a lot by high school students: “When am I ever going to use Algebra or history in real life?” The short answer is that you probably won’t, but we need you to show that you can tackle high school before we want you building bridges or performing brain surgery. The long answer is that high school is about developing thinking skills, so when it comes time to do things as an adult, students are ready to use their mind to solve problems and achieve success. The Practicality of an Impractical Education In grammar school, we learned essential skills: reading, writing, and arithmetic. But it is harder to see the point of high school classes like Algebra, English Literature, Ancient History or Physics. So, if students are never going to actually use cosine, recite the causes of World War I, or write a 5-paragraph essay as an adult, what is the point? When my students ask why they have to learn what they are learning, I often ask them, “if your friends were accepted into medical school right now, do you think they would become very good doctors?” Generally, the answer is “no”. Most students recognize that they themselves and their peers are not really ready to tackle adult tasks. Their brains are not ready yet. Their ability to learn, think, comprehend, or problem-solve are not developed enough. That is why we teach what we teach in high school. We are working to develop these underlying cognitive skills that are required in our society. What are the “Skills” It’s possible to just memorize their way through school, but that will leave a student only able to follow instructions. What other skills can students develop in each class? Math and Science: To actually solve a problem (not just repeat memorized steps) someone must comprehend difficult concepts, solve logically, and use rigid, linear thinking. All of these cognitive abilities are essential to succeed in a business world in which we are forced to tackle problems for which there is no answer key or teacher’s notes. English and History: We disseminate information through the written word. When students are reading The Joy Luck Club or a history textbook, it is important that they develop the ability to thoroughly understand what they are reading. This skill is probably more important than the actual facts or themes in the reading. That’s not to say that learning history or understanding literature isn’t important – it is. But from a practical standpoint, it is more important that students learn to read for content than the content itself. The same goes for an essay. Is it really important that the world knows their opinion on the Industrial Revolution? Probably not, but one day every student will have a message they want to get out there, and when that happens, the ability to express oneself through the written word will be essential. Next month we can go over ways to develop these skills in each class. Paul the Tutor (aka Paul Osborne) runs Paul the Tutor’s Education Services online and on Piedmont Avenue. They specialize in tutoring and test prep for non-traditional learners and traditional students. Paul is dyslexic, holds a Masters from the Harvard Graduate School of Education and authored of the LD SAT Study Guide. In September 2020 the city council passed a resolution accepting Prop 68 funds and agreed to designate a project by the end of 2021. After considering grant criteria, the city said the Recreation Department continues to have an acute need for additional program space, according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “Our best bet for providing outdoor, inclusive education and programming is through the Recreation Department and their programs,” Gonzales said. The commissioners voted 10-2 in favor of recommending the project to city council with modifications. Since October, staff revised the concept to eliminate traditional fencing and instead proposed a combination of native hedge plantings and removable fencing that could be installed when the space needs to be enclosed, rather than be a permanent fixture. “[During COVID] we’ve maximized the use of any and every inch of space that we could find outside,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “For the last 18 months, we’ve offered preschool programs outdoors… and have carved out [outdoor] space at the Recreation Department building and designated spaces around Piedmont parks so we can continue to offer childcare programs.” Recreation staff have created programs that are centered on outdoor and nature play, Putzer added. She offered anecdotes of Hillside Preschool as evidence of a successful childcare program that has transitioned to become a completely-outdoor program. “[The children] put raincoats and rain boots on when it rains, they grow and eat their own tomatoes

articles.text: [and other produce]. The transformation of our program to outdoors has been extremely successful. Even when COVID is behind us, we will make our outdoor preschool a permanent program offering, and this project is very exciting,” she explained. Putzer added that the space would be very popular for informal use, Girl Scout meetings, as an intimate wedding space or other gatherings. “The design is beautiful, and clearly it’s needed, and is a good use of this space,” said council member Conna McCarthy. “I’m enamored with the outdoor education concept,” said council member Betsy Andersen, who agreed that the space is an appropriate site for this project. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. The Twelve Days of Christmas – the Song On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fourth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fifth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the sixth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the seventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eighth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the ninth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the tenth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eleventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the twelfth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Twelve drummers drumming, eleven pipers piping, ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree.

articles.text: ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!” All services are available for streaming at the listed times or watching at one’s convenience 24/7 after the service has ended. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team beat neighboring Head-Royce 2-1 on Friday, December 10 at home, but lost 6-3 to Campolindo yesterday, December 14 at the Cougars’ field in Moraga. The victory over Head-Royce in the “Oakland Hills Derby” came against a Division 4 North Coast Section opponent. A number of players on both teams are well acquainted with each other on and off the field. “Head-Royce defended well,” noted PHS coach Dan Chubbock. “I thought we were the stronger team of the two. Our teams have several players who have played on club teams and are friends. It really makes for one of our best games with a lot of cheering and heckling back-and-forth between the two teams. It’s all very good natured fun.” “I’d like to set up more games with Head-Royce, to be honest. Maybe next year we can do a double-header with them. It’s definitely one of the strongest Michaela Bini had an assist in the game with Campolindo.

articles.text: Staff Photos A.J. Harris scored a career-high 35 points against Washington HS to help Piedmont claim third place at the Rob Vares Memorial Tournament at Washington High School in Fremont. Playing without team leader Jojo Murphy, Piedmont’s basketball team finished third in the Rob Vares Memorial Tournament hosted last weekend by Washington High School in Fremont. Led by scoring ace AJ Harris, the Highlanders blew out Mission San Jose 73-39 in the opening game on Thursday, December 9, but lost narrowly to Oakland High in the semifinals on Saturday, 56-53. Later the same day they defeated the host school 62-55 to claim 3rd place. The semifinals and finals were moved to Saturday following a power outage at the school on Friday. “We had to play two games on Saturday after a power outage. We played a really tough game against Oakland then had to come back that night against Washington,” said assistant coach Jason Harris. “We had to play a good team on their home court. It was a really good team effort. We’re holding teams to 40 percent on field goals, 25 percent on threes. We have a good defensive team,” added Harris who was filling in for coach Ben Spencer at the tournament. A.J. Harris had a huge tournament, with 24 points and seven rebounds against Mission San Jose, 22 points and 14 rebounds in the semifinal with Oakland, and a career-high 35 points to go along with 13 boards in the finals vs. Washington. His 35 points eclipsed by one point the top high school game of his older brother, Luke, now playing for Carlton College as a freshman. “He wants everyone to know that it’s one more point that what Luke got,” said coach Harris, the father of A.J. and Luke. “He’s always looked up to Luke and tried to be just as good.” Raydan Holmes earned All-Tournament honors after scoring 14 points against Mission San Jose and 13 against Oakland. Rayden Holmes scored 14 points against Mission San Jose and 13 against Oakland. Both he and Harris were named to the All-Tournament team. “Raydan did really well after being asked to play point guard on the fly,” said coach Harris “I thought he did a great job stepping up. We’re finding that he’s our third scorer. That’s always been an important part of our teams.” The loss to Oakland was a nail-biter. Piedmont trailed by five points at the half and was within one basket at the end. “We got down early and kept fighting and really played hard. We didn’t shoot the ball great, but played super hard, said coach Harris. 3rd-place Finals vs. Washington The Highlanders jumped out with a strong 25 point first quarter to lead 25-17 and led 41-30 by halftime. The Huskies cut the lead 1980 Mountain Boulevard, #212 510-339-9313

articles.text: The Piedmont boys’ soccer team defeated San Lorenzo 4-1 on Friday, December 10 on the road. Two days earlier they sustained their first loss of the season, 3-2 against Mt. Eden in Hayward on December 8. Piedmont’s big win against San Lorenzo was a strong response to its loss to Mt. Eden, where the Monarchs pulled off a late upset with two goals in the final five minutes. “We played with a maturity that we haven’t showed a lot of,” said coach Todd Sullivan after the victory against San Lorenzo. “The loss came from a crazy position with five minutes to go, but we controlled the second half. That’s soccer. [The win] was a good reaction to what happened.” “We were in control against Mt. Eden. [Against San Lorenzo] we just wanted to take charge and put in a good performance. We have a [holiday] break and wanted to do well before that,” added senior Anders Payne, who scored his first goal in Friday’s game. San Lorenzo Recap The Highlanders’ first goal came in the 18th minute on a counter attack following a SLZ free kick. Senior captain Andre Stankiewicz whipped in a pass to Aiden Woolwine, who slotted in a hard shot to the keeper’s right. Piedmont went up 2-0 in the 32nd minute when Payne was able to walk one in. In the buildup, Stankiewicz drew a foul one yard above the penalty area to enable a free kick opportunity for Conner Curtis. His spot kick ricocheted off the cross bar and back toward Payne, whose initial header skipped off the cross bar, again, then back to his midsection for the tap in. “It was my first goal in four years,” he said. Luckily, Conner put in on target and I was just there,” said Payne. In the second half, Darius Grammer put PHS up 3-0 in the 49th minute. The play started when Patrick Alexander, appearing at right midfielder after being a center back, won the ball in SLZ’s defensive third and played it through to Woolwine on the Staff Photos Conner Curtis had a right-footed goal against San Lorenzo and a leftfooted score against Mt. Eden. Aiden Woolwine had a goal and had an assist in a 4-1 victory over San Lorenzo. right wing. Woolwine sent a cross all the way to Grammer on the left post, who took it off his chest then followed through for a leftfoot finish. The Grizzlies scored their only goal on a counter attack in the 58th minute, but Piedmont responded with a final goal by Curtis with one minute to play. In the buildup, Ian Work sent a long pass to Woolwine, who instinctively sent a through-ball to Curtis charging forward. Curtis’ right footed shot from 21 yards skipped past the keeper at the left post. Mt. Eden Recap Piedmont led 2-1 until the waning minutes of action, when it allowed two goals in the final five minutes of play. Mt. Eden is now 5-0-2 and leads the Shoreline Division with a 4-0 record against league opponents. Curtis scored in the 5th minute when his free kick on the left sideline trickled in. His spot-kick was a pass targeting Soren Dixon, but his shot attempt missed and the ball successfully bounced in. The Monarchs tied in the 29th when their forward Gilberto Rivera took an athletic shot on the volley between two Highlanders’ defenders from 25 yards. Piedmont scored with 10 minutes left in the game on a remarkable goal from Curtis when the ball fell his way after Mt. Eden defender’s header. A yard above the area, Curtis took one-touch with his right foot to free himself up, and then followed with a hard left footed curling shot past the keeper. But Mt. Eden wasn’t done, Rivera bagged his second goal in the 77th minute on a free kick from 6-yards above the area—

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team finished fourth in last weekend’s Paris Twins Classic at Binks Rawlings Gym, the 11th annual event. They opened with a 69-32 win over Lompoc on Thursday, December 9, then lost 65-57 to Cardinal Newman in the semifinals on Friday, and lost to Vanden 74-52 on Saturday, December 11. Valley Christian walked off with top honors this year with a 59-32 drubbing of Cardinal Newman. The Vanden Vikings brought a strong lineup and are now 5-1 after a narrow 59-52 semifinals loss to Valley Christian. “It is definitely a tough tournament,” said host coach Bryan Gardere, whose team has won the tournament only once, in 2017. “It’s still early in the season so these are teaching moments. We weren’t ready to play early and there were some very good shooters in this tournament.”. First Round: PHS 69, Lompoc 32 The Highlanders’ defense had a strong showing in the opening game with Lompoc, allowing no more than 10 points in any quarter. The Highlanders defeated Lompoc a week ago in the Bryan Ayer Classic at Lompoc. Piedmont led 18-6 by the end of the first quarter and added 27 points in the second quarter to steam ahead 45-14 by halftime. PHS led 55-24 by the end of the third period and closed out the win with 14 points in the 4th quarter. Natalia Martinez scored 24 points in Piedmont’s win vs. Lompoc.

articles.text: With an enrollment typically below 900 students, it is not uncommon for students to play more than one sport. Here is a look at four athletes currently competing on a winter team. ANTONIO RIVERA Water Polo & Basketball Antonio Rivera, a senior, finished the fall season as a firstteam All-League recipient on the water polo team, helping lead the Highlanders to their first league championship in the Western Alameda County Conference. Rivera scored five goals in the championship win over Berkeley, while helping his team reach the Division 2 North Coast Section Finals. As the No. 3 seed, Piedmont lost 7-4 to No. 1 Marin Academy on November 10. The team finished with a 19-6 record. Rivera was the leading scorer on the team and helped the team to its most successful season ever. This winter he has a key role on the boys’ basketball team as a first-year varsity member. He played on the junior varsity squad as a freshman and sophomore. Antonio Rivera helped lead the boys’ water polo team to its first League Championship in the fall, and is currently a member of the basketball team. NINA GOLDBERG Soccer & Football Nina Goldberg, a senior, is a four-year starter on the soccer team Nina Goldberg is a four-year starter on the varsity soccer team and joined the football team last fall as a specialty kicker. Anders Payne is a member of both the soccer and golf teams. Morgan Hunt is the goalkeeper on the soccer team and is a starter on the softball team.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Five Bay Area rainy day hikes to consider By Jonathan Comeaux With more rain in the forecast over the next week, looking out the window could be daunting for some hikers feeling those gray and gloomy vibes. But luckily for us in the Bay Area, there is a wealth of parks to choose from where hikers can get plenty of exercise and avoid heavy rain with help of the vast tree coverage. So grab your rain gear, hiking boots, and consider this group of five areas where you can enjoy the wet weather. Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve, Oakland Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve is a small treasure in Oakland Hills, East Bay Regional Parks District called Huckleberry an “ecological gem” with its year-round display of blossoming Staff Photos Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills is considered an ecological gem with its year-round display of blossoming plants. It has an ideal canopy for rain cover. A winter favorite, manzanita at Huckleberry is currently in bloom. A local favorite, Redwood Regional Park, has many trails protecting hikers from rain. French Trail in Redwood Regional Park is an enjoyable tree-covered hike. plants. The canopy of California Bays, Redwood trees, and Manzanita make it an ideal and small 3.4 mile loop. Manzanita trees, with their vibrant red burl, are currently in bloom. Redwood Regional Park, Oakland A local favorite, Redwood Regional Park is a default location for residents in the Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont. Several trails provide extensive tree coverage. Consider the French Trail, Chown Trail, Madrone Trail, Fern Trail, and Redwood Peak Trail as hikes that will put you beneath a canopy of trees. The West Ridge Trail provides an avenue where you can find each of the trailheads, parking at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area. Another connecting trail, which is well covered, is the Stream Trail, with parking at Canyon Meadow Staging Area. Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland Adjacent to Redwood Regional on Skyline Boulevard, you’ll find trails with more foot traffic compared to the former, but equal amount of tree coverage along the Big Trees Trail, Sequoia Bayview Trail, Palos Colorados Trail, and the Sunset Trail. Purisima Creek Redwoods In San Mateo County, Purisima Creek’s Harkins Ridge provides a beautiful journey through the hills surrounding San Mateo. Consider the Purisima Creek Trail, which is adjacent to the now active Purisima Creek. You will walk by large stumps of old growth trees with some second-growth trees scattered throughout the area. Cataract Falls, Mt. Tamalpais On the north side of Mt. Tamalpais above Mill Valley is one of its most popular trails, the Cataract Falls Trail. You will be well protected by a canopy of redwood trees towering over you. The rain has brought waterfalls back to Cataract Creek, which will line your entire walk. Although only a four-mile hike, you’ll gain over 1,000 feet in elevation over steep steps and tree roots. Joaquin Miller Park also has redwood trees covering hikers from the rain. Purisima Creek Redwood Preserve has a vast amount of redwood trees, some much older than the ones in the East Bay Hills. Cataract Falls is located on the north side of Mt. Tamalpais. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse presents a production of Twelfth Night now through January 15, 2022. The show was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine and the Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaption of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a Duke. Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. San Francisco Playhouse’s production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk music score by Shania Taub. To purchase tickets visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ Feste (Sam Paley, center) opens Twelfth Night with the people of Illyria, Tiana Paulding (left), Michael Gene Sullivan, Amanda Le Nguyen, Cathleen Riddley, Caleb Haven Draper, Tasi Alabastro, Jon-David Randle, and Amanda Farbstein. sfph/upcoming-plays/. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required to attend the production. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street, San Francisco. For information call (415) 677-9596.
articles.title: SF Playhouse Twelfth Night musical now through January 15

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s current production of Charles Mee’s Wintertime will end on Sunday, December 19. Berkeley Rep welcomes back Mee and director Les Waters, who have teamed up in the past to bring Fetes de la Nuit and Big Love to the stage. Wintertime is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family, who arrive at their summer house in the winter woods for a supposedly secret rendezvous—and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” Tickets are available at https://tickets.berkeleyrep.org/ events?k=wintertime&hidedate. Berkeley Rep requires all patrons to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification, and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre, 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley. Photo by Kevin Berne Carmen Berkeley as Ariel (left), Jomar Tagatac as Bob and James Carpenter as Frank in Berkeley Rep’s production of Wintertime.

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company is currently performing Georgiana and Kitty: Christmas at Pemberley through Sunday, December 19. The play, the final installment of the Christmas at Pemberley trilogy, was written by MTC Playwright in Residence Lauren Gunderson and former Director of New Play Development Margot Melcon. Georgiana and Kitty follows Mr. Darcy’s younger sister Georgiana and the youngest Bennet sister, Kitty. Georgiana, shy but creative, is living under the scrutiny of her brother, and Kitty, now free of the influence of her gregarious sister Lydia, is Georgiana’s practical best friend. It is Christmastime at Pemberley and the pair impatiently await the arrival of Henry Grey. The world premiere of Georgiana and Kitty: Christmas at Pemberley is a co-commission of Marin Theatre Company, in partnership with the Jungle Theater in Minneapolis and Northlight Theatre in Chicago. To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.marintheatre.org/. Marin Theatre Company is located at 397 Miller Avenue in Mill Valley. For information call (415) 388- 5200. Photo by Kevin Berne Marin Theatre Company’s production of Georgiana and Kitty: Christmas at Pemberley, with Lauren Spencer as Georgiana Darcy (left), Aidaa Peerzada as Emily Grey, Emilie Whelan as Kitty Bennet, Zahan Mehta as Henry Grey, Adam Magill as Thomas O’Brien, Alicia M.P. Nelson as Margaret O’Brien and Madeline Rouverol as Sarah Darcy.
articles.title: Marin Theatre’s Christmas at Pemberley now through Dec. 19

articles.text: After a good (or, more accurately, bad) year’s COVID absence, the Chanticleer singers were back once more in exemplary form. We can properly celebrate Christmas again with their predictably profound and joyful sounds. The dozen male vocalists – the only ones in the entire hall without masks – won sustained ovations Sunday from the crowd at the Cathedral of Christ the Light in Oakland, as well as from Bishop Michael Barber in his low-key attendance as just one of many fans in the pews. We may not be back to normal yet, but no one will suppress the unbridled joy of the 2021 Christmas-holiday season. The usual elements of a cappella (unaccompanied) singing, multi-lingual repertoire and highrange countertenors were supplemented by innovations of the new music director, Tim Keeler. This meant linking of composers from vastly different centuries and backgrounds setting the same carol texts. So, the familiar carol “Lo, a Rose E’er Blooming” featured living composer Jonathan Woody as catalyst between Michael Praetorius and Hugo Distler, spanning four centuries in total. The more it’s the same, the more it’s different. This being the 400th anniversary of Praetorius’ passing, the emphasis was on German texts, as well as unharmonized Latin hymnody by the brilliant 12th century polymath German nun (and now saint), Hildegard von Bingen. Chanticleer may have its customary problems with German pronunciation (it’s an “umlaut allergy,” some always quip), but their Latin was articulate and unassailable. Singing as The San Francisco-based men’s choral group Chanticleer. they do on pitch without a conductor or instrument accompanying is akin to walking a high wire over Niagara Falls. The group is both virtuosic and expressive, without any question. The expressiveness is especially attractive in the cathedral with its rich sonic resonance, where announcements carry throughout with no microphones anywhere. Sounds in long decay time waft in the air richly and enduringly before fading. This is emblematic of a typical Catholic church, according to an acoustics lecture I heard at Cal, while typical Protestant churches feature a shorter sonic decay time favoring intelligibility of sermons more than song. It’s no news that Chanticleer represents a pinnacle of vocal art. Most unusual of all is its ability to reproduce both male and mixed choral music, as half of the ensemble consists of rare countertenors singing in the alto range, about an octave and a half above middle C – usually younger men reaching for the sky acoustically. Adept countertenors belong in the Fort Knox of vocalists – the gold of the species. This element was lustrous in “Rose of Roses” by the Swedish composer Fredrik Sixten, a work commissioned by Chanticleer, where a countertenor is offset against robust lower male voices in texts extolling Mary the mother of Jesus symbolized by the Rose. Among the other contemporary pieces was Melissa Dunphy’s “The Elements of the Sun Broke into Song,” which starts as chant but broadens out harmonically in ancient texts ascribed to Enoch, an antecedent of Noah. And some of the most beautiful sounds emerged from the Latin “Ave, spes nostra” by Vicente Lusitano, an alluring antiphon with lingering resonances filling the hall. Never to be forgotten is the Chanticleer signature work “Ave Maria” by Franz Biebl, an obscure Bavarian composer who achieved world fame through this antiphonal vocal opus with delectable crescendos as adopted by Chanticleer. Thereafter the singers finished off with lighter seasonal selections and the customary spirituals arranged by former Chanticleer singer and director Joseph Jennings. The encore for the enthusiasts present was “Christmas Time is Here” by the late San Francisco jazz musician Vince Guaraldi. Recalling the Magi of old, Chanticleer is itself a nomadic ensemble based locally, singing one night in many locales this year through December 23 in Northern California. MUSIC NOTES – The group had no public performances for 15 months ending in June, during which period they turned out three full-length films…Company members Keeler and Adam Ward produced new arrangements for this concert set…One of the memorable countertenors in this program was Logan Shields, the only singer with eyeglasses. Jeepers creepers, where’d you get those peepers? CHANTICLEER CHRISTMAS CONCERTS – Includes San Francisco on Dec. 18-19; and Santa Clara, Sacramento, and Carmel. For information, see: www.chanticleer.org.
articles.title: Clear sailing again for Chanticleer Chorus

articles.text: This is the last weekend to catch the Christmas Revels’ 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. articles.text: December is a time to come to Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek to see Garden of d’lights, its large collection of water-conserving and drought-resistant plants illuminated during the holidays through December 23. The exhibit is a safe outdoor experience that is suitable for all ages. Thousands of lights and lasers transform the Garden’s cacti, succulents and trees into magical, multicolored botanical sculptures, making it unique in the entire Bay Area. The garden houses plants from various hemispheres, so there is always something in bloom. Due to Covid-19, tickets must be purchased in advance with timed ticket entry. Capacity is restricted to 120 per entry group time. Time slots are available for 5:30 p.m., 6:30 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Ruth Bancroft Garden lights up during December. articles.text: Chitra Ganesh, Sultana’s Dream, 2018, portfolio of 27 linocuts; Mai-Thu Perret, Les guerilleres I, 2016 Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) on the UC Berkeley campus is presenting an art exhibition entitled New Time: Art and Feminisms in the 21st Century now through January 30, 2022. The exhibition explores the values, strategies, and ways of life and culture in current feminist art. Artworks made in 2000 and beyond are the primary focus, but many installations on view span several generations, mediums, and geographies. The exhibition is organized around eight themes: hysteria; the gaze; revisiting historical subjects through a feminist lens; the fragmented female body; gender fluidity; labor, domesticity, and activism; female anger; and feminist utopias. New Time is inspired by Bay Area poet Leslie Scalapino’s feminist poem of the same name. Many female artists, groups, musicians, and activists are featured, including Judy Chicago, Laura Aguilar, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Nicole Eisenman, Kiki Smith, and Amy Sillman. To learn more, visit https:// bampfa.org/program/new-timeart-and-feminisms-21st-century.
articles.title: New exhibit at Berkeley Art Museum now through January 30

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California has rescheduled the opening of Edith Heath: A Life in Clay to January 29, 2022. The exhibition was rescheduled due to water damage in the museum. The retrospect will be on display through October 30, 2022. A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artists’ career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by Oakland Museum’s Curator of A sampling of ceramics by Edith Heath. Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org.
articles.title: Edith Heath exhibit to open Jan. 29 at Oakland Museum

How the Word Is Passed: A Reckoning with the History of Slavery Across America, by Clint Smith. Little, Brown & Company. For this timely and thought-provoking book, Smith, a poet and journalist, toured sites key to the history of slavery and its present-day legacy. Smith holds up a mirror to America’s fraught relationship with its past, capturing a potent mixture of good intentions, earnest corrective, willful ignorance and blatant distortion. Invisible Child: Poverty, Survival and Hope in an American City, by Andrea Elliott. Random House. The book expands on her acclaimed 2013 series for “The Times” about Dasani Coates, a homeless New York schoolgirl, and her family. Elliott spent years following her subjects in their daily lives, through shelters, schools, courtrooms and welfare offices. The book is a searing account of one family’s struggle with poverty, homelessness and addiction. On Juneteenth, by Annette Gordon-Reed. Liveright Publishing. Exploring the racial and social complexities of Texas, her home state, Gordon-Reed asks readers to step back from the current heated debates and take a more nuanced look at history. Such a perspective comes easy to her because she was a part of history – the first Black child to integrate her East Texas school. On several occasions, she found herself shunned by whites and Blacks alike, learning at an early age that breaking the color line can be threatening to both races. Red Comet: The Short Life and Blazing Art of Sylvia Plath, by Heather Clark. Alfred A. Knopf. It’s daring to undertake a new biography of Plath, whose life, and death by suicide at 30 in 1963, have been thoroughly picked over by scholars. Determined to rescue the poet from posthumous caricature as a doomed madwoman and Clark aims to “reposition her as one of the most important American writers of the 20th century.” Clark, a professor of poetry in England, delivers a transporting account of a rare literary talent enlivened throughout by quotations from Plath’s letters, diaries, poetry and prose.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Berkeley Symphony Nigel Armstrong (left), Emanuela Nikiforova, Ivo Bokulic, and Isaac Pastor-Chermak performed a stirring concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, December 12 The Berkeley Symphony does things right, and much of the credit must go to Artistic Director Rene Mandel. Their ongoing series of chamber music concerts, now in its ninth year at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is a perfect example. All seemed calm on the surface in advance of Berkeley Symphony musicians’ opening chamber music concert of the 2021-22 season. And then I was informed of some heroic performances. A couple of the performers who were originally announced to play the concert had to cancel due to schedule conflicts. In ordinary times that might spell disaster, and usually the concert might be canceled. But it wasn’t. The substitute players played heroically. Winter from Antonio Vivaldi‘s ubiquitous Four Seasons served as a perfect warm up. That did not prepare the large and enthusiastic audience who had come on a cold and very wet Sunday afternoon for the surprise that awaited them. After the Vivaldi, guest violinist Nigel Armstrong strode to the stage and delivered Brian Nabors’ Theme and Variations for Solo Violin. His bow jumped over the strings like a graceful kangaroo, and there were other spectacular techniques as well. Armstrong made the difficult look like child’s play. His bow skipped along the string like a smooth stone skittering across the surface of a lake. That’s called a flying staccato. Not only that but Nabors’ composition calls for bowed notes to be combined with Pizzicato notes played simultaneously. Paganini invented this technique, but composer Brian Nabors gave it a 21st century touch. If it was difficult and virtuosic. What made it all the more interesting was that it was played with consummate ease. articles.text: The In the Tradition Piano Trio: Anthony Pegram (drums), Bill Jackman (piano), and Rich Trevor (bass). The In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, December 19, showcasing the Center’s Steinway Grand Piano. The Trio consists of pianist Bill Jackman, bass player Rich Trevor, and drummer Anthony Pegram, who perform as an old-school, classic jazz piano trio. The concert, entitled Music for the Holidays, will be a benefit for the Center and will include a collection of jazz, Latin, swing, and ballads. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years. He was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher and has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combos and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Jack London Square. The concert will be performed at 2 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door, or may be purchased in advance at https://bpt. me/5316993. Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 21 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia K. Forsyth Nº 45 in a biweekly series Americans in Paris was invited to the apartment of Guy and Jeanine Saperstein, a Piedmont couple who recently moved to France with their belongings and two small dogs. The occasion was Thanksgiving with their family members who flew in for the holiday, including their son Leon and wife Sunny, Piedmont residents who are planning to move to Paris at the end of the school year. Grandson Westlee is taking French lessons twice a week to be prepared. The clan is settling on the Left Bank at the very foot of the Eiffel Tower. Jeanine is powering through unpacking boxes. At her side is Bettye, her French majordomo who knows instinctively where everything should go. Guy and Jeanine had switched apartments with niece Unmi Abkin for a better layout plus the rarities of American-style bathrooms, walk-in coat closet, and chic powder room. Unmi and her husband Roger Taylor, both chefs from Northampton, Massachusetts, are just around the corner living in the Paris apartment the Sapersteins purchased this past summer. Roger and Unmi’s daughter Thanksgiving with the Sapersteins Coco, now in seventh grade at the International School of Paris, studies French for two hours daily. Unmi and Roger are busy testing recipes, following Curry & Kimchi, Unmi’s cookbook published in 2019. Roger is mapping the Paris neighborhoods by bicycle. Guy and Jeanine’s apartment is up a spiral staircase to the fifth floor in a limestone-block building on an elegant tree-lined avenue bordering the Champs de Mars. The stately roomy apartment is inviting and warm, and comfortably furnished during a period of transition. Moving is, at core, about adjustment; and theirs is from a California manse chock full of friendships and memories to change up life’s perspective and travel more while based in one of the most desirable of European cities. articles.text: Over the many years that I’ve been writing this column, I feel consistently called to consider the theme of slow, conscious living: slowing down, savoring, and weaving the stories of artisans and the lives of the makers into the products we consume. I think these values are a carry-forward from the many years I spent in the restaurant business watching chefs thoughtfully select the produce, the vendors, and even the place settings for their restaurants. My mission of creating beauty as a spiritual practice evolved over time. It wasn’t always there. In fact, the truth is quite the opposite. In my youth I had the gift of contrast. I worked in a wide range of food industry establishments, starting with McDonalds at age 16, the Sizzler at 17, and working my way up through the ranks of various restaurants until I wound up 15 years later as a seasoned restaurant professional working in the highest-end establishments San Francisco had to offer. During that time, I frequented many restaurants as a “professional” foodie and enjoyed hundreds of meals prepared by many of our wonderful Bay Area chefs. I also traveled, touring (and eating my way) through France and Italy. I even had one lucky week of getting to cook with Jean Pierre Moule, a founding chef with Alice Waters at Chez Panisse. I watched. I learned. I developed a strong understanding that the food that satisfied all the senses — not just my palate, but my heart and soul – was food that had been prepared slowly, thoughtfully, and served in an environment where beauty and simplicity were strongly revered. The most memorable of my experiences as a restaurant professional were the years I spent on the sidelines of Alice Waters’ incubator-by-proxy when I was in a five-year relationship with a waiter at Chez Panisse. In those years, I breathed, devoured, savored, cherished, and treasured my lived experience as a devotee of Alice’s church of slow cooking. LMBI designers Hannah Gipperich and Tiara Thomas enjoying the day. while enjoying a Lindsey Shere dessert and pinching myself that I had come so far from my food roots of quick-style American dinners. While Alice likely knows nothing of my existence, I am forever grateful that I got to witness from afar the slowness, the attention and presence, and the time-honored processes of marinating, curing, and savoring she brought to my life. “Slow” became my mantra, and ultimately it became the foundational ethos of my approach to interior design. Quality cannot be rushed and there’s no getting around that fact. I share this story as a lead-in to the similar joy I felt a few weeks ago on a trip to Healdsburg, where many of the memories of my restaurant world came rushing back. It was a return visit to the home base of our beloved vendors at Studio Bel Vetro, and included a luncheon at Sandra Jordan Fabrics, hosted by Sandra along with winemaker/artist and Berkeley native Mark Harris. The visit was devised and hosted by Sloan Miyasato and the company’s outside sales representative, Ryan Hammond. The day was filled with color and character, with talks and tours featuring artisan-crafted objects and the people who make them, networking with delightful Exquisite appetizer cones await guests. design industry colleagues, and imbibing with fantastic wine, food, and scenery — for beauty makers, by beauty makers. It would be hard to say what my favorite part of the trip was… the community connection, the glass-blowing presentation, or the slow meal served. Thanks to a beloved colleague, Phillip from Sandra Jordan, I learned that one of their gracious employees is none other than the granddaughter of famed Chez Panisse dessert chef Lindsey Shere. Earlier in the day I shared with Phillip that once, on a Chez Panisse staff wine-tasting trip to Navarro Winery in the ‘90s, as I walked through the vineyard with Lindsey Shere. We discovered that her father and my grandfather were both coal miners in a small town in Black Diamond, Washington. With Emily Shere’s presence at this event, it felt like my life was coming full circle. Being human is, in its best moments, about slowing down and pausing, savoring. This event was all of that: slow design, slow food, slow fabrication, slow entrepreneurship, slow relationship; slow meaning: deliberate, thoughtful. My soul was enriched by the connections and reconnections made with my team, colleagues, and old friends; my aesthetic need for beauty was met by the gorgeous lighting, glassware, textiles, food — even the drive. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors have once again shown their community spirit in giving back to those less fortunate. On Wednesday, November 17, they met at the Community Hall to show support for two community service projects: • Toys for Tots Toys for Tots, operated nationally by the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve and coordinated locally by the Piedmont Fire Department, has been a worthy cause for 25 years. Piedmont Seniors purchased new, unwrapped toys for children of all ages to be put in the toy donation bins at the Fire Station. Many lower income children and their parents have come to depend on this important program to ensure that their children have a joyful Christmas. The Fire Department welcomes more donations during this holiday season. • Socks for Seniors Piedmont Seniors has supported Socks for Seniors for 9 years. Through the Lutheran Ministry of Oakland, the Seniors have donated dozens of colorful and holiday socks for underserved members of the East Bay community. 2021-22 has hit this vulnerable group particularly hard. One of the local nursing homes lost 1/3 of its population this year. articles.text: Tips for year-end and beyond from your local Scout Council As you may recall, with the Federal Tax Law that was signed into law on December 22, 2017, most taxpayers have or will claim the Standard Deduction and have lost the benefit of Itemized Deductions. Charitable contributions are still deductible, but in many cases, with the limitations of deductible taxes and mortgage interest, coupled with the elimination of miscellaneous deductions, many will fall below the Standard Deduction amount. Keep in mind that California did not conform to the Federal Tax Law changes. Here are some strategies for you to consider: ● For those who are subject to the RMD (required minimum distribution) rules for your retirement accounts, you are eligible to do a QCD (qualified charitable distribution). With a QCD you can distribute up to $100,000 of your annual RMD to the church or other qualified 501(c)(3) public charity, enabling you to avoid paying income taxes on that amount. ○ When you reach age 70-1/2 you are subject to the RMD rules. However, changes were made with the SECURE Act, signed into law on December 10, 2019, whereby if your 70th birthday is on or after July 1, 2019, you do not have to take withdrawals until you reach age 72. ○ If you are subject to the RMD rules and do not take the required distribution, you are subject to a 50% tax penalty on the undistributed amount. ○ With the CARES Act, the IRS suspended the required distributions only for the tax year 2020. ○ For the tax year 2021 and beyond, the required distributions again apply. ● Consider bunching up multiyear charitable contributions into one year, along with your other eligible deductions, to exceed the Standard Deduction amount. These are strategies to be discussed with your personal tax advisor. John Chiang is a CPA and a member of the Piedmont Council BSA Finance Committee.
