articles.text: Features Book cover: Michael Lewis’ non-fiction The Premonition: A Pandemic Story First Mondays Reading Group gathers on a chilly morning on December 6 by the Japanese tea House in Piedmont Park. Pictured are: Albert Chen, Phil Witte, Karin Fetherston, Ken Young, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Mike and Nancy Henn, Lois Price, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Fourteen members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group gathered in front of the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on a cool afternoon on Monday, December 6, for a discussion of their December book, Michael Lewis’ non-fiction The Premonition: A Pandemic Story. Carol and Swee Ling brought Santa-worthy sacks of refreshments that the readers barely made a dent in. The dictionary defines “premonition” as “a strong feeling that something is about to happen, especially something unpleasant.” If the group had a premonition last Monday, it might have been about the weather. The temperature dipped to 52 by the time the group finished its discussion prior to 3 p.m. Michael Lewis is a great storyteller. On the back cover of The Premonition, John Williams of the New York Times Book Review writes, “I would read an 800-page history of the stapler, if he (Lewis) wrote it.” Members of the group who had read previous works by Lewis, such as Moneyball, The Big Short, The Blind Side, and Liar’s Poker, would agree with Williams. The group felt it is an important and thought-provoking book, but also one that raises concerns about our country. Lewis tells the story of how the pandemic came to be, but also how it was able to spread so quickly in the United States. He writes that the American coronavirus pandemic was a perfect storm of the reaction of President Trump, the long history of politicization of the Center for Disease Control (CDC) and the lack of a unified public health care system – all coming together with horrible consequences. This is also the story of a random group of experts whose jobs it was to put together plans for responding to pandemics in general. When the Covid-19 virus struck our country and our government’s response was sorely lacking, these public health officers, doctors, and researchers took the initiative to try to save Americans from the Covid-19 disaster. Charity Dean, a public health doctor in California, saw the danger of the virus before the rest of the country did. She tried unceasingly to get state officials to look at the data and act to keep the virus from spreading. In doing so, she put her reputation and her job in jeopardy. There also was another group of doctors trying to do the same thing at the federal level. This book is a particular indictment of the CDC. Years ago, a CDC official took steps to avoid a potential pandemic that turned out not to be serious, but his career was ruined because of his action. It is no wonder that very few leaders of government agencies are willing to take proactive, let along heroic actions in times of trouble. The changes in leadership can also contribute to ineffectiveness. Additionally, government positions that were once reserved for career public servants have been politicized. According to Lewis these political appointees may not have the competence or appropriate motivations to do what is needed, and right for our country. Some members of the reading group were initially concerned that a book about government public health activities would not be interesting. It was just the opposite. The readers found The Premonition to be very readable and entertaining. They enjoyed the profiles of the “good and heroic” people, as well as the “bad” people who did not live up to what the country needed during the pandemic. The failure of our government to act quickly and meet the pandemic’s challenge was frustrating and disappointing. Our health system does not work as well as it should, and our political system seems broken. The inability of our government to take action in this health crisis was also troubling for the readers. After more than an hour of discussion outdoors, the readers were feeling the December temperature and agreed it was time to select future books and adjourn. They had previously selected the novel Hamnet by Maggie O’Farrell for January and The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown for February. The group also selected The Midnight Library by Matt Haig for their March read. The group’s next discussion will be on Monday, January 3, and start at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting the group will meet in person at the Tea House. If the forecast is for cold or rain, the group will have their discussion via a Zoom call. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Please contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: Susan Simon Crown, 57, of Piedmont died Monday morning, November 22, 2021, after a twenty-month battle with pancreatic cancer. Susan died at home, surrounded by her husband Greg, her children Katherine and George, and family as she had wished. Throughout her cancer journey, she continued to live a full, connected life with the things she cared about as a priority, and surrounded by the people she loved. Her family, sisters, and nieces and nephews were a tremendous comfort and support for her. She found time to share with others who were on the same journey, offering encouragement and the benefit of what she had learned in her treatment. Susan was remarkable in her ability to be grateful, compassionate, connected, and present despite successes and setbacks and the unpleasantness that she had to endure. Born in Poughkeepsie, NY, she was the daughter of Joseph and Mary Louise Crown, the third of four sisters. She attended the local high school where she rowed crew on the Hudson River, earned her bachelor’s degree in English and Design at Hartwick College in Oneonta, NY, and then landed a job in Boston at Bain & Company. She moved into marketing in the nascent computer publishing industry with a stint at PC Computing, and then relocated to San Francisco to work at Berkeley Systems. In the late 1990s, she joined an early startup to lead their marketing effort. Like many of the dot com era the startup didn’t work out, but she did meet her future husband Greg at the company. Susan and Greg were married in October of 2001 in the Hudson Valley among fall colors – Susan’s favorite time of year. After the birth George, her 2nd child, the couple relocated from San Francisco to Piedmont. As her children reached their teens, Susan channeled some of her energy into a new career with J. Hilburn as a men’s clothing Susan Crown stylist. As with many of Susan’s personal connections, her clients frequently became friends. Susan was never happier than when she was combing a beach intent on finding that special heart-shaped rock or bit of “rare” blue sea-glass. Whether on Rodeo Beach in Marin County, or a beach on Cape Cod, MA or Little Compton, RI, Susan could find the most amazing heart rocks and collectible bits. She avidly collected and curated them and could always tell you where she found each one. More than once TSA questioned the weight and contents of her carry-on bag as she returned from an East Coast trip loaded with precious finds. Susan had a passion for children’s issues and tirelessly supported the San Francisco Court Appointed Special Advocates (SFCASA), organization. She served on the board for many years, drove incredible fundraising (for which she was honored), and spent countless hours personally volunteering. She had a tremendous knack for turning “passion into action” to improve the experiences of youth and families trying to navigate the foster care system. In addition to family and friends, hearts, and CASA, Susan’s other great love was art. She was a strong supporter of art education through local nonprofit work. She had a lifelong personal interest in painting which she renewed and deepened in recent years. Art classes with her sisters Mary and Jane, and frequent small works in watercolor and acrylic created wherever she had a quiet moment gave her both peace and satisfaction. She was nurturing and kind, creative, tenacious, and a fighter for the people and things she loved. Susan had bottomless energy and passion for her family, her friends, and for her causes. She was energized by people she met and with whom she connected. She could make a new friend for life in the space of an airplane ride. Her family and community have lost her, but we are so grateful that she shared herself and her love with us and thereby made us rich. Susan is survived by her husband Greg, children Katherine and George, sister and brother-in-law, Mary and William in MA, sister Jane in NC, beloved nieces and nephews in MA and universities in Washington DC and VA, and dear friends all across the country. A celebration of Susan’s life will be held at the Episcopal Church of St. Mary the Virgin on Union Street in San Francisco at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, January 5th. In lieu of flowers, please make contributions in Susan’s memory to the pancreatic cancer support organization “Let’s Win” (https://letswinpc.org) or the “Pancreatic Cancer Action Network” (https://www.pancan.org). articles.text: Madeleine Hickling, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away on December 2, 2021. Madeleine Henning Hickling died on December 2, 2021 from complications of kidney disease that first became apparent after a bout of liposarcoma in the 2000s. A native of St. Cloud, Minnesota, Maddy lived in the Bay Area since 1960, when she met and married her husband, Douglas Hickling. Maddy had many interests in the community and over the years participated in several organizations including the University YWCA Auxiliary, Town and Gown Club, the Bellevue Club, and the Piedmont Area Republican Women. Maddy took pride in being a native Minnesotan and a graduate of the U of Minnesota, where she studied psychology and joined Kappa Kappa Gamma Sorority. Maddy remained involved in the KKG alumni association for decades and valued the friendships she made as an alumna. Until recently Maddy kept up with several childhood friends from St. Cloud who, like her, graduated from the St. Cloud State Laboratory High School and later relocated to California. Until the final days of her life, Maddy was highly engaged with the world around her and keenly appreciated things that brought beauty and comfort to everyday life. She was an avid gardener who loved raising flowers and vegetables and herbs. She had a green thumb with houseplants, especially orchids. She participated in the East Bay Earthworms gardening group for many years. She also enjoyed home interior decoration and design, which led her to a career in residential real estate serving Piedmont, first as an agent with Century 21, then later with Mason-McDuffie (which became Better Homes Realty). pages.text: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 25 Obituary Maddy Hickling dies December 2 Madeleine Hickling, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away on December 2, 2021. Madeleine Henning Hickling died on December 2, 2021 from complications of kidney disease that first became apparent after a bout of liposarcoma in the 2000s. A native of St. Cloud, Minnesota, Maddy lived in the Bay Area since 1960, when she met and married her husband, Douglas Hickling. Maddy had many interests in the community and over the years participated in several organizations including the University YWCA Auxiliary, Town and Gown Club, the Bellevue Club, and the Piedmont Area Republican Women. Maddy took pride in being a native Minnesotan and a graduate of the U of Minnesota, where she studied psychology and joined Kappa Kappa Gamma Sorority. Maddy remained involved in the KKG alumni association for decades and valued the friendships she made as an alumna. Until recently Maddy kept up with several childhood friends from St. Cloud who, like her, graduated from the St. Cloud State Laboratory High School and later relocated to California. Until the final days of her life, Maddy was highly engaged with the world around her and keenly appreciated things that brought beauty and comfort to everyday life. She was an avid gardener who loved raising flowers and vegetables and herbs. She had a green thumb with houseplants, especially orchids. She participated in the East Bay Earthworms gardening group for many years. She also enjoyed home interior decoration and design, which led her to a career in residential real estate serving Piedmont, first as an agent with Century 21, then later with Mason-McDuffie (which became Better Homes Realty). Seasonal rituals and holidays were important to her, and she established fun family traditions like eating special meals in the dining room on holidays Halloween and Valentine’s Day and hosting family Christmas and Easter celebrations. Maddy is survived by her children, Anne Hickling of Phoenix, Arizona, and William Hickling of Alameda. She is also survived by her sister, Emily Henning Warden of Berkeley, and two grandchildren, Luke and Julian Rodriguez, of Phoenix. She is predeceased by her husband, Douglas Hickling, who died in 2014. Susan Crown dies November 22 in Piedmont Susan Simon Crown, 57, of Piedmont died Monday morning, November 22, 2021, after a twenty-month battle with pancreatic cancer. Susan died at home, surrounded by her husband Greg, her children Katherine and George, and family as she had wished. Throughout her cancer journey, she continued to live a full, connected life with the things she cared about as a priority, and surrounded by the people she loved. Her family, sisters, and nieces and nephews were a tremendous comfort and support for her. She found time to share with others who were on the same journey, offering encouragement and the benefit of what she had learned in her treatment. Susan was remarkable in her ability to be grateful, compassionate, connected, and present despite successes and setbacks and the unpleasantness that she had to endure. Born in Poughkeepsie, NY, she was the daughter of Joseph and Mary Louise Crown, the third of four sisters. She attended the local high school where she rowed crew on the Hudson River, earned her bachelor’s degree in English and Design at Hartwick College in Oneonta, NY, and then landed a job in Boston at Bain & Company. She moved into marketing in the nascent computer publishing industry with a stint at PC Computing, and then relocated to San Francisco to work at Berkeley Systems. In the late 1990s, she joined an early startup to lead their marketing effort. Like many of the dot com era the startup didn’t work out, but she did meet her future husband Greg at the company. Susan and Greg were married in October of 2001 in the Hudson Valley among fall colors – Susan’s favorite time of year. After the birth George, her 2nd child, the couple relocated from San Francisco to Piedmont. As her children reached their teens, Susan channeled some of her energy into a new career with J. Hilburn as a men’s clothing Susan Crown stylist. As with many of Susan’s personal connections, her clients frequently became friends. Susan was never happier than when she was combing a beach intent on finding that special heart-shaped rock or bit of “rare” blue sea-glass. Whether on Rodeo Beach in Marin County, or a beach on Cape Cod, MA or Little Compton, RI, Susan could find the most amazing heart rocks and collectible bits. She avidly collected and curated them and could always tell you where she found each one. More than once TSA questioned the weight and contents of her carry-on bag as she returned from an East Coast trip loaded with precious finds. Susan had a passion for children’s issues and tirelessly supported the San Francisco Court Appointed Special Advocates (SFCASA), organization. She served on the board for many years, drove incredible fundraising (for which she was honored), and spent countless hours personally volunteering. She had a tremendous knack for turning “passion into action” to improve the experiences of youth and families trying to navigate the foster care system. In addition to family and friends, hearts, and CASA, Susan’s other great love was art. She was a strong supporter of art education through local nonprofit work. She had a lifelong personal interest in painting which she renewed and deepened in recent years. Art classes with her sisters Mary and Jane, and frequent small works in watercolor and acrylic created wherever she had a quiet moment gave her both peace and satisfaction. She was nurturing and kind, creative, tenacious, and a fighter for the people and things she loved. Susan had bottomless energy and passion for her family, her friends, and for her causes. She was energized by people she met and with whom she connected. She could make a new friend for life in the space of an airplane ride. Her family and community have lost her, but we are so grateful that she shared herself and her love with us and thereby made us rich. Susan is survived by her husband Greg, children Katherine and George, sister and brother-in-law, Mary and William in MA, sister Jane in NC, beloved nieces and nephews in MA and universities in Washington DC and VA, and dear friends all across the country. A celebration of Susan’s life will be held at the Episcopal Church of St. Mary the Virgin on Union Street in San Francisco at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, January 5th. In lieu of flowers, please make contributions in Susan’s memory to the pancreatic cancer support organization “Let’s Win” (https://letswinpc.org) or the “Pancreatic Cancer Action Network” (https://www.pancan.org). articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Tree Lot is seeing record popularity this year. With only 60 trees not yet sold as of December 7, the Scouts have arranged for delivery of 300 more trees in time for this weekend. The new shipment includes 200 Douglas Firs of 6-7 feet and 100 Noble Firs of 5-6 feet. All trees are due to arrive by Friday, to meet customers’ needs through the weekend and into the following week. The initial shipment of 1,450 trees arrived the day after Thanksgiving but was missing 150 Silvertips of the 300 ordered due to drought and fire. Silvertips availability has been limited statewide this year. December 7 marks the earliest date the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot has been on the verge of selling out. It is the first time in the 53-year history of the tree lot that a supplemental shipment was ordered. “We’ve ordered more Noble and Douglas fir trees, but they won’t last long. So come one, come all, and get ‘em fresh from the farm, or delivered right to your door,” said volunteer David Ashton, who orders the trees. The Scouts got a head start this year with 250 trees preordered online prior to the opening day. articles.text: As an alumna of Piedmont schools and now a parent of a Havens 1st grader, I wanted to share why I support the Giving Campaign and ask others to join me. I attended Piedmont schools from K-12. Now, as I walk my daughter to school, I am reminded of my special experience growing up in Piedmont. I remember kindergarten at Wildwood and walking to school every day where beloved teachers Mrs. Weidkamp and Mrs. Schoenberg introduced us to classroom learning. As a first grader, I sang “On the Sunny Side” every day with Mrs. Morrison. In high school, I perfected my bird-calling skills (and yes – my claim to fame – my Wildwood friend and I won the bird-calling contest and performed on the David Letterman show). I was lucky to have fabulous, amazing, wonderful teachers – many of whom I am still in touch with today, decades later. From small class sizes and aides in elementary school, to library time and electives in middle school, to AP classes in high school, I greatly benefited from the generosity of our community. Fast forward 20 years. My husband and I are living in Piedmont with our three children. This fall, our daughter, Lily, started at Havens as a first grader. We started off this school year nervously – how would our daughter adjust to first grade? Would Havens live up to the memories and expectations I had of Piedmont schools? We were thrilled to see that from her very first day, Lily was over the moon at Havens. Principal Dolid, Mrs. Fredericks, and the resource specialists have made this a smooth and wonderful experience. Lily is confident, she is engaged, and she simply loves school. We feel a great sense of comfort and peace in knowing that our kids will have an amazing public school experience here in Piedmont. Piedmont schools deserve our very best to ensure our young ones can continue to develop, thrive, and grow. We hope you’ll join us in supporting Piedmont Schools through the Piedmont Giving Campaign this year.
articles.title: Full circle with Piedmont schools

articles.text: The holiday season is a time for gathering, showing one another love and warmth, and thinking about resolutions for the new year. This season also provides opportunities to reduce waste, emissions, and our climate footprints throughout the holidays. From the gifts we give, to the ways we wrap those gifts, decorate, travel, and even the food we eat, our decisions make an impact on the world around us. If you’re searching the internet for ethical, eco-friendly holiday ideas, a simple google search will give you many ideas. However, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks for greening the holiday season. While the winter holiday season brings many of us good cheer, it also contributes more solid waste to landfills, harm to the environment, and emissions to our carbon footprint. Each year, Americans throw away approximately 25% more trash during the Thanksgiving to New Year’s holiday period than any other time of the year. This contributes an extra 25 million tons of garbage nationally, about 1 million extra tons per week. When thinking about how to reduce your climate footprint this holiday season, consider the three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle. • Reduce From gift giving to wrapping to decorations, we often purchase single-use materials and contribute to unnecessary greenhouse gas emissions. One way to reduce your greater carbon footprint is by shopping locally. Shopping locally reduces the transportation emissions of goods and the overall carbon footprint of the product. Local shopping guides like those from Visit Oakland and Berkeley Holidays offer a wide range of ideas close to home for all audiences and price points. Other options to reduce gift-related waste are some clutter-free gift ideas including experiences, classes, memberships, and consumables. • Reuse Another way to reduce your carbon footprint this holiday season is through gifting secondhand items. Local thrift, vintage, and antique stores give products a second life, keeping them out of landfills and reducing emissions associated with the creation of new products and the transportation of said products. Not only do thrift, vintage, and antique stores decrease the carbon footprint of your gifts, but they also often contribute to local charities, boosting local community development. Gifting durable, reusable items and necessities will also ensure that your gift is used and lasts the test of time. Re-gifting is another sustainable option, especially for events like white elephant gift exchanges when the gift is not personalized and could be for someone you don’t know well. • Recycle Purchasing recycled-content products, or products contained in recyclable packaging materials decreases the waste that enters landfills. When wrapping gifts, consider recycling wrapping paper, reusing wrapping fabrics or bags and items such as ribbons and bows, or making your own from magazines, maps, or newspapers, such as an old edition of the Piedmont Post. If it’s necessary to purchase new wrapping paper, look for products that are recyclable and made from recycled materials. In some cultures, like the Japanese tradition of furoshiki, gifts are wrapped in cloth. Some potential cloth wrapping materials include tea towels or scarves, which make the wrapping cloth part of the gift itself. Better yet, give a gift that requires no packaging like an experience, class, membership, or donation in someone’s honor. Other opportunities for greening the holiday season this winter include turning off holiday lights during the day and when you go to bed, donating edible food, composting food scraps and your Christmas tree, minimizing personal vehicle use, and serving meals to your guests using reusable foodware when entertaining. Further editions of the Climate Corner will focus on additional opportunities to reduce your climate footprint and green the holidays this year. Still, Lillevand cautioned that fiscal numbers related to the project are not solidified. Because there are so many “unknowns” in design and site development, there may be impacts to cost. She added that, in early 2022, before the City Council signs off on a final design, “there will be a lot more clarity and understanding of costs.” Taxpayers will start seeing an impact related to the bond issuance in December 2022. The bonds are secured by, and payable from, ad valorem property taxes levied by the city and collected by Alameda County. The annual tax rate to repay the bonds is expected to be no more than $25.40 per $100,000 of assessed value, which is lower than originally anticipated – Measure UU estimated the tax rate to be $26.20 per $100,000 of assessed value. Lillevand added that the “overall debt service is almost identical to the estimate contained in Measure UU, and with a tax rate below the estimate contained in the measure.” The bonds were issued as a single-series bearing a tax-exempt rate of 5%, resulting in an issue premium of $5.8 million. The total bond proceeds will be $25,329,463. The bond proceeds are not the same as the design and construction budget for the pool. The project budget is currently under development. ELS Architects, the firm chosen by the city to design the new pool, is estimating costs at roughly $21 million. “Given escalating construction costs, inflation, and supply chain challenges, we are extremely fortunate that we will have significant contingency moneys to support the development of a community pool,” Lillevand said. Still, Lillevand cautioned that fiscal numbers related to the project are not solidified. Because there are so many “unknowns” in design and site development, there may be impacts to cost. She added that, in early 2022, before the City Council signs off on a final design, “there will be a lot more clarity and understanding of costs.” Taxpayers will start seeing an impact related to the bond issuance in December 2022. The bonds are secured by, and payable from, ad valorem property taxes levied by the city and collected by Alameda County. The annual tax rate to repay the bonds is expected to be no more than $25.40 per $100,000 of assessed value, which is lower than originally anticipated – Measure UU estimated the tax rate to be $26.20 per $100,000 of assessed value. articles.text: On Friday, December 3, the Piedmont City administration announced that the public is once again invited to attend public meetings in City Hall. The regularly scheduled city council meeting on Monday, December 6, was the first in over 90 weeks that allowed the public to attend. Members of the public may still participate in meetings on Zoom. “It’s great that [council members] get to meet both in the council chambers, and for the first time since the pandemic began, we can welcome guests,” said Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. The next city council meeting will be held on Monday, December 20 at 7:30 p.m. Looking back at 2020 The City Council under former mayor Bob McBain declared a local emergency at a March 16, 2020 meeting in an effort to address the growing pandemic. The item to adopt a resolution ratifying proclamation of local emergency was not originally included in that meeting’s agenda, but was added by City Administrator Sara Lillevand late Monday afternoon. Days before that meeting, Gov. Gavin Newsom suspended provisions of the Brown Act, which would have otherwise required notice of the addition. City Hall was then closed to the public for nonessential business March 16 through March 25, 2020.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post returned to Piedmont High to report from inside classrooms after a 20-month hiatus due to Covid safety measures. Equipped with a mask and with vaccination card, school approval and health screener results in hand, this reporter visited the new STEAM building to see what Marna Chamberlain’s College Preparatory Physics class was working on. On Thursday December 2, Chamberlain’s period four Physics class continued building and refining solar ovens in groups of two. The immediate goal was to design and create a solar oven capable of heating up something edible. The overarching aim was to try to create solutions to the issue of inequity, locally and globally, regarding access to energy. Drawing her students’ attention to the bigger picture, she said, “Remember, we are addressA solar oven on the Makers Lab patio heats up some s’mores. PHS Physics Teacher Marna Chamberlain reviews 11th grader Audrey Harmon’s solar oven project. ing equity and finding solutions that are sustainable and realistic for their given target population.” No stranger to the project, Chamberlain had students building and donating them to Native Americans in 2014, and later arranged for students to build solar panels with a USB charging port and to be sent to Uganda and Haiti. “Our design could be used locally by kids as a fun project. Moms might have these basic supplies like cotton balls, shoeboxes, and construction paper around the house,” added student Eva Levingston. The amenities of the new science lab were at their disposal, and ingenuity, problem-solving and innovation were on display. Miter saws, razor blades, drills, hot glue guns were the tools, and cardboard, plywood, tin foil, saran wrap, spray paint and plexiglass were the favored supplies. Some students used shoe boxes as their base, others modified pizza boxes and some ovens resembled wooden bird houses. Students were given free rein to choose their own design without many constraints so there was considerable variety between groups. Many students had the goal of making water safe for consumption. But with only an hour of time to have the ovens out in the winter sun, many opted instead to make s’mores or Rice Krispies treats. Students were directed to research the dual properties of light, both as a particle and as a wave, and to use that knowledge in conjunction with the material science of the building supplies. Senior Ana Romanczuk and Junior Milani Juarbe explained their design. “We have aluminum foil so we can reflect the light through saran wrap. Everything inside will be black, so the heat will get attracted to it, and it will end up getting trapped inside.” Students also learned about the Angle of Isolation – choosing the best angle to position the light reflecting material of the ovens, like tin foil or mirrors. Chamberlain explained the importance of recording accurate data and following the scientific method even if designs and tests don’t work out as planned “Sometimes, efficiency goes down after attempting improvements, and that is okay. Even in something like rocketry, the first model may perform the best,” she said. From March 2020 to March 2021 all classes at PHS were taught remotely on computers because of the Covid pandemic. Now that school has been back in person full-time since August, students in classes like Physics have the chance to experience the full process of creation and experimentation. With the new STEAM building on the high school campus, Piedmont students have the latest in technology to advance their studies. Perseas Gioukaris (left) and Eva Levingston hold up their solar oven, which has feet on the bottom to limit heat transfer. Kevin Blodgett (left) and Harry Pasion test their solar oven by recording the temperature inside with an aquarium thermometer.
articles.title: INSIDE THE CLASSROOM Marna Chamberlain’s physics class builds solar ovens

articles.text: The Piedmont Pioneers, a middle school First Tech Challenge (FTC) robotics team, continues in its sixth year of competition. The Pioneers’ current challenge requires building a robot capable of going over or around large barriers, and to pick up, transport, and deliver scattered spheres and This year’s team consists of six members, three responsible for programming software and three dedicated to engineering the hardware. Eighth grader Cassie Colby captains the software team of 7th graders Aliya Vora, and Edward Balasingham. The software team writes code in java to program their robot in two different modes, autonomous, and driver control. The autonomous programs enable the robot to move accurately as it does various tasks. The driver control program maps actions to buttons on a video game controller, allowing the “driver’’ to move the robot around like a video game. The hardware team is led by 8th grader Nathaniel Welch and includes 7th graders Grey Sanford and Elsa Wallway. Their team designs and constructs the robot and all of its physical features. They have built a claw to pick up the objects on the field and created an elevated drive train to scale the barriers on the field. The Pioneers meet at least three times a week, in addition to attending scrimmages and competitions. FTC is not just about building, programming, and competing; every year the Pioneers fundraise thousands of dollars, through corporate sponsors and grants. Additionally, they log every practice in their engineering Nathaniel Welch (left), Grey Sanford, Edward Balasingham, Cassie Colby and Aliya Vora make changes to their FIRST Tech Challenge robot at their first scrimmage in November. Community Arts Programming 7th grader Grey Sanford works on the drive train of the Pioneer’s robot in early September. notebook, recording attendance, plans of action, accomplishments, with supporting photos and notes. They also conduct outreach in the community through mentoring sessions and other events. The Pioneers strive to embody gracious professionalism in all interactions with other teams, companies, and teammates, and to exude the FTC core values which include problem-solving, improving, innovating, and having fun. FIRST is an amazing program with levels suitable for kids from K-12. FTC, the Pioneers level, is for 7-12 graders. FIRST Robotics gives participants first-hand experience in programing, building, researching, and fundraising. In addition, the program helps kids build sportsmanship, and communicating skills. Volunteers wearing purple in support of the Giving Campaign were at every school site, and teachers made thank-you signs to express gratitude to families for their support of the Giving Campaign. articles.text: The holidays are back and we are still in this strange moment k nown as “Covid-times.” Although, for those of us with kids under the age of about six, it’s just known as “normal-times” because they don’t really remember a time when we went to the grocery store without a mask or gathered with large groups without thinking about everyone’s vaccine status. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, December 8, 2021 Thinking Outside The Classroom Holiday Family Stories of Before and Now By Nina Meehan The holidays are back and we are still in this strange moment k nown as “Covid-times.” Although, for those of us with kids under the age of about six, it’s just known as “normal-times” because they don’t really remember a time when we went to the grocery store without a mask or gathered with large groups without thinking about everyone’s vaccine status. For those of us who do remember “before-times,” it seems like a long time ago at this point. I have been reflecting on the power of noticing and honoring before and now, in general. Our kids grow and change. The holidays are a marking point for how things are different. For instance, my 13-year-old once wanted Legos for Hanukkah. Now he wants V-Bucks. Robyn Fivush, director of the Family Narratives Lab in Emory University’s Department of Psychology has studied the impact of family stories on children. The more that children are familiar with the narrative of their lives, they have higher “self-esteem, higher levels of social competence, higher quality friendships, and less anxiety and stress.” (https://news.emory.edu/stories/2020/04/esc_covid_19_family_stories/campus.html) So, this holiday season, why not take some time to write some before and now stories? Start by taking it year by year and looking at photos or just remembering where you were at different ages. Share memories with your family this holiday season. Remembering together is how we create family narratives, but also going back before our children remember to their very first winter holiday can be very meaningful. Here is a specific frame you can use to explore before and now: • When you were ____ years old, you were so excited to receive _____ as gifts. • Now you are ____ years old, and I can see that ____ is on your wish list. • When you were ____ years old, I can remember you eating so much _____ at the holiday meal. • What do you think you will eat the most of this year? • When you were ____ years old, we went on that wonderful trip to_____. My favorite memory of you on that trip was ______. • If we could travel anywhere in the world this year, where would you want to go? • When you were ___ years old, • we had a hard holiday because ______. I felt sad/lonely/ angry at that time. What could be hard about this holiday for you? There are so many fun ways to explore memories through stories, and important ways to reflect on harder times as well. Perhaps, your child will remember something that you don’t. And, if you both can’t remember a detail or a year, feel free to use this prompt: • We don’t remember this holiday, but what if this crazy thing happened (MAKE UP A CRAZY HOLIDAY ADVENTURE FOR YOUR FAMILY)? However you choose to share stories, I hope your holiday is memorable and filled with cheer. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre and the host of Creative Parenting Podcast. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: As the weather gets colder and more drizzly, I find it good to curl up with my tuxedo cat, a fluffy duvet, and a nice cup of tea. To round it out, I love a good mystery. Mysteries come in all flavors. I joined a Mystery Book Club for several years at my local library, enabling me to expand my usual stable of mystery authors. I enjoy books featuring forensic investigators, smart female detectives, England, especially during the Victorian period, and ethical dilemmas. Most of the books are light on graphic violence. Here are a variety of choices, all of which I have read. Enola Holmes Mystery Series by Nancy Springer. Philomel Books. 2006. The Case of the Missing Marquess. 236 pages. This would be a good series for a family read. I enjoyed her character as an adult and I can see middle schoolers also enjoying her adventures. Her first story, The Case of the Missing Marquess has been made into a movie on Netflix. The setting is the English countryside and Victorian London. Enola is the teenaged sister of Sherlock and Mycroft Holmes. She is eccentric and high spirited, solving her own mysteries, while her brothers try to keep her from getting into too much trouble. She is generally a few steps ahead of them. She is also a master (mistress?) of disguise. voices. Anyone who has visited or attended Harvard will recognize many of the landmarks. The House on Vesper Sands was named an Indie Next Pick, Library Reads Pick, Apple Books’ Best Book, Powells’ Pick, Amazon Fiction & Literature’s “Best of the Month,” and one of Daily’s Best Historical Novels of 2021. An Anonymous Girl by Greer Hendricks & Sarah Pekkanen. St. Martin’s Group Publishing. 2019. 375 pages. A young woman joins a psychological study at the local university, drawn by the opportunity to make some much needed money. But, as the requests become more and more bizarre, she wonders what she has gotten herself into. The novel takes place in New York and is told from alternating points of view from Jessie and the psychologist. The House on Vesper Sands by Paraic O’ Donnell. 2021. 408 pages. The book is characterized as a Victorian Gothic set in 1893 London. It is eerie and requires suspension of belief. This was a period of seances, spirits, and mesmerism. The book opens with a seamstress jumping from the window of an Earl’s London residence. The main characters are a female journalist and two coppers. Some people have found it brilliant; others found it confusing. There are lots of characters to keep track of, but I found it a satisfying read. I certainly didn’t figure it out ahead of time. Before the Fall by Noah Hawley. Grand Central Publishing. 2017. 397 pages. Scott Burroughs, an unsuccessful artist, at the last minute, ends up as a passenger on a private jet from Martha’s Vineyard to New York. 18 minutes into the flight the plane crashes into the ocean. Scott and J.J., a fouryear-old, are the only survivors. Suddenly, Scott is in the limelight as a hero. He tries to hide from the press, but things keep getting worse, fueled by the news which has become sensationalized entertainment. But what caused the crash that killed seven people? articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team is off to a strong start after shutting out rival Bishop O’Dowd 1-0 on Wednesday, December 1, beating Shoreline opponent Tennyson 2-0 on Friday, December 3, and tying Oakland Tech 1-1 on Monday, December 6. The 1-nil defeat of O’Dowd marked Piedmont’s first win over the Dragons since the 2015- 16 season, and was evidence of Piedmont’s ability to constantly pressure its opponent and limit the scoring opportunities. “We have a very solid back line, I expected us to be good defensively this year. In the second half, we were head and shoulders above O’Dowd. We’re working and building up to our best. With fingers crossed, this is a sign of our future,” said coach Todd Sullivan. However, the squad’s 1-1 tie with Oakland Tech on Monday night resulted in the Bulldogs celebrating as if they had won. ‘It was poor quality tonight. Oakland Tech was ready for it and we weren’t… It was almost like the O’Dowd game but in reverse. (Tech) worked harder than we did. Luckily we got a result, but have a lot to work on ahead of the winter break,” said Sullivan. Four matches into the season, PHS hasn’t allowed a goal. but his shot was saved. Daniel had another look in the 24th minute after winning the ball but his shot clanged off the left. Russell Tan also had a shot go wide in the 37th. In the second half, Stankiewicz did well to win a penalty kick in the 51st minute, but Piedmont’s shot sailed high. O’Dowd had just two shots on target throughout the night, and had six shot attempts go wide. With some slick footwork, Daniel weaved his way around Tennyson’s left back and smashed a leftfooted shot to the top-right bin. Daniel 2, Tennyson 0 PHS opened league competition with a 2-0 win over Tennyson on Friday, December 3 at Witter Field. The Highlanders went into halftime tied ay 0-0, but scored in the 45th and 54th minute, both by Daniel. The opening goal at 45’ was a disastrous moment for the Lancers. After playing the ball back to their keeper, Daniel pressed the goalie and scored by blocking Tennyson’s pass attempt into the net. In the 54th, Daniel bagged his brace after receiving a nice long pass from Conner Curtis. Oakland Tech Recap Piedmont’s most recent game was a 1-1 tie with non-league Oakland Tech on Monday, December 6. The Highlanders scored in the 2nd minute when the Bulldogs’ keeper made a mistake on a throw, tossing it inadvertently to Conner Curtis who tapped in the ball from slightly above the penalty area. The Bulldogs tied the match in the 26th minute on a free kick opportunity, sending a low shot that slightly deflected off of Piedmont’s defensive wall and found its way into the net. Aiden Woolwine broke the scoreless duel with five minutes left in the game after the Dragons’ keeper fumbled a cross back into the field of play. Woolwine jumped at the chance, ad sent a right-footed rocket into the net for the game winner. “It felt good! When the ball fell, I knew I was going to hit it. The ball flicked off one of their players and found me in the right place,” recalled Woolwine ecstatically. In the buildup, Andre Stankiewicz targeted Woolwine on a corner. After a deflection, Woolwine sent a pass back to Stankiewicz on the wing near the touch line; Stankiewicz then whipped in another cross toward the near post, where the BOD keeper lost the ball back into play. Aiden Woolwine scored the game-winner in the 75th minute against O’Dowd.

articles.text: 11th annual girls’ basketball tournament at PHS After a one-year hiatus due to the global pandemic, the Paris Twins Classic returns to Binks Rawlings Gym this week from Thursday through Saturday, December 9-11. It is the 11th year of the annual tournament named for Sports Hall of Fame athletes Courtney and Ashley Paris, who led Piedmont to two consecutive state championships. “Our tournament is going to be thick with competition. We’ve only won this one time, and it’ll be tough to do it again. We’re excited,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Piedmont will face Lompoc in the opening game tomorrow, Thursday, December 9 at 8:00 p.m. Piedmont recently beat Lompoc 74-40 on December 2 at the Lompoc tournament. The Highlanders won the tournament after being a finalist last year. Also competing on the opening day at 3:30 p.m. will be Cardinal Newman, which holds a 4-2 overall record and had a 29-4 record last year. It plays Grant Union from Sacramento. a team with a 6-1 record. Piedmont will play the winner of that game on Friday, December 10 at 6:30 p.m. Game 2 is slated for 5:00 p.m. tomorrow with Vanden of Fairfield (2-0) playing Sacred Heart (2-1). Vanden recently beat Pleasant Valley 73-35 and Chico 72-39. “Vanden is another tough school; they made it to the second-round of the State Tournament [in the winter of 2020]. It’s a really deep tournament,” said Gardere. Game 3 is at 6:30 p.m., featuring Freedom HS Oakley (2-1) against Valley Christian of San Jose (4-0). The winners of Vanden vs. Sacred Heart will face the winner of Freedom vs. Valley Christian on Friday at 8:00 p.m. The Championship game is scheduled for Saturday, December 11 at 2:30 p.m. with a 3rd place game at 1:00 p.m.
articles.title: Paris Twins Classic opens tomorrow

articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ basketball team started its season in a big way. Playing 300 miles from home in Lompoc, they won the annual Bryan Ayer Classic for the second time in three years. On Thursday, December 2, they rolled over Santa Barbara, 57-34; trounced host Lompoc on Friday 74-40, and won the finals 62-34 over Orcutt Academy. It marked the 14th annual tournament following last spring’s pandemic shortened season. In 2019, PHS lost to Santa Barbara in the championship 64-54. Sophomore Natalia Martinez was named MVP of the tournament, and juniors Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill were named to the All-Tournament team. “I am proud of our whole team. We aren’t close to the final product, but definitely off to solid start,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We can build from this weekend. Trinity [Zamora], Natalia [Martinez], Maddie [Hill] and Hannah [Govert] led the way. Kat Melian truly stepped up in her first action on varsity. I’m so proud of her,” Finals vs. Orcutt Academy Piedmont led 18-7 at the end of the first quarter and ballooned to 39-17 by halftime. It was after three quarters before finishing with a 62-34 victory for the championship. In the first quarter, Piedmont made five three-pointers, two each by Zamora and Hill, and one by Hannah Govert. Martinez exploded for 13 of her 27 points Natalia Martinez was named the tournament’s Most Outstanding Player. I the second quarter, including 4 for 5 at the free throw line. Martinez added 10 more points in the third quarter including 4 of 4 at the line. Hill had a 3-pointer, and Shay Ottaviano scored her first varsity field goal. Final stats include Martinez with 27 points, six rebounds, two assists, and five steals. Zamora scored 16 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals, and two blocks. Hill came away with 12 points, two rebounds, three assists, and two steals. Govert scored three points, seven rebounds, four assists, and two blocks. Melian had five rebounds, two steals. Ottaviano scored four points, two rebounds, one steal. Semifinals vs. Lompoc In the semis, Piedmont defeated Lompoc 74-40 after going into the half with a 32-20 lead. They finished the night with 18 steals and poured in 10 three-pointers in the second half. Freshman Shakila Zuberi scored three points in her varsity debut. Final stats include Zamora with 25 points, 12 rebounds, five assists, three steals, and two blocks. Martinez had 28 points, seven boards, nine assists, and six steals. Hill scored 13 points, two rebounds, three assists, and five steals. Govert scored three points, three boards. Melian had two points and four rebounds. Zuberi had three, and two rebounds. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 13 Staff Photos Paris Twins Classic opens tomorrow 11th annual girls’ basketball tournament at PHS By Jonathan Comeaux After a one-year hiatus due to the global pandemic, the Paris Twins Classic returns to Binks Rawlings Gym this week from Thursday through Saturday, December 9-11. It is the 11th year of the annual tournament named for Sports Hall of Fame athletes Courtney and Ashley Paris, who led Piedmont to two consecutive state championships. “Our tournament is going to be thick with competition. We’ve only won this one time, and it’ll be tough to do it again. We’re excited,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Piedmont will face Lompoc in the opening game tomorrow, Thursday, December 9 at 8:00 p.m. Piedmont recently beat Lompoc 74-40 on December 2 at the Lompoc tournament. The Highlanders won the tournament after being a finalist last year. Also competing on the opening day at 3:30 p.m. will be Cardinal Newman, which holds a 4-2 overall record and had a 29-4 record last year. It plays Grant Union from Sacramento. a team with a 6-1 record. Piedmont will play the winner of that game on Friday, December 10 at 6:30 p.m. Game 2 is slated for 5:00 p.m. tomorrow with Vanden of Fairfield (2-0) playing Sacred Heart (2-1). Vanden recently beat Pleasant Valley 73-35 and Chico 72-39. “Vanden is another tough school; they made it to the second-round of the State Tournament [in the winter of 2020]. It’s a really deep tournament,” said Gardere. Game 3 is at 6:30 p.m., featuring Freedom HS Oakley (2-1) against Valley Christian of San Jose (4-0). The winners of Vanden vs. Sacred Heart will face the winner of Freedom vs. Valley Christian on Friday at 8:00 p.m. The Championship game is scheduled for Saturday, December 11 at 2:30 p.m. with a 3rd place game at 1:00 p.m. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team won its second championship in three years at the Bryan Ayer Classic in Lompoc in central California. Piedmont wins Bryan Ayer Classic in Lompoc By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont girls’ basketball team started its season in a big way. Playing 300 miles from home in Lompoc, they won the annual Bryan Ayer Classic for the second time in three years. On Thursday, December 2, they rolled over Santa Barbara, 57-34; trounced host Lompoc on Friday 74-40, and won the finals 62-34 over Orcutt Academy. It marked the 14th annual tournament following last spring’s pandemic shortened season. In 2019, PHS lost to Santa Barbara in the championship 64-54. Sophomore Natalia Martinez was named MVP of the tournament, and juniors Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill were named to the All-Tournament team. “I am proud of our whole team. We aren’t close to the final product, but definitely off to solid start,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We can build from this weekend. Trinity [Zamora], Natalia [Martinez], Maddie [Hill] and Hannah [Govert] led the way. Kat Melian truly stepped up in her first action on varsity. I’m so proud of her,” Finals vs. Orcutt Academy Piedmont led 18-7 at the end of the first quarter and ballooned to 39-17 by halftime. It was after three quarters before finishing with a 62-34 victory for the championship. In the first quarter, Piedmont made five three-pointers, two each by Zamora and Hill, and one by Hannah Govert. Martinez exploded for 13 of her 27 points Natalia Martinez was named the tournament’s Most Outstanding Player. I the second quarter, including 4 for 5 at the free throw line. Martinez added 10 more points in the third quarter including 4 of 4 at the line. Hill had a 3-pointer, and Shay Ottaviano scored her first varsity field goal. Final stats include Martinez with 27 points, six rebounds, two assists, and five steals. Zamora scored 16 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals, and two blocks. Hill came away with 12 points, two rebounds, three assists, and two steals. Govert scored three points, seven rebounds, four assists, and two blocks. Melian had five rebounds, two steals. Ottaviano scored four points, two rebounds, one steal. Semifinals vs. Lompoc In the semis, Piedmont defeated Lompoc 74-40 after going into the half with a 32-20 lead. They finished the night with 18 steals and poured in 10 three-pointers in the second half. Freshman Shakila Zuberi scored three points in her varsity debut. Final stats include Zamora with 25 points, 12 rebounds, five assists, three steals, and two blocks. Martinez had 28 points, seven boards, nine assists, and six steals. Hill scored 13 points, two rebounds, three assists, and five steals. Govert scored three points, three boards. Melian had two points and four rebounds. Zuberi had three, and two rebounds. Game #1 vs. Santa Barbara Facing last year’s tournament champ in the opening game, Piedmont began the fourth quarter with a slim 5-point lead, 37-32. But it outscored Santa Barbara 20-5 in the final period to win comfortably, 57-34. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team hosted its Holiday Tournament from Thursday through Saturday, December 2-4. It marked the return of Piedmont’s early-December tourney, formerly sponsored by the Otis Spunkmeyer Cookie company, to help welcome the start of the season. The tradition started more than 15 years ago by former coach Chris Lavdiotis. “Hosting a tournament means so many things on many different levels,” noted coach Ben Spencer. “We’re getting back to normal, it means our athletic department can build funding again, and most importantly, our kids can compete at a high level against some of the best teams in the Bay Area. The Piedmont Holiday Tournament (formerly the Otis Spunkmeyer Invitational) has been a great tradition for our program. It means that the basketball season is officially here,” The Highlanders lost in the finals against Northgate 56-42 on Saturday. PHS defeated Freedom 56-47 in the semifinals on Friday after opening with a 67-40 win over Terra Linda on Thursday. Piedmont was moved up from Div. 4 to Div. 3 (larger enrollment schools in North Coast Section) after last year’s highly successful season. None of the games came against divisional opponents; Northgate is Div. 2, Freedom is Div. 1, and Terra Linda remained a Div. 4 team. The Highlanders defeated Northgate 88-82 in the spring of 2021, so the Broncos were back looking for a little payback. “I thought Northgate came ready to play knowing that we beat them last year. They came out with a lot of energy and did well defending our two key players. Our defense is a bit ahead of our offense, which will pay larger dividends later in the season,” said assistant coach Shamaree Worley. “We have to keep working on the offense and getting more people to contribute as scorers to take the load off of A.J. and JoJo.” A.J. Harris led the way in the finals with 16 points against Northgate. He had 19 points against Freedom, and 21 against Terra Linda. JoJo Murphy opened with 24 points against Terra Linda, followed by 20 points against Freedom. He tweaked his ankle toward the end of the semifinals and played through pain to score eight points I the finals. The PHS student section showed up in numbers for the PHS Holiday Tournament. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team hosted its Holiday Tournament, falling in the finals to Northgate 56-42. Finals vs. Northgate Northgate opened with a 17-8 lead, and Piedmont trailed 30-24 at the half. PHS struggled in the third with just three points, falling behind 42-27 by the start of the fourth, closing out 56-42. The Broncos started strong by building a 13-3 lead before Bautista Costa knocked down a 3-pointer, following by Harris scoring to narrow the deficit as Murphy sat on the bench. Murphy entered in the second period and made a visible impact as space on the floor opened. Harris had eight points in the quarter with two 3-pointers, while Murphy had four. Harris opened the second half with a 3-pointer after a steal, but that was all Piedmont would be able to do. Northgate’s defenders made three blocks and had a pair of steals during a 17-0 scoring run stretching into the fourth quarter. PHS did well to put up 15 points and narrow the deficit to 49-36 in the final period. Murphy had four and Harris had three in the fourth quarter. Final stats: Harris with 16 points, Murphy had eight, Spencer Settlemier had six points, Raydan Holmes had five. Semifinals vs. Freedom Piedmont opened with a 15-7 lead in the first quarter and went up 31-16 by halftime. The Highlanders went into the fourth with a 47-33 lead and closed out strong 56-47. Murphy opened strong in the first quarter with seven points including a 3-pointer. Another strong defensive quarter in the second helped PHS keep a 15-point advantage by halftime. Murphy put in six points and Harris scored seven points, Coach Ben Spencer sends in guard Matthew Riordan. A.J. Harris scored 16 points against Northgate, 19 points against Freedom, and 21 against Terra Linda. JoJo Murphy had 24 points in the opening game vs. Terra Linda, and had 20 against Freedom He scored eight points in the finals while playing on a nagging ankle.

articles.text: Photo by Stephanie Shrieve Piedmont High School students represent more than half of the 13-member roster of the Red Rock Alameda 16s Boys Club Volleyball Team: team captain Wilson Wong (2nd from left; Owen Kelly, John Champion, Brayden Day (libero), Shunji Higashi, Ryan Stokes, and Danny Allen. The team is coached by PHS varsity coach Leslie Blakeley (2nd from right). Seeded No. 40, the Red Rock Alameda 16s Boys Club Volleyball Team finished the Northern California Volleyball Association (NCVA) qualifier tournament in Roseville as the No. 15 team. Seven players on the roster are from Piedmont High, and the team is coached by PHS varsity coach Leslie Blakely. Piedmont players include juniors Brayden Day (libero), Owen Kelly (opposite hitter), Ryan Stokes (middle hitter/ blocker), and Wilson Wong (team captain & outside hitter). The team also includes sophomores Danny Allen (libero and defensive specialist), John Champion (opposite hitter), and Shunji Higashi (setter). In the first round Red Rock upset the No. 10 seeded team, Absolute Volleyball Club’s 16 Blue team. They moved up in ranking to No. 21 after second round game in Roseville, and then moved up to No. 17 following a win in Ripon. Their ranking went to No. 16 following a win at Santa Clara. The squad, seeded No. 15, now prepares for the Regional Championship Tournament in Roseville on December 11-12. Red Rock Volleyball Club has five locations throughout the Bay Area, including indoor courts at the Bladium in Alameda. They offer clinics and camps for boys and girls from grades 2-12. Red Rock also offers a year-round beach volleyball program, including beach courts at Alameda Beach and Moraga Commons. For more information about Red Rock Volleyball Club, visit https://www.redrockalameda.com/

pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Big-wave watching along the coast – wintertime at its best By Jonathan Comeaux Winter has arrived and King tides are higher than average along the Northern California shore. Although visitors to the coast should be wary of their surroundings this time of year, swells typically are roaring in December, January and February; attracting big-wave lovers from all over the world to gaze at the Pacific Ocean’s moving-mountains of water. Wave forecasts are for 10+ foot swells from Sunday to Wednesday, December 11-15. Here are four locations the Post previously visited. Be sure to check for any sudden closures the day of your hike given the nature of big waves. Tomales Point Taking the 9.7-mile out-andback Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay. It overlooks remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific Coast to your left with Tomales Bay and the town of Dillon Beach to your right. The hike starts at Pierce Point Ranch, a historic farmstead in Pt. Reyes that has informative markStaff Photos Tomales Point of Marin County has 10-foot waves forecasted between tomorrow and December 14. Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Preserve. Tule Elk are considered the smallest subspecies of elk. Muir Beach is expecting 8-11-foot waves from December 9-15. A four-mile walk between Muir Beach and Tennessee Valley Beach along the Coastal Fire Road provides great wave-viewing. ers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The near five-mile walk to Tomales Point is next to the Tule Elk Reserve, where herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves are roaming. The ending is a bluff overlooking tide pools and an array of birds: pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while red-tailed hawks and turkey vultures are often spotted looking for food as well. According to wave forecasts, this area will have 10+ foot swells on Thursday, December 9. Waves will taper down to six-feet on Friday and Saturday but explode to 15-foot swells on Sunday and Monday, December 11-12. December 13-14 is still likely to have waves over 10 feet. Muir Beach Muir Beach is among the most popular destinations for Bay Area residents. Starting an 8-mile day of hiking at Tennessee Valley Beach in Marin County and venturing to Muir Beach on the Coastal Fire Trail provides a strenuous but awe-striking view of the Pacific Ocean all the way. The hike along the coast requires some sharp ascending and descending, as the Coastal Trail has well over 1,000 feet in elevation gain each way. Wave reports indicate that Thursday, December 9 will produce swells of 8 feet and will increase to 10-feet by Sunday morning and 12-14 foot waves on Monday. Swells are expected to range from 11 feet on the early morning of Tuesday, December 14, and 11-feet again the morning of December 15. On this popular trail you’re likely to pass over 150 hikers on a weekend days. Rodeo Beach Rodeo Beach just north of San Francisco is an ideal location for urban exploring through former military bunkers. The beach is a starting point to venture around the Marin Headlands. A popular overlook location is Hill 88, a former radar control station. Rodeo Beach is a popular area for beginning surfers due to its quick breaks and typical smallscale waves. However, King tides will likely produce waves of 6-7 feet on Thursday and Friday, December 9-10 Saturday, December 11 will produce some 7-9 foot waves in the late afternoon before the monsters arise on Monday through Wednesday, December 13-15. Forecasts expect 10-13 foot waves on Dec. 13, more 13-15 foot swells on Dec. 14, while Dec. 15 anticipates 10-11’ waves. Thursday, Dec. 16 still had 7-9 foot waves forecasted. Half Moon Bay & California Coastal Trail The capital of surfing in the U.S. is Half Moon Bay’s Pillar Point with its annual Mavericks competition happening anytime typically between mid-December and February. With the anticipated King tides this week, 15-foot swells are expected from Mavericks all the way south to Pescadero, it will peak at 19 feet on Monday and Tuesday, December 13-14. Even Surfers Beach along the Half Moon Bay Jetty ­ – often considered a location for beginners will have 13-foot waves on December 13-14. With high wave activity this weekend, the best location for safe wave-viewing will be the California Coastal Rodeo Beach north of San Francisco has 10-15 foot swells expected the next 3-4 days. Hill 88, a former military radar station overlooking the Pacific Ocean, has a million-dollar view of the Golden Gate Bridge. The California Coastal Trail overlooks stretches of shoreline from a bluff, safely above the big waves crashing below. A photo of Half Moon Bay’s Poplar Beach at sunset. Trail between El Grenada and Eel Rock. Starting at Surfers Beach, the California Coastal Trail travels 4.5 miles along a bluff overlooking stretches of shoreline towards Poplar Beach, where 7’ swells on Sunday, December 12, will increases to 12-14 feet by December 13-14.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet The Nutcracker returns to Paramount Theatre December 18-19. Oakland Ballet will present its production of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker, the weekend of December 18-19. Oakland Ballet dancers bring Lustig’s classic holiday ensemble to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will deliver Tchaikovsky’s magnificent musical score. Performances are at the Paramount Theatre at 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Friday, December 18, and at 1 p.m. on Sunday, December 19. The performance is approximately two hours including intermission. Doors open one hour before the performances. An encore reception will take place following performances, where guests will have an opportunity to meet and mingle with dancers and Lustig while enjoying champagne and holiday treats. Purchase tickets for these performances by visiting https:// oaklandballet.org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker/.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet to perform The Nutcracker Dec. 18-19

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will present its production of the popular Tchaikovsky ballet, Nutcracker, this Friday, December 10, with performances scheduled through December 30. SF Ballet performs the ballet every year with more than 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco. San Francisco Symphony will perform Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older, no children under the age of three will be permitted. To attend a performance or event at the War Memorial Opera House you must present proof of full vaccination status, alongside a matching photo ID. Masks are required for all. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/nutcracker/ to view production times and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Christmas Revels will present its 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland from December 11-19. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. Children are welcome at all performances if fully-vaccinated against COVID-19. Group discounts are available at www.CaliforniaRevels.org or by calling the box office at 510- 452-9334.

By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Ballet will present its production of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker, the weekend of December 18-19. Oakland Ballet dancers bring Lustig’s classic holiday ensemble to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will deliver Tchaikovsky’s magnificent musical score. Performances are at the Paramount Theatre at 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Friday, December 18, and at 1 p.m. on Sunday, December 19. The performance is approximately two hours including intermission. Doors open one hour before the performances. An encore reception will take place following performances, where guests will have an opportunity to meet and mingle with dancers and Lustig while enjoying champagne and holiday treats. Purchase tickets for these performances by visiting https:// oaklandballet.org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker/. San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker opens this Friday, December 10. San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker opens on Friday By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet will present its production of the popular Tchaikovsky ballet, Nutcracker, this Friday, December 10, with performances scheduled through December 30. SF Ballet performs the ballet every year with more than 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco. San Francisco Symphony will perform Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older, no children under the age of three will be permitted. To attend a performance or event at the War Memorial Opera House you must present proof of full vaccination status, alongside a matching photo ID. Masks are required for all. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/nutcracker/ to view production times and to purchase tickets. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Christmas Revels performances in Oakland December 11-19 Christmas Revels will present its 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland from December 11-19. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. Children are welcome at all performances if fully-vaccinated against COVID-19. Group discounts are available at www.CaliforniaRevels.org or by calling the box office at 510- 452-9334. articles.text: Thanksgiving is a distant memory. Black Friday signals the race toward Christmas. Can it be coincidence that I am reminded of the mantra of the Indianapolis 500… “Start your engines.“ It is good to ask ourselves tough questions which can also be inspirational. For example… What does it take to be a concert performer? The nerves of a bull fighter, the grace of a ballerina. The enterprise of a politician, and the endurance of a marathon runner. It also helps to have the intelligence of Socrates, the artistic concept of Picasso, and don’t forget a little bit of the heart. Be sure to study nature in all of its variety. Try to play passages of music differently every time and still be musically correct in every way. Never pander to the audience. Be sincere and forthright. Always retain your dignity both personally and artistically. While you do this you must, at the same time, be flexible. All of these things were made crystal clear on Sunday when I was a judge at the Northern California Young Talents music competition in Livermore. Rimma Radayeva is the driving force. Her organization of the festival ran like clockwork. There was not one glitch for five straight hours. All of the students and their families live the inspiration of the American dream. Their diligence and hard work is exemplary. It was not that everyone played perfectly. What was important is that they played with diligence and inspiration. Holiday music was not neglected either this weekend. There was a beautifully staged production of “Scrooge…The Musical“ at the Mormon Temple Hill auditorium. This was a fully-staged production with a full symphony orchestra and impressive sets. The orchestra was conducted crisply by Matt Mackey, resulting in the orchestra playing in inspired fashion. I kept watching Mackey and I asked myself “who is this guy?” He is a really good conductor. I found out that he is the Band Director at Elk Grove High School outside Sacramento. Those kids are sure lucky. The rest of the production was first class. It is interesting to note that everyone on stage and behind stage is an amateur, but you’d never know it. Everything was of professional quality. The audience rose as one at the end to applaud – a standing ovation that was well deserved. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg… If you know where to look. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints’ Oakland California Temple is located in the Oakland Hills at 4766 Lincoln Avenue. A scene from the colorful production of “Scrooge - the musical” at the Mormon Temple Hill auditorium.
articles.title: The pleasure of their company

articles.text: Musicians Steve Oda (sarode), Michael Lewis (table), and Pushpa Oda (tanpura). Musicians Steve Oda, Michael Lewis and Pushpa Oda will perform a selection of North Indian classical music this Saturday, December 11, at Piedmont Center for the Arts beginning at 7 p.m. The music will be followed by a dance performance by Kali Futnani, a senior teacher at Bharata Kalanjali in Berkeley. Futnani began her dance training at Kalanjali in Berkeley, which was founded by K.P and Katherine Kunhiraman. She has a BFA from Kalakshetra College of Fine Arts in Chennai, India. Kali continued her training under K.P. Yesodha in Chennai for six years, performing with the company throughout India before returning to the Bay Area. Bharatanatyam is a South Indian classical dance style that was performed in the temples of Tamil Nadu for thousands of years before coming to the stage. Bharatanatyam has both rhythmic and dramatic aspects. The theory of rasa, the nature of the aesthetics as transcendental and emotional experience, is central to all Indian arts. Through movement set to rhythmic patterns and storytelling through hand gestures and expression, the audience and the performer have a shared experience through art. Tickets are $20 at the door, and $10 for students with high school or college identification. All events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require proof of vaccination and proper masking while indoors.
articles.title: Indian classical music and dance at PCA on Sat. night

articles.text: The In the Tradition piano trio will perform at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, December 19, showcasing the center’s Steinway Grand Piano. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a benefit for the Center, entitled Music for the Holidays, and will include a collection of jazz, Latin, swing, and ballads. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B - eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for The In the Tradition Piano Trio: Anthony Pegram (drums), Bill Jackman (piano), and Rich Trevor (bass). jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 2 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door, or can be purchased in advance at https://bpt.me/5316993. Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required.
articles.title: In the Tradition Piano Trio at PCA December 19
