articles.text: Four East Bay artists will present an exhibition entitled A Boundless Moment at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday and Sunday, December 11-12. Gallery hours are from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. The exhibition will showcase the works of Carl Heyward, Akiko Suzuki, Usha Shukla, and Colleen Gianatiempo. Heyward is a NEA (National Endowment for the Arts) grant recipient and a former Masters of Fine Arts instructor at the San Francisco Academy of Art University. His work has been featured at various art galleries in the Bay Area and internationally. “Yarrow 03” oil on canvas, 36x36” by Usha Shukla Artist Usha Shukla Suzuki is a textile and mixed media artist based in San Francisco. Since 2014, she has participated in the Global Art Project with partner Heyward. “My work expresses the invisible nature of thought, of skin sensation, the poetry of Love and Eros or the presentiments that occur prior to thought. Intuitive works are born from everyday life as are novels,” Suzuki said. “The words borne out of the flood of my imagery become poetry and are visualized in works as abstractions through paint, collage, sewing and fiber works.” Shukla was born and raised in New Delhi, India; the vibrant colors of the Indian countryside greatly influence her artwork. She completed a graduate program at the Academy of Art University, San Francisco, with a focus on painting. She paints primarily large abstracts in vivid colors and has a unique process of “mark-making.” Gianatiempo is a mixed media artist, educator, and designer living in the East Bay. “My journey as an artist began when I was 3 years old. I remember cutting up family photos and drawing on walls with lipstick. I learned early on that it’s possible to express the world around me in different ways and this is where my passion began,” Gianatiempo said. “Nature is my main influence as I always marvel about the design and beauty it beholds,” she said. “I work in many mediums and thrive most when I can experiment and discover new techniques. I have been told that I am the Mary Poppins of art supplies! Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required at all Piedmont Center for the Arts events. “Silent Majority” blue textile 63x56” by Akiko Suzuki

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony music series opens Dec. 12 in Piedmont Composer Jessie Montgomery The long-standing chamber music series with Berkeley Symphony musicians and friends continues this Sunday, December 12, with a concert at the Piedmont Center of the Arts at 4 p.m. Four extraordinary Berkeley Symphony string players will assemble for a dynamic exploration of classic and contemporary chamber music with a thrillingly improvisatory feel, culminating with Debussy’s iconic impressionist masterpiece. Violi nists Nigel A r mstrong and Emanuela Nikiforova will be joined by violist Ivo Bokulic and cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak in a performance of Jessie Montgomery’s Voodoo Dolls for String Quartet, Brian Nabors’ Theme and Variations for solo violin, Winter from Four Seasons by Antonio Vivaldi, and Claude Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org, by calling Berkeley Symphony’s box office at 510-841-2800, ext. 1, or at the door. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Proof of vaccination and photo ID is required. Nigel Armstrong, violin Nigel Armstrong is a dynamic and creative artist both within and beyond the realm of classical music. From his musical beginnings as a member of “The Little Fiddlers” in Sonoma, to collaborations with tango musicians in Argentina, he has enjoyed using the violin in a versatile manner throughout his life. As soloist Nigel has performed with orchestras such as the Dusseldorf Symphony, the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, the St. Petersburg Philharmonic, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the Boston Pops, and with conductors including Sir Neville Marriner and Carlos Miguel Prieto. He received the 2nd Prize, the Ole Bull Prize, and the Nordheim Award at the 2010 Menuhin Competition Senior Division in Oslo, Norway, and got the 4th Prize plus the Prize for the Best Performance of the Commissioned Work (STOMP, by John Corigliano) at the XIV International Tchaikovsky Competition. As a chamber musician his concerts have taken him across the US and abroad--highlights have included opportunities to share the stage with the Tokyo String Quartet and pianist Jonathan Biss. Since 2009 he has appeared as concertmaster with the Colburn Orchestra, LA’s American Youth Symphony, the Curtis Symphony Orchestra, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the New York String Orchestra in their annual Carnegie hall performances. Beginning in the 2016/17 season he serves as concertmaster of the Santa Cruz Symphony. A graduate of the Colburn School and the Curtis Institute of Music. He also recently had the opportunity to live with and learn from the Plum Village community founded by Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh, where he spent a year. Emanuela Nikiforova, violin A native of Bulgaria, Emanuela Nikiforova benefited from the influence of the Russian violin school at Varna and Sofia middle and high music schools, and the influence of Yfrah Neaman and Neaman’s esteemed student, Professor Kevork Mardirossian (Louisiana State University School of Music). She is also influenced by Yehudi Menuhin and Argentinian Alberto Lysy at the International Menuhin Music Academy in Gstaad, Switzerland. And by Camilla Wicks at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Nikiforova has performed on three different continents from a young age as a soloist, chamber and orchestra musician. She is a former member of Camerata Lysy, Camerata Bariloche, Philharmonica de Buenos Aires, Sarasota Orchestra and Baton Rouge Symphony, and a current member of the Santa Rosa, Marin, Berkeley, Oakland and Silicon Valley symphonies, a substitute at the San Francisco Ballet, Opera San Jose, California and Napa symphonies and others. Nigel-Armstrong Ivo Bokulic Ivo Bokulic, viola Born in Croatia, raised in Chicago, and based in San Francisco, Ivo Bokulic is Associate Principal Violist of the San José Chamber Orchestra and also holds positions with Opera San José & Berkeley Symphony. An active freelance musician in the Bay Area and beyond, Ivo performs with groups such as the New Century Chamber Orchestra, Utah Festival Opera, Santa Rosa Symphony, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, California Symphony, Reno Philharmonic, Marin Symphony, Oakland Symphony, Fresno Philharmonic, Modesto Symphony Orchestra, Santa Cruz Symphony, and One Found Sound. As a member of Isaac Pastor-Chermak San Francisco’s Magik*Magik Orchestra, Ivo has toured, recorded, and performed with acts such as Death Cab for Cutie, Sting, Father John Misty, Gregory Porter, and Third Eye Blind. He holds both Bachelor and Master of Music degrees from the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, where he studied with Jodi Levitz. He plays a viola made in 1999 by Hiroshi Iizuka. Isaac Pastor-Chermak, cello Isaac Pastor-Chermak leads an active musical life as a cellist, teacher, conductor, and administrator. A career orchestral player, on any given weekend he can be found performing as Principal Cellist of the Waterloo-Cedar Falls Symphony; Associate Principal Cellist of the Stockton Symphony; Assistant Principal Cellist of Opera San Jose and Fresno Philharmonic; and a member of the Berkeley Symphony, Monterey Symphony, Santa Cruz Symphony, Santa Barbara Symphony, and Dayton Philharmonic. He fills his summers with teaching and chamber music projects. In addition, he is Assistant Principal Cellist at the Eisenstadt Classical Music Festival in Austria, and Co-Principal Cellist of the Lake Tahoe Music Festival. In past seasons, he has enjoyed time as Principal Cellist of Portland Opera, as well as membership in the West Virginia Symphony and Walla Walla Symphony. He maintains a wide range of chamber music commitments with favorite colleagues. He is the cellist of Black Cedar Trio, the only flute-cello-guitar ensemble in the United States. He frequently partners with pianists Miles Graber and Alison Lee in sonata programs. As a recording artist he regularly appears in both live and studio recordings. “Backlash Bach,” a CD featuring Bach’s Sonatas BWV 1027-1029, was released in 2020. “The Shadow Dancer,” featuring Elliott Miles McKinley’s String Quartet No.8, was released in 2019. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 21 Composer Jessie Montgomery 9th annual Chamber Music concerts begin Sunday Berkeley Symphony music series opens Dec. 12 in Piedmont The long-standing chamber music series with Berkeley Symphony musicians and friends continues this Sunday, December 12, with a concert at the Piedmont Center of the Arts at 4 p.m. Four extraordinary Berkeley Symphony string players will assemble for a dynamic exploration of classic and contemporary chamber music with a thrillingly improvisatory feel, culminating with Debussy’s iconic impressionist masterpiece. Violi nists Nigel A r mstrong and Emanuela Nikiforova will be joined by violist Ivo Bokulic and cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak in a performance of Jessie Montgomery’s Voodoo Dolls for String Quartet, Brian Nabors’ Theme and Variations for solo violin, Winter from Four Seasons by Antonio Vivaldi, and Claude Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org, by calling Berkeley Symphony’s box office at 510-841-2800, ext. 1, or at the door. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Proof of vaccination and photo ID is required. Nigel Armstrong, violin Nigel Armstrong is a dynamic and creative artist both within and beyond the realm of classical music. From his musical beginnings as a member of “The Little Fiddlers” in Sonoma, to collaborations with tango musicians in Argentina, he has enjoyed using the violin in a versatile manner throughout his life. As soloist Nigel has performed with orchestras such as the Dusseldorf Symphony, the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, the St. Petersburg Philharmonic, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the Boston Pops, and with conductors including Sir Neville Marriner and Carlos Miguel Prieto. He received the 2nd Prize, the Ole Bull Prize, and the Nordheim Award at the 2010 Menuhin Competition Senior Division in Oslo, Norway, and got the 4th Prize plus the Prize for the Best Performance of the Commissioned Work (STOMP, by John Corigliano) at the XIV International Tchaikovsky Competition. As a chamber musician his concerts have taken him across the US and abroad--highlights have included opportunities to share the stage with the Tokyo String Quartet and pianist Jonathan Biss. Since 2009 he has appeared as concertmaster with the Colburn Orchestra, LA’s American Youth Symphony, the Curtis Symphony Orchestra, YOA Orchestra of the Americas, and the New York String Orchestra in their annual Carnegie hall performances. Beginning in the 2016/17 season he serves as concertmaster of the Santa Cruz Symphony. A graduate of the Colburn School and the Curtis Institute of Music. He also recently had the opportunity to live with and learn from the Plum Village community founded by Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh, where he spent a year. Emanuela Nikiforova, violin A native of Bulgaria, Emanuela Nikiforova benefited from the influence of the Russian violin school at Varna and Sofia middle and high music schools, and the influence of Yfrah Neaman and Neaman’s esteemed student, Professor Kevork Mardirossian (Louisiana State University School of Music). She is also influenced by Yehudi Menuhin and Argentinian Alberto Lysy at the International Menuhin Music Academy in Gstaad, Switzerland. And by Camilla Wicks at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Nikiforova has performed on three different continents from a young age as a soloist, chamber and orchestra musician. She is a former member of Camerata Lysy, Camerata Bariloche, Philharmonica de Buenos Aires, Sarasota Orchestra and Baton Rouge Symphony, and a current member of the Santa Rosa, Marin, Berkeley, Oakland and Silicon Valley symphonies, a substitute at the San Francisco Ballet, Opera San Jose, California and Napa symphonies and others. Nigel-Armstrong Ivo Bokulic Ivo Bokulic, viola Born in Croatia, raised in Chicago, and based in San Francisco, Ivo Bokulic is Associate Principal Violist of the San José Chamber Orchestra and also holds positions with Opera San José & Berkeley Symphony. An active freelance musician in the Bay Area and beyond, Ivo performs with groups such as the New Century Chamber Orchestra, Utah Festival Opera, Santa Rosa Symphony, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, California Symphony, Reno Philharmonic, Marin Symphony, Oakland Symphony, Fresno Philharmonic, Modesto Symphony Orchestra, Santa Cruz Symphony, and One Found Sound. As a member of Isaac Pastor-Chermak San Francisco’s Magik*Magik Orchestra, Ivo has toured, recorded, and performed with acts such as Death Cab for Cutie, Sting, Father John Misty, Gregory Porter, and Third Eye Blind. He holds both Bachelor and Master of Music degrees from the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, where he studied with Jodi Levitz. He plays a viola made in 1999 by Hiroshi Iizuka. Isaac Pastor-Chermak, cello Isaac Pastor-Chermak leads an active musical life as a cellist, teacher, conductor, and administrator. A career orchestral player, on any given weekend he can be found performing as Principal Cellist of the Waterloo-Cedar Falls Symphony; Associate Principal Cellist of the Stockton Symphony; Assistant Principal Cellist of Opera San Jose and Fresno Philharmonic; and a member of the Berkeley Symphony, Monterey Symphony, Santa Cruz Symphony, Santa Barbara Symphony, and Dayton Philharmonic. He fills his summers with teaching and chamber music projects. In addition, he is Assistant Principal Cellist at the Eisenstadt Classical Music Festival in Austria, and Co-Principal Cellist of the Lake Tahoe Music Festival. In past seasons, he has enjoyed time as Principal Cellist of Portland Opera, as well as membership in the West Virginia Symphony and Walla Walla Symphony. He maintains a wide range of chamber music commitments with favorite colleagues. He is the cellist of Black Cedar Trio, the only flute-cello-guitar ensemble in the United States. He frequently partners with pianists Miles Graber and Alison Lee in sonata programs. As a recording artist he regularly appears in both live and studio recordings. “Backlash Bach,” a CD featuring Bach’s Sonatas BWV 1027-1029, was released in 2020. “The Shadow Dancer,” featuring Elliott Miles McKinley’s String Quartet No.8, was released in 2019. Preludes and Prologues, his debut CD with pianist Alison Lee, was released this year in January. articles.text: Wrath Winery in Soledad, California. One hopeful sign that some of the necessary social isolation that the pandemic required is the return of live in-person wine tasting events. The first one I attended was sponsored by the Family Winemakers of California in August. The second was last month and was held by Wrath Winery in Soledad, between Salinas and King City in Central California. For the past several years Wrath has been putting on their version of “La Paulee” the traditional party held in Burgundy to mark the end of the harvest each year. In Burgundy this is a big deal. The vintners join in for a three-day Bacchanal, the highlight of which is a huge dinner held at Clos Vougeot chateau with up to a thousand attendees. The vintners bring loads of their wine to be shared with others. In addition to eating and drinking, there is singing and speeches and the whole thing lasts into the wee hours. The Gendarmes (French Highway patrol) are given the night off. The Wrath La Paulee was a little tamer than that but loads of fun. On a beautiful October Saturday afternoon. the winery set up tables and umbrellas adjacent to the San Saba vineyards on the Wrath estate. They invited about a hundred of their neighbors, growers, workers and wine club members to attend. They served their delightful Chardonnay and many, many, many bottles of Pinot Noir from not only Wrath but neighboring wineries Tondre, Boekennoogen and McIntyre. The food was delicious. and everyone was in good spirits. At a later date I was able to retaste the Wrath wines and take proper tasting notes. I have to say the Santa Lucia Highlands region is quickly becoming one of the premier locations to grow Pinot Noir. The wines below show great depth and complexity and are certainly worth searching out. • 2019 Wrath Pinot Noir San Saba Vineyard, $49 This beautiful vineyard is the one that surrounds the winery buildings in a sheltered nook that Wrath Winery focuses on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. articles.text: Glowfari returns to Oakland Zoo for second year of magical illumination. Tickets for Glowfari, the popular holiday illumination of Oakland Zoo, are available now through January 20. Advance ticketing is required. Glowfari features hundreds of life-size glowing animal lanterns throughout the Zoo and will display all-new light fixtures for the event’s return this year. It takes the place of last year’s Zoolights, and features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates. The event is appropriate for all ages and invites attendees to take a mile-long illuminated stroll through the campus and ride the gondola to see the remarkable, 65-foot “Queen Ant Tunnel.” Finish the evening with a visit to Santa and ride the express train through the zoo’s winter wonderland. Glowfari is available to visit from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. except on Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. In January, the event will be available Wednesday through Sunday.
articles.title: Glowfari lights up Oakland Zoo during holidays

By Pierre DuMont One hopeful sign that some of the necessary social isolation that the pandemic required is the return of live in-person wine tasting events. The first one I attended was sponsored by the Family Winemakers of California in August. The vintners bring loads of their wine to be shared with others. In addition to eating and drinking, there is singing and speeches and the whole thing lasts into the wee hours. The Gendarmes (French Highway patrol) are given the night off. The Wrath La Paulee was a little tamer than that but loads of fun. On a beautiful October Saturday afternoon. the winery set up tables and umbrellas adjacent to the San Saba vineyards on the Wrath estate. They invited about a hundred of their neighbors, growers, workers and wine club members to attend. They served their delightful Chardonnay and many, many, many bottles of Pinot Noir from not only Wrath but neighboring wineries Tondre, Boekennoogen and McIntyre. The food was delicious. and everyone was in good spirits. At a later date I was able to retaste the Wrath wines and take proper tasting notes. I have to say the Santa Lucia Highlands region is quickly becoming one of the premier locations to grow Pinot Noir. The wines below show great depth and complexity and are certainly worth searching out. • 2019 Wrath Pinot Noir San Saba Vineyard, $49 This beautiful vineyard is the one that surrounds the winery buildings in a sheltered nook that Wrath Winery focuses on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. is a cool, dry site. In addition to Pinot Noir, San Saba also produces, Chardonnay, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Fahlenghina. The wine opens savory with earth, smoked meat, and dried herbs over a core of lush black berry fruit. Medium-bodied, it explodes in the mouth, offering bursts of juicy, perfumed fruits, very finely grained, and finishing long and layered. Very impressive. • 2019 Wrath EX Pinot Noir, $27 The holy grail of today’s wine lover is a well-made, delicious Pinot Noir that does not cost an arm and a leg. Holy grails are hard to find, so this (relatively) inexpensive bottling is a good candidate to fit the bill. Wrath has cut back on the oak and let the fresh cherry juiciness of Pinot fruit come to the forefront. It is light and gentle on the palate with a clean, supple finish. • 2019 Wrath Pinot Noir Tondre Grapefield, $49 Wrath purchases these grapes from the Tondre Family – close neighbors just to the west. The wine delivers expressive spice notes of clove, cinnamon and anise over a red currant and cherry core. It is big, dense, and well-structured, packing a great intensity of fruit, finishing with lingering mineral notes. This big boy is delicious now but will improve with a few years in the cellar. • 2019 Wrath Pinot Noir McIntyre Vineyard, $49 Very prettily perfumed on the mineral-driven nose, offering up cherry, strawberry and violet accents. Light to medium bodied, it’s very intensely flavored showing exotic spices, minerals, and ripe fruit character, with fine grainy tannins and mouthwatering acidity leading to a long, satisfying finish. • 2019 Wrath Pinot Noir Swan/828, $35 The name of this wine comes not from the vineyard but from the clones used to produce it. The Swan clone was developed by pioneering Joseph Swan Winery in Sonoma County. Here it is paired with another clone 828 to make an intriguing Pinot Noir. It shows gorgeous depth and delineation in its flowers, spices and red berries. This is a beautifully detailed, nuanced Pinot loaded with class and sheer personality. A soft, caressing finish rounds things out in style. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside throughout the month to see the 16-acre estate in all its festive glory. The non-profit, registered landmark, will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. The impressive myriad of decorations that were installed last month enhances the estate’s historic and renowned elegance. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing over a dozen decorated trees inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of twinkling lights in all colors that don the gardens and drape the interior. Walking through the 16-acre estate, you will find 22 festooned Christmas trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreate the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in early to mid-1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as brightly in daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. You can cozy up by the fire pits in the Woodland The ballroom chandelier glistens from below. The ballroom features a pair of Baccarat crystal Louis XVI style fifty-light chandeliers. The dining room features elegant and festive meal settings. Garden Court with mulled wine or hot apple cider, day or night. A bonus with daytime admission is the opportunity to take a selfie with Santa Claus. He will pay a Attendees view one of the many festooned trees in the estate. visit to the historic mansion this weekend and next, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Evening admissions may be purchased for any day between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m., although evening tickets are selling fast. Daytime admission is available every day between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. Visit www.filoli.org to reserve tickets. Staff Photos Each tree at Filoli is uniquely decorated; no two are the same. Fairy light fixtures adorn all corners of the gardens. The outdoor stage is a perfect spot for a photo opportunity, or to cozy up with a warm cup of apple cider. Trees on the garden grounds are dressed in hues of purple and red.

articles.text: Piedmont Seniors at the Oakland Zoo: (front) Mona Jamieson (left), Margaret Brownell, Janet Epstein, Greg Jurin, Yorkman Lowe, and Madeline Mooore; back row: Jim Ayotte, Irene Westler, Susan McCreary, and Sandra Curach. Not pictured: Havaleh Kapellas. The Piedmont Seniors ventured out on their second excursion since the COVID-19 shutdown to visit the nearby Oakland Zoo. The zoo was established in 1922, and is currently home to over 850 native and exotic animals. The zoo is recognized for its outstanding animal care, particularly its elephant care program. There is also a children’s petting zoo and when you explore the grounds, you will see chimpanzees, squirrel monkeys, a variety of birds, camels, giraffes, and more. If you haven’t been there in quite a while you are in for a big surprise. In 2018 the zoo expanded to form the California Trail. The best part was traveling in an aerial gondola from the existing zoo. The gondola ride continues at a slow pace at the entrances and exits. The view at the top is spectacular and one can see miles of the East and West Bay Areas! Once the members arrived after a 4 minute enclosed ride, the group saw black bears, American bison, eagles, gray wolves, coyotes, and even mountain lions. There is a pleasant lunch spot at the top, where one can order tasty food at the Landing Café. Again, the scenery is spectacular and such a great spot to enjoy a relaxing meal. The zoo website is “high-tech”, and it is easy to order lunch from their website. You simply select your food and choose the time when you want to pick it up. Should you choose to remain on the lower level, you can also use their website to order food at the Tuskers Grill. There is a terrific train ride that is available that goes all around the perimeter of the zoo, which gives a nice overview of what visitors will be seeing. This train is situated just outside of the zoo entrance near the children’s rides. Separate tickets are needed for these attractions. There is a “not-to-be-missed” special attraction, Glowfari. which is currently taking place through January 30. You will see hundreds of larger than life glowing animal lanterns with all new displays for 2021. Last year the Zoolights exhibit was also very popular. The proceeds support the operating expenses of the zoo as well as funds needed to care for the ongoing support of the animals. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 25 Piedmont Seniors enchanted with Oakland Zoo Piedmont Seniors at the Oakland Zoo: (front) Mona Jamieson (left), Margaret Brownell, Janet Epstein, Greg Jurin, Yorkman Lowe, and Madeline Mooore; back row: Jim Ayotte, Irene Westler, Susan McCreary, and Sandra Curach. Not pictured: Havaleh Kapellas. By Janet Epstein The Piedmont Seniors ventured out on their second excursion since the COVID-19 shutdown to visit the nearby Oakland Zoo. The zoo was established in 1922, and is currently home to over 850 native and exotic animals. The zoo is recognized for its outstanding animal care, particularly its elephant care program. There is also a children’s petting zoo and when you explore the grounds, you will see chimpanzees, squirrel monkeys, a variety of birds, camels, giraffes, and more. If you haven’t been there in quite a while you are in for a big surprise. In 2018 the zoo expanded to form the California Trail. The best part was traveling in an aerial gondola from the existing zoo. The gondola ride continues at a slow pace at the entrances and exits. The view at the top is spectacular and one can see miles of the East and West Bay Areas! Once the members arrived after a 4 minute enclosed ride, the group saw black bears, American bison, eagles, gray wolves, coyotes, and even mountain lions. There is a pleasant lunch spot at the top, where one can order tasty food at the Landing Café. Again, the scenery is spectacular and such a great spot to enjoy a relaxing meal. The zoo website is “high-tech”, and it is easy to order lunch from their website. You simply select your food and choose the time when you want to pick it up. Should you choose to remain on the lower level, you can also use their website to order food at the Tuskers Grill. There is a terrific train ride that is available that goes all around the perimeter of the zoo, which gives a nice overview of what visitors will be seeing. This train is situated just outside of the zoo entrance near the children’s rides. Separate tickets are needed for these attractions. There is a “not-to-be-missed” special attraction, Glowfari. which is currently taking place through January 30. You will see hundreds of larger than life glowing animal lanterns with all new displays for 2021. Last year the Zoolights exhibit was also very popular. The proceeds support the operating expenses of the zoo as well as funds needed to care for the ongoing support of the animals. Even Santa will be there and you can ride the Express Train through the Winter Wonderland. This wintertime event is extremely popular and sells out! You need to purchase timed tickets for crowd control. pages.text: Wednesday, December 8, 2021 27 Photos by Sierra Nevada Photos Nearly 50 Scouts and parents from Troop 11 had a river rafting trip on the American River the weekend of September 18. Troop 11 Scouts enjoy rafting on American River By Elles Krieckhaus Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 went rafting on the South Fork of the American River the weekend of September 18 not far outside Sacramento. About 50 Scouts left early Saturday morning and drove in carpools. After learning about boating and water safety, we got on the water and went down the river smiling. The weather was warm and the water was great when we were able to get out of the rafts and swim. We stopped about halfway down the stretch of river and our guides provided a delicious lunch for us. After lunch, we got back in the rafts and entered a steeper part of the river canyon, where we went down some crazy rapids including Satan’s Cesspool, Hospital Bar, and Recovery Room. Everyone got wet but no one had to visit a real emergency room. After our adventure on the water, we unpacked the rafts and helped put them on trucks, then took a bus back to our campsite. Once back at camp we changed into dry clothes and set up our campsite. Some Scouts set up tents and others experimented with tarps to build shelters. Each Patrol cooked its own dinner, which included Sloppy Joes, tacos, and spaghetti. Campfires were not allowed due to the high fire danger, so we spent time learning knife and ax skills and playing cards by lantern light. As we went to bed, we observed the full moon had a bright ring around it and the clouds were moving in, a sign of rain. The Scouts sleeping in tents were happy they did when it started raining late that night. But those in the tarp shelters stayed mostly dry too, except for one of the parents. We got up early on Sunday, made breakfast in our patrols, packed up, and left. And I at least slept the rest of the day. Oars up! Troop 11 rafters tackle Satan’s Cesspool. articles.text: are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something that draws us toward a new and larger vision, maybe we should be thankful, not only for what we have now, but also for the opportunity to create and build something more inclusive, more peaceful, more beautiful, that might be described as one nation under God. Perhaps this understanding of what a real blessing is will help us not be discouraged by chaos, but rather, inspire us to pick up our shovels, hammers and levels and begin to build a better future for all. The Rev. Scott Denman is Rector of St. John’s Episcopal Church, 1707 Gouldin Road in the Montclair District of Oakland. For information, call 339- 2200. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, December 8, 2021 Scout Tree Lot Continued from page 1 Scout Drew Kobal helps to secure a tree on a customer’s car. This past weekend, December 4-5, the lot sold over 450 trees. “Our Scouting community has really stepped up to volunteer. We have had volunteers from all our troops, packs, and the Community Service Venturing Crew. Some very energetic Cub Scouts have been our best salespeople,” said Smegal. “The tree lot is one of the most visible events that Piedmont Scouting puts on throughout the year. It’s an important reason that Piedmont Scouting has such a high saturation level of youth, especially now having embraced girls. It’s one of the most successful and robust programs in the world, particularly in light of it being such a small council,” said Ashton with a smile. Deliveries via online ordering are still available at www.scouttreelot.org. Troop 1 Scouts Samantha Pell (left) and Madeleine Poon, help a customer look up an order on the system. Although Piedmont is small with a very limited number of public buildings, it is interesting to note that the tallest are given to education! Considering what we currently have against successful small city models, I think the town center could be improved in future development by the addition of the following: 1. A main plaza – not so big, but strategically located at ground zero in the city, functioning as the natural meeting place. 2. Some more commercial – small convenient venues that would increase activity and vitality. 3. Mixed use residential – just like commercial, increasing activity and vitality. 4. Enhanced urban design between different parts of center, including planting, hardscape, lighting and signage. 5. Subordination and reduction of cars. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through will@MakingDesignSense.com The Veterans’ Memorial Building and Police Station and the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse and Havens School both flank busy Mulberry’s with their own nicely designed secondary plazas. articles.text: How long would it take you to run three miles through Piedmont? For Walter Teitelbaum, a 21-year-old Piedmont High alum and cross-country runner, it only took 16 minutes. Teitelbaum was declared the overall winner of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, finishing ahead of more than 2,200 runners and nearly one minute faster than the 2nd and 3rd place runners. While waiting for the start of the Thanksgiving morning 8:30 a.m. 5-kilometer race, runners and onlookers were treated to a half dozen fanfares by seven symphony musicians playing bona fide Belgian and French hunting horns. It was an appropriate announcement of one of the city’s largest public events of the year. Runners stretched out on Highland Avenue in front of the Exedra in a line a half-block long. The route was the same as in previous years, winding its way along Highland, Wildwood, and La Salle Avenues, crawling up the incline on Sea View before dashing down Mountain Avenue and onto Craig and Vista to the finish line. In addition to competitive runners and recreational runners, there was an abundance of families with strollers, including multiple race winner Crosby Freeman, running with his wife Jessica while pushing a stroller with 10-week old Spencer Freeman. And there were plenty of people sipping cocoa and coffee while giving their dogs a little morning workout.
articles.title: Turkey Trot returns with 2200+ runners

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8, at 5 p.m. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) helped the city’s Public Works employees install holiday lights on the Community Center’s 80-foot redwood tree yesterday, morning November 30. With Public Works Supervisor Dana Low (left), Cathy Glazier, Terri Ashton, Sara Kimball, and Lisa Lomenzo carry a large string of lights Tuesday morning to be placed on the redwood tree above the Community Hall. Nick Millosovich and his crew installing lights on the tree from a cherry picker, PBF members completed their 57th year of decorating the tree one day before the annual Tree Lighting ceremony. The community is invited to attend the ceremony in front of the Community Hall tonight, December 1, at 7 p.m. Piedmont Garden Club members also provided help with the unraveling, testing and holding up the 1,500 lights yesterday morning at 9:00 a.m. The morning’s activity of carrying lights with friends, sharing stories and posing for pictures used to be a tedious two-day process before the lights were switched over to LED in 2013. With the glass incandescent bulbs PBF would plan on replacing 20% of them each year due to being burned out or broken. PBF

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Turkey Trot organizers thank all the runners, walkers, cheering families and friends, volunteers and sponsors for making the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot a success. Welcomed clear skies greeted the more than 2,000 runners and walkers in the race this year. It is a matter of great pride to see Piedmont bringing friends and families of multiple generations from all over the country to participate in this Thanksgiving Day community tradition. Coordinating a race of this size takes many hands and the organizers are incredibly grateful to have the support and unwavering commitment of the City of Piedmont, the Piedmont Public Works Department, the Piedmont Police Department, and the Piedmont Fire Department. The excellent work of a large and energetic group of volunteers working on Wednesday and on Race Day made everything seem effortless. Their spirit of service and dedication to the community and the Piedmont Turkey Trot is greatly appreciated. Many thanks to the sponsors: Transports, Village Market, Corcoran Global Living, Piedmont Grocery, MB Jessee Painting, J. articles.text: Firefighter/paramedic Todd Gerard will officially retire from the Piedmont Fire Department on Sunday, December 5 after 28 years of service. He joined the department in 1993 and brought with him years of experience as a trained paramedic. “Todd Gerard has been a steady, calm fixture in Piedmont for nearly three decades,” noted Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “His skills, experience, and easy-going nature will be sorely missed.” Gerard grew up in Huntington Beach in Southern California. He came north to attend American River College in Sacramento where he obtained his degree in Fire Science. “After I completed school, I realized I’m not a hot weather person, so I moved to the Bay Area to look for work,” he said. Gerard started working with a local ambulance company in 1987, becoming a field supervisor for Acme Western Ambulance Services in the East Bay until 1991. He received his paramedic training at Chabot College in Hayward, and then signed on as an Alameda County Paramedic in 1992. A claim to fame is that he served as an on-site paramedic for the TV show Nash Bridges. “I worked on movie sets for about three years part-time. It was fun, but the hours were long – all night, all day,” Gerard said. “I worked on sets when I started working in Piedmont.” Nearly 35 years of paramedic service earns Gerard a well-deserved retirement, to which he modestly replied, “It’s just what I do. After all these years. I love being a paramedic.” His extensive background in paramedic services earned him a position with the Piedmont Fire Department in 1993. He was hired full-time after a year of working each shift in the Department part-time. In the last 10 years, Gerard noted that Piedmont Fire crews have been helping with wildfires more often and throughout the state – from Napa County to Santa Barbara. One of the most devastating fires during his time with the department, the 2017 Thomas Fire, had Piedmont crews stationed in Southern California for two weeks. Piedmont crews were assigned to tactical and structural Piedmont Paramedic-firefighter Todd Gerard. protection, working round-theclock, 24 hours on and 24 hours off. At the time, the fire was the third-largest in state history. Gerard was sent to assist with a second crew of Piedmont firefighters and paramedics, along with Capt. Jon Fitzpatrick, engineer Russ San Filippo, and firefighter/paramedic Zach Heliker. “Each year since then, the fires have gotten bigger and bigger,” Gerard said. Last year, Northern California experienced the most destructive wildfires on record, and Piedmont crews were there to assist. Gerard’s focus as a paramedic was an integral part of the crew; ready to administer medications, provide advanced life support, and perform CPR. Gerard gave credit to his crew members. “My focus [as a paramedic] was not actually fighting the fires or carrying [the lines]. I’m almost 60, so I let the younger guys handle that,” he said with a smile. Firefighter/paramedic Brian Gidney, who has worked with Gerard since 2005, described him as an ideal firefighter. “Todd retiring is very exciting and a well-deserved end of his career. But to not have him around will be hard to adjust to,” Gidney said. “To describe Todd is akin to describing much of an ideal firefighter. He is calm in a way that reassures everyone around him; he cares for others truly like they were his own family; and he is driven is to be a helper and problem solver. “Above all, Todd is one of the most humble people I’ve ever known. Personally and professionally, he has been an example to live up to – and I know I’m not the only one who feels that way.” Gerard said he is looking forward to retirement so he can devote time to his passion for skiing, a sport he has done nearly his entire life. He acknowledged that he will really miss the department. “It has been my family for all these years,” he noted. He observed that they will miss him, too, but said they may miss his famous oatmeal-l banana pancakes even more. Gerard will retire in Reno, Nevada, where he intends to continue in public service as a volunteer with the Red Cross or another non-profit organization. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop at 5:30 p.m. tomorrow, December 2. In the creation of the 2023- 2031 Housing Element, which is a chapter of the General Plan, the City of Piedmont will consider all types of land uses, housing types, building types and heights, residential densities, code changes, and housing programs, such as subsidies and incentives, in order to meet the state-mandated goal of accommodating 587 new housing units by 2031 and to affirmatively further fair housing in Piedmont. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson noted, “All options for new housing units must be on the table because accessory dwelling units alone will not be enough to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation.” Community members interested in participating may participate in the workshop by visiting https://piedmont-ca-gov.zoom. us/j/85005754222. Participants are asked to have a smartphone in hand for live polling during the virtual workshop.
articles.title: City to host Housing Element workshop tomorrow

Dave Ashton, who has ordered all the trees for many years, confirmed the Scouts were not able to buy as many Silvertips as they had hoped. Price hikes and limited availability of trees have been common everywhere on the West Coast. “The price increases [for customers] were modest in comparison to the cost increases [to the scouts]. We did not pass all the costs on, in hopes of providing the highest value trees available in the area,” said Ashton. The lot has plenty of Noble Firs, of all sizes, and still holds a decent supply of Douglas Firs too. Garlands, wreaths, and mistletoe are also available for purchase. To a person, the Scouts are overjoyed to be back selling trees in person, roaming the tree lot, and enjoying hot chocolate on the chilly nights. “I enjoy meeting the customers, and I would say I am a good salesman,” said Cub Scout Jackson Apodaca. “I like working with my friend Rob Ashton. Last year he got a badge for working 20 hours here, so he is just about the perfect Scout.” Apodaca added that his goal this year is to “work as many hours as I can without getting sleepy.” There will be no sales trailer this year to eliminate contact indoors between customers and the Scouts. Transactions are by debit or credit card only. Scouts and staff will wear masks when interacting with customers as a courtesy. Customers visiting the lot are asked to wear a mask as a courtesy. “It’s a common comment that the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot offers the best trees in the region, and it’s an added bonus that we are such a beneficial charity for our local kids,” said Ashton with a smile. articles.text: As the leaves begin to blow and the trails are carpeted in gold and red and brown, Camp Augusta is now settling down for a long winter’s nap. With acorns and pine needles scattered about the wood chips and a delicious feast shared by the staff who live on site, we were digesting our meal as well as our memories from this past summer. Though we were all grateful for a great many things, one shared theme was our gratitude for the reality of running summer camp for the hundreds of campers who played outside with us this, our 90th year! We all experienced a renewed sense of wish, wonder and surprise and many of our campers (and staff) were reminded of what it is to be a kid again. Hopefully the glow is still there. You know the one: when your camper returns from camp and they seem the same - yet different. A little bit dirtier, a little bit happier, a little bit more hmmm…. mature or centered within themselves? The golden glow starts to fade as the school year ensues and the fall arrives, but hopefully the embers are still there. Embers to rekindle the recent memories of a time not long ago when they were sleeping outside, running through the woods and basking in the glory of childhood. We truly have so much gratitude for the sounds of play returning to Augusta for our 90th year after such a quiet 2020. The laughter, the songs, the campfire, the hello hugs and the goodbye tears. The warm glow of the fire reflecting on young faces eager for the next adventure. Gratitude for you all, a community who recognizes the importance of the work Augusta does and your support through the last two years. And, to our anonymous donor who recently contributed $30,000 to kick start our end-of-year annual fundraising campaign. With gratitude and love being buzzwords this time of year, especially after the last two years of well, you know….Camp Augusta is thinking of all of you – grateful for your trust and confidence. For entrusting your children to our care to learn of a greater sense of self, without them really even realizing they are doing it, while here with us in the woods of Augusta. Thank you to our community – the old, the new, and to those we haven’t even met yet. Campingly yours, Randy Grayson Director, Camp Augusta p.s. articles.text: Shani Boyd, the Children’s Librarian at Piedmont Avenue Library, has many challenges to deal with in her new job and lots of energy to face them. She chose to specialize in children’s librarianship largely because she got so much satisfaction from reading fantasy when she was growing up. As early as middle school in Marin County she was serving as part of a teen advisory group for the local library. Still living in Marin, she drives to Oakland every day to develop programs for children, order materials, and support students in the community. It is a challenge during COVID to provide activities for kids while keeping them safe. Part of the job includes wiping down toys for check-out after they are used and before they go back out. She figures out how to do Storytime with proper distancing – not the kind of problems that usually come to mind when you think of a librarian’s job. But since August, Shani has been in the library every day, doing all that and taking her turn at staffing the circulation desk, too. Shani came to the Piedmont Avenue Branch library immediately after receiving a Master’s in Library Science degree from San Jose State, preceded by an undergraduate degree from University of the Pacific. She is still getting acquainted with the job and with her work team and the community. She has many ideas, much enthusiasm and she is eager to help keep Piedmont Avenue Library the community resource it has always been. When you are there, say hello and welcome Shani Boyd. Ruby Long is a neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications.
articles.title: Piedmont Avenue Branch Library update

articles.text: Shake, Rattle, and Roll program for elementary ages begins in Jan. The Piedmont Recreation Department is offering a new after-school program called Shake, Rattle and Roll for elementary school-aged children, which offers opportunities for creative movement, music, and rhythmic exploration. Sign-ups are available for classes in January 2022, with three sessions throughout the school year. The program will be taught by Piedmont Adaptive P.E Specialist Raul Jorcino, and Nancy Henderson, a retired Albany Adaptive P.E Specialist. Jorcino and Henderson have more than 70 years of combined experience in adaptive physical education. “Both Nancy and Raul are truly amazing individuals, and we’ve formed this dream team. Nancy and I were able to create an inclusive program in the summer and school year [in Albany]. She and I have been working on what these programs will look like [in Piedmont],” Phalen said. The program is suited for children with neurodiverse needs in grades K-5. Henderson will teach the first two sessions, and Jorcino will teach session three. The program will be from 3:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. at Beach School. Session 1: Thursdays, January 13 - February 17 Session 2: Thursdays, March 3 - April 4 Session 3: Thursdays, April 21 - May 26. Classes will be limited to 10 children. Interested parents may call the Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 to enroll. Teen Sidekicks Teenaged “sidekicks” will be paired with campers in adaptive programing to help build relationships and strengthen children’s recreational skills. The Recreation Department is currently seeking volunteers ages 14 or older to commit to an entire session, Thursday afternoons for six weeks. Community service hours are available upon request, and volunteers may receive a letter of recommendation. Students interested in becoming a sidekick should contact Eva Phalen at ephalen@piedmont. ca.gov for an application

articles.text: Yasaman Ford assists with editing of film footage as a part of the Reel Stories team. Yasaman Ford, a PHS graduate in 2016, will be co-teaching the Reel Stories Women’s Filmmaking Weekend December 3-5 at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley. The popular and original program enables adult women to experience film production in an accelerated two and a half day event. Ford attended her first Camp Reel Stories program before her sophomore year at Piedmont High School and returned to its summer program for the next three years. It was at Reel Stories where her passion for film and feminism ignited. While attending UCLA’s School for Film and Television during the year, Ford would come home every summer to share her growing knowledge and experience of film with students through Reel Stories and Piedmont’s Summer Enrichment Program. Ford joined the Reel Stories Team as a Program Coordinator and Lead Media Instructor in March 2020. Founded in 2013 by Executive Director Esther Pearl, Reel Stories is the only female owned and operated non-profit film program for women in the country led by professionals. In addition to teaching filmmaking, Ford also creates and collaborates on film and digital media projects. Ford’s own work as a filmmaker ranges from narrative production design to directing documentaries, freelance motion graphics and editing. She aims to educate others, from toddlers to teenagers, on the importance of representation in the media. This year the program will be back in-person at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley, the only female-owned production studio. Signups for the December 3-5 weekend program are available online at: bit.ly/RSWoWe. The end of the first semester of school presents unique challenges every year as daylight fades even before homework and study gets started. All the while, everyone at school – students, teachers, administrators – may have one foot out the door to holiday vacations. It is no different this year, and everyone may be even more anxious to have double holidays to make up for last year. So, how do students stay on track? A tutor can help, especially before finals at the end of the first semester. Sometimes all that is needed is a new perspective and a little one-on-one help. As primarily a math tutor, I often encounter surprise when I mention that I didn’t major in mathematics in college. I explain that mastery of material does not necessarily equate to mastery in teaching, connection with students or most importantly, results. I credit my success as a math tutor to my communication skills in translating numbers to words. The beauty of math for some can also be a fatal attribute for others, as it is void of language. I have found that people who can put numbers and concepts into words often are not math experts, but are individuals with backgrounds like sociology, linguistics or English. Communication skills as a tutor are invaluable. Knowing
articles.title: Yasaman Ford leads Reel Stories filmmaking weekend

articles.text: Over the last two years many of us have reflected on what it means to be a more inclusive society. As much as this heavy work starts within, it also begins with our little ones. Starting with our children, even the youngest, is a great way to change the narrative on what it means to see the world in a more inclusive way. There are many holidays celebrated this time of year, and I am reminded of how Christmas can define the “season.” However, this is an excellent opportunity to expose children to different cultures, practices and traditions. Many holiday celebrations incorporate storytelling, or histories, to pass on traditions. Exploring celebrations different from our own offer children the opportunity to not only experience different traditions but to also see common values - family, love, respect and honor. This exploration allows children to develop an understanding of the world around them and that is more inclusive of others. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, December 1, 2021 Yasaman Ford leads Reel Stories filmmaking weekend Thinking Outside The Classroom Yasaman Ford assists with editing of film footage as a part of the Reel Stories team. By Jay Russell Yasaman Ford, a PHS graduate in 2016, will be co-teaching the Reel Stories Women’s Filmmaking Weekend December 3-5 at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley. The popular and original program enables adult women to experience film production in an accelerated two and a half day event. Ford attended her first Camp Reel Stories program before her sophomore year at Piedmont High School and returned to its summer program for the next three years. It was at Reel Stories where her passion for film and feminism ignited. While attending UCLA’s School for Film and Television during the year, Ford would come home every summer to share her growing knowledge and experience of film with students through Reel Stories and Piedmont’s Summer Enrichment Program. Ford joined the Reel Stories Team as a Program Coordinator and Lead Media Instructor in March 2020. Founded in 2013 by Executive Director Esther Pearl, Reel Stories is the only female owned and operated non-profit film program for women in the country led by professionals. In addition to teaching filmmaking, Ford also creates and collaborates on film and digital media projects. Ford’s own work as a filmmaker ranges from narrative production design to directing documentaries, freelance motion graphics and editing. She aims to educate others, from toddlers to teenagers, on the importance of representation in the media. This year the program will be back in-person at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley, the only female-owned production studio. Signups for the December 3-5 weekend program are available online at: bit.ly/RSWoWe. ADVICE FROM A TUTOR By Jay Russell The end of the first semester of school presents unique challenges every year as daylight fades even before homework and study gets started. All the while, everyone at school – students, teachers, administrators – may have one foot out the door to holiday vacations. It is no different this year, and everyone may be even more anxious to have double holidays to make up for last year. So, how do students stay on track? A tutor can help, especially before finals at the end of the first semester. Sometimes all that is needed is a new perspective and a little one-on-one help. As primarily a math tutor, I often encounter surprise when I mention that I didn’t major in mathematics in college. I explain that mastery of material does not necessarily equate to mastery in teaching, connection with students or most importantly, results. I credit my success as a math tutor to my communication skills in translating numbers to words. The beauty of math for some can also be a fatal attribute for others, as it is void of language. I have found that people who can put numbers and concepts into words often are not math experts, but are individuals with backgrounds like sociology, linguistics or English. Communication skills as a tutor are invaluable. Knowing test-taking strategy, and working through the material while making mistakes can make a tutor more effective than a math genius with a Ph.D. When I was 20 years old, my first private tutoring assignment was for a class I had never taken, Statistics. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

The Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team held Cardinal Newman scoreless in a 0-0- tie to open the 2021 season at Witter Field on Monday, November 29. It sent a message that Piedmont is for real this year as it prevented last year’s North Coast Section champion from scoring any goals. Earlier this year in February Piedmont, ranked No. 9, nearly upset No. 1 Cardinal Newman in a 1-0 loss in the NCS Quarterfinals. “We definitely had more impetus going forward. We looked really solid at the back. [Cardinal Newman was] never a threat, even though we were playing high,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Piedmont’s attack had its fair share of chances, and its defense did well to keep Cardinal Newman’s looks at net minimal. The Highlanders looked good on the counter-attack, but lacked the finishing when finding a final pass or clear shot. “They were a very young team we were playing against. I think we were the one to take the ball more forward in the second half. I think it was a very good first game,” said Sullivan. It was an impressive performance by Piedmont’s midfield and back line, keeping their line high and often stealing possession at midfield to hold the ball in the final third. Wearing the captain’s armband is senior central midfielder Andre Stankiewicz, who did Conner Curtis had three shots on target. well at maintaining the ball and sending useful passes forward to Conner Curtis, Russell Tan, and Aiden Woolwine in the attack. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont lost its season-opener at St. Ignatius in San Francisco on November 27. Piedmont’s basketball team fell 76-62 to St. Ignatius in San Francisco for its season-opener on Saturday, November 27. The Wildcats compete in the Central Coast Section. “We just didn’t come ready to play, we got outworked on both ends of the floor,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “We had 2-3 bad minutes in the second quarter and that was the ball game. We’re preaching defense and will go back to the drawing board.” A.J. Harris led the way with 28 points, while JoJo Murphy had a difficult game with 18 points after returning from an ankle injury. “A.J. had a great night; he was 11 of 16 from the floor. JoJo hadn’t practiced in around two weeks and had a tough night shooting. He was short on many shots that he typically makes, so perhaps his ankle wasn’t all the way there,” said Spencer. St. Ignatius did well to move the ball around to find open shooters, and their tall center managed to block three shots and force Piedmont into difficult shots around the basket. “They were really well coaches and very disciplined. They have 12 seniors and they were able to maintain composure and work really well together,” said Spencer. Piedmont trailed 14-11 at the end of the first quarter, but St. Ignatius blew the game open with a 41-27 lead by halftime. The Wildcats held a 58-46 lead to start the fourth, and closed out the victory at 76-62. “They are in a tough league with some big schools and are a great team to play. As poorly as we played, it was good to see us hang in it and inch closer,” Spencer added. The Highlanders crept closer in the third quarter, but the Wildcats a lead of 14 points for the remainder of the game. “We were able to get the lead down to seven in the third quarter and were able to compete in the fourth. This is a really good time to learn and experience the physicality it takes to play at the varsity level,” said Spencer. articles.text: Piedmont’s fall sports teams officially concluded their season in November, with 24 All-League recipients from seven different teams. PHS earned two Athlete of the Year awards in cross country by Jack Stein and Ellie Black. This marks a return to the end-of-season awards by the Western Alameda County Conference after a year hiatus due to the global pandemic. Becker and Mahany led the way for Piedmont at doubles all fall. They entered with the No. 2 seed in the league tournament, and defeated Berkeley 7-5, 6-1 before losing to O’Dowd in the semifinals in three sets, 4-6, 7-5, 6-4. Girls Volleyball The volleyball team struggled, finishing with a 3-12 record. Shelby Cavenaugh earned a second-team All-League selection after helping lead the team in spikes as an outside hitter. Honorable Mentions were also awarded to senior captain Ruby Shaffer and libero Eden Lorin. Boys Cross Country Jack Stein’s winning time of 15:34.8 at the Western Alameda County Conference Finals earned him the Runner of the Year award after he defeated a field of 70 runners. Also earning a first-team selection was Parker Long; he placed 5th in 16:20 at the WACC Finals. Receiving second-team honors were Julien Lee, who finished 10th in 16:35.02. Xander Schulte-Sasse also earned a second-team choice; finishing 13th in 16:41.71 at League. Staff Photos Photo by Steve Zirkelbach

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team and two individual members of the girls’ team competed last Saturday in the State Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno. Piedmont was led by Jack Stein in, who just missed a podium finish (top 10) with a 12th place finish in a field of 209 runners in a personal best time of 15:43.4. Individual qualifiers Ellie Black finished 17th of 207 in 18:44, and teammate Josie OesPhoto by Steve Zirkelbach Jack Stein led the way with a time of 15:43.4 to finish 12th of 209 runners. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Dr. Gutlaizer and Ellen and Liza Konnert Ellie Black finished 17th of 207 with a time of 18:44. terer was 62nd in 19:46. The boys’ team placed 11th among 25 schools. “It was exciting to watch Jack pass the first mile in 5:49. Ellie Black and Josie Oesterer both ran PRs on the course. I’m very proud of this group for making it to the finish line with such a strong showing,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Stein finishes his high school career as Piedmont’s No. 2 alltime runner on the Woodward Park course behind Steve Brown’s time of 15:31 in 1994. Brown was seen at the Piedmont Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving Day, spending some time with his family and former PHS cross-county coach Doyle O’Regan. Stein set the course record for PHS at Hayward High one week earlier at the North Coast Section Finals with a time of 15:29.4. In Fresno, he eclipsed his previous best at Woodward Park by nearly a full minute, lowering his time from 16:40.2 to 15:43.4. “I thought Saturday went really well. The State meet is really cool to be a part of and it was my first time going. It was a huge PR that opens up opportunities for me. I wasn’t expecting to be that high on the list; it’s a really competitive course, and to be up there on the list is really humbling,” said Stein. Rounding out Piedmont’s top five, junior Christian Taylor was next in 82nd with a time of 16:52.1; junior Parker Long placed 88th in 16:56.1; sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse came in 92nd with a time of 16:59.3 and sophomore Julien Lee placed 107th in 17:13.9.

articles.text: Bryan Gardere, a PHS alum, began coaching Piedmont’s girls basketball team prior to the 2002- 2003 season. He arrived with a fire in his eye and mission to create a respected basketball program in the East Bay. His team won the first State Championship in school history, then added a second title one year later. In his 19 hears at the helm, his teams have also won four North Coast Section championships and four league titles. His current team includes at least three players drawing college interest. When asked for his comments upon entering his 19th season, he laughed and replied, “That’s crazy, man. I haven’t even talked about it. I remember starting just like it was yesterday. Those were some really good times. It feels like it hasn’t been that long, but when you think about it, we’ve had maybe 12 athletic directors, 4-5 principals, hundreds of kids. The kids on this year’s team weren’t even born! “I didn’t know what high school basketball was about when I came here, I walked into a very solid team. To start something Bryan Gardere has helped send a long list of student-athletes to college. and still be is strange to think about. I can’t complain for one second,” he said. articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson San Francisco Ballet performs the “Waltz of Flowers” in Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker. San Francisco Ballet will present its production of Helgi Tomasson’s Nutcracker, premiering on December 10 and running through December 30. The 2022 season will be dedicated to Tomasson, who has announced his retirement next year after 37 years as Artistic Director. San Francisco Ballet’s production of Nutcracker with music by Tchaikovsky, is performed every year with a kaleidoscope of more than 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older. No children under the age of three are permitted. All ticket holders at the War Memorial Opera House must present proof of full vaccination status, along with a matching photo, and masks are required. To purchase tickets and to view production times, see: https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker/.
articles.title: San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker begins Dec. 10

articles.text: Musicians Steve Oda, Michael Lewis and Pushpa Oda will perform a selection of North Indian classical music on Saturday, December 11 at Piedmont Center for the Arts beginning 7 p.m. The music will be followed by a dance performance by Kali Futnani, a senior teacher at Bharata Kalanjali in Berkeley. Futnani began her dance training at Kalanjali in Berkeley, which was founded by K.P and Katherine Kunhiraman. She has a BFA from Kalakshetra College of Fine Arts in Chennai, India. Kali continued her training under K.P. Yesodha in Chennai for six years, performing with the company throughout India before returning to the Bay Area. Bharatanatyam is a South Indian classical dance style that was performed in the temples of Tamil Nadu for thousands of years before coming to the stage. Bharatanatyam has both rhythmic and dramatic aspects. The theory of rasa, the nature of the aesthetics as transcendental and emotional experience, is central to all Indian arts. Through movement set to rhythmic patterns and storytelling through hand gestures and Kali Futnani expression, the audience and the performer have a shared experience through art. Tickets are $20 at the door, and $10 for students with high school or college identification. All events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require proof of vaccination and proper masking while indoors.
articles.title: Indian classical music and dance concert at PCA on December 11

articles.text: Christmas Revels will present its 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland from December 11-19. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. Children are welcome at all performances if fully-vaccinated against COVID-19. Group discounts are available at www.CaliforniaRevels.org or by calling the box office at 510- 452-9334.
articles.title: Christmas Revels performances in Oakland December 11-19

Mee’s Wintertime new through December 19 Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) has returned to in-person performances with Charles Mee’s Wintertime, running through Sunday, December 19. For this production, Berkeley Rep welcomes back Mee and director Les Waters, who have teamed up in the past to bring “Fetes de la Nuit” and “Big Love” to the stage. “Wintertime” is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family who arrives at their summer house in the winter woods for a supposedly secret rendezvous – and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” The production features Micah Peoples, Carman Berkeley, Nora el Samahy, Thomas Jay Ryan, James Carpenter, and David Ryan Smith. Tickets to Wintertime are now on sale at https://www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/wintertime/. Berkeley Rep requires all patrons to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification, and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre at 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley.

articles.text: Simone Young will conduct the San Francisco Symphony live at Davies Symphony Hall December 2 through December 4. articles.text: Benefit concert at Center for the Arts on December 19 The In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, December 19, showcasing the Center’s Steinway Grand Piano.
