articles.text: Art review by Jaime Robles The Art of Banksy, a collection of iconic prints and art by the anonymous UK street artist, opened at San Francisco’s Palace of Fine Arts this month and its stay has been extended through Sunday, February 27, due to popular demand. The exhibition includes many of Banksy’s most famous works. The little girl watching a heartshaped balloon float away, a chimpanzee coiffed and bejewelled like Queen Elizabeth, the street protestor throwing a bouquet of flowers. There are helicopters adorned with huge pink bows, squads of military wearing “happy face” masks, and rats. Lots of rats doing all kinds of ratty things. “If you feel dirty, insignificant or unloved, then rats are a good role model. They exist without permission, they have no respect for the hierarchy of society, and they have sex 50 times a day.” So reads one of the many Banksy-attributed quotes stenciled on the black walls of the winding corridors that run through the exhibition space. Photos by Jaime Robles “Laugh Now” screen print from The Art of Banksy. This piece shows the characteristic soft edge of the spray can paint and stencil technique used by Banksy in his street art. Banksy is a wonderful artist. His work was one of the earliest and most representative of street art that used stenciled rather than freehand spray can drawing. He has stated that he used stencils so that he could more quickly produce his art and escape the police patrolling the streets that make up his canvases. Stencils gave his work a distinctive and recognizable style. Banksy also has a sharp satiric mind and passionate beliefs about poverty and the cruelty it endures under the uncaring machinations of a capitalist State. Part of his genius is his ability to convey those beliefs in simple and succinct black-and-white images. His art is both impressionistic and precise at the same time, giving it an immediate and arresting quality. The Art of Banksy is a kind of catalog of the guerrilla exhibitions that Banksy organized or was part of during his early days as a street artist. And it adds to the history of street art as a movement within the UK, a collective in-your-face protest of politics and the politics of art. The effort and the imagination are impressive not only for this singular artDorothy undergoes a basket check. ist but for the contributing young street artists themselves, whose work and passion are surely underrated by the slick purveyors of taste and high art within the UK – and the US. A video interview with Banksy’s early days screen printer, Ben Eine, is projected on several screens throughout the show. Eine explains the history and process of the prints while showing his own impressive display of tattoo art on his forearms and neck. The artwork has been gathered from collectors reportedly from around the globe, but the exhibition is unauthorized. On his personal website page called Product Recall, Banksy lists the exhibition along with others shown worldwide from Budapest to Tel Aviv to Las Vegas. The anonymous Banksy. The dollar cost of the entrance fee to each exhibition is listed and an opening paragraph reads enigmatically: “Members of the public should be aware there has been a recent spate of Banksy exhibitions none of which are consensual. They‘ve been organised entirely without the artist’s knowledge or involvement. Please treat them accordingly.” While it’s true the exhibition entrance fee comes in at a hefty $39.99, complete with a capitalist classic, the penny discount, and you have to exit through a gift shop of Banksy cups, T-shirts and food concessions, the exhibition itself is a lot of fun. Full of wry truth-telling and humor that is both desperate and loving. There has always been poignancy to street art. And great generosity. All of these are in full display at in Banksy’s art. For a cheaper ride and a smallscreen experience, you can also try visiting Banksy’s website. It’s well worth it. In compliance with the City of San Francisco’s vaccine mandate, visitors of The Art of Banksy will be required to present proof of full vaccination with valid ID in order to attend the exhibit. Masks are mandatory for all attendees. Please consult the website for additional information on COVID- 19 protocols.
articles.title: From streets to palace: The Art of Banksy

articles.text: A concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts last week was of such magnitude that for the first time in my life, I find myself literally speechless. The concert on Saturday afternoon, November 20, was sponsored by the Kodaly Foundation for Music Education. A young pianist from Indonesia, Jessica Suandrianna, was the featured soloist. This is a name and a musician you will want to remember. Only 28 years old, she proved herself to be masterful in every way. She has all the technique a pianist could ever hope for. That she puts it to the service of the highest levels of artistry is extraordinary. Everything about her playing is artistic and profound. This is an extraordinary combination and rather unknown to musicians of her generation. Jessica walks onto the stage with a simplicity and a dignity that is disarming. There is an economy of movement which produces the greatest results. The rarely heard piano Sonata by Edvard Grieg was notable for elegant voicing, absolute independence of the hands, and a resonant tone that sounded orchestral. After the Grieg sonata came four piano pieces by Brahms which transported to us into a German dream land. Once again, the piano became an orchestra. There was will-of-the-wisp lightness and then, quick as a cat, came the thunder and the lightning – and all the pastel colors in between. Pathos and romanticism were brought to the fore in two nocturnes by Frederick Chopin, and then another change of pace with Debussy’s L’ile joyeuse. Then once again came a change of mood and color with a new composition by the Indonesian composer Ananda Sukarlan. This extraordinary program was brought to a conclusion by another new composition entitled Tryptich of an Encounter, written for piano four hands by the Belgian pianist- teacher Gilbert de Greeve who was in the Center to join Ms. Suandrianna. He was a teacher of hers and remains her mentor. Quite frankly, their performance was the finest example of four hand piano playing I have ever heard. They played as one. The interplay between the two was as beautiful to watch as it was to listen to. Mentor Gilbert de Greeve (left) joined his brilliant student Jessica Suandrianna for some 4-hands piano works at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 20.
articles.title: Masterful pianist visits Piedmont

articles.text: Opening reception on Saturday, Dec. 4 at 5 p.m. Four East Bay artists will present an exhibition entitled A Boundless Moment at Piedmont Center for the Arts this weekend, Saturday and Sunday, December 4-5, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. The exhibit will be open to the public again the following weekend, December 11-12. The exhibit will showcase the works of Carl Heyward, Akiko Suzuki, Usha Shukla, and Colleen Gianatiempo. Heyward is the recipient of a National Endowment for the Arts grant and a former Masters of Fine Arts instructor at the San Francisco Academy of Art University. His work has been featured at various art galleries in the Bay Area and internationally. Suzuki is a textile and mixed media artist based in San Francisco. Since 2014, she has particArtist. Colleen Giantiempo Artist Carl Heyward ipated in Global Art Project with partner Heyward. “My work expresses the invisible nature of thought, of skin sensation, the poetry of Love and Eros or the presentiments that occur prior to thought. Intuitive works are born from everyday life as are novels,” Suzuki said. “The words borne out of the flood of my imagery become poetry and are visualized in works as abstractions through paint, collage, sewing and fiber works.” Shukla was raised in New Delhi, India, where the vibrant colors of the Indian countryside greatly influenced her artwork. She completed a graduate program at the Academy of Art University in San Francisco, with a focus on painting. She paints primarily large abstracts in vivid colors and has a unique process of “mark-making.” Gianatiempo is a mixed media artist, educator, and designer living in the East Bay. “My journey as an artist began when I was 3 years old. I remember cutting up family photos and drawing on walls with lipstick. I learned early on that it’s possible to express the world around me in different ways, and this is where my passion began,” Gianatiempo said. “Nature is my main influence as I always marvel about the design and beauty it beholds,” she said. “I work in many mediums and thrive most when I can experiment and discover new techniques. I have been told that I am the Mary Poppins of art supplies.” An opening reception will be held this Saturday, December 4, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Gallery hours will be open to the public, with no reservation required, on Sunday, December 5 from noon to 3 p.m., and again on December 11 and 12 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required at all Piedmont Center for the Arts events.

articles.text: Olivia Wilde and Oscar Isaac in Life Itself. Life Itself, written and directed by Dan Fogelman, is framed by the trope known as the unreliable narrator, meaning a narrator whose credibility is brought into question. It is a familiar plot device used in literature and film and is oft repeated like a mantra in Fogelman’s story. The film opens with Will Dempsey (Oscar Isaac) standing at the counter of a small coffee shop. Taking his cup of coffee, he adds tabs of Xanax, sips, and then begins to sing and talk loudly as the owner and a barista push him toward the door. It’s immediately established that he is not only the protagonist of the story, but strangely quirky and untethered from his surroundings. The essential question posed in this brief setup is, why? What has brought him to this point in his life? The next scene takes place in the office of Will’s therapist (Annette Bening). She is questioning him about his recent mental health; his answers in previous sessions have always been oblique and evasive. But today he grudgingly begins to talk about his courtship and then marriage to Abbey (Olivia Wilde), which is revealed in a long flashback. She was a university student and he a writer. At a house party they sit on the front porch steps and she asks him why he has never asked her out. Will tells her that if he crossed that threshold there would be no turning back regarding his devotion to her. As is revealed, their relationship is heartbreakingly intimate, joyful, and Will is shown telling Abbey that he will dedicate his life to making her life more than wonderful. And it is Abbey, holding her senior thesis, who introduces the idea that becomes the film’s mantra: it isn’t just the literary narrator who is unreliable but it is life itself. Meanwhile, the therapist presses Will to confront his recent events and their unexpected and tragic outcome, one that involves a truth that is more than he can bear. His affect is evasive, shrouded with emotional revetments, and a head-shaking resistance against a traumatic memory that he distorts in order to cope. In the many flashbacks, the lengthy vignettes, and the dramatic pauses, each is filtered through Will’s prism thus making it impossible for the audience to rely on what he has shared as being either truthful or remotely normative. It’s at this point that the story shifts to Will’s 21-year-old daughter, Dylan (Olivia Cooke), who is living with her grandfather (Mandy Patinkin). For reasons that are self-evident she is overwhelmed by a sense of angst, her default response to her life one of anger and resistance. This brief chapter ends with her sitting on a bus stop bench in the middle of the night and slowly drifting off into a soft, barely conscious sleep. Now, abruptly, Life Itself makes a complete change of location (Spain), language (Spanish with subtitles), and characters. The setting is a bucolic olive plantation owned by Senior Saccione (Antonio Banderas), a wealthy single man. We are introduced to Javier Gonzalez (Sergio Peris-Mencheta) and Isabel (Laia Costa). Javier works on the plantation and Isabel is his new wife. They live in a casita near the main house. This narrative is straightforward, though subtle hints convey that possible heartbreak is just within reach. Fogelman is a master of the lachrymose. The audience can intuit that regardless of all appearances, life is not linear; rather, it’s a gestalt of various directions, making the point that Abbey is an unreliable narrator. One last point: Recall that the script for Life Itself was written by Fogelman, who created the theme of the unreliable narrator. And it is Fogelman who inserts unexpected tragedies before abruptly flipping the narrative to one that at least promises some clarity. It’s as if Fogelman wanted to create a film that is more like a novel in structure and exposition. He crafts a kind of tale that allows him to examine certain themes that thread their way through our lives, always different in texture though also universal in experience. I give Fogelman kudos for this film, for risking all to examine life in all its vagaries. For those who love film as a way to tell stories and mirror life’s experiences, I say, go see this film. Then ponder and wrestle with its strengths and its weaknesses. Life Itself. Directed by Dan Fogelman. Starring Oscar Isaac, Olivia Wilde, Antonio Banderas. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. articles.text: First things first: Win Win is not a sports film, though the title and ad posters seem to promise a plot that revolves around a team and its coaches. It’s much more. While it does focus on high school wrestling, the film is never formulaic. It is not about winning on the mats, or about a weak team transformed into a group of wunderkins; rather, it is about flawed yet decent people who out of kindness fashion an improbable family. Begin with Paul Giamatti. If you’ve not seen him in “Sideways,” then make a point of renting this film. It was his breakthrough movie, launching his career as more than a minor character actor. Giamatti would be the first to acknowledge that he is not your typical leading man: sad-eyed, overweight, and balding. Yet he is so good – brilliant, really – at portraying certain characters that it’s always a delight to watch someone so talented work. Giamatti relishes the role of Mike Flaherty: a struggling lawyer with few clients, a volunteer high school wrestling coach, married to Jackie, nicely portrayed by Amy Ryan, father to two girls, and living in a modest home. While the movie has been billed as a comedy, it is much more. Win Win is essentially about good people and situations in which they do the best they can while realizing even their best may not be enough. Until it is. Unexpectedly, into the Flaherty home comes a teenage kid, Kyle, played by Alex Shaffer. As Mike soon discovers, he is a gifted wrestler who is also troubled – his mother is in rehab and his grandfather is living in a nursing home. He has run away from home, hoping to move in with his grandfather no matter that he is a stranger to him. Mike convinces Jackie that they should take in the boy until his mother can be found. She believes they now have Eminem living in their basement, a delinquent rapper who is beyond help. Writer/director Tom McCarthy does not portray Kyle stereotypically, which makes the movie far richer and more engaging. The film soon evolves into a soft, subtle, very human tale, serious and comedic. The ensemble of actors is superb, to include Kyle’s mom, Cindy, nicely rendered by Melanie Lynskey, as well as the veteran actor Burt Young, who plays the aging grandfather suffering from early dementia. Win Win is proof that small movies are still being made that exemplify excellent storytelling, deeply human, filled with delightful, well-intentioned, imperfect people. Win Win. Directed by Tom McCarthy. Starring Paul Giamatti, Amy Ryan, Bobby Cannvavale, Jeffrey Tambor, Melanie Lynskey and Burt Young. 2 hrs., 27 min. Rated R.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, December 1, 2021 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Life Itself – a story of life’s vagaries Olivia Wilde and Oscar Isaac in Life Itself. By Chris Honoré Life Itself, written and directed by Dan Fogelman, is framed by the trope known as the unreliable narrator, meaning a narrator whose credibility is brought into question. It is a familiar plot device used in literature and film and is oft repeated like a mantra in Fogelman’s story. The film opens with Will Dempsey (Oscar Isaac) standing at the counter of a small coffee shop. Taking his cup of coffee, he adds tabs of Xanax, sips, and then begins to sing and talk loudly as the owner and a barista push him toward the door. It’s immediately established that he is not only the protagonist of the story, but strangely quirky and untethered from his surroundings. The essential question posed in this brief setup is, why? What has brought him to this point in his life? The next scene takes place in the office of Will’s therapist (Annette Bening). She is questioning him about his recent mental health; his answers in previous sessions have always been oblique and evasive. But today he grudgingly begins to talk about his courtship and then marriage to Abbey (Olivia Wilde), which is revealed in a long flashback. She was a university student and he a writer. At a house party they sit on the front porch steps and she asks him why he has never asked her out. Will tells her that if he crossed that threshold there would be no turning back regarding his devotion to her. As is revealed, their relationship is heartbreakingly intimate, joyful, and Will is shown telling Abbey that he will dedicate his life to making her life more than wonderful. And it is Abbey, holding her senior thesis, who introduces the idea that becomes the film’s mantra: it isn’t just the literary narrator who is unreliable but it is life itself. Meanwhile, the therapist presses Will to confront his recent events and their unexpected and tragic outcome, one that involves a truth that is more than he can bear. His affect is evasive, shrouded with emotional revetments, and a head-shaking resistance against a traumatic memory that he distorts in order to cope. In the many flashbacks, the lengthy vignettes, and the dramatic pauses, each is filtered through Will’s prism thus making it impossible for the audience to rely on what he has shared as being either truthful or remotely normative. It’s at this point that the story shifts to Will’s 21-year-old daughter, Dylan (Olivia Cooke), who is living with her grandfather (Mandy Patinkin). For reasons that are self-evident she is overwhelmed by a sense of angst, her default response to her life one of anger and resistance. This brief chapter ends with her sitting on a bus stop bench in the middle of the night and slowly drifting off into a soft, barely conscious sleep. Now, abruptly, Life Itself makes a complete change of location (Spain), language (Spanish with subtitles), and characters. The setting is a bucolic olive plantation owned by Senior Saccione (Antonio Banderas), a wealthy single man. We are introduced to Javier Gonzalez (Sergio Peris-Mencheta) and Isabel (Laia Costa). Javier works on the plantation and Isabel is his new wife. They live in a casita near the main house. This narrative is straightforward, though subtle hints convey that possible heartbreak is just within reach. Fogelman is a master of the lachrymose. The audience can intuit that regardless of all appearances, life is not linear; rather, it’s a gestalt of various directions, making the point that Abbey is an unreliable narrator. One last point: Recall that the script for Life Itself was written by Fogelman, who created the theme of the unreliable narrator. And it is Fogelman who inserts unexpected tragedies before abruptly flipping the narrative to one that at least promises some clarity. It’s as if Fogelman wanted to create a film that is more like a novel in structure and exposition. He crafts a kind of tale that allows him to examine certain themes that thread their way through our lives, always different in texture though also universal in experience. I give Fogelman kudos for this film, for risking all to examine life in all its vagaries. For those who love film as a way to tell stories and mirror life’s experiences, I say, go see this film. Then ponder and wrestle with its strengths and its weaknesses. Life Itself. Directed by Dan Fogelman. Starring Oscar Isaac, Olivia Wilde, Antonio Banderas. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. articles.text: Shelby, the star pooch in A Dog’s Way Home, was discovered in a dog shelter after she was saved from a Tennessee garbage dump. As far as the kids are concerned, A Dog’s Way Home finds the PG sweet spot and stays there. They’ll take to it like, well, ducks to water. But then it’s a story about a nifty dog named Bella and her owner, Lucas (Jonah Hauer King), a med student living with his mom, Teri (Ashley Judd). Lucas and his fellow med student, Olivia (Alexandra Shipp), find Bella as a pup, living with cats and kittens under an abandoned wreck of a house, and it’s Lucas who takes the wiggly, excitable, playful pooch home. She is literally a rescue dog; the house is about to be bulldozed. A year goes by, Bella grows up, and is spotted by a villainous animal control guy, Chuck (John Cassini), who makes it his mission to catch her on the street, unleashed. He claims she’s a pit bull. Worried that Bella could be impounded and even put down, Teri and Lucas send her to stay briefly with relatives in Farmington, New Mexico, while they search for a place to live outside of the city limits and out of Chuck’s jurisdiction. Bella is, of course, homesick, misses Lucas and Terri, and at the first opportunity makes a break for it, not realizing that she is 400 miles away from home. And so begins Bella’s twoyear adventure. It proves to be a mildly harrowing journey that involves humans, a pack of stalking wolves, two men who want to adopt her, an orphaned mountain lion cub that tags along, an avalanche, and learning to survive on leftovers in garbage bins. But Bella determinedly makes her way toward home and Lucas. Kids will love all of it. Plus, the filmmakers, having adapted A Dog’s Way Home from the bestselling novel by Bruce Cameron, decide to give the film a Bella voice over (by Bryce Dallas Howard) allowing her to share her impressions of all that she encounters. No worries regarding animals talking. Kids are totally on board with anthropomorphizing animals. Remember a Disneyesque small wooden boy and an iconic mouse. Plus. humans talk to dogs all the time and swear they get an answer topped off with a wagging tail. This is a family friendly film with a great story. Bella meets lots of kind people along the way. A Dog’s Way Home. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Now streaming
articles.title: A Dog’s Way Home a sweet story of Bella

articles.text: The live action feature The Kid Who Would Be King opens with a brief animated prologue of the Arthurian legend and then skips to present day England, the setting for this fresh, energetic tale. At its center are a 12-yearold boy, Alex (Louis Ashbourne Serkis), and his best bud Bedders (Dean Chaumoo). Their first year in secondary school has just begun. Two bullies, Kaye and Lance (Rhianna Dorris, Tom Taylor) have singled out Alex and Bedders to torment. When one of their confrontations is broken up by a school administrator the four are given detention. In the late afternoon, Alex is on his way home when is chased by Kaye and Lance. He runs into an abandoned construction site to hide and it’s there that he discovers a sword sticking out of a block of concrete, and, grasping the hilt, he manages to pull the blade free. He later shows it to Bedders, and they conclude that it is the Excalibur, the sword of King Arthur. The next day, a mysterious kid comes to the school, and seeks out Alex and Bedders. He tells them that he is actually the wizard Merlin (Angus Imrie), who has the power to age backward. When Alex is skeptical, the strange boy transforms himself into the older Merlin (Patrick Stewart), and he tells the boys that Alex is a descendent of King Arthur. He has come to ask for help to defeat the newly awakened wicked sorceress, Morgana (Rebecca Ferguson), Arthur’s half-sister, who, with her army of demon knights, is about to leave her underworld during a solar eclipse and lay waste to the world. It’s also her mission the find and take possession of the Excalibur. Merlin explains that the only hope for England is Alex. With the Excalibur, he knights Bedders, and with optimism includes Kaye and Lance. The four, discussing the chivalric code, in all its guileless decency, form what will resemble the Arthurian round table. They pledge that they will defend the world from evil and are then trained by Merlin in swordsmanship. And thus begins what will be an epic, heroic adventure during which they confront Morgana and do battle with her demon knights. Unexpectedly the Excalibur is destroyed, but then restored. Alex also learns the history of his family, and his connection to Arthur/ The Kid Who Would Be King is an exciting and compelling saga with a rousing conclusion that ends with the entire student body at Alex’s school is knighted and joins in the battle against Morgana. Tweens and newbie teens will be captivated by the story, filled with action, but absent even a drop of blood. The Kid Who Would Be King. Directed by Joe Cornish. Starring Louis Ashbourne Serkis, Rhianna Dorris, Patrick Stewart, Tom Taylor. 2 hrs. Rated PG.
articles.title: The Kid Who Would Be King a delightful story

articles.text: The season of caring is upon us and Montclair Village is ready to celebrate its return during the upcoming 2021 Holiday Stroll on Thursday, December 9 from 5:30-8:00 p.m. Since COVID came on the scene 19 months ago it’s become clearer than ever how important the Village is, not only as a vibrant commercial center and provider of essential services, but as a community gathering place for people who care about each other. The Montclair Village Association is excitedly planning the 18th Annual Holiday Stroll and invites community members to make the Village a December destination for festive shopping, dining and overall merriment. Some of the highlights you can expect are: • Performances by the Pacific Boys Choir and Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees • Strolling with costumed student dancers from the Oakland Ballet and a fanciful Ice Queen on stilts • Family photos with Santa in a Winter Wonderland setting • Toy donation drive hosted by the Oakland Fire Department • Shopping and dining in festively decorated retail businesses • Commemorative mug sales along with Village Plaza updates • Opportunity to chat with District 4’s City Councilmember Sheng Thao It’s a wonderful thing that so many local businesses have survived the last 19 months and that joyful traditions like the Holiday Stroll are returning, especially during this time of year. As Montclair Village Association’s Executive, Director Daniel Swafford stated, “Businesses are versatile — what they do really well is persevere and adjust to changing times, but we have to look to the fact that we are in this together, and what creates our sense of community, are the unique experiences and relationships our neighborhood businesses provide.” Montclair Village is looking forward to your support and participation in celebrating community by offering everything it can to ensure this season of caring is a special one. For more information about the festivities being planned, follow Montclair Village on Instagram and Facebook and visit MontclairVillage.com regularly for updates. Oakland’s famous Tap Dancing Christmas Trees will be on hand to welcome shoppers during the annual Montclair Village Stroll on December 9.
articles.title: Holiday Stroll returns to Montclair Village Dec. 9

articles.text: One of our favorite fall and winter fruit combinations is pears and cranberries. This cake speaks of the seasons and is welcomed on a dessert table for brunch, coffee or teatime, and dinner. I enjoy its simplicity but use your imagination on how to serve it according to the situation. A simple dusting of confectioner’s sugar or a dollop of softly whipped cream will go nicely. Or sliced as is won’t compromise its visual appeal. Choose either d’Anjou or Bosc pears if available, as they will hold up during the hour or so of baking, retaining both shape and some texture when fully baked. In comparison Bartlett pears can turn very soft and mushy. I usually load up on fresh cranberries as soon as I see them in stores. I keep a bag out for immediate use and toss the rest in the freezer, so cranberries are usually available at our house. If you don’t happen to have this small quantity on hand, substitute with raspberries or other fruit. Using frozen is fine, also. articles.text: If your parents are getting close to retirement age, or are already retired, it may be time to talk with them about financial and aging issues, some of which may involve difficult conversations. For the sake of everyone in your family, don’t avoid these “taboo” topics. You’ll need to be careful about approaching these subjects with your parents. Mention ahead of time that you’d like to talk to them about their future plans and reassure them that you want to understand their wishes, so their affairs will be taken care of as they would like. If your parents are agreeable, choose a location comfortable for them and ask whom they might like to invite (or not invite). Then, think about how to open the conversation, preferably not with what they want to do with their money – this could be interpreted as your seeking information about your inheritance or being skeptical about their financial decisions. Instead, build a broad-based discussion about their vision for their aging years. A series of shorter conversations may allow you to cover topics more comfortably, one by one, rather than trying to solve everything at once. Try to address these areas: • • Health care – You’ll want to learn if your parents have established the appropriate health-related legal documents – a health care power of attorney, which gives someone the authority to make important decisions about their medical care if they become unable to do so themselves, and a living will, which spells out the extraordinary medical treatments they may or may not want. Independence – As people age, they may begin to lose their independence. Have your parents considered any options for long-term care, such as a nursing home stay, or the services of a home health aide? And do they have plans in place? If they plan to receive support from family members,
articles.title: Don’t avoid ‘taboo’ topics with older parents

Pear Cranberry Cake – a holiday treat for all By Deborah Quok One of our favorite fall and winter fruit combinations is pears and cranberries. This cake speaks of the seasons and is welcomed on a dessert table for brunch, coffee or teatime, and dinner. I enjoy its simplicity but use your imagination on how to serve it according to the situation. A simple dusting of confectioner’s sugar or a dollop of softly whipped cream will go nicely. Or sliced as is won’t compromise its visual appeal. Choose either d’Anjou or Bosc pears if available, as they will hold up during the hour or so of baking, retaining both shape and some texture when fully baked. In comparison Bartlett pears can turn very soft and mushy. I usually load up on fresh cranberries as soon as I see them in stores. I keep a bag out for immediate use and toss the rest in the freezer, so cranberries are usually available at our house. If you don’t happen to have this small quantity on hand, substitute with raspberries or other fruit. Using frozen is fine, also. Pear Cranberry Cake Adapted from Back from Scratch INGREDIENTS • 1 cup unsalted butter, softened • 1 cup granulated sugar • 3 large eggs, room temperature • 2 cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 1/3 cup milk or half and half, room temperature Don’t avoid ‘taboo’ topics with older parents If your parents are getting close to retirement age, or are already retired, it may be time to talk with them about financial and aging issues, some of which may involve difficult conversations. For the sake of everyone in your family, don’t avoid these “taboo” topics. You’ll need to be careful about approaching these subjects with your parents. Mention ahead of time that you’d like to talk to them about their future plans and reassure them that you want to understand their wishes, so their affairs will be taken care of as they would like. If your parents are agreeable, choose a location comfortable for them and ask whom they might like to invite (or not invite). Then, think about how to open the conversation, preferably not with what they want to do with their money – this could be interpreted as your seeking information about your inheritance or being skeptical about their financial decisions. Instead, build a broad-based discussion about their vision for their aging years. A series of shorter conversations may allow you to cover topics more comfortably, one by one, rather than trying to solve everything at once. Try to address these areas: • • Health care – You’ll want to learn if your parents have established the appropriate health-related legal documents – a health care power of attorney, which gives someone the authority to make important decisions about their medical care if they become unable to do so themselves, and a living will, which spells out the extraordinary medical treatments they may or may not want. Independence – As people age, they may begin to lose their independence. Have your parents considered any options for long-term care, such as a nursing home stay, or the services of a home health aide? And do they have plans in place? If they plan to receive support from family members, • • • • • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1/2 teaspoon almond extract 1 large pear, d’Anjou or Bosc, cut into 12 wedges 1/4 cup cranberries, whole 1/4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the center position. Preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the sides and bottom of a 9-inch spring form pan. 2. In a small bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt. Set aside. 3. In a large mixing bowl, cream the softened butter and sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, 3 – 4 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add eggs, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Add vanilla and almond extracts and beat to incorporate. 4. Add about one-third of the flour mixture to the butter mixture, then half of the milk. Repeat with another one-third of the flour, the remaining milk, and finally the remaining flour; mixing just until combined after each addition. Do not over mix. 5. Transfer the batter into the prepared pan, smoothing the top to an even level. Arrange the pear slices in a decorative fashion, then distribute the cranberries. 6 Bake until lightly browned, about 30 minutes. Sprinkle with sliced almonds, and continue baking another 30 minutes, or until a wooden pick inserted in the center comes out clean. 7. Let cool in the pan for about 10 minutes, remove the sides of the springform and continue to cool slightly. The cake may be served warm or at room temperature. Add a dusting of confectioner’s sugar or softly whipped cream to serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. • • do their expectations match yours? Financial goals – Focusing on the personal and financial aspects of the legacy your parents want to leave can be a valuable conversation. Have your parents updated their will or other arrangements, such as a living trust? Have they named a financial power of attorney to make decisions on their behalf if they become incapacitated? Do they have the proper beneficiary designations on their insurance policies and retirement plan accounts? If you can position these issues as being more about your parents’ control over their financial destiny, rather than “who will get what,” you’ll more likely have a productive conversation. Last wishes – You’ll want to find out if your parents have left instructions in their will about their funerals and last wishes. Express to them that you, or another close family member, should know who is responsible for making sure their wishes are met. Money, independence and aging can be sensitive topics. Don’t think you have to go it alone. You can enlist help from another close family member. articles.text: Barbara Fox Roach passed away peacefully in her sleep in her beloved Piedmont home on Monday, November 8, 2021, after a courageous six-month battle with cancer. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne Kalmar, also of Piedmont. The two enjoyed 10 wonderful years together, traveling the world, vacationing at their homes in Carmel and Palm Desert, and playing golf with friends at Claremont Country Club in Oakland and Monterey Peninsula Country Club in Pebble Beach, until Arne’s passing in 2016. A life-long Republican and philanthropist, Barbara contributed to numerous charitable, community, and political organizations, including the Cancer League, the Oakland Museum, the Russian National Orchestra, the San Francisco Opera, the Oakland Symphony, the Oakland Zoo, and the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West in Cody, Wyoming. As a member of the board of the Oakland Zoo, Barbara played an important role in the zoo’s fundraising efforts and its transformation into a world-class institution. Her passion for politics eventually led her to work on the re-election campaign of Pete Wilson to the U.S. Senate and to Barbara Roach, a resident of Piedmont for 60 years, died on November 8 at age 90. become a member of the Lincoln Club of Northern California and the Media Research Group. Barbara will be remembered for her lively wit, vivacity, and friendly nature. She was always an engaged listener who loved to share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children – Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin Henry “Hank” Roeth (Haley), Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. Barbara was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Donations in Barbara’s memory may be made to the Oakland Zoo, the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West, or a charity of choice.

articles.text: Bill Blackwell died peacefully on Thanksgiving in the Piedmont home he shared with his wife, Marjorie for 41 years. Born William Dinsmore Blackwell in Indianapolis, Indiana on August 25, 1939, he was the son of Raymond Earl Blackwell and Dorothy Dinsmore Bloom. At age 5, his family moved to Louisville, Kentucky. An architect by profession, Bill had a diverse and successful career that included numerous design and planning projects in the U.S. and abroad, as well as other creative activities, over a span of 60 years. His work was his life. From a small public high school in Anchorage, Kentucky, he won an appointment to the U.S. Naval Academy in 1947. After completing 2½ years at the Academy, he transferred to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to pursue his dream of becoming an architect. He received a bachelor’s degree in architecture from MIT in 1953 and was immediately inducted into the Army. As a young sergeant in Korea, he was able to contribute to the design and relocation of Signal Corps facilities under wartime conditions. Following discharge, he returned to Louisville and worked for three years with a prominent architectural firm. His projects included a master plan for the University of Louisville, designs of a student union building and of a large Methodist church. In 1958, he moved to California and, under the GI Bill, earned a master’s degree in architecture from the University of California, Berkeley. In 1960, Bill joined the architectural firm of Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill in San Francisco. Over six years, his projects included design of the structural research laboratory at the UC Richmond Field Station, a complex radiochemistry laboratory at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, and a conceptual plan for the redevelopment of Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House to the Capitol in Washington, DC. In 1966, he joined the San Fra ncisco Redevelopment Agency to work on planning and design of the Western Addition Redevelopment Area. His efforts resulted in deleting widening of Turk Street and reducing parking requirements, making 17 blocks of housing economically feasible. Bill recognized early on the need for more housing in the City. In 1972, he wrote a growth scenario for San Francisco, based on a grid pattern, that would enable more people to live within walking distance of neighborhood shops, parks, transportation and other amenities. He also drafted a zoning ordinance, passed by the San Francisco Planning Commission, that allows higher densities through development of narrow-lot townhouses. Bill was a craftsman who designed and built his own furniture. He had a one-man show of his furniture designs as part of the Bay Area Art Explosion in 1967. Subsequently, he was Bill Blackwell at a recent 4th of July Parade in Piedmont. invited to join the Market Street Joint Venture Architects and was a lead designer in 1969 of the traffic signals and other items of Market Street’s outdoor furniture, some of it still in place. In 1973, Bill joined the architectural/engineering division of the Bechtel Corporation, then headquartered in San Francisco. Projects included the design of an airport reception pavilion for the late King Hussein of Jordan, participation in planning the new city of Jubail, Saudi Arabia, classified projects for several government agencies, facility planning for IBM and Applied Materials, proposals for reconstruction of the Pentagon and redevelopment of Mather Air Force Base in Sacramento. He was rewarded by Bechtel for engineering excellence. Bill is the author of Geometry in Architecture, published by John Wiley & Sons in 1984 and translated into a Spanish version by Editorial Trillas in Mexico. He was working on a new book, Explorations in Geometry, at the time of his death. In 1986, he created and published a unique world map centered on the Bay Area, which was sold by the former Random House map store in San Francisco and other Bay Area map/book stores. Bill’s interest in color and symmetry led to creation of geometric paintings that were exhibited at the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute in Berkeley, Berkeley YWCA, Route One Gallery at Pt. Reyes Station, Hearst Art Gallery at St. Mary’s College, the Metro Center in downtown Oakland, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art sales and rental gallery, and Piedmont Center for the Arts. Bill was a man of ideas. In 2009, during a debate over design of a new Transbay Transit Terminal that included costly construction of underground space for future High Speed Rail (HSR), he proposed bringing HSR from San Jose to an expanded Caltrain station at Fourth and Townsend streets to save billions in underground track and terminal construction in downtown San Francisco and provide needed space for taxis, parking and local buses Bill Blackwell early in his career as an architect with Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. at the HSR station. If Bill had his way, daylight saving time (if at all) would begin on the first day of spring and end on the first day of fall; calendars would begin on Monday, the beginning of the work week, and end on Sunday; political campaigns would last no more than three months; the NCAA basketball tournament would pit a oneseed against a nine, a two-seed against a ten, etc. to make the first round more meaningful. Bill was always well prepared for meetings (business and social) and liked to arrive early to “get the best seat” at the table. He often recalled with pleasure the many personal encounters and friendships he made along his path through life, especially those that involved ice cream and cookies. Bill Blackwell is survived by Marjorie Leland Blackwell, his wife of 41 years, and eight nieces and nephews, who live in the Midwest and on the East Coast. He is predeceased by his sister, Margaret Emily Koenig, and brother-in-law Rowland Koenig. The family is grateful to dear friends for their love, support, and kindness during a difficult time, and to Continuum Hospice for excellent care. To remember Bill, please plant a tree in his name or make a contribution to the math department at Franklin College, Franklin, Indiana, or to a charity of your choice. A memorial service will be held at a later date. For information, please email marjb@sbcglobal.net.

articles.text: James (“Jim”) Chapple Soper, a longtime resident of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully with his children by his side on November 15, 2021. He was 92. Born on January 15, 1929 in Billings, Montana, he was the son of Erastus Burrows Soper III and Dorothy Chapple Soper. A resident of Piedmont beginning in 1939, Jim attended Wildwood Elementary School and Piedmont High School and was an Eagle Scout. His family moved to Taft in Kern County for his senior year of high school, and he graduated from Taft High School before returning to Piedmont. He went on to Stanford University where he was a member of the Sigma Nu fraternity and the Army ROTC. He graduated with a Bachelor of Arts degree. Jim developed many lifelong friendships at Stanford and remained an active alum. While in his third year at Stanford University School of Law, Jim met the love of his life, Suzanne Simon. After graduating from law school, Jim and Suzi were married in Pomona on October 24, 1953. The couple spent their first years of marriage at Fort Sill Oklahoma, and Copperas Cove, Texas, where Jim was stationed as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Army. Following his service, Jim returned to live in Piedmont and began his career as an attorney in Oakland. Jim and Suzi raised their family on Oakmont Avenue, the street where Jim grew up and where his parents continued to live into their senior years. Jim and Suzi lived in two houses on Oakmont. When they outgrew one, they moved across the street. They dearly loved their Oakmont neighbors. Jim began his career at Fitzgerald Abbott & Beardsley (now Donahue Fitzgerald) in Oakland in 1956, and continued to practice law there for 60 years, retiring at age 86. Jim chaired the firm’s Business and Corporate Transactions and Estates & Trusts Practice Groups for many years. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had another strong turnout of 29 walkers on November 17. One of the areas they had not visited was the Sandringham/Selborne/Estates/ Inverleith loop near the top of Hampton Avenue. The walkers said they were ready for the challenge, and off they went on one of the longest walk of the year and one with some steep climbs. Before they began, Recreation Department Supervisor Eva Phalen told the walkers about new, unique adult programs developed for 2022. The higher elevation in this section of Piedmont seems to make the color of the leaves on the trees a little more vibrant late in the fall season. Realizing that this might be the last really good Wednesday for fall colors, seeing some beautiful trees was another excellent reason to take this walk. The long line of walkers went up Highland Avenue with Hampton Park their initial destination. They took their usual route down Sheridan and up Wildwood Avenues. A quick passage through the always lovely Hall Fenway took the walkers to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. They went past Crocker Park (also known to locals as Bear Park). then crossed La Salle Avenue, going through the columns that marked the entrance to the early Piedmont St. James Woods neighborhood. The boundaries of this large development are still marked by original, tile inlay sidewalks. The walkers continued their ascent of Hampton and came to a set of trees with striking red leaves that were more vibrant than those of the trees below. The group came to Sandringham and went up to the Marlborough Court cul-desac, and then another half block to Sandringham Place, another cul-de-sac. Along the street there is a medium sized tree whose bunches overhang the sidewalk and create what is almost like a leaf tunnel. When the group came to Selborne Drive they stopped to admire a beautiful, clear view of the Bay in the distance. Going up Selborne took the walkers to Estates Drive and a short climb up to upper and lower Inverleith Terrace. The walkers took Inverleith back to Hampton, and along the way passed liquidambar trees with more vibrant red leaves and a bottlebrush tree with a very active hummingbird. The group went down La Salle and St. James Drive, back to Hampton and retraced their steps to the Exedra. It had been a little over a five-mile walk, the longest Wednesday walk that anyone could remember, but very enjoyable – and probably good preparation for the Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A resident of Piedmont beginning in 1939, Jim attended Wildwood Elementary School and Piedmont High School and was an Eagle Scout. He went on to Stanford University where he was a member of the Sigma Nu fraternity and the Army ROTC. He graduated with a Bachelor of Arts degree. The couple spent their first years of marriage at Fort Sill Oklahoma, and Copperas Cove, Texas, where Jim was stationed as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Army. Jim and Suzi raised their family on Oakmont Avenue, the street where Jim grew up and where his parents continued to live into their senior years. Jim and Suzi lived in two houses on Oakmont. articles.text: On October 7, the Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) recommended that the City Council adopt a Safer Streets Plan with four additional recommendations. Committee member Eugene Brown said, “appropriate considerations and recommendations have been made and I would look at this as a mid-point in a continually evolving process that will continue to be evaluated and modified as circumstances dictate”. Pursuant to California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15072, the city staff prepared an Initial Study for public review. Having received no comments, staff is recommending that City Council adopt a Negative Declaration based on the Initial Study. On Monday, December 6, the City Council will consider adopting a resolution to approve the draft plan. Following adoption, implementation of the Plan’s recommendations, programs and policies will begin. City staff will continue to monitor existing bike and pedestrian traffic conditions in the City. “The Piedmont Safer Streets report is a vital document that will act as a blueprint for prioritizing the locations and the types of bicycle and pedestrian safety improvements over the next five years. Public Works and Engineering look forward to addressing the issues identified at the highest priority locations first and making this community a safer place to walk and bike”, said Daniel Gonzales, City’s Public Works Director. The Final Draft Plan is available for public review on the City’s website. The December 6 City Council meeting agenda and staff report for the Plan will be posted on the City’s website no later than Friday, December 3. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, December 1, 2021 City to consider OK for Safer Streets Plan on Dec. 6 On October 7, the Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) recommended that the City Council adopt a Safer Streets Plan with four additional recommendations. Committee member Eugene Brown said, “appropriate considerations and recommendations have been made and I would look at this as a mid-point in a continually evolving process that will continue to be evaluated and modified as circumstances dictate”. Pursuant to California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15072, the city staff prepared an Initial Study for public review. Having received no comments, staff is recommending that City Council adopt a Negative Declaration based on the Initial Study. On Monday, December 6, the City Council will consider adopting a resolution to approve the draft plan. Following adoption, implementation of the Plan’s recommendations, programs and policies will begin. City staff will continue to monitor existing bike and pedestrian traffic conditions in the City. “The Piedmont Safer Streets report is a vital document that will act as a blueprint for prioritizing the locations and the types of bicycle and pedestrian safety improvements over the next five years. Public Works and Engineering look forward to addressing the issues identified at the highest priority locations first and making this community a safer place to walk and bike”, said Daniel Gonzales, City’s Public Works Director. The Final Draft Plan is available for public review on the City’s website. The December 6 City Council meeting agenda and staff report for the Plan will be posted on the City’s website no later than Friday, December 3. Send any comments or questions on the Plan to Associate Planner Gopika Nair at gnair@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: As of November 30, all but 14 Piedmont students aged 12 and older have provided proof of COVID-19 vaccination to the school district. It equates to a vaccination rate of 99% among the 1,222 students in that age bracket. The deadline to submit proof of vaccination was November 17 and is mandatory to attend school in person. On January 5, 2022, the first day of the second semester, students without proof of vaccination or a medical exemption from a physician, will be referred to independent study. The school district has not received any formal submissions of medical exemptions. “As of [November 30], we are not aware of any student who is definitely opting for Independent Study starting January 5,” said PUSD Communication Director Brian Killgore. The school district mandated vaccinations for all age eligible students on September 22, and three weeks later extended the requirement to teachers and anyone working on or visiting school campuses. Children aged 5-11 became eligible to receive the Pfizer covid vaccine on November 3, and the district’s vaccination policy immediately included them in the mandate. These students have until January 14 to provide proof of full vaccination (defined as two weeks after a second dose). The district will send families with students aged 5-11 directions for submitting proof of vaccination later this week.
articles.title: Only 14 students age 12 and older yet to submit vaccination proof

articles.text: The ginkgo trees around the city Sent their leaves cascading on the lonely sidewalks. The breeze of fall intensifies To raw and brisk now, matching our communal moods, And tears at banners left in protests Of a nation keen divided When the thousands marched for social justice While recalling Mr. Floyd. The willows are emitting sighs of deep despair. A sharp-edged crescent moon with sickle points Admonishes: The easy days are past, Stand ready for the rising tides. Is it Lincoln’s statue showing furrowed brow in sudden consternation When confronted by a virus most notorious Locking up our nation’s prized museums And shutting down too many schools As tokens of this viral hour of infamy? Citizens afar are face to face with Frequent fearsome cyclone storms That, one behind the other, rage, While twisters inland Heedlessly devour homes and hospitals. California’s gobbled up by wildfires Leaving ashen villages and vineyards Never burned before, then stuffing in the wake A suffocating smoke to choke the innocent and elderly. The world has stopped abruptly in its tracks. The jovial corner druggist, broke, Closed up his shop for good. Our spunky third-grade teacher with her babe in arms Stood hours long in unemployment lines. We need a spark of newfound courage now emerging From survivors of this snake-bit era, Intently sweeping out the trash of past complacency, Intent to win this battle with Corona. These times will test our fortitude Till peaceful armies of our solons Sound a conch horn to inaugurate a budding era And unleash our nation’s wonders in totality again For all of us to see, assimilate and feel. Posterity awaits to weigh our strength Confronted by tsunamis of adversity. Paul Hertelendy is a classical music and dance reviewer, a published poet, and a Piedmont resident. articles.text: Editor: In 15 years what is the probability that the State will mandate that all non-essential facilities be disconnected from the electrical grid and the natural gas distribution network and either be operated off-grid using energy generated and stored on site or be closed? Will a public aquatic facility be considered essential? What is your level of faith in the unpleasant predictions currently made by the climate models? We should scale down the 2016 vision for our new aquatic facility in order to minimize its energy use. The first question should be, what is our energy budget (measured in MWh not $)? Within that budget which of the many community needs can be met? What can be built and operated now and be made to evolve smoothly in the future, given foreseeable technology improvements? The current on-going process is backward. It was appropriate when resources were infinite and there was no need to choose between powering schools or pools. The one outlined above will ensure that the City can afford the operating costs in the short term and keep the pool open in the long term. Frugality is a forgotten, ancient virtue whose value will become more and more apparent with time. –Bernard Pech For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has experienced a slight increase in crime in July, August, and September compared with the same period in 2020. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers detailed crime data at a city council meeting on November 15. There were 253 reported offenses in the third quarter of 2020, as compared to 267 reportable offenses in 2021, showing a slight increase. Violent crime numbers have remained flat, but the city has seen a substantial increase in larceny theft. In July, August, and September, there were a total of 59 thefts reported to the department. What continues to drive the increase in larceny is the phenomenon of catalytic converter thefts, Chief Bowers explained. The catalytic converter houses precious metals that are harvested once they are stolen. “We caught several people in the process of stealing them, or caught [them] on our license plate readers. It’s something many regional communities are experiencing, and it’s very frustrating. It was not surprising to us to find that there is organization to [the crime].” “We find them, take them to custody, but shortly thereafter [the suspects] will be released,” Bowers said. “If they don’t have a criminal history, they could be released fairly quickly. [Crime] organizations are bailing them out in these catalytic converter thefts.” According to the department’s Uniform Crime Report third quarter comparison, there were more crimes overall in 2020 and 2021 as compared to 2019. There were 86 and 85 reportable offenses in 2021 and 2020, respectively, and 69 in 2019. “To deal with these [issues], the department continues to leverage an awareness that we need to be out-and-about, present, and driving around,” Chief Bowers said. Bowers also credited the departments use of technology, including the Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) program. The department made 24 arrests through the third quarter of 2021, an increase from 14 arrests made during the same period last year. “The APLRs help prevent crime,” Bowers said, a program the city has maintained since 2013. Mayor Teddy Gray King asked Bowers to provide details on the program’s impact, given that safety camera programs can be a divisive issue in some communities. “It’s a tool that is great for law enforcement, but a tool that many people have questions about, and rightfully so,” Bowers said. “We have the absolute privilege to use this [APLR] technology… we have to continue to be as transparent as possible in how we’re using this. That was the thought behind the transparency portal.” The department has maintained a transparency portal for over a year that can be found by visiting https://piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/police/ transparency_portal. The public is invited to provide feedback, comments, and concerns about the ALPR program, in partnership with Flock Safety. The department is currently in the process of implementing a public safety camera program, approved by City Council earlier this year. The current phase of the implementation consists of working with the data fiber provider and utility company to bring the necessary infrastructure to camera locations; Bowers noted the department’s appreciation for the assistance of the city Public Works Department and Director Daniel Gonzales in the process. Juvenile officer Officer Nicole Casalnuovo has rotated out of the Juvenile Officer position which has been filled by Officer Hugo Diaz. Chief Bowers added that school district administrative staff were included on the interview panels and “provided important input in the evaluation” process. “[Diaz] has a substantial background of working with youth, has volunteered with at-risk youth programs in Oakland, and he’s very adept at working with teenagers,” Chief Bowers said. “No surprise, he did exceptionally well in the interviews. The overarching focus and goal is to guide [youth]. Hugo has been great, and his communication with the [PUSD] Wellness Center and school staff has been focused on team-building, to help young people in crises.” The department uses funding from the Department of Justice Tobacco Grant to re-stablish the Juvenile Officer position in 2017. The department reapplied for the grant in 2021 but did not receive funding. Bowers explained that he has maintained communications with the grant administration and intends to reapply during the next filing period.
articles.title: Police Dept. 3rd quarter crime stats

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8, at 5 p.m. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions may contact the City Clerk’s office at 510-420-3040. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. City seeks volunteers for Bond Oversight Committee By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8, at 5 p.m. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: On November 10 the Piedmont School Board approved a universal set of “Single Plans for Student Achievement” goals for all three Piedmont elementary schools. Beach School Principal Michael Corritone presented a report developed by administrators and faculty. Corritone began by reviewing the goals from the last school year, 2020-2021. At that time, the elementary schools’ first goal of Single Plans for Student Achievement focused on continuity of instruction despite online-only distance learning. The second goal was to plan to safely and efficiently switch to hybrid learning. Literacy and mathematics, were the main targets at elementary school last year and were measured by meeting “Essential Learning Outcomes.” “Of course things were unbelievably challenging for everybody,” Corritone stated. “In the end, we were really pleased 85% of students reached those [goals] in mathematics. Those that didn’t meet all those targets were referred to summer school.” The new goals presented showed a marked change from the pandemic-based goals of the previous year. Goal One: “All students and staff will feel physically safe and emotionally supported as part of a caring and inclusive community.” Efforts towards this goal, include the quarterly administration of the Social Emotional Health Screeners. Family Identity Surveys with a diversity, equity and inclusion focus were also sent out at the start of the year. A total of 29% of all elementary school families responded to the Identity Survey which had 12 multiple choice or open-ended questions. On a question regarding a “sense of connection with the community” 30-39% percent responded with either “kind of”, “not very much at all”, or “not at all.” Havens Principal Anne Dolid aims for 50% participation in the next iteration of the survey and less that 10% of families describing their community connection as “kind of”, “not very much at all”, or “not at all.” Goal Two: “All students will engage in relevant learning experiences that foster life-long curiosity, creativity, collaboration, critical thinking, communications and responsible citizenship.” Corritone explained efforts toward this goal included the implementation of a new science curriculum adopted from Carolina Smithsonian. Elementary students have three new units of study: Physical, Earth and Life Sciences. Engineering will be added next year. Goal Three: “Teachers and staff, with district partners will ensure an outstanding educational experience for every student through collaboration, innovation, and professional growth.” These “Single Plans” were primarily developed on Wednesday afternoons when elementary students get out early for staff development.

articles.text: A laser cutter was delivered to the new engineering lab at Piedmont High School’s engineering lab in the STEAM building on November 17. It was in use by students for the past year by Piedmont students in the garage of John Lambert and his wife Helen Potter, key organizers of the Makers group in town. “It was pretty tough to move. It weighs 700 pounds. When we installed it into position in our garage it had 3/4” inch bolts that go down onto the floor, so we had to crank those feet back up onto the casters, prior to moving it,” Lambert explained. With the help of four school district staff members, Lambert and Potter loaded the laser cutter onto a truck for the four-block ride to the high school campus. The machine is a Nova 35, CO2 laser produced by Thunder Laser, capable of cutting anything non-metallic. The laser requires only a regular 120 volt circuit and pulls 100 watts. It cuts by burning through materials at the thickness of a human hair. A separate unit called a chiller cools the CO2 glass tube down so it doesn’t break. An air compressor pumps air through the laser head to keep smoke out of the mirror and a large exhaust fan removes the smoke produced by the burning of the laser. Lambert has been indispensable in the setup process. The laser cutter needed to be perfectly level prior to operation. Since it is now at the school, the power switch needed to need to be replaced for safety with a keyed switch. Lambert ordered the specific part and installed the keyed switch himself. “It took me about an hour to take it apart and replace it, but the school district was extremely happy,” he said. The Makers have mainly been cutting parts for prototyping with the laser cutter out of cardboard, plywood, and acrylic. The actual mechanisms used on Makers robots are easier to produce out of metal or other materials once the prototypes are in hand. The funds for the laser cutter were raised through donations to Piedmont Makers, about $10,000. “This one (cutter) can’t do metal. We are actually looking for one that can, a fiber laser, which is probably our next purchase, but they are more expensive, in the range of $50,000-$60,000,” Lambert said with a smile. Currently, Physics teacher Marna Chamberlain has a guitar-making class that will use the laser cutter. Her class has curriculum relating audio to physics by building speakers. Their class will eventually design and build their own guitars, with the help of the laser cutter. There are many more application for the laser cutter the school can utilize. “We sent the school some examples of a biology teacher who was cutting the shapes of human organs out of felt, and using those to build the intestinal system or circulatory system in biology,” explained Potter. Piedmont Makers has seen exponential growth in participants, and is now has 50 teams and 340 students participating. The addition of the new laser cutter will help answer the swelling demand for more engineering resources in Piedmont. John Lambert (front) and PUSD facility staff carefully position the 700-pound laser cutter onto a lift gate for transport to PHS.
articles.title: Laser cutter delivered to high school STEAM lab

It was in use by students for the past year by Piedmont students in the garage of John Lambert and his wife Helen Potter, key organizers of the Makers group in town. “It was pretty tough to move. It weighs 700 pounds. When we installed it into position in our garage it had 3/4” inch bolts that go down onto the floor, so we had to crank those feet back up onto the casters, prior to moving it,” Lambert explained. With the help of four school district staff members, Lambert and Potter loaded the laser cutter onto a truck for the four-block ride to the high school campus. The machine is a Nova 35, CO2 laser produced by Thunder Laser, capable of cutting anything non-metallic. The laser requires only a regular 120 volt circuit and pulls 100 watts. It cuts by burning through materials at the thickness of a human hair. A separate unit called a chiller cools the CO2 glass tube down so it doesn’t break. An air compressor pumps air through the laser head to keep smoke out of the mirror and a large exhaust fan removes the smoke produced by the burning of the laser. Lambert has been indispensable in the setup process. The laser cutter needed to be perfectly level prior to operation. Since it is now at the school, the power switch needed to need to be replaced for safety with a keyed switch. Lambert ordered the specific part and installed the keyed switch himself. “It took me about an hour to take it apart and replace it, but the school district was extremely happy,” he said. The Makers have mainly been cutting parts for prototyping with the laser cutter out of cardboard, plywood, and acrylic. The actual mechanisms used on Makers robots are easier to produce out of metal or other materials once the prototypes are in hand. articles.text: Dr. Laura Huppert M.D., the Piedmont High Valedictorian in 2006, has now added published author to her long list of accolades with the release of Huppert’s Notes: Pathophysiology and Clinical Pearls for Internal Medicine. The text, published by McGraw-Hill, is a condensed medicine reference for medical students and internal medicine residents and is based upon her own personal notes. After excelling at Piedmont, Huppert attended Harvard University where she earned All-American honors in rowing and a B.A. in Molecular and Cellular Biology. She attended Harvard Medical School, and then moved back to the Bay Area to join the Internal Medicine residency program at UCSF. She currently is in her third year of Hematology/Oncology Fellowship at UCSF. The book’s genesis arose at Harvard, where, as a medical student, she searched for a succinct medical resource to aid in her studies but could not find a source that met her needs. So she began her own set of notes, which she compiled throughout medical school and residency at UCSF. While taking an extra year to teach in UCSF’s Chief Laura Huppert’s newly published medical textbook Huppert’s Notes functions as a one-stop shop and memory aid for medical students and internal medicine residents with all the must-know facts. Residency Program, an editor at McGraw-Hill saw her notes and approached her about publishing them. “There is so much to learn in internal medicine, and as we continue to advance our understanding of medicine it is only becoming more complex. Therefore, it is becoming more challenging to distill the key concepts in a way that students can approach it,” she said. Huppert identified a need in the medical community and filled it. “There is an intellectual jump from learning the basic biology of heart attacks and pneumonia to all of a sudden knowing how to care for somebody with these conditions in a clinical setting. I wanted something to bridge those gaps to help students become good doctors without using 10 different resources,” Huppert said. Many of the big medical textbooks are several thousands of pages. With the helpful reviews and edits from a team of colleagues and UCSF faculty Huppert’s Notes, at 464 pages, transforms her actual notes and hand sketches into a standardized authority that can fit in a lab coat. I knew I wanted to try to do independent research and he helped me take it to the next level by endorsing me to get a position in a lab and by mentoring me with my science fair projects,” Huppert recalled.
