articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Members of the Pacific Boys Choir will perform at this year’s Montclair Village Holiday Stroll. The season of caring is upon us and Montclair Village is ready to celebrate its return during the upcoming 2021 Holiday Stroll on Thursday, December 9 from 5:30-8:00 p.m. Since COVID came on the scene 19 months ago it’s become clearer than ever how important the Village is, not only as a vibrant commercial center and provider of essential services, but as a community gathering place for people who care about each other. The Montclair Village Association is excitedly planning the 18th Annual Holiday Stroll and invites community members to make the Village a December destination for festive shopping, dining and overall merriment. Some of the highlights you can expect are: • Performances by the Pacific Boys Choir and Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees • Strolling with costumed student dancers from the Oakland Ballet and a fanciful Ice Queen on stilts • Family photos with Santa in a Winter Wonderland setting • Toy donation drive hosted by the Oakland Fire Department • Shopping and dining in festively decorated retail businesses • Commemorative mug sales along with Village Plaza updates • Opportunity to chat with District 4’s City Councilmember Sheng Thao It’s a wonderful thing that so many local businesses have survived the last 19 months and that joyful traditions like the Holiday Stroll are returning, especially during this time of year. As Montclair Village Association’s Executive Director Daniel Swafford stated, “Businesses are versatile — what they do really well is persevere and adjust to changing times, but we have to look to the fact that we are in this together, and what creates our sense of community, are the unique experiences and relationships our neighborhood businesses provide.” Montclair Village is looking forward to your support and participation in celebrating community by offering everything it can to ensure this season of caring is a special one. For more information about the festivities being planned, follow Montclair Village on Instagram and Facebook and visit MontclairVillage.com regularly for updates.
articles.title: Holiday Stroll returns to Montclair Village

articles.text: Possibility of more than 2,000 runners this year Thousands of people from Piedmont and beyond will converge near Piedmont Park tomorrow, November 25, for the 20th annual Turkey Trot. The 5-kilometer race will begin at 8:30 a.m., and all signs are that it could draw more than 2,000 runners. The popular Thanksgiving morning event took a hiatus last year due to COVID-19 and gathering restrictions. This year, it returns with all the same traditions. Runners will meet before the race begins in front of the Exedra at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Coffee and hot chocolate will be served at Corcoran Group, formerly Highland Partners, at the beginning and the end of the race. There will also be plenty of refreshments afterwards. The 5-kilometer race will begin along Highland Avenue and continue onto Wildwood Avenue and La Salle Avenue, before looping back along Sea View and Mountain Avenues. The route is considered a good workout for serious runners and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their time. For many others, it’s simply a lively social event before the Thanksgiving festivities begin at home. Although anyone can join the race, those who have registered are in the running to win some sweet prizes. (For registration, jersey and bib pickup information, see separate article on page 1.) Winners will be announced at an awards ceremony after the last runner crosses the finish line. Prizes are awarded to the top three runners in each age category, from youth to seniors over 80. All winners will receive a racing cap, a fresh bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers, and a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery. The overall male and female winners will receive a turkey from Village Market, and running shoes from Transports. Proceeds from the Turkey Trot support Piedmont High School cross country and track-and-field teams. The bulk of proceeds are given to the City of Piedmont to fund sports facilities maintenance.
articles.title: On Thanksgiving, it’s Turkey Trot time in Piedmont

articles.text: Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their chairs and music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce – musically – the start of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. The big treat for runners (and spectators) this year will be the sign of eight symphony musicians from the Bay Area on hand to play music written for hunting horns 200 years ago. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a retired French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument they all are pitched in the key of D, they all have the same length of tubing – approximately 14 feet. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmont resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Piedmont resident Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, the mastermind. As the word spread among horn players, the group has grown to an ensemble of eight. that would communicate to hunters various aspects of the hunt. However, over more than two centuries music was developed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see one with a very large circumference, called the trompe de chasse “Dauphine.” The trompe de chasse d’Orleans has a smaller circumference. The trompe de chasse Lorraine resembles an animal horn. But because

pages.text: Wednesday, November 24, 2021 11 Scout Tree Lot Continued from page 1 season rapidly approached, we met weekly, addressing every aspect of the lot from ordering, to permits, hiring drivers, organizing Troop participation, building the chute, operating the forklift and power equipment, lighting, marketing, computer systems, training board members to cashier, WiFi, etc…the list makes my head spin. Behind the curtain I found the most dedicated group of people — in fact, two members of the committee have been working on the Tree Lot for roughly 50 years each: Dave Ashton since 1973 and Kevin Fischer since 1968–both started at the lot as Scouts. Right behind them at 40 plus years are Brian Kelleher and Greg Pike. Relative newcomers, Mark Dukas, Troy Alering, and Chris Lee have chalked up 20 or 30 years, but who’s counting? And former Tree Lot Chairmen, Ronnie Baum and Jim Reilly have been regularly tapped by Tom Smegal as he learns the ropes as head honcho this year. Kevin Fischer is in charge of organizing the Order of the Arrow to set up and take down the lot, including setting up the electrical and lighting plans. Dave Ashton is in charge of ordering all the trees. Beginning in March and April each year, he’s in contact with growers throughout California and Oregon. Brian Kelleher has been ordering all the wreaths – magnolia, mixed cedar and fir, and candle wreaths for many, many years. He likes this role because it’s fun to work with his old Scouting Tree Lot Chair Tom Smegal (left) and Immediate Past Tree Lot Chair Jim Riley survey the tree lot after it was set up on Saturday, November 20. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, November 24, 2021 HIKING WITH JON Chasing the sunset at Mission Peak By Jonathan Comeaux Mission Peak Summit is among the most popular trails in the East Bay Regional Park District and considered the most frequented attraction in the City of Fremont. On a Sunday morning and early afternoon, the location can become a highway of foot traffic, bikers, families, and dog walkers making their way to the Mission Peak Summit Pole for a photo opportunity. However, making your way to the Mission Peak Trailhead by 3 p.m. allows for a more secluded trek. The bonus is that it provides a striking view of a burning orange sunset over the Bay Area as the sun departs below the mountains surrounding the South Bay Peninsula. Standing at the Summit Pole, the view overlooks Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge with the Dumbarton Bridge and Fremont further to your right. You can watch the The view from the Mission Peak’s Summit Pole with Fremont off in the distance. Staff Photos The view of the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, with the Dumbarton Bridge, and a golden California sky. The view of the East Bay after 5:00 p.m. The rolling hills of the Mission Peak Regional Park. The sun creeping below the mountains surrounding the South Bay Peninsula. lights go on from Hayward to Union City, with a glimpse of the San Mateo Bridge and San Francisco off in the distance. To the South are Milpitas, the cityscape feeding toward San Jose, and the remaining Mission Peak Regional Preserve. Turning to the East you will see the rolling hills of the Sunol Regional Wilderness and Ohlone Regional Wilderness. A normal visit to the 2,520- foot summit, such as our visit in March 2020, would be difficult to keep a 6-foot distance for those who are COVID-19 conscious. This time, however, it wasn’t difficult to keep ample space from fellow patrons on the wide gravel trail despite passing 170 hikers on the way up. Instead of the usual mass gathering at the Summit Pole, there were never more than 10 people, giving us a surprising opportunity to snap a few shots. A dozen night-owl hikers were still trekking up to the summit on our way back down. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up the 3.25-mile trail on the way to Mission Peak, elevation 2,500 feet. With a flashlight in hand, there was never a point when we would get too far ahead or too far behind other hikers, providing a feeling of safety under the night sky. Be sure to pack plenty of water to stay hydrated, add some granola or source of energy, and a charged battery for videos of an unforgettable sunset. This hill means you’re on the home stretch towards the summit. Hikers often pass by cows and calves grazing in the fields. The rocky cliffs of the Mission Peak Regional Park towards the summit.

articles.text: Stein leads with 2nd place finish; Black, Oesterer qualify as individuals Piedmont’s cross-country teams returned to Hayward High to toe the line for the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship on Saturday, November 20. The boys’ team placed 3rd out of 19 schools and earned a trip to the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno this Saturday, November 27. It will be the first appearance at the State Meet for the boys’ team since 2017. The girls’ team narrowly missed going to State, placing 4th among 13 schools. However, its lead runners, Ellie Black and Josie Oesterer, both qualified as individuals. It is the first time in 10 years the PHS girls’ team has not qualified for the State championship. Jack Stein and Ellie Black led the way for their teams, notching personal records in the process. Stein continued a highly successful season by placing 2nd overall in a field of 144 runners with a time of 15:29.4. He improved his personal record time by six seconds, eclipsing Reece Proctor’s time in 2016 by three seconds for the current course record at Hayward High since its reconstruction in 2016. “My goal coming in was to qualify for state with a top-three finish, and I also wanted to beat Reece Proctor’s course record. I was two seconds away in the WACC Championship and I really wanted to get his time. It feels awesome,” said Stein. “Reece’s team was one we all looked up to. He was a star and we heard his name all the time,” added Stein. Crosby Freeman set the PHS record at the North Coast Section meet in 2001 with a time of 15:15. Behind Freeman is Mark Ceraldi in 2005 with a time of 15:24. Stein now ranks in at No. 3 and Proctor No. 4 All-Time at the NCS meet on the course at Hayward, but Stein is now the record holder on the revised course. Ellie Black places 4th at NCS Black was 4th overall among 105 runners, finishing with a time of 18:10.7. Oesterer earned the final qualification spot for Fresno by finishing 12th in 19:07.6. “I definitely looked up the other girls in the race and what their best times were this season, so I kind of knew what to expect,” Black said. “My plan for the first mile was to make sure I didn’t go out too fast and die out in the race. I tried to get up the hills as fast as I could,” she said describing her strategy mile by mile. She missed the early portion of the season rehabbing from an injury, but retuned when she was 100 percent. The added strength after recovery has led to successive personal records at the Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Piedmont’s boys’ cross country runners wear their bronze medals after placing third at the North Coast Section championships and qualified for the State Championship this Saturday, November 27 in Fresno. Pictured are: Julien Lee (left), Cooper Downing, Alex Ware, Xander Schulte-Sasse, Parker Long, Christian Taylor, and Jack Stein. Jack Stein leads a pack of runners at Hayward High. Piedmont’s girls’ cross-country team at the starting line of the North Coast Section championships November 20 at Hayward High. Pictured are: Josie Oesterer (942), Ellie Black, Camille Snyder, Jamie Schwarz, and Ella Yasar. WACC Championship on November 6 with a time of 18:38.6, and now demolishing that time at the NCS Finals. “My overall goal for this season was to run healthy, and once I got going I was setting PRs; it felt really good,” she added, Looking ahead to the CIF State Meet in Fresno this weekend, both Stein and Black are keeping valuable details in mind regarding the course. “I’m definitely hoping for a PR but getting around that course in 16 minutes would be awesome. Woodward Park is a tough course with a lot of hills. Stein leads with 2nd place finish; Black, Oesterer qualify as individuals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s cross-country teams returned to Hayward High to toe the line for the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship on Saturday, November 20. The boys’ team placed 3rd out of 19 schools and earned a trip to the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno this Saturday, November 27. It will be the first appearance at the State Meet for the boys’ team since 2017. The girls’ team narrowly missed going to State, placing 4th among 13 schools. However, its lead runners, Ellie Black and Josie Oesterer, both qualified as individuals. It is the first time in 10 years the PHS girls’ team has not qualified for the State championship. Jack Stein and Ellie Black led the way for their teams, notching personal records in the process. Stein continued a highly successful season by placing 2nd overall in a field of 144 runners with a time of 15:29.4. articles.text: Former Piedmont tennis player Mackie McDonald is currently ranked No. 55 on the ATP World Tour, one ranking below his career high. Without any remaining ATP Tournaments for 2021, the 26-year old pro will return in January 2022 and will undoubtedly appear in the Australian Open on January 17-30. ATP 250 events like the Antalya Open from Jan. 4-11, or the Murray River Open are typical preparatory trials ahead of the Grand Slam in Australia. Since his appearance in the U.S. Open in September, he defeated No. 49 James Duckworth of Australia in the Round of 128 on October 7 at Indian Wells’ BNP Paribas Open. He matched up against No. 2 Daniil Medvedev in the second round on October 9, ultimately losing in straight sets, 6-4, 2-6. At the VTB Kremlin Cup in Moscow, McDonald defeated No. 80 Yoshihito Nishioka on October 20 in straight sets, 6-3, 6-4 in the Round of 32. However, No. 124 Frenchman Gilles Simon upset McDonald in the Round of 16 on October 21. McDonald’s last win came on October 26 in the St. Petersburg Open Round of 32 against No. 113 Egor Gerasimov of Belarus in straight sets, 7-5, 6-4. He lost to Spain’s No. 19 Roberto Bautista Agut in the Round of 16 by scores of 6-3, 6-2 on October 28. McDonald appeared earlier this month at the ATP 250 Stockholm Open in Sweden on November 9, but lost in three sets, 2-6, 6-3, 5-7, to No. 50 Davidovich Fokina in the Round of 32. Photos courtesy of Mackenzie McDonald’s Official Instagram Mackie McDonald finishes 2021 with the No. 55 ranking on the ATP World Tour. Mackie McDonald will return to action on January 17 at the Australian Open.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald closes year as No. 55 on ATP World Tour

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team hosted Granada yesterday for their annual preseason North Coast Section Foundation game and lost 74-56. The season formally opens on Saturday, November 27 at St. Ignatius in San Francisco. “I look at tonight as a solid game all around and positive on the defensive and rebounding side. A couple of lapses here and there, but I think we did a better job rebounding tonight than we did at any point last season,” said coach Ben Spencer. Prior to the game, junior A.J. Senior captain JoJo Murphy cheers on his teammates. Junior A.J. Harris scored 29 points on Tuesday. He was named to WestCoastPrep’s Top 25 Bay Area basketball players. Harris made local headlines on WestCoastPreps.com by being named to their list of Top 25 players. He is eying a big season as a leader on the team alongside JoJo Murphy and will be a major factor in Piedmont’s success this year. “It was great to get some notoriety but at the end of the day, we’re just trying to win basketball games; the ranking stuff really doesn’t matter to me,” said Harris. Harris had a solid outing in the November 23 exhibition game, scoring 29 points. He did well matching up against Granada’s size, including its 7-foot tall center. “I thought I played well, our team showed signs of good things, but there’s also a lot we can work on like executing our offense better,” said Harris. They had some big guys and athletic guys, so we have to work on guarding those types of players better.” Coach Ben Spencer reaches out for a high five. articles.text: Sophia Zalewski, Piedmont High School’s Valedictorian in 2020 and its record-setting distance runner, throughout high school, was part of the team from Carnegie Mellon that placed third at the Div. 3 Mid-Atlantic Region Cross-Country Championship on Saturday, November 13 at Big Spring High School in Newville, Pennsylvania. She placed 22nd in a field of 216 runners with a time of 24:23.7. Her team qualified for the Division 3 NCAA Cross Country Championship one week later. Her team placed 18th of 32 schools on a 6,000 meter course at Tom Sawyer Park in Louisville, Kentucky. Zalewski finished 187th among 292 runners with a time of 23:01. She is competing as a freshman after the fall 2020 season was wiped out due to the global pandemic. “It felt really great getting to run at nationals and be part of such a strong team. Our woman’s team this year is the best it’s been in a long time, and it’s really encouraging to know I am contributing to that and getting to race with a great group of girls,” she said. Zalewski’s emergence on the program wasn’t without adversity. She required seven months to heal from a stress fracture, and rehabbing during a global pandemic thousands of miles from home added to the frustration. Zalewski returned to running in the middle of the season and competed in just a couple of events prior to the Mid-Atlantic Championship meet. “It felt great to race again for the first time since before COVID Sophia Zalewski ran with Carnegie Mellon at the Div.3 Cross Country NCAA Championship in Louisville, Kentucky on Saturday, November 20. and be part of the team environment that I love so much. Making the nationals team was very motivating. It was so much fun to run with a team again and get back in the competitive mindset,” she added. During her high school career in Piedmont, Zalewski typically competed in 5,000-meter events. She is the school’s all-time record holder on nearly every course, including a 17:50.7 at the WACC Championship at Hayward High, 18:17.8 at the CIF State Championship in Fresno, and 18:44.4 at the Capital Cross Challenge in Sacramento. In spite of the winter weather in Pennsylvania, she is happy to be running again. “I am definitely enjoying Pittsburgh and the East Coast. Fall is incredible because the leaves turn colors and the entire park is a vibrant red and yellow, which we don’t see as much in California. I’m still adjusting to the cold, but I really like experiencing seasons,” said Zalewski. Already eying 2022, she’s eager to continue her progress from the lengthy foot injury and help lead Carnegie Mellon to more success. “I’m regaining fitness and want to come back stronger for next year,” said Zalewski. Sophia Zalewski (right, 95) and the Carnegie Mellon team at the starting line. Sophia Zalewski (second from right) and her team after placing third at the Div. 3 Mid-Atlantic Region CrossCountry Championship on Saturday, November 13.
articles.title: Sophia Zalewski in Div. 3 National Cross-country Championship

articles.text: Staff Photo JoJo Murphy is looking forward to a big season. Winter is coming, and with it comes Piedmont High School’s principal winter sports, basketball and soccer. Here is a look at four key players on each varsity roster: JoJo Murphy, Boys’ Basketball JoJo Murphy enters his senior year after leading spring’s 11-5 team in several categories; points at 409, knocking down 55 three-pointers with a sterling 43% shooting percentage, to go along with 105 rebounds, 58 assists, and 46 steals. Murphy had five games of over 30 points, including a careerhigh of 38 against San Leandro on May 7. He also knocked down seven 3-pointers against Bishop O’Dowd in the season-finale on June 4. He was the Post’s’ Sophomore of the Year in 2020 after unseating former starter DaRon Benson for a first-team spot. He scored 385 points that year and helped lead Piedmont to a Div.4 NCS Championship. Murphy earned WestCoastPreps.com’s Bay Area Athlete of the Year award last June. He will have strong support this season from junior A.J. Harris and senior Raydan Holmes. Trinity Zamora, Girls’ Basketball Trinity Zamora, a junior, was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year and Freshman of the Year in 2021 and 2020. She was named to Bay Area News Group’s Top-25 players from last spring, lead Piedmont to a 15-3 record. She competed in national tournaments throughout the country over the summer. Staff Photo Trinity Zamora. Winner of the Post’s Sophomore of the Year and Freshman of the Year awards in 2020 and 2021. Zamora is a double-double machine for the Highlanders, so it’s no surprise she’s drawing collegiate attention. She had seven consecutive games last season in which she had double digits in scoring and rebounding. She had a 22-rebound performance in a 73-67 win over Oakland Tech on May 22. It was the highest number since former SF State forward Kelea Pickeral-Dennis pulled down 38 rebounds in 2015. The girls’ basketball will have a roster that will compete on the main stage of NCS. Keep an eye also on returning starters Natalia Martinez and Maddie Hill. Conner Curtis, Boys’ Soccer Conner Curtis is the soccer team’s leading scorer the past two seasons. articles.text: Oakland Ballet’s The Nutcracker returns to the Paramount Theater next month. Oakland Ballet will present its production of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker on Saturday and Sunday, December 18-19, at the Paramount Theater in downtown Oakland. Performances are at 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Saturday, and 1 p.m. on Sunday. Lustig’s classic holiday production will be brought to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. As a special treat, Oakland Symphony will provide live music and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will add vocal music from Tchaikovsky’s score. Running time is approximately two hours including intermission. An encore reception will take place following performances, allowing guests to mingle with dancers and meet Lustig while enjoying champagne and holiday treats. Regular Box Office hours are Fridays from 12-4 p.m., with extended hours on Thursdays on December 2 – 16. Tickets are available online at: https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker/.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet’s The Nutcracker at Paramount Dec. 18-19

articles.text: Cassandra Sessions to be performed December 2 - 26 Shotgun Players will present The Cassandra Sessions: Recording this World, with in-person performances at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley beginning December 2 and running through December 26. The Cassandra Sessions, conceived and performed by Beth Wilmurt and Jake Rodriguez, features the songs of Berkeley native and folk song legend Malvina Reynolds. Inspired by Greek mythology, the performance is a new musical theater piece about making music and its significance in the world. Live-stream performance dates will be available on Friday, December 10 and Friday, December 17, both at 8 p.m. If unable to attend or watch a live-stream performance, video-on-demand will be available from December 23 Photo courtesy of Houston Chronicle The Cassandra Sessions features the music of folksinger Malvina Reynolds. through January 9. To purchase tickets and to learn more, visit shotgunplayers. org/online/article/cassandra.
articles.title: Shotgun Players to recreate music of Malvina Reynolds

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse is presenting the musical Into the Woods on stage now through December 23. The show premiered on November 19 after a year and a half hiatus due to COVID-19. Into the Woods tells the story of a baker and his wife who attempt to lift a family curse and have a child. They are visited by a witch who promises she can fulfill the request, but on her terms only. The couple must travel into the nearby woods and search for four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold. The production features a cast of familiar fairytale characters, including Rapunzel, Cinderella, Jack, and Little Red Riding Hood. Music and lyrics are by Stephen Sondheim for this play adaption of James Lapine’s book of the same name. The play is directed by Alex Rodriguez, with Anthony Rollins-Mullens as narrator. The show stars Alexis Lazear, Reggie White, and Rebecca Pingree in the lead roles. To purchase tickets, visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse. org.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse is performing Into the Woods live through December 23

articles.text: Christmas Revels will present its 36th season of holiday events with performances of “La Sirène” at the First Congregational Church of Oakland from December 11-19. This year’s show features a full chorus, elaborate costumes, traditional music and dance, and a sea monster. California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. First Congregational Church of Oakland is located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. All guests must be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19; a COVID-19 Safety Policy will be in effect. Children are welcome at all performances if fully-vaccinated against COVID-19. Group discounts are available at www.CaliforniaRevels.org or by calling the box office at 510- 452-9334.

articles.text: You were sure that you hit the wrong concert on the wrong night, unless you caught the fineprint program insert. Neither the conductor nor the opening symphonic work matched the earlier billing, which had featured the recuperating Michael Tilson Thomas on the podium of the S.F. Symphony. But MTT, still curtailing commitments, had given way to emergency fill-in Ludovic Morlot, most recently music director of the Seattle Symphony. And as you learned in the late-hour fineprint, the French-born Morlot had subbed Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite, a fanciful children’s tale thematically compatible with the work to follow. Morlot stayed on to lead the commissioned world premiere of Timothy Higgins’ Trombone Concerto, with Higgins himself as soloist. In music, the remarkable Higgins is akin to triple-threat stars in sports – he is a composer and arranger as well as principal trombonist in the orchestra. His was a beautifully craft concerto in traditional harmonies and textbook structure inspired by Higgins’ emotional reactions to his/their impending baby. That welter of emotions led to a full-throated, full-orchestra exuberance. Writing sophisticated orchestrations at times with glints of Richard Strauss’ style, Higgins could easily pass for a fulltime composer A second of his motivations was to show off the variety of sounds and textures in his instrument – in the range, in the expressiveness, in its agility. The agility of the instrument in fast runs was ingratiating. Yet more memorable was its descending into intimate moments, with softness and legato in the night music of the middle movement. There he not only fashions a lovely trio of oboe (Eugene Izotov), clarinet (Carey neoclassical work quoted the old Shaker tune “Simple Gifts.” The score was originally entitled “For Martha,” intended for the nonpareil modern dancer Martha Graham and her company. Graham changed the title, quoting a poetic line of Hart Crane about a watery spring. This evolved into quite another type of springtime in its references. This was also a signal achievement for Copland, that one-time Brooklyn boy and most urbane of composers visualizing, in the evolution, an early song and early settlers in rural Pennsylvania. MTT knows and works the piece well, this time stretching out slow passages enticingly. He never skimped on the sharp accents and dissonances, and he got alluring performances from the orchestra, even with piccolo player Catherine Payne moved up to the flute first chair playing memorable solos, for which she was accorded a bow at the end. In the end, the SF Symphony had averted the night’s potential disasters. MUSIC NOTES –– Higgins had incorporated into his concerto a personal lullaby he sang to the babe even prior to birth, imbedded so deeply into the opus that few could discern the where and which. The SFS played Copland’s expanded full-orchestra version of Appalachian Spring, far richer than the Spartan ensemble used for the dancers’ world premiere of the work. As soloist Higgins brought this off exuberantly and somehow managed to maintain excellent pitch throughout with that infinity of slide positions integral to his brass device which, more than most instruments, often seems to resist maintaining pitch. articles.text: Photo by David Schroeder Joseph Marcheso will direct Dido and Aeneas at Opera San Jose on November 28. Opera San Jose’s production of Henry Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas will end on November 28, with performances at California Theatre. Dido and Aeneas is an opera in a prologue and three acts, with a libretto by Nahum Tate. The production is directed by Joseph Marcheso, and features mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz as Dido and baritone Efrain Solis as Aeneas. Soprano Maya Kherani stars as Belina and award-winning bass-baritone Nathan Stark is the Sorcerer. Running time is 60 minutes with no intermission. Dido and Aeneas opens Opera San Jose’s in-person season in the California Theatre. The season launched with a streaming production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri. Dido and Aeneas will be followed by productions of Bizet’s Carmen, and Bernstein’s West Side Story. “This season, we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love – and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” said General Director Khori Dastoor. Proof of vaccination and masks are required for all attendees while on the California Theatre grounds. Audiences will enjoy earlier performances times for Opera San Jose’s return to the stage. Evening performances will begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees at 2 p.m. To purchase tickets to upcoming live performances, visit https://www.operasj.org/ subscriptions/. ®

articles.text: B.B. King had a great blues education. The Reverend Archie Fair showed B.B. his first chords (I, IV and V) on a $15 Silvertone guitar Rev. Fair bought from Sears Roebuck. B.B. was seven. His favorite musicians in his youth were Blind Lemon Jefferson and Lonnie Johnson. B.B.’s mother’s first cousin, Bukka White, recorded on Victor and Vocalion records. B.B. loved Bukka’s bottleneck slide guitar tone and later fashioned the shimmering sound into his famous vibrato. He bought his first guitar, a Stella acoustic, at age twelve and taught himself to play scales and read music a little with a Nick Manaloft book from Sears. B.B. played on Son Boy Williamson II’s KWEM in West Memphis, then on KDIA, Memphis. At KDIA he was a singer and DJ, first called “Beale Street Blues Boy”, later shortened to “B.B.”. After hearing T-Bone there, B.B. had to get an electric guitar. As a DJ in the forties, B.B. heard lots of musicians (after the army in ’44-’45). His influences include T-Bone Walker, Oscar Moore, Charlie Christian, Django Reinhardt, and Tiny Grimes. B.B. felt he couldn’t play chords well and performed solely as a singer and single-note guitar improviser. Ike Turner introduced B.B. to the recording industry. In 1952, his “3 O’Clock Blues” was number one on the Billboard R&B charts. After many 1950’s hits including “Every Day I Have the Blues” and “Sweet Little Angel”, B.B. became popular among sixties rock artists including Clapton and the Stones. Although B.B. studied scales as a kid, he built his style on licks and phrases he picked up from guitarists and vocalists. He thought vocally in conceiving phrases. Analyzing B.B.’s solos academically shows bits of different scales. He’d use a few notes of minor pentatonic (C-Eb-F-G-Bb in C) and of major pentatonic (C-D-E-G-A in C) in the same phrase. A phrase might use C minor pentatonic, yet end on the “A” from C major pentatonic. B.B. phrased with breaths like a vocalist. His signature style includes his shimmering vibrato (often while a note is picked repeatedly), a single high-pitched “button” note for emphasis and a wide-range bent note played on an offbeat. Use the link below to see and hear my improvisations in B.B.’s Style: www.guitarimprov. com/B.B.King’sFortiesRoots.pdf His guitar was named after a woman fought in a brawl at a dance where B.B. performed and the two men knocked over a lit barrel of kerosene. In the ensuing fire, B.B. retrieved his guitar and named it “Lucille”. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www. guitarimprov.com.
articles.title: The story of B. B. King

Then, not much later he played Stuart Canin basks in the adulation of the audience at a concert on Sunday, November 21. Photos by Dave Weiland Violinist Stuart Canin (left) was joined by pianist Helene Wickett and violinist Rene’ Mandel in a memorable concert November 21, 2021 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. the violin for the Big Three world leaders at the Potsdam Conference in bombed out Germany at the end of World War II. And who attended this command performance? None other than President Truman, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin. Such was his early fame. Canin then won the Paganini competition in Genoa, Italy in 1959. Sunday’s concert in Piedmont was a lesson for music lovers. Canin was joined on stage by violinist Rene Mandel and pianist Helene Wickett. The opening piece from Shostakovich’s Five Pieces brought a tear to this critic’s eyes. From then on, the concert developed in magnitude. Many concert musicians are content to play the same repertoire season after season. Not Canin. He learned the immensely difficult Divertimento for Violin and Piano by Stravinsky just for the occasion. It was played with such virtuoso Insouciance that it looked easy. Did I see Canin with a wry smile on his face? The concert concluded with a dramatic performance of Beethoven’s Sonata No. 7. Throughout the concert, the ensemble was impressive, with Wickett on piano and Mandel joining Canin for the Shostakovich. Some miracles are biblical. Sunday’s was musical. The miracle was not so much that Stuart Canin is 95. That might be sufficient for mortals. The miracle is that at 95 he is still masterful and at the top of his game! All the others are gone. Stuart Canin remains – master of all he surveys. That’s the stuff dreams are made of. At the tender age of 95, Stuart Canin was in full commend of his instrument. articles.text: Finding Nemo is a computer-generated Pixar film that debuted in 2003 and was an instant hit. This animated film greeted a whole new generation of youngsters, eager to engage in an adventurous search for a small clownfish named Nemo (Alex Gould) who has gone missing. This orange, white, black striped little guy lives in the Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Australia. His father is Marlin (Albert Brooks), his mother Coral (Elizabeth Perkins). She has recently laid a number of eggs, but as it turns out all but one are damaged during a barracuda attack. The lone survivor is Nemo. Marlin is, of course, overprotective of his only little clownfish son. But Nemo rebels. He decides to swim but is too close to a speedboat and is captured by scuba divers. Marlin, aghast, tries to follow the boat, but in vain. He meets up with Dory (Ellen DeGeneres), a blue tang fish, who apparently suffers from shortterm memory loss, but still offers to help Marlin find Nemo. And thus begins the quest – at times frantic – to find Nemo, who has been taken to live in an aquarium in a Sydney dentist’s office (Bill Hunter). articles.text: Shark Tale is a Dreamworks animated feature starring a bluestreak cleaner wrasse fish named Oscar (Will Smith) and a timid vegetarian shark named Lenny (Jack Black). This odd-couple hangs out in the Southside reef. Oscar dreams of becoming rich and famous while working at the local Whale Wash, and Lenny has to deal with his mobbed up family, led by his dad, Don Edward Lino, who worries that his son, a shark, prefers not to eat fish. Don decides that Lenny needs some gangster mentoring and assigns the tack to his older son, tough-talking Frankie (Michael Imperoli). When Oscar reports to work, he is called into the office of his boss, Sykes (Martin Scorsese), a puffer fish, who not only owns the Whale Wash, but on the side is a loan shark to whom Oscar owes money. Sykes tells Oscar that it’s time to pay the debt, some 5,000 clams, the next day, or else. Oscar, broke, is rescued by his best friend Angie (Renee Zellweger) who gives him a shiny pink pearl, which Oscar quickly pawns. The next day, Oscar brings the money to the racetrack where he intends to pay Sykes, but hears that there is a sure thing sea horse running, named Lucky Day/ He bets all of his cash to win. It’s an exciting race with Lucky A scene from Dreamworks’ Shark Tale. in the lead; however, at the last moment, just before the finish line, Lucky trips and loses and so does Oscar. Sykes, hearing that Oscar cannot pay him, sends two of his enforcers, Ernie and Bernie (Ziggy Marley and Doug E. Doug), Jamaican jellyfish, to deal with Oscar. And so we’re introduced to Oscar who is always on the verge of trouble. He happened to be in the vicinity of an anchor, which is dropped and hits Frankie, killing him. Suddenly the locals of Southside reef are referring to Oscar as a “shark slayer,” a tale that he doesn’t dispute. After all, fame is fame, and he enjoys his new reputation. Of course there are lots of machinations taking place: there’s behind the scenes double-dealing, chases and plotting, all involving Angie, Lenny, and a seductive female Lion fish named Lola (Angelina Jolie), who gives Oscar a big kiss, making Angie jealous. And there is, of course, Don Lino, believing Oscar killed Frankie, and is seeking revenge. At one point he sends his lefthand man, Luca (Vincent Pastore), an octopus, to track down Oscar. Finally, Oscar steps forward, and confesses that it was an anchor that killed Frankie and not him. Lenny and Don Lino reconcile, and Oscar becomes the manager of the Whale Wash. It’s all a comedy of errors that the kids will enjoy, highlighted by the jive-talking Oscar. Shark Tale. Directed by Bibo Bergeron & Vicky Jenson. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Will Smith, Robert DeNiro, Renee Zellweger. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG

articles.text: I met Randy and Krys Wulff 20 years ago when I first moved to Piedmont. We would see each other at church but it was only when they went into the wine business that I really got to know them. After successful careers in law and arbitration (Randy) and optometry consultation (Krys) they decided to start a winery. They bought a house and vineyard in Napa Valley and at first mostly sold their grapes to other high-quality producers. Then they relocated to a house on Atlas Peak with a killer view of the valley. They began planting Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petite Verdot in 1995 on an estate vineyard surrounding the house, and Lobo Atlas Peak was off and running. As the vines aged the wines improved each year. The Wulffs hired talented UC Davis educated, Frenchtrained winemaker Victoria Coleman and veteran vineyard manager Mario Bazan to round out the team. Everything seemed to be going great until October 8, 2017 – the Atlas Peak Fire. Krys was out of town and when Randy woke in the middle of the night he saw a wall of flames bearing down on the house. He managed to escape with the two cats and nothing else. The house and guest house burned to the ground but most of the vineyard managed to survive. It has been four years now and like a phoenix, a new improved house and guest house have risen from the ashes. The property has such a beauty and serenity now it is hard to imagine the destruction that was wreaked upon this place. Grapes are amazing plants. There is an old saying…if you have a piece of land so poor that absolutely nothing will grow – plant grapes. They are tough guys. So maybe it is not surprising that a fire that decimated everything but the chimney could not destroy the vineyards. The grapes from the Lobo Atlas Estate vineyard are producing at the top of their form. In addition to the new vineyard. the Wulffs continue to produce wine from their original valley floor vineyard. In fact, this year Lobo Vineyards went from small, family-owned, little-known winery to small, family-owned, winery on the cover of Decanter magazine. That’s right, this year Decanter listed Lobo Napa Valley as one of California’s top Cabernet Sauvignons. Quite an honor to say the least. Several years ago Lobo joined with a couple of other wineries to develop a state of the art winery and tasting room called The Caves at Soda Canyon. They offer fantastic tasting experiences with amazing views of Napa Valley from the terrace. Appointments can be made by visiting the website www.lobowines.com • or calling 707-224-8322. Wine purchases are best made directly from the winery via the website. 2020 Lobo Chardonnay The 2020 Lobo Chardonnay is a beauty. Ripe, concentrated and fresh, with lots of golden fruits, a touch of oak, crème bruleee and minerality, it’s medium to full-bodied, complex and layered, with a classy, balanced fruit

articles.text: Part 33 in a biweekly series. As I visit cities, towns, and villages in different parts of the world, the thing I enjoy most is walking through the downtowns, Distinctive landmarks traditionally punctuate the core of a city, such as these church towers in Ljubljana, the relatively small capital city of Slovenia. Besides their aesthetic appeal, they keep us in touch with the local history, while at the same time providing orientation and wayfinding for both pedestrians and autos. Public spaces of town centers don’t have to be (in fact should not be) very big to form a truly energized, vital core area where people come together and interact. This proposed small city plaza in Mexico is designed purposely tight to the surrounding shops, restaurants, and commercial uses to facilitate a synergistic and exciting environment. the cores, the centers. In fact, I would say the value of these areas is the most important thing I have learned after decades of observation and practice in the various fields of environmental design. They define the heart of a place. Always easily recognizable by the change of use from private to public, the change of building size and type, and the resulting increased pedestrian activity, there is a whole different feeling and energy associated with even the smallest scale successful center. It brings with it a sense that you have arrived, that this is the gathering place, the heart of the community. In a larger context like the Bay Area, the city of San Francisco itself could describe the core. In huge Mexico City, the Centro Histórico (Zocalo) neighborhood is considered by most to be the heart and soul of the metropolis. And in a small California town like Healdsburg, the beautiful little town square is clearly, as Gertrude Stein might have described it, the “there” there. In the end, what makes town centers successful is how well they provide for and enhance the various aspects of public life. They include a mix of civic, commercial, recreational, and residential uses that are designed in such a way to facilitate interaction among people. In short, they foster community. This incredibly important concept is universal, with continuous historic precedent: from the bustling, agoras in ancient Greece, to the civic plazas in Europe and South America to, (what were) the exciting “downtowns” across the USA…to…unfortunately, the weak imitators like shopping malls surrounded by huge parking lots of our era. In Piedmont, the town center is obvious as the residential pattern changes to the collection of public buildings and public spaces located in the geographical middle of the town. In my mind, “public” buildings include not only the civic buildings, like the city hall and schools, but also commercial, and religious buildings which although not publicly owned, take on the same role as venues for bringing people together. Included in this mix is Piedmont Center for the Arts with its exhibits and performances as an energizer and community enhancer, and soon the new theater being built at the high school will do the same. One great advantage of the small size of our relatively dense core is the ease of walking between uses and functions – the exact opposite of the familiar contemporary pattern of single uses surrounded by huge parking lots. How successful is Piedmont’s town center? What do you think? Many successful components are in place here, working pretty well

articles.text: Guests gathered at the beautiful Piedmont residence of Melissa and Ali Partovi to recognize and thank sponsors and donors to the Cancer League’s upcoming annual black-tie event, Holly Ball. Lucy Ridgway, Cancer League President, welcomed guests along with Jenna Caldwell, 2021 Holly Ball Chairperson. “We love celebrating our sponsors who make it possible for us to fund groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages,” said Ridgway. The event was organized by Cancer League members Rebecca Heywood and Brooke Wall and brought sponsors and donors together to give Cancer League members the opportunity to extend their gratitude to the ball’s generous benefactors. This year’s sponsors include the David & Susan Martin Foundation, Jeannine & Ben Gillikin, Gary Kovacs, John Muir Health/UCSF Health, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Jenna & Jack Caldwell, The Grubb Company, Celine & Alistair MacTaggart, and Camilla & Shahan Soghikian. The Annual Holly Ball will be held on Friday, December 3 at the Claremont Country Club. This year’s theme is “A Medieval Knight”. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? –Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: • • • • • • • Our residents, Peter Hewitt As a new grandparent, all you may want to do is get your hands on that new baby. You’ll want to hold her in your arms and gaze down at her for hours, expound on which family member she resembles most, and tell tales about what it was like back in your day when you had your first little one. Whatever you do, don’t do it! Try to keep in mind what the new parent is going through. If this is their first baby, the emotional and intellectual transition is tremendous. When you first arrive at the home where a newborn has just joined the family, the parents may feel so overwhelmed with their new roles and responsibilities that they may not be able to tell you what they need or want. If you are a grandparent who will be making regular visits during the first few weeks of the baby’s life, it can help to have a little meeting with the parents-to-be a few weeks before the due date and get to know what they imagine that they may need postnatally. A little preparation goes a long way and can make a real difference for the new parents. Talk about who the baby resembles other than in passing Recount your own labor stories or new parent experiences Ask parents to give detailed instructions or make multiple decisions for you Stay too long or expect to be treated as a guest Tell the new parents what you think they should be doing about ANYTHING at this point Comment on the choice of breast-feeding or bottle-feeding Make anything about you or your new status as grandparent, other than to express joy and Madeline Reiter, are happy to be part of the Give Back Committee at The Lake Merritt - Independent Living. This can-do husband and wife team helped form the committee last year as a way to help fellow residents find new ways to give back to the community. I asked them if they were continuing any family traditions of giving back? “In the past we volunteered at Berkeley Friends Church serving dinners to the homeless as well as collecting food and essential items for them,” Peter replied. Madeline added, “Many of our fellow residents have expressed a desire to address this need as well.” New parents are needy, exhausted, and anxious to do everything right for their baby. The best way to show your love and support is to focus on them and their new role. Do what you can to help the birthing parent rest and recover physically and reinforce the notion that the couple is doing a great job. The parents’ stress levels can be heightened if there are other small children in the home, so any time that you can occupy the older sibs is helpful. Don’t assume anything is routine, even for an experienced parent. Grandparents can go wrong even when they have the best intentions. If you are able to keep the focus off of yourself and onto the new little family, you strengthen the parents’ confidence and encourage their belief that they are good at their role. These Do’s & Dont’s can help you help your adult children get off to a great start raising their family. “After discussions, we’re partnering with St. Vincent de Paul and Meals on Wheels this year,” Madeline said. Right now, residents at The Lake Merritt are assembling tote bags which, led by Pete, are being decorated in holiday themes “This is something that has been very close to our hearts for many years,” Pete said. Resident David Adams is also a proud member of the committee. David is championing fundraising for Meals on Wheels of Alameda County. “We all need food to eat and DO: • Have a key to the front door to avoid ringing the doorbell • Learn where the lights are, how the dishwasher and washer/dryer work, where the trash goes, etc • Know where the cleaning supplies are kept • Make a few favorite meals you can put in the freezer • Have fresh fruit and cut veggies available in the fridge • Keep the new mom’s favorite healthy snacks nearby in a big bowl • Make sure the new mom has a large water bottle nearby that you can keep filled • Ask what the parents might need for grocery shopping, pet care • Keep a phone charger, laptop, pen and paper near the new mom at all times • Keep Kleenex, hand sanitizer, and masks handy • Find out the preferences for visitors, and how you can help guide guests • Tell the new parents they are doing a great job many people here in our neighborhood are having trouble getting enough food,” David said. “The impact of COVID-19 has greatly increased this need over the past 20 months. I believe now more than ever we need to step up to help.” David’s goal is to continue fundraising throughout 2022, giving quarterly donations to the charity. articles.text: Being a caregiver for a loved one can be rewarding and fulfilling, even renewing relationships later in life. However, depending on the illness that someone is living with, caregiving can also be physically and emotionally draining and lead to health issues for a well-meaning caregiver. A look at the numbers In a recent report from Blue Cross-Blue Shield, 57% of caregivers were found to be “experiencing clinically significant levels of stress, anxiety or depression.”. During the peak of the COVID- 19 pandemic in 2020, the report found that 1 in 4 caregivers were “feeling more stress trying to balance work and family.” The Family Caregiver Alliance provides a variety of statistics on caregiving pulled from many sources. They note several interesting facts, including: • That caregiving spouses have poorer health than other types of family caregivers • That older caregivers—those over age 65—rate a physical strain of caregiving as “high” • That caregivers for someone who is living with Alzheimer’s • disease or dementia also rate a physical strain of caregiving as “high” 40% to 70% of family caregivers have clinically significant symptoms of depression. But why? Family members often jump into caregiving with no experience or training. Caregiving for a loved one can start out small, doing a few favors or helping out here and there. Then, as a progressive illness such as dementia worsens and the needs for their assistance increase, the stress can also increase. In some instances, a loved one has time to be a companion to an elder who just needs a little company and help driving to the grocery store. However, some conditions require physical help such as lifting someone in and out of bed or the tub and this can cause injuries to the caregiver. When someone has a progressive illness that leads to a deterioration in their abilities to take care of their own daily activities, it can lead to a family member taking on more and more personal care for which they are unprepared, as well as the emotional stress of watching their parent or spouse changing. It is important for these caregivers to avoid burnout and injury; the toll of caregiving on health worsens over time. Professional care with a trained caregiver can augment a family caregiver’s efforts and potentially reduce stress and the chance of illness. For some people in need of assistance, it takes a care team. Being aware of the risks of caring for a family member is important so that caregivers can seek out the support they need to maintain their own wellness. Support groups (in-person or virtual), training, and other longterm care options can be considered to decrease stress on a family caregiver. articles.text: Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr. died on November 12 at age 85. Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr., father of John C. Weaver III and son of Violet Jurs Weaver and John Carrel Weaver, passed away at Highland Hospital on November 12, 2021, where he had once served his medical residency. He was 85. Born on August 12, 1936, he lived in the Rockridge neighborhood until moving to Piedmont in 1942. In 1954 he graduated from Piedmont High School, went on to graduate from Stanford University, followed by medical school at Northwestern University. He served his internship at Highland Hospital in Oakland from 1962 to 1963. Following that he served on active duty as a physician with the Marine Corps in Okinawa and Japan. He returned to serve his medical residency at Highland Hospital, followed by a fellowship in Nephrology at San Francisco General Hospital (UCSF) from 1968 to 1969. He joined what became the Oakland Medical Group in 1969, and in 1970 started the Chronic Hemodialysis Program at Providence Hospital in Oakland. He was the first physician to provide dialysis services in the East Bay. de la Raza in Oakland, the West Oakland Community Health Center and rural clinics in Tuolumne, Copperopolis and Garberville, California. A lifelong learner, he studied Spanish to better serve his patients. He enjoyed exploring the world. His travels took him to six of the seven continents, highlighted by his time in Japan, where he studied the language and toured the country extensively by train, visiting Hiroshima and Nagasaki and climbing Mount Fujiyama. He also visited Hong Kong, Thailand and the Philippines. As a boy, he participated in athletics. After winning the Piedmont Junior High School free-throw shooting championship at age 13, he participated in high school football and basketball, predominantly warming the bench and “hoping the coach might send me in, but more afraid he might.” His community involvements and club memberships included the Piedmont Community Church, Alameda-Contra Costa Medical Association, the Claremont Country Club and 50 years as a member of Oakland Rotary Club. Through Rotary, he visited all the Central American countries for international projects with the World Community Service Committee. In addition to travel, John enjoyed fishing, duck hunting and golf. A lifelong embracer of conservative ideals, he proudly flew the American flag from his porch railing above the Oakland Estuary. John is predeceased by his parents and by his former wife, Brenda Best Weaver. He is survived by his son, John C. Weaver III, of San Francisco, sisters Stephanie Mooers of Piedmont and Julie Weaver Jurs of Portland, Oregon. He also leaves behind nieces and nephews Michael Mooers of Grass Valley, Jeff Mooers of Lafayette, and Tom Mooers of Sierra City. He is also survived by nephews and nieces Justin Anderson, Mary Kate Horwood, Emily Anderson Johnson and Jennifer Garcia Navarro, all of the Seattle, Washington area. He later worked with East Bay Nephrology Group and Santa Rosa Medical Clinic in Coachella, CA. A generous volunteer, he traveled extensively to bring his medical skills to underserved areas in California and around the world. His work took him to Thailand, American Samoa, Cambodia, Malawi and Peru. Closer to home, he worked with Clinica

articles.text: Barbara Fox Roach passed away peacefully in her sleep in her beloved Piedmont home on Monday, November 8, 2021, after a courageous six-month battle with cancer. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children, Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin (Hank) Roeth, Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. She was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Donations in Barbara’s memory may be made to the Oakland Zoo, the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West, or a charity of choice. pages.text: Wednesday, November 24, 2021 25 Obituary Longtime Piedmont resident John C. Weaver, Jr. dies November 12 Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr. died on November 12 at age 85. Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr., father of John C. Weaver III and son of Violet Jurs Weaver and John Carrel Weaver, passed away at Highland Hospital on November 12, 2021, where he had once served his medical residency. He was 85. Born on August 12, 1936, he lived in the Rockridge neighborhood until moving to Piedmont in 1942. In 1954 he graduated from Piedmont High School, went on to graduate from Stanford University, followed by medical school at Northwestern University. He served his internship at Highland Hospital in Oakland from 1962 to 1963. Following that he served on active duty as a physician with the Marine Corps in Okinawa and Japan. He returned to serve his medical residency at Highland Hospital, followed by a fellowship in Nephrology at San Francisco General Hospital (UCSF) from 1968 to 1969. He joined what became the Oakland Medical Group in 1969, and in 1970 started the Chronic Hemodialysis Program at Providence Hospital in Oakland. He was the first physician to provide dialysis services in the East Bay. de la Raza in Oakland, the West Oakland Community Health Center and rural clinics in Tuolumne, Copperopolis and Garberville, California. A lifelong learner, he studied Spanish to better serve his patients. He enjoyed exploring the world. His travels took him to six of the seven continents, highlighted by his time in Japan, where he studied the language and toured the country extensively by train, visiting Hiroshima and Nagasaki and climbing Mount Fujiyama. He also visited Hong Kong, Thailand and the Philippines. As a boy, he participated in athletics. After winning the Piedmont Junior High School free-throw shooting championship at age 13, he participated in high school football and basketball, predominantly warming the bench and “hoping the coach might send me in, but more afraid he might.” His community involvements and club memberships included the Piedmont Community Church, Alameda-Contra Costa Medical Association, the Claremont Country Club and 50 years as a member of Oakland Rotary Club. Through Rotary, he visited all the Central American countries for international projects with the World Community Service Committee. In addition to travel, John enjoyed fishing, duck hunting and golf. A lifelong embracer of conservative ideals, he proudly flew the American flag from his porch railing above the Oakland Estuary. John is predeceased by his parents and by his former wife, Brenda Best Weaver. He is survived by his son, John C. Weaver III, of San Francisco, sisters Stephanie Mooers of Piedmont and Julie Weaver Jurs of Portland, Oregon. He also leaves behind nieces and nephews Michael Mooers of Grass Valley, Jeff Mooers of Lafayette, and Tom Mooers of Sierra City. He is also survived by nephews and nieces Justin Anderson, Mary Kate Horwood, Emily Anderson Johnson and Jennifer Garcia Navarro, all of the Seattle, Washington area. He later worked with East Bay Nephrology Group and Santa Rosa Medical Clinic in Coachella, CA. A generous volunteer, he traveled extensively to bring his medical skills to underserved areas in California and around the world. His work took him to Thailand, American Samoa, Cambodia, Malawi and Peru. Closer to home, he worked with Clinica READ IT IN THE POST Longtime Piedmont matriarch Barbara Roach dies at 90 Barbara Fox Roach passed away peacefully in her sleep in her beloved Piedmont home on Monday, November 8, 2021, after a courageous six-month battle with cancer. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children, Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin (Hank) Roeth, Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. She was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Donations in Barbara’s memory may be made to the Oakland Zoo, the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West, or a charity of choice. articles.text: Helen Cecile Peoples Buty peacefully passed away on October 30. Born in Hankow, China in 1929, she was the daughter of Lewis Jackson Peoples and Marguerite Ann Tahaney. Helen was a wife, mother, friend, business woman, athlete and world traveler. She spent her early childhood in China, but with the onset of World War II, the family was forced to return to San Francisco. When her father was released from Santo Tomas Internment Camp, the family settled in Louisburg, North Carolina, and then Washington DC. Helen attended Western High School and American University, where she was a member of Delta Gamma sorority, the debate team as well as a varsity swimmer where she won a collegiate medal. Helen was the youngest woman to join the Red Cross and during the Korean Conflict was stationed in Pusan, South Korea. Upon her return, she became a secretary at Kaiser Permanente and helped to develop their centralized patient admissions system. She was married to Francis Helen enjoyed world travel. She cruised the seven seas and visited every continent with her family and friends. Helen excelled at sports, and especially loved tennis which she played until the spry age of 82. When Helen wasn’t traveling, working, playing tennis, dominoes or bridge she was entertaining. She was a gracious hostess and fabulous cook. Her home was open to those in need of a place to stay, strangers and friends alike. Many family friends enjoyed extended stays at the Buty family home. Helen is survived by son Louis, his wife K, daughters Mary and Madeline, and their husbands Rick and Jason. She is also survived by grandchildren, Gina, Joe, Wynton and Zachary and by six nephews, two nieces, several cousins as well as grandnieces and grandnephews. A Memorial Service will be held next year at 11:00 a.m. on April 29, 2022 at St. Theresa Catholic Church in Oakland.
