articles.text: William Henry Fraley, born February 15, 1928, to Ferdinand and Marion Saphir Fraley, died peacefully on November 4, 2021, after 93 eventful and unforgettable years. Known as Bill to all who loved and knew him, he grew up in Piedmont, graduating from Piedmont High School in 1946 and later from the University of California at Berkeley. He married the lovely Patsy Craig in 1953, served as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Army in France in the mid 1950’s, and then settled into a long and successful career as a Planning Commissioner for Alameda County. Bill and Patsy lived their entire lives together in Piedmont. Bill was a wonderfully unique character – funny, and with a bemused and unpredictable view of the world around him and everyone in it. Bill was “old school,” a can-do, get-it-done kind of guy with a personality that filled the room wherever he went. Bill was a consummate outdoorsman and Gold Country historian. He was a back-country fisherman, high Sierra backpacker and cross-country trekker, and the creator and driver of the Yubierra cabin retreat in the Gold Country at Goodyear Bar, providing more than 50 years of enormous pleasure to his family and friends. Such good times there. Bill was an avid cyclist and will always be remembered for his screaming downhill runs at the Markleeville Death Ride and many similar places. Whatever the difficulty or downturn of any life adventure, Bill bore it with a grin and a solution. Near the end of his life, walking down Piedmont Avenue for lunch, he would stop some unsuspecting young man, point A 1946 photo of Bill Fraley. Bill Fraley, a graduate of Piedmont High School in 1946, died on November 4, He was 93. up to the distant hill overlooking Mountain View Cemetery, and proudly declare, “I’m going up there, right there!” You finally made it up there, Bill, God bless you always! Bill is survived by his nieces Ingrid in Germany, Carine in France, a nephew Miguel in France, by two children, Kirk and Nina, and first and always foremost by his dear wife and dedicated companion of 68 years, Patsy Craig Fraley, who loved him more than life itself. articles.text: On Thursday, December 2, the City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop at 5:30 p.m. In the creation of the 2023- 2031 Housing Element, which is a chapter of the General Plan, the City of Piedmont will consider all types of land uses, housing types, building types and heights, residential densities, code changes, and housing programs, such as subsidies and incentives, in order to meet the state-mandated goal of accommodating 587 new housing units by 2031 and to affirmatively further fair housing in Piedmont. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson noted, “All options for new housing units must be on the table because accessory dwelling units alone will not be enough to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation.” Community members interested in participating can access the workshop in the following ways: • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont-cagov.zoom.us/j/85005754222 • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont. • • ca.gov/government/meeting_ videos Telephone: Dial (669) 900- 9128 and enter webinar/meeting number 850-0575-4222 Television: Watch on KCOM, Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T UVerse Channel 99 Register before the meeting to be entered for a raffle prize drawing at https://bit.ly/community_wskp_1 In addition to the device being used to participate in the meeting, participants are asked to have a smartphone in hand for live polling during the virtual workshop.

articles.text: NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Notice is hereby given that the City Council of the City of Piedmont will hold a Public Hearing in the City Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue on Monday, December 6, 2021 at 7:00 p.m. or as soon as possible thereafter to consider the following item: Second (2nd) Reading of Ordinance 763 N.S. Adopting by Reference and Opting in to the Alameda County Waste Management Authority’s Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance (2021 02); Repealing and Replacing Divisions 9.02, 9.03, 9.05, 9.10 and 9.11, and Adding a New Division 9.12, “Organics Reduction and Recycling” of the Piedmont City Code. Adoption of this ordinance will codify the Alameda County Waste Management Authority’s Organics Reduction and Recycling Ordinance (2021-02), make changes to divisions 9.02, 9.03, 9.05, 9.10 and 9.11, and add division 9.12 to the Piedmont City Code to comply with the requirements of SB 1383. This meeting will be held virtually in response to the COVID- 19 pandemic. You can access the meeting by accessing meeting # 822-7828-4201 on the Zoom platform. Additional methods for accessing the meeting can be found on the meeting agenda on the City Council web page at: https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city_council/. You may choose to write your opinion and address the response to the Piedmont City Council via email at citycouncil@ piedmont.ca.gov or via U.S. Mail at Piedmont City Council, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. All City Council meetings are televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station on Channel 27, and will be available through streaming video on the City’s website https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/meeting_videos. All interested persons are invited to attend the hearing and express opinions upon the item listed above. If you challenge the nature of this proposed action in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone else raised at the Public Hearings described in this notice, or in written correspondence delivered to the Piedmont City Council at, or prior to the Public Hearing. Further information on this item may be obtained on the City’s web page at https://piedmont.ca.gov. The staff report, containing the full text of the ordinance, including the ordinance to be adopted by reference, is available at https://piedmont.ca.gov/ common/pages/DisplayFile.aspx?itemId=18132803. Paper copies of the materials are available at the City Clerk’s Office, City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont for public inspection. John O. Tulloch City Clerk City of Piedmont November 16, 2021

He stated that the steps and landing are in poor condition, with evidence of rot; the exposed aggregate is weathered and has created a surface that is slippery when wet, posing a safety concern. The walkway is also dimly lit at night. The project that went to bid places an emphasis on improving pedestrian safety, and includes reconfigured colored concrete steps with a non-slip finish; decorative metal handrails on both sides of steps; two ornamental light standards similar in design to the Community Hall pole lights; a water efficient drip irrigation system; and native shrub plantings around the plaza. HM Construction was identified as the lowest responsive bidder, and the prices are consistent with the current bid climate, Gonzales confirmed. At $225,464, it is above the engineer’s estimate for the total cost of the project, which was $155,000. The bid opening was held on October 6, with eight bidders showing interest in the project, a number Gonzales noted at the time as high for a relatively small project. “The more expensive item [in this project] is lighting, which is more expensive than anticipated. This is a small project and small site. Electrical services on a small site do tend to be more expensive,” Gonzales said. “Lighting is an important component in having a safe pathway.” “The lighting is important. We’ve heard from our Police Chief on multiple occasions that we should keep [park areas] welllighted for safety reasons,” said council member Conna McCarthy. Councilmember Betsy Andersen added that the path leads to the Tea House and Community Hall, both rental spaces with elevated safety concerns. “I can see [for] larger events that people [will] enter from that corner of the park. Having this as a safe entry is very important,” she said. The bid documents allow eight weeks for the work to be completed; now approved by City Council, work is estimated to begin shortly and be completed in early February 2022. City Council awarded a contract for the Highland Guilford Steps and Handrail project to HM Construction at a November 15 meeting. The project was prioritized to address safety concerns regarding the deteriorating condition of steps near Guilford Road in Piedmont Park. Earlier this year, a resident reported a trip and fall that occurred on the stairs. The Highland and Guilford steps are located at the southern entrance to the Cherry Tree Walk and the Tea House in Piedmont Park and will connect with the entry to the Community Hall. It was originally envisioned as an informal pedestrian walkway, designed with exposed aggregate concrete and railroad ties fashioned as informal steps. pages.text: Wednesday, November 24, 2021 29 City to host Housing Element Workshop on Dec. 2 On Thursday, December 2, the City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop at 5:30 p.m. In the creation of the 2023- 2031 Housing Element, which is a chapter of the General Plan, the City of Piedmont will consider all types of land uses, housing types, building types and heights, residential densities, code changes, and housing programs, such as subsidies and incentives, in order to meet the state-mandated goal of accommodating 587 new housing units by 2031 and to affirmatively further fair housing in Piedmont. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson noted, “All options for new housing units must be on the table because accessory dwelling units alone will not be enough to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation.” Community members interested in participating can access the workshop in the following ways: • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont-cagov.zoom.us/j/85005754222 • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont. • • ca.gov/government/meeting_ videos Telephone: Dial (669) 900- 9128 and enter webinar/meeting number 850-0575-4222 Television: Watch on KCOM, Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T UVerse Channel 99 Register before the meeting to be entered for a raffle prize drawing at https://bit.ly/community_wskp_1 In addition to the device being used to participate in the meeting, participants are asked to have a smartphone in hand for live polling during the virtual workshop. Coming out of High School in 2006 Huppert was named one of the USA Today Top 20 High School Students in America. Huppert’s passion for research in the laboratory blossomed at Lawrence Berkeley Lab, and she continued research-based lab work on tuberculosis at Harvard, until she found her true calling. “I realized in college that I really loved working in the lab but also loved working with people, so medicine was kind of a natural place where I could still do science but also work with patients,” she said. Entering her Internal Medicine residency at UCSF, Huppert initially considered focusing on infectious diseases or pulmonary (lungs), but was instead drawn to the field of oncology (cancer). “These are exciting times for oncology, and there have been so many advances in the last two decades. Plus, I really appreciate the long-term patient interactions that you get to have with your patients as an oncologist,” she said. After undergrad and medical school studies, three years of residency and three years of fellowship, Huppert approaches the work force with her own textbook in hand. Huppert is now in the process of applying for a position as a breast medical oncologist. Following that workshop, ELS and city staff will collect and record findings from each team and synthesize data into a final concept. Council Member Betsy Andersen, who attended both community workshops, noted the large turnout on November 16, with more than 80 people in attendance. “I am delighted that ELS Architecture and Urban Design was able to use the conceptual design from 2016 as a launch pad for these community workshops. Since we only have one pool facility for our residents, time is of the essence to get it rebuilt,” said Andersen, who was integral in the 2020 Yes on Measure UU campaign. The measure passed with a two-thirds majority of yes vote in November 2020, allowing the city to issue up to $19.5 million in bonds with bond revenue going to fund a new aquatic complex. Anderson noted that both workshops were attended by Olympic swimmers Dana Vollmer Grant, who works for ELS, and her friend and former Olympic and Cal teammate, Nathan Adrian, who lives in the East Bay and teaches swim lessons. “Judging from the great turnout at these workshops, the community is eager to help move this project forward. articles.text: The City of Piedmont held a dedication ceremony Sunday afternoon, November 14, formally unveiling the Corey Reich Tennis Center at Vista and Bonita Avenue. Formerly known as the Recreation Tennis Courts and operated by the city’s Recreation Department, the four-court complex was named in honor of Corey Reich, a Piedmont High grad who returned from college after being diagnosed with ALS. He has been an assistant tennis coach since then for the high school men’s and women’s tennis teams. Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) hosted the invite-only dedication where permanent tennis records are now on display along with a gleaming new sign at the entry. In her opening address, Mayor Teddy Gray King said, “As a member of the Piedmont City Council for over seven years, I can say definitively that the rehabilitation and improvement of these courts is a great accomplishment. “Corey had a storied tennis career at Piedmont High School, and [was in] college when he was met with a heartbreaking diagnosis. But Corey came back to Piedmont and blazed a new career with the varsity tennis teams. articles.text: The City of Piedmont received an ‘AAA’ long-term rating from Standard & Poor’s (S&P) Global Ratings, the highest possible rating issued by the credit rating agency. Cities that receive this rating are considered to have the highest degree of safety regarding timely servicing of financial obligations and to have the lowest credit risk. S&P assigned the long-term rating to the city’s proposed $19.5 million bond series for the new community pool. The credit rating agency noted Piedmont’s “very strong local economy, reflected in the city’s mature residential base, very high resident incomes, and access to diverse employment in the San Francisco Bay Area,” according to its accompanying document. The city also exhibited “historical maintenance of very strong reserves and liquidity, good financial management, and use of multiyear budget forecasting,” the S&P ratings document stated. The rating will allow the city to sell the bonds at lower interest rates. The bonds will be sold on November 18, and interest on bonds is tax-exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King acknowledged the significance of the credit rating when speaking at a community pool town hall hosted by the League of Women Voters (LWV) on November 4. “We were just granted a AAA credit rating, which is just extraordinary,” Mayor King said. “It’s going to result in tremendous savings for our city as we pursue this project.” Mayor King also noted that the city has never issued general obligation bonds, so this is the first credit rating issued to the city. Bonds will be available in $5,000 denominations. Community members interested in purchasing the bonds may contact Bank of America Securities at 510-208-3850. articles.text: The Piedmont Turkey Trot took a hiatus last year due to COVID-19 restrictions but returns in person this year on Thanksgiving morning, November 25. The 20th annual Turkey Trot will be the same 3-mile route on city streets (see attached map). The Trot is a good workout for serious runners, and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their times from previous races. The race always begins early Thanksgiving morning, – hence its tagline, “Move your feet before you eat!” The Turkey Trot brought in more than 1,200 runners in 2010. The Trot, then in its 9th year, had grown into a large social event. Piedmont residents and neighbors came together walking, jogging, dog-walking, and stroller-pushing. That year also marked a more official race. It was the first year the race used a professional timing service and clock at the finish line. Piedmont Post offered a new award that year for the largest registered family in the trot. The city encouraged runners to “go green,” and observe sustainable practices by supplying water jugs and compostable cups to quench runners’ thirsts. The morning run was followed by refreshments and awards on the high school campus. The day before the Turkey Trot, on November 24, 2010, Piedmont Post asked residents, “Why do you trot on Thanksgiving?” Catherine Teare said it’s truly the “first big party of the holiday season.” Her daughter Sadie, 5, said that her family trots because they’re fast. John and Gigi Orta said what they like best about the trot are the “t-shirts, seeing all our Piedmont friends, and getting icees at Mulberry’s when it’s Front-runners begin the race in the 2017 Piedmont Turkey Trot, the year with the highest participation.

articles.text: I must take issue with the recent article published in the Post labeled “pouring cold water on net zero pool”. This appears to be a misrepresentation of the comments made by the design team. I believe the gist of the comments was mainly aimed at the reality of issues that the team is aware of and appears to be dedicated to addressing. The article label tends to put the onus on the team, which is unfair and inaccurate. Nevertheless, here are other points to be considered. 1. space for electrification has been an issue for them and those of us advocating all-electric. However, the design has not yet been advanced enough to answer this question; there are still options that need to be considered, e.g., Solar PVT solar tube panels, (smaller size but same capacity as those being considered), and high efficiency heat pumps 2. Other options relate to how EBCE’s contribution could offset needed capacity, and the possibility of off-site solar panels 3. Another salient point raised in the article was “could the city forgo addition design features...” IMO, this has to be seriously considered, it points to the heart of the issue of how much we are willing to sacrifice in favor addressing climate change which, as we all know, the effects of which fall on the futures of these very children that will use the pool. This is a dilemma of needs vs. wants/desires...are we willing to step up to seriously embrace that challenge? Tom Webster is a member of Piedmont Connect.
articles.title: Giving credit where credit is due

articles.text: A few weeks ago I wrote that the dictionary is not the arbiter of usage; rather, I made the point that language is dynamic, ever changing, and mirrors societal change. Words suddenly appear, some are tweaked, others all but vanish as we constantly search for ways to give meaning to our experience. Recently I saw an article by Amy Harmon in the New York Times in which she discusses the continuing struggle we have encountered while engaging in a national dialogue about race – the expressions, phrases and the vocabulary. This debate grew especially intense after a long summer of protests in response to the death of George Floyd in 2020. Change was demanded, outrage rippled and surged as streets filled with demonstrators, fists raised as exclamation points, signs and banners held high, putting into words the need for social justice. The assumption was that language, not just spoken but written, could bend culture. From that tumultuous summer came a new lexicon that at times was puzzling and yet still made its way into the public’s consciousness. And so, using Harmon’s wording and my own comments, let me offer some examples. In the recent West Virginia election, conservatives suggested that “Critical Race Theory” was being taught in the public schools. It wasn’t. But perhaps more important, its meaning (with the exception of university seminars) was elusive and its complex definition all but ignored. CRT was also linked to Black Lives Matter, as has the word “microaggression,” another expression that begs for clarification. And there is the placement of an “x” at the end of “Latinx,” a recent appellation that replaces Latino, which is masculine, with a word that is considered gender neutral. Harmon explored the term “implicit bias,” which derived from the work in the 1990s by psychologists, who focused on people who harbored subconscious stereotypes. She noted that “implicit” has recently been replaced with the word “complicit,” an intentional change. And there is, of course, the stand alone word “racism,” which has recently been linked to “systemic” or “structural,” two words that reflect a far broader meaning and imply that racism is not just personal prejudice but extends to laws relating to voting, education, and bank-lending. Harmon also includes in her list the word “BiPoc” (pronounced bye-pock), that can now be found in the new Merriam-Webster Dictionary and widely used on social media. It is meant to demonstrate the severity of racial injustice that is perpetrated against Black and Indigenous people. It does not mean bisexual people of color. Two other words now in use when discussing racial injustice are “equality” and “equity.” The latter has moved into the mainstream, and is meant to convey the embedded disadvantages caused by past and present discrimination. Ultimately, what Harmon is attempting to say in her article is that words do matter. While at times their meaning can be puzzling, even confusing, the goal is still to comment, however imperfectly, on the human condition – such as it is. Chris Honore is a reviewer and longtime columnist in the Post. He may be contact by e-mail at: honore307@gmail.com.
articles.title: The Cartography of Language – Redux

articles.text: Editor: Scouting in Piedmont is a very tight-knit community of people who have all been pursuing scouting for a long time. As such, the scouting community in Piedmont doesn’t experience too much expansion. I believe this is due to a lack of exposure to scouting in general. Scouting is a place where scouts can grow and develop into bright new members of society. Scouting instills life-long valuable lessons that I believe should be stressed upon everyone, whether through school or another source. For scouting to grow into something bigger it is necessary to gain more exposure through media. This brings me to why I am reaching out. I personally think it would be great if scouting can receive more exposure through the Piedmont Post aside from the occasional Eagle Scout newspaper clippings. I love and support what the Piedmont Post is doing for the community of Piedmont and keeping everyone interconnected, and it would be wonderful if scouting was more included in that. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, November 17, 2021 Opinion Giving credit where credit is due By Tom Webster Editor: I must take issue with the recent article published in the Post labeled “pouring cold water on net zero pool”. This appears to be a misrepresentation of the comments made by the design team. I believe the gist of the comments was mainly aimed at the reality of issues that the team is aware of and appears to be dedicated to addressing. The article label tends to put the onus on the team, which is unfair and inaccurate. Nevertheless, here are other points to be considered. 1. space for electrification has been an issue for them and those of us advocating all-electric. However, the design has not yet been advanced enough to answer this question; there are still options that need to be considered, e.g., Solar PVT solar tube panels, (smaller size but same capacity as those being considered), and high efficiency heat pumps 2. Other options relate to how EBCE’s contribution could offset needed capacity, and the possibility of off-site solar panels 3. Another salient point raised in the article was “could the city forgo addition design features...” IMO, this has to be seriously considered, it points to the heart of the issue of how much we are willing to sacrifice in favor addressing climate change which, as we all know, the effects of which fall on the futures of these very children that will use the pool. This is a dilemma of needs vs. wants/desires...are we willing to step up to seriously embrace that challenge? Tom Webster is a member of Piedmont Connect. Request for more Scouting stories in the Post Editor: Scouting in Piedmont is a very tight-knit community of people who have all been pursuing scouting for a long time. As such, the scouting community in Piedmont doesn’t experience too much expansion. I believe this is due to a lack of exposure to scouting in general. Scouting is a place where scouts can grow and develop into bright new members of society. Scouting instills life-long valuable lessons that I believe should be stressed upon everyone, whether through school or another source. For scouting to grow into something bigger it is necessary to gain more exposure through media. This brings me to why I am reaching out. I personally think it would be great if scouting can receive more exposure through the Piedmont Post aside from the occasional Eagle Scout newspaper clippings. I love and support what the Piedmont Post is doing for the community of Piedmont and keeping everyone interconnected, and it would be wonderful if scouting was more included in that. Sincerely, –Theo Markopoulos The Cartography of Language – Redux By Chris Honoré A few weeks ago I wrote that the dictionary is not the arbiter of usage; rather, I made the point that language is dynamic, ever changing, and mirrors societal change. Words suddenly appear, some are tweaked, others all but vanish as we constantly search for ways to give meaning to our experience. Recently I saw an article by Amy Harmon in the New York Times in which she discusses the continuing struggle we have encountered while engaging in a national dialogue about race – the expressions, phrases and the vocabulary. This debate grew especially intense after a long summer of protests in response to the death of George Floyd in 2020. Change was demanded, outrage rippled and surged as streets filled with demonstrators, fists raised as exclamation points, signs and banners held high, putting into words the need for social justice. The assumption was that language, not just spoken but written, could bend culture. From that tumultuous summer came a new lexicon that at times was puzzling and yet still made its way into the public’s consciousness. And so, using Harmon’s wording and my own comments, let me offer some examples. In the recent West Virginia election, conservatives suggested that “Critical Race Theory” was being taught in the public schools. It wasn’t. But perhaps more important, its meaning (with the exception of university seminars) was elusive and its complex definition all but ignored. CRT was also linked to Black Lives Matter, as has the word “microaggression,” another expression that begs for clarification. And there is the placement of an “x” at the end of “Latinx,” a recent appellation that replaces Latino, which is masculine, with a word that is considered gender neutral. Harmon explored the term “implicit bias,” which derived from the work in the 1990s by psychologists, who focused on people who harbored subconscious stereotypes. She noted that “implicit” has recently been replaced with the word “complicit,” an intentional change. And there is, of course, the stand alone word “racism,” which has recently been linked to “systemic” or “structural,” two words that reflect a far broader meaning and imply that racism is not just personal prejudice but extends to laws relating to voting, education, and bank-lending. Harmon also includes in her list the word “BiPoc” (pronounced bye-pock), that can now be found in the new Merriam-Webster Dictionary and widely used on social media. It is meant to demonstrate the severity of racial injustice that is perpetrated against Black and Indigenous people. It does not mean bisexual people of color. Two other words now in use when discussing racial injustice are “equality” and “equity.” The latter has moved into the mainstream, and is meant to convey the embedded disadvantages caused by past and present discrimination. Ultimately, what Harmon is attempting to say in her article is that words do matter. While at times their meaning can be puzzling, even confusing, the goal is still to comment, however imperfectly, on the human condition – such as it is. Chris Honore is a reviewer and longtime columnist in the Post. articles.text: California is preparing for a winter surge of COVID-19 cases despite a relatively high vaccination percentage among its population, Gov. Gavin Newsom said on November 10. “We have seen some signs that suggest concerns,” Gov. Newsom said during a press briefing. “We have learned over the [last two] years that COVID-19 takes advantage when we put our guard down.” Still, hospitalization rates are much lower this November than one year ago. For example, on November 3, the number of intensive care unit (ICU) patients in the state dropped below 1,000; ICU rates weren’t that low since the end of July. Medical experts warn that, although a large portion of Bay Area residents are vaccinated, those who are most vulnerable and require booster shots are not receiving them. Booster shots are available to all Californians age 18 and older, and are strongly recommended for those over the age of 65. “Waning immunity is real, and boosters do fix waning immunity at least for multiple months, but we are not giving out as many as we need to,” UCSF Epidemiology Professor George Rutherford said. The California Department of Public Health on November 9 announced that local health jurisdictions and providers should proactively outreach to patients who are 65 and older, have underlying medical conditions, or received the Johnson and Johnson COVID vaccine. “In addition, providers should not miss an opportunity to vaccinate the unvaccinated or provide boosters by offering vaccine during routine or non-routine visits to medical offices, clinics, pharmacies, and hospitals,” State Public Health Director Tomas Aragon said. When announcing vaccine availability for children ages 5 to 11, Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicolas Moss stressed the importance of inoculation for everyone eligible. “With each new population that becomes eligible for vaccination, we move one step closer to ending the COVID pandemic,” he said. “Now is the time to get yourself and your children vaccinated as we approach winter and the holidays, where we expect to see an increase in cases.” According to the California Department of Public Health, holiday travel and gatherings fueled surges last year, 2020. New case percentages was at its highest in the San Francisco Bay Area the week of December 21, 2020. The state concurrently changed regulations and guidance in the midst of surges to attempt to control the rapid spread of the virus. The color-coded tier system was introduced by Gov. Newsom last year, before Thanksgiving, a major holiday for travel. For those planning to travel for the holidays, the State of California recommends taking a number of precautions. The state advises to keep gatherings small, ensure guests are vaccinated, host parties outdoors when possible, and get tested for COVID-19 prior to and after traveling. articles.text: Deadline to apply is December 8 The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall by Wednesday, December 8 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. Scan to book your estimate!

This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see one with a very large circumference, called the trompe de chasse “Dauphine.” The trompe de chasse d’Orleans has a smaller circumference. The trompe de chasse Lorraine resembles an animal horn. But because Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their chairs and music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce –- musically – the start of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. The big treat for runners (and spectators) this year will be the sign of eight symphony musicians from the Bay Area on hand to play music written for hunting horns 200 years ago. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a retired French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument they all are pitched in the key of D, they all have the same length of tubing – approximately 14 feet. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmpnt resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Piedmont resident Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, the mastermind. articles.text: Scouts in Piedmont’s Troop 11 hold their newly issued certificates for a Citizenship in Society merit badge, soon to be a requirement for Eagle Scouts. Sixteen Scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 11 participated in field testing a new Eaglerequired merit badge. Citizenship in Society provides Scouts with opportunities to learn more about the world by encouraging them to explore information on diversity, equity, inclusion and ethical leadership, and to learn why these qualities are important in society and in Scouting. The inaugural class consisted of Lauren Ashton, Bill Ashton, Kajsa Benson, Arun Brahma, Muriel Crawford-Jakubiak, Kane Crawford-Jakubiak, Alex Hattan-Kutter, Annika Hattan-Kutter, Drew Kobal, Jeff Kobal, Elles Krieckhaus, Marguerite Laub, Sammy Lee, Audrey Scherer, Eric Anderssel Venner and Everett Villger. Piedmont Council was one of only 40 councils nationwide selected to complete and provide feedback on the merit badge requirements in advance of the launch of the new merit badge. Scouts from Troop 6 also participated and provided important feedback prior to the launch. This merit badge became official November 1 and will become a requirement for the rank of Eagle Scout as of July 1, 2022. For more information, contact Scout Executive Katherine Benson at Katherine.benson@scouting.org. The Piedmont Council BSA serves boys and girls in age-appropriate programs including Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing, Exploring, and Sea Scouts. The aims of character, fitness, citizenship and leadership development and delivered through a program full of adventure and fun.

articles.text: Laura Pochop As Laura and I enter our family’s final year in the Piedmont schools, our contribution to The Giving Campaign means more to us than ever. Not just a donation, but a huge thank you to our schools and the teachers for everything they have given to our family. This year when we wrote our check to The Giving Campaign, we felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude and a tremendous appreciation for all that the Piedmont schools have done for our three kids. We have a few precious months left in the schools. Our son Charlie is a senior and he is almost to the finish line. This is a bittersweet time for sure. Eighteen years have passed since our first, Tess, entered Ms. Sandy’s kindergarten class in the fall of 2003. It brings tears to our eyes to think of those first days at drop off when we met the other new parents on the Havens playground. Those “new” parents are now our life-long friends; those kindergartners are now adults; and Havens looks like a Four Seasons Hotel. The incredible things our schools and teachers have given our kids are too numerous to count and difficult to put into words. Put simply, our children are good people. They are kind and thoughtful. No doubt our kids are going to thrive and we’re incredibly proud of them. We credit their teachers and the Piedmont schools, and we are profoundly grateful. We hope the parents of seniors, and particularly those like us who are months away from being empty nesters, will consider a donation to The Giving Campaign. This year, more than any other, it feels like the right thing to do. of heart and spirit.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 17, 2021 11 Americans in Paris Continued from page 10 naval high command are set up with computer-screens and illustrated slideshows. The ballroom and reception hall are assisted by audio-visual reenactments that cleverly give context. Today it’s odd to reflect about how remote the location was to Paris-proper, but even at the end of the 18th century this area east Marquetry floor, antechamber to dining room. Its age is 250 years. Les Cabinet des Glaces (mirrors) of the Tuileries was still hinterland. The twin limestone palais were built at a countryside setting so rough the site bordered on a drainage ditch, and the exterior grounds were without electric lighting except for a floodlight mount on each building. These factors mattered two decades later when revolution broke out and the royal warehouse was looted. The crown assigned the Royal Garde-Meuble to maintain and protect the furniture as early as 1764. But, as the nation fell into chaos and the king’s grasp on power slipped away, the deux palais on a country road were not well-guarded. One commander reported that he needed 60 guards and he had only 12. It was common knowledge that the inventory at the keep was not just limited to the royal furniture: the keep contained the royal collection of diamonds. An extraordinar y theft occurred in September 1792 at the height of political intrigue and chaos for Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette who were by then under prison guard after the Flight to Varennes, a foiled attempt to flee east by coaches to Germany and assemble a foreign army to crush the revolutionaries. Thieves freely entered the Garde-Meuble spending five days digging out their bounty and stealing the crown’s collection of massively large diamonds. Some gems were recovered, but not the 68-carat Blue Diamond believed to have been carried to England where it was professionally cut to camouflage the massive stone. The 45-carat Hope Diamond on display at the Smithsonian, the French claim, is the French Blue. articles.text: Piedmont’s water polo team, seeded No. 3, lost to No. 2 Marin Academy in the North Coast Section semifinals 7-4 at Redwood HS in Larkspur on Wednesday, November 10. It was their first semifinals appearance since 2018 after reaching the quarterfinals in 2019 prior to the pandemic. The team finished a successful season with a 19-6 record. It was a defensive battle from the get-go. The Highlanders led 3-2 with less than a minute before halftime, but Marin tied it with 11 seconds to spare. articles.text: Piedmont girls’ basketball team heads into the season as favorite in Division 4 of North Coast Section after finishing last spring with a 15-3 overall record. They are likely to compete with Bishop O’Dowd for the league title in the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont defeated O’Dowd 66-55 to finish last spring’s shortened season, setting up a future rivalry Foothill Championship in WACC. “Our schedule is ruthless; It’s going to be tough, but it should be a really fun season,” said PHS coach Bryan Gardere. :We’re trying to build off what we did last year and keep building.” Piedmont heads into the season with considerable talent and several returning starters: 2021 Sophomore of the Year winner Trinity Zamora, 2021 Freshman of the Year winner Natalia Martinez, and junior leader Maddie Hill. Aniya Perine also earned starting minutes last year along with Brie Sotelo, and Hannah Govert was another valuable defender. Two new transfer students Eva Levingston and Perseas Gioukaris will make their debut with the Highlanders this winter. Leading the charge will be Zamora. The tall, versatile forward does it all for Gardere. “Many argue that Trinity is one of the leading players in Northern California. She had a good summer, she’s been working really hard and you can really see it. Her jumper, how she handles the ball, her athleticism and fitness. She’s ready to take her game to the next level,” said Gardere. Martinez is another player gaining attention after putting together a season that won her the Post’s Freshman of the Year Staff Photos Trinity Zamora, a junior, is eying a big season for Piedmont. award from all school sports. “Natalia has put in so much work, you’ll be able to recognize the second you watch her play. Her left-hand finishing, jumper, and her range. She’s really, really, committed herself to adding layers to her game. She has worked really hard on her craft, and it’s clear she loves basketball,” said Gardere. Gardere predicts that Hill, a junior and three-year starter, will have a “breakout” season. “I think Maddie will have a big year. She’s already been a big part of what we do. She’s improved her game as well and really put some time in,” said Gardere. However, the turnout was lower this year than in the past, with only 15 players for the varsity and JV team. The Highlanders have a handful of scrimmages planned – at Salesian in Richmond on November 20, at Ygnacio Valley in Concord on November 23; then an Alumni Game on November 26. The regular season gets underway when the Highlanders travel to Lompoc for the annual Bryan Ayer Classic on December 2-4. Piedmont will play its first home game om the Paris Twins Classic at the Binks Rawlings Gym in Piedmont the week of December 9-11. Natalia Martinez won the Post’s Freshman of the Year award last spring.

articles.text: Judy Chicago’s On Fire at 80 is on display at the DeYoung Museum. A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago is now on display at the de Young museum in San Francisco, continuing through January 9. Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The exhibit was curated in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States, and pays homage to Chicago who fought against the suppression of women’s creativity. She founded the first feminist arts education program in the country at California State University in Fresno. To purchase tickets to the exhibition, visit https://deyoung. famsf.org/exhibitions/judy-chicago.
articles.title: Judy Chicago retrospective at de Young Museum

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, presents an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition will be on display through February 27. The show is a solo exhibition by Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo, who is displaying more than 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artists’ paintings that actively center Black subjectivity anchored by his extremely calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working between Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. articles.text: PHMozart’s opera Cosi fan tutte returns to War Memorial Opera House on November 21. San Francisco Opera presents Cosi fan tutte in live performances beginning November 21 with performances through December 3. Cosi fan tutte is the second chapter of the opera company’s Mozart-Da Ponte trilogy, set in an American house across a 300-year timespan. The opera is conducted by Henrik Nanasi and directed by Music Director Eun Sun Kim, who celebrates her inaugural year with San Francisco Opera. The opera stars Nicole Cabell, Irene Roberts, Ben Bliss, John Brancy, Ferruccio Furlanetto, and Nicole Heaston, and is sung in Italian with English supertitles. articles.text: 2022 season will celebrate tenure of Helgi Tomasson San Francisco Ballet will present the popular holiday treat Nutcracker, premiering December 10, with performances through December 30. The company produces the ballet every year with a kaleidoscope of more than 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production will be accompanied by the Ballet orchestra performing the score by Tchaikovsky. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older. Children under age three are not permitted. Proof of full vaccination and photo ID are required, and masks must be worn. To view production times and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sf ballet.org/ productions/nutcracker/ Celebrating Tomasson San Francisco Ballet’s 2022 season will celebrate the tenure of its Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson, who has been with the company for 37 years. San Francisco Ballet’s production of Nutcracker returns to the War Memorial Opera House on December 10. “From my very first days in San Francisco, my goal has been to build a ballet company that draws from the past while looking forward. Thirty-seven years later, I’m proud that San Francisco Ballet’s distinctiveness derives from this duality: a brilliant ability to bring the classics to life as well as an unquenchable curiosity for exploring new ways of moving,” he said. “In planning my final Season with San Francisco Ballet, I reflected upon the many artists and works that have inspired me throughout my career. I designed a final Season that offers both a heartfelt look back at the artistry of my almost four decades here – a love letter to this company and all of its supporters.” Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. He has choreographed more than 50 works for the Company, including fulllength productions of Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, Romeo & Juliet (taped for Lincoln Center at the Movies’ Great American Dance), Giselle, and The Nutcracker (taped for PBS’s Great Performances). “Helgi is a visionary whose creativity, brilliance, and stewardship of the Ballet is reflected both in the caliber of the Company’s work, as well as in the thoughtful transition plan that he helped conceive to support the organization’s ongoing vitality,” said Sunnie Evers, Co-Chair of the San Francisco Ballet Board. SF Ballet Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson.

articles.text: In a special chamber music concert offered by Berkeley Symphony, legendary violinist Stuart Canin will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday afternoon, November 21, at 4 p.m. Titled Stuart Canin & Friends, he will be accompanied by Helen Wickett on piano, and joined by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel. The program includes Five Pieces for Two Violins and Piano by Shostokovich, Stravinsky’s Divertimento for Violin and Piano, and Beethoven’s Sonata for Violin and Piano in C Minor. Tickets are available through Berkeley Symphony by calling the Symphony Box Office at (510) 841-2800, ext. 1, or online at https://tickets.berkeleysymphony.org/TheatreManager/1/ online?performance=532. Stuart Canin, Violin Stuart Canin was born in New York City and studied the violin with famed pedagogues Hans Letz and Ivan Galmanian. As a young violinist Canin received nationwide attention at age 10 when he appeared on the Fred Allen radio show and performed Schubert’s The Bee, helping start the famous radio feud between Allen and Jack Benny. During World War II Canin was sent lo Europe as an infantryman. When the war ended he was sent to Paris to help entertain Allied troops. In July 1945 he and pianist Eugene List were called to Potsdam, Germany for a private concert for U.S. President Harry Truman, English Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian Premier Josef Stalin. The event was reported throughout the world. He returned to the U.S in 1946 and continued his music education. In 1953 he was appointed music professor at Iowa State. In 1956 he was a Fulbright professor at the Hochschule in Freiburg, Germany. Three years later, in 1959, he won the International Paganini Violin Competition in Genoa, Italy, selected over 24 other violinists. He was the first American to win the prize. He joined the faculty at Oberlin Conservatory of Music in 1961 as a professor, and left in 1966 to accept a position as Concertmaster of the Chamber Symphony of Philadelphia. In 1970 Seiji Ozawa appointed him Concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony, where he remained for 10 years. Starting in 1980, he worked on music scores for Hollywood films, eventually working in more than 650 films. He returned to San Francisco in 1992 and founded the New Century Chamber Orchestra. Helene Wickett, Piano Hélène Wickett has appeared as piano soloist with major orchestras and in solo recitals throughout Europe and America. Her orchestral appearances include 70 different concertos with major orchestras, including San Francisco Symphony, Boston Symphony, Cleveland Orchestra, Dallas Symphony, at the BBC in London and orchestras in France, Austria, Holland, Ireland, Sweden, Spain, Norway and Denmark, Poland, and the Czech Republic. She has played solo programs in virtually every western musical capital, including acclaimed recitals at London’s Wigmore Hall, Paris’ Opéra Comique, Salle Gaveau and Salle Cortot, Rome’s Villa Medici, Washington’s Kennedy Center and New York’s Carnegie Hall. She studied with Alfred Brendel, Nadia Boulanger, Robert Casadesus, Geneviève Joy, Elena Guirola Hitchcock, and Benjamin Kaplan. The winner of the Pro Musici’s Foundation Competition, she has had works dedicated to her by Darius Milhaud, Andrew Imbrie, Robert Rodriguez and Hsueh-Yung Shen. She also performs as an orchestral violinist and violist, having studied with Stuart Canin, Henryk Szeryng and Jacob Krachmalnick. Fluent in half a dozen languages, she works with singers and assists opera productions from the keyboard and as supertitle operator. She currently teaches privately in San Mateo. Rene’ Mandel, Violin Rene Mandel enjoys a night off from his role as Executive Director of Berkeley Symphony and a rare opportunity to perform as violinist. A Los Angeles native, he began playing the violin the Violinist Stuart Canin age of 8. At 14, he performed as soloist with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, conducted by Calvin Simmons. At 20, he became a member of the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra and became Principal 2nd violin. In 1993 he was a founding member of the New Century Chamber Orchestra under Stuart Canin. He has performed as soloist with the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, the New Century Chamber Orchestra, and the Knoxville Symphony. As an orchestral violinist, he has performed and toured with the San Francisco Symphony and the Los Angeles Philharmonic. As a chamber musician, he has performed throughout the United States and Europe. His teachers included Mr. Canin at UC Santa Barbara, where he earned his Bachelor of Music degree. In 2006 he served as Orchestra Manager and Artistic Administrator for Berkeley Symphony under the direction of Kent Nagano. From 2009-2011 he was Director of Artistic Operations/Executive Producer for the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, again under Kent Nagano. He returned to the Bay Area in July 2011 as Executive Director for Berkeley Symphony, under the direction of Joana Carneiro. Starting in 1980, he worked on music scores for Hollywood films, eventually working in more than 650 films. He returned to San Francisco in 1992 and founded the New Century Chamber Orchestra. Helene Wickett, Piano Hélène Wickett has appeared as piano soloist with major orchestras and in solo recitals throughout Europe and America. Her orchestral appearances include 70 different concertos with major orchestras, including San Francisco Symphony, Boston Symphony, Cleveland Orchestra, Dallas Symphony, at the BBC in London and orchestras in France, Austria, Holland, Ireland, Sweden, Spain, Norway and Denmark, Poland, and the Czech Republic. She has played solo programs in virtually every western musical capital, including acclaimed recitals at London’s Wigmore Hall, Paris’ Opéra Comique, Salle Gaveau and Salle Cortot, Rome’s Villa Medici, Washington’s Kennedy Center and New York’s Carnegie Hall. She studied with Alfred Brendel, Nadia Boulanger, Robert Casadesus, Geneviève Joy, Elena Guirola Hitchcock, and Benjamin Kaplan. The winner of the Pro Musici’s Foundation Competition, she has had works dedicated to her by Darius Milhaud, Andrew Imbrie, Robert Rodriguez and Hsueh-Yung Shen. She also performs as an orchestral violinist and violist, having studied with Stuart Canin, Henryk Szeryng and Jacob Krachmalnick. Fluent in half a dozen languages, she works with singers and assists opera productions from the keyboard and as supertitle operator. She currently teaches privately in San Mateo. Rene’ Mandel, Violin Rene Mandel enjoys a night off from his role as Executive Director of Berkeley Symphony and a rare opportunity to perform as violinist. A Los Angeles native, he began playing the violin the Violinist Stuart Canin age of 8. At 14, he performed as soloist with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, conducted by Calvin Simmons. At 20, he became a member of the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra and became Principal 2nd violin. In 1993 he was a founding member of the New Century Chamber Orchestra under Stuart Canin. He has performed as soloist with the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, the New Century Chamber Orchestra, and the Knoxville Symphony. As an orchestral violinist, he has performed and toured with the San Francisco Symphony and the Los Angeles Philharmonic. As a chamber musician, he has performed throughout the United States and Europe. His teachers included Mr. Canin at UC Santa Barbara, where he earned his Bachelor of Music degree. In 2006 he served as Orchestra Manager and Artistic Administrator for Berkeley Symphony under the direction of Kent Nagano. From 2009-2011 he was Director of Artistic Operations/Executive Producer for the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, again under Kent Nagano. He returned to the Bay Area in July 2011 as Executive Director for Berkeley Symphony, under the direction of Joana Carneiro. articles.text: With a resplendent silvery half-moon radiating over the City, you knew this would be a very special concert. Apprehension had been palpable as the recently retired music director Michael Tilson Thomas, turning 77 next month, underwent brain surgery to remove a tumor. Forced to cancel guest engagements with four orchestras, he made it back November 12-13 despite all adversity. He was a mite shaky, a mite cautious, but as confident and verbose as ever conducting the San Francisco Symphony. The instant he came on stage a rousing shout and a standing ovation by the audience brought things to a standstill, coming from a crowd fervently wishing for his total recuperation. Clearly, he is and was esteemed and beloved. His program was a careful one, devoid of unfamiliar music or technical knots. The highlight was the 15-minute Notturno (Nocturne) from 2004 composed by the conductor himself – a flight of fancy for solo flute (Demarre McGill) and string orchestra. The stamp of Italy was on the score, which even quoted discreetly from the Sextet of Donizetti’s opera Lucia di Lammermoor in the strings’ pizzicato. On hearing it, you might mistake this for a 19th century work – modernisms were studiously avoided in order to plumb a specific milieu. Demarre is a stellar new name on the scene, though not McGill; his brother, the renowned clarinetist Anthony, has played the area repeatedly. Demarre, currently with the Seattle Symphony, would make a terrific match as principal with Michael Tilson Thomas returned to conduct the San Francisco Symphony on November 12 and 13. the SFS, which now has a yawning vacancy, particularly if he ever could stay still. Performing MTT’s piece, he was restless and wide-ranging, adding a visual element to the auditory. Demarre could fill a double void in the SFS, which like many professional orchestras around the country has no Black personnel playing on stage regularly. He played the fast-flying and bird-call effects to the hilt, as trilling as they were thrilling. He produced a sensual flow in the many lyrical sections and brought off quasi-improvisatory sections delectably. The SFS’s string orchestra fell in behind him, as if long-time collaborators. In his flawless impromptu introduction to the piece, MTT spoke of the work as an existential quest, with the flutist pondering, what am I doing here? McGill, I thought, answered that query several times over with his committed playing. The concert had as bookends Mozart’s Six German Dances, which Mozart had dashed off in record time over a single brief sitting, and the first (Spring) of the Schumann Symphonies, which to these ears have always resonated as a quasi-Prussian opus of unwavering severity – perhaps springtime at a boot camp. MUSIC NOTES MTT’s successor, Esa-Pekka Salonen, has his work cut out for him, not only conducting regularly, but also working to help fill at least 11 vacancies on the SFS roster, including the #1 and #2 members of the flute section. In addition, there are slots open in the cello section (including the principal), two more in the clarinets, and assorted openings in violin, viola, bassoon, trombone and percussion. MTT is returning to the podium in measured steps. For Nov. 18-20, he is conducting only Copland’s Appalachian Spring, which he has led many times. The rest of the program will feature Ludovic Morot on the podium.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will present Charles Mee’s acclaimed play, Twelfth Night, from Wednesday, November 24 through January 15, 2022. Twelfth Night was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaption of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a Duke - Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. San Francisco Playhouse’s production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk score by Shania Taub. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required to attend the production. Visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/ upcoming-plays/ for play times and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: A scene from Stuart Little. Stuart Little is a live action/ animated family friendly feature, based on the 1945 best-selling novel by E.B. White. Kids, for generations, have been enamored with this small anthropogenic mouse, and will find much to enjoy in this adaptation. The story begins when Mr. and Mrs. Little (Hugh Laurie and Geena Davis) visit an orphanage where they meet and decide to adopt Stuart (Michael J. Fox). When they bring him home, he is not greeted all that warmly by the older son, George Little (Jonathan Lipki), who resents having a new brother. And there’s the family cat, Snowball (Nathan Lane) who takes one look at Stuart and views him as dinner. And so, things don’t get off to a good start for Stuart. George unintentionally throws him down the laundry chute along with the laundry. Mrs. Little manages to put him in the washing machine where Stuart swallows a mouthful of detergent. Before long Stuart begins to feel lonely and a bit of an outcast from the family. As a result, the Littles return to the orphanage and speak with its owner, Mrs. Keeper (Julia Sweeney), asking if it would be possible to find Stuart’s biological parents. And thus begins Stuart’s adventure. He does end up bonding with George when he helps him win a remote-controlled sailboat race. Meanwhile Snowball’s alley cat friend, Monty (Steve Zahn), visits the Littles’ home and discovers that Stuart is a new addition to the family. Snowball and Monty report Stuart’s presence to the leader of the alley cat cohort, Smokey (Chazz Palminteri), who devises a nasty plan for Stuart. The Littles learn from Mrs. Keeper that Mr. and Mrs. Stout (Bruno Kirby and Jennifer Tilly) arrived at the orphanage, claiming to be Stuart’s real parents (they’re in collusion with Smokey) and they have left with Stuart. But the Littles soon learn from Mrs. Keeper that Stuart’s parents died years before in an accident, and that the Stouts are imposters. The Littles, upset, call the police, who begin the search for Stuart, whose life they fear is in danger. There are exciting moments, tense chases through Central Park, and lots more going on, to include a rescue of Snowball by, as it turns out, Stuart. Ultimately, Snowball and Stuart return home, and the Little family is happily reunited. Kids will love the excitement, and the animation/live action is seamless and wonderfully done. Stuart Little. Live action and animated family comedy. Directed by Rob Minkoff. Starring Geena Davis, Hugh Laurie, and the voice of Michael J. Fox. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG.

There are great songs from every country that are achingly beautiful and ever so sad. Some of the most beautiful are from Naples. But country and western songs are great also, and sometimes amusing, like the Hank Williams classic, “Move it on over”. They say it all works out if you play the song backwards; you get your house back, and your dog and your girl. Ah, but if only life were so simple. Music is very expressive within the context of the battle of the sexes. But running parallel is the ever-present battle of the generations. Is it possible to mediate this one? You can be the judge. They answered as one: “Heifetz used to play fast… Didn’t he? And Kreisler wrote those junky little pieces.“ My blood pressure went up a little bit, and I asked, “Is this how you dismiss two of the greatest Historical perspective – The glory of the past Next week: the superiority of today’s performers geniuses of all time?“ Such arrogance, I thought. How did we arrive at this juncture? A brief examination is needed. From its beginnings around 1600, music was on an ever-increasing spiral culminating in Jascha Heifetz on violin and Vladimir Horowitz on piano. With them, the pinnacle was reached. What happened subsequently is debatable. Most of the great players of the past were inventors and almost all of them were composers. We must assume that they were fine players because they played their own music. Every country and every region was unique. The performers were subject to how they felt at the moment, and so their playing was variable. Even Heifetz, who was known to demand Olympian perfection of himself, messed up on occasion. So did the towering genius of a Niccolo Paganini and Anton Rubenstein. Many of the players of the past would admit after playing below their own standard, “I played like a pig.” Today’s players never make mistakes, and in that regard they are superior to just about any player of the past. But they lack humanity, as well as individual personality and individual uniqueness. But technical perfection they have. Some, like myself, feel that the fascinating elements of individual sound and personality have vanished. These elements are the victims of the general trend toward the depersonalization of modern man. The walk through the art museum of time has resulted in paint-by-number perfection. This is the current state of affairs as I see it. Unlike memorable country and western songs, it doesn’t help to play it backwards. The old guard has spoken. Enough already. articles.text: Howard Ratner (Adam Sandler), a New York jeweler, is a man riffing through life – manic, frenetic, impulsively self-destructive, a catastrophe of bad decision-making. From the opening scenes of Uncut Gems Howard is like a frog in a simmering pot of water and it’s he who is turning up the flame. It’s clear from the fraught get-go that this character study will not end well. The only question asked of the audience is how much sustained, fevered frenzy can be endured as Sandler delivers one of his best dramatic performances. A compulsive gambler, he rushes along the gritty streets of New York, engaging in the briefest of conversations, pausing just long enough to make (or promises to make) a deal, or come up with some overdue cash. His hustle is perpetual, his reedy, grating voice pitched just close enough to panic to sound like fingernails on a chalk board. There’s no moment in Uncut Gems of expository relief. His life is frantically dodgy, bowling pins thrown in the air. He seems perpetually oblivious to the fact that his shtick grows increasingly frayed: he’s in hock to some thugs, one being his brother-inlaw (Eric Bogosian), for serious money. He’s also obsessing about a South African rock embedded with uncut stones that he’s going to take to auction, convinced it is worth some $300,000. While the rock is the story’s McGuffin, it’s also a detour, as events ricochet through his life. He actually lets a famous basketball star (Kevin Garnett playing himself) take the rock with him for the night, leaving as collateral his Celtic championship ring, which Howard promises to hold until the next day when the rock is returned. He, of course, sells the ring and bets the cash on a Celtics game. Meanwhile, Howard is juggling an angry wife (Idina Menzel), a young mistress (Julia Fox), and argues with both, loudly (loud is his default setting), all while conducting his life like a Adam Sandler stars in Uncut Gems. pyramid scheme. The anxiety (for the audience) is relentless as he pinballs from side to side in search of a flipper, kvetching and promising and careening toward a climax that is breathtaking and takes place inside his hot house gem shop. This long scene is focused on the outcome of that Celtics game. Howard paces and yells as baskets are missed or made. The thugs, there to collect money owed, throw him malevolent looks while sitting on the other side of a shatterproof glass security wall. This is the same outfit that stripped Howard naked, threw him into the back of his SUV, wanting to impress upon him that they take his debt seriously. Some final thoughts about Uncut Gems: Sandler is extraordinary in his portrayal of Howard Ratner. He mines every quirk, every irrational moment. He inhabits the character, giving depth to a man who engages when he should retreat, seeks confrontation when he should walk away, agrees when he should disagree, is obnoxious when diplomacy is called for. He’s a mess, yet remains optimistic, a driven gamer who thrives on chaos. It’s impossible not to watch Sandler chew up the scenery. For sibling directors Josh and Benny Safdie it’s clear that Howard is the quintessential uncut gem. Uncut Gems. Directed by Ben and Joshua Safdie. articles.text: Dane DeHaan, Christoph Waltz and Alicia Vikander star in Tulip Fever. The year is 1634. The place is Amsterdam, a thriving port city defined by international shipping, art patronage and likely the first western commodities bubble: a frenetic speculation in tulip bulbs, most especially a bulb referred to as “the breaker.” In the backrooms of taverns, buyers and sellers carried on the purchase and sale of bulbs with all the enthusiasm of traders on the floor of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Most coveted was the white tulip – the breaker – that had a glorious streak of crimson on one petal. It sold for stunning prices, hence the title of the film, Tulip Fever. But this is not simply a story about the fortunes made and lost in tulip speculation (to include occasional suicides in one of the many canals). Indeed, while the operative word is “fever,” it also applies to an adulterous triangle between a young woman, Sophia (Alicia Vikander), who was all but purchased from a local orphanage by a wealthy merchant, Cornelis (Christoph Waltz), a sixty-something man. Having lost his first wife and child in childbirth, he is now looking for a vessel to carry an heir. Sophia, lovely, grateful to suddenly find herself surrounded by affluence, does what she can to encourage the hopes of impregnation. However, after three years, and no success, Cornelis considers returning Sophia to the orphanage. In the interim, he decides to immortalize himself and Sophia in a painting and hires a young artist, Jan van Loos (Dane DeHann), to create a formally posed portrait. And so enters into the home a young, vital, attractive painter who cannot take his eyes off of Sophia whose luminous visage is reflected in the light of the morning sun as she stands near a window holding a breaker tulip. Hence, while tulip fever grips Amsterdam, a different fever grips Sophia and Jan It is immediately clear that their carnal attraction will likely end badly. How the last half of act two and act three crystalize involves a convoluted plan that requires a certain suspension of disbelief. Perhaps it’s a cliché that the husband is the last to know. When he learns of the ninemonth charade that has been swirling around him he is flummoxed. Involved in this drama is the Abbess of the orphanage (Judi Dench), an ethically challenged, lecherous doctor, a type of surrogate pregnancy involving Sophia’s housemaid, Maria (Halliday Granger), and an obscure but interesting ending. Did I like the story? I did. It is lushly told, beautifully costumed, with a consummately gifted cast, beginning with three Oscar winners: Dench, Vikander and Waltz. Tulip Fever. Directed by Justin Chadwick. Starring Alicia Vikander, Dane DeHaan, Christoph Waltz. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Tulip Fever – a film with 3 Oscar winners

By Chris Honoré Howard Ratner (Adam Sandler), a New York jeweler, is a man riffing through life – manic, frenetic, impulsively self-destructive, a catastrophe of bad decision-making. From the opening scenes of Uncut Gems Howard is like a frog in a simmering pot of water and it’s he who is turning up the flame. It’s clear from the fraught get-go that this character study will not end well. The only question asked of the audience is how much sustained, fevered frenzy can be endured as Sandler delivers one of his best dramatic performances. A compulsive gambler, he rushes along the gritty streets of New York, engaging in the briefest of conversations, pausing just long enough to make (or promises to make) a deal, or come up with some overdue cash. His hustle is perpetual, his reedy, grating voice pitched just close enough to panic to sound like fingernails on a chalk board. There’s no moment in Uncut Gems of expository relief. His life is frantically dodgy, bowling pins thrown in the air. He seems perpetually oblivious to the fact that his shtick grows increasingly frayed: he’s in hock to some thugs, one being his brother-inlaw (Eric Bogosian), for serious money. He’s also obsessing about a South African rock embedded with uncut stones that he’s going to take to auction, convinced it is worth some $300,000. While the rock is the story’s McGuffin, it’s also a detour, as events ricochet through his life. He actually lets a famous basketball star (Kevin Garnett playing himself) take the rock with him for the night, leaving as collateral his Celtic championship ring, which Howard promises to hold until the next day when the rock is returned. He, of course, sells the ring and bets the cash on a Celtics game. Meanwhile, Howard is juggling an angry wife (Idina Menzel), a young mistress (Julia Fox), and argues with both, loudly (loud is his default setting), all while conducting his life like a Adam Sandler stars in Uncut Gems. pyramid scheme. The anxiety (for the audience) is relentless as he pinballs from side to side in search of a flipper, kvetching and promising and careening toward a climax that is breathtaking and takes place inside his hot house gem shop. This long scene is focused on the outcome of that Celtics game. Howard paces and yells as baskets are missed or made. The thugs, there to collect money owed, throw him malevolent looks while sitting on the other side of a shatterproof glass security wall. This is the same outfit that stripped Howard naked, threw him into the back of his SUV, wanting to impress upon him that they take his debt seriously. Some final thoughts about Uncut Gems: Sandler is extraordinary in his portrayal of Howard Ratner. He mines every quirk, every irrational moment. He inhabits the character, giving depth to a man who engages when he should retreat, seeks confrontation when he should walk away, agrees when he should disagree, is obnoxious when diplomacy is called for. He’s a mess, yet remains optimistic, a driven gamer who thrives on chaos. It’s impossible not to watch Sandler chew up the scenery.
