articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough’s first novel, Elvis and the World as it Stands, published in August, is now available for purchase online and in select stores. Riddiough’s debut novel is appropriate for students age 10 and up and is a narrative of loss and chosen families, told from the point of view of a newly-adopted kitten named Elvis. Riddiough said she drew the story from her own experience as a volunteer for East Bay SPCA, and decided upon the unorthodox approach of using an animal as the protagonist and narrator. In the book, Elvis is adopted by the Pemberton family, but in the process is separated from his sister, Etta. Elvis’ mission is to be reunited with Etta. “I volunteered with the East Bay SPCA’s feline department with my daughter Julia, and there were many kittens over that period that were adopted out to their forever homes, but in the process were separated from [siblings] they had bonded to,” she said. “I wanted to explore that feeling of not having control over what happens to you.” Riddiough mirrored the feelings of hopelessness Elvis the cat felt to his human companion and deuteragonist Georgina Pemberton, a 10-year-old girl who is navigating the grief of her parent’s separation. The book balances these heavy themes of divorce and loss with the light-hearted animal characters that become Elvis’ friends Book jacket of Elvis and the World as it Stands. Author Lisa Riddiough and confidants, which includes an overly-optimistic hamster and an inquisitive goldfish. “I have an ensemble cast of animal characters that live in the home Elvis is adopted into. I tried to bring in humor to balance the heavier topics,” Riddiough explained. Georgina’s affinity for Lego toys and building well-known skyscrapers with them allows the book to touch lightly on 9/11, extending the theme of “a loss of control.” The title Elvis and the World as it Stands makes reference to the kitten who is beginning to make sense of the world around him. “The events surrounding that day (Sept. 11) made a lot of adults around the world feel a sense of losing control,” Riddiough said. “But the important [message in the novel] is, how do we move forward? For Elvis and Georgina, it is with the support of friends and family, and a strong sense of purpose.” Riddiough began taking writing classes in her mid-forties through the University of California extension. When writing her first book, she said she was “amazed” at how much she learned through the publishing process and working with an agent. The story sold at the beginning of the COVID lockdown and was published in August this year. Riddiough’s next book, Letters to Live By: an alphabet book with intention, will be released in January 2022. The book is dedicated to a Piedmont middle school teacher who Riddiough said her children greatly admired. Signed copies of Elvis and the World as it Stands are available at A Great Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair Village. Riddiough currently lives in Sacramento.
articles.title: Lisa Riddiough’s novel Elvis and the World as it Stands now available

articles.text: The Recreation Department, on October 11, designated John Wilk as Sports Coordinator for all youth sports from kindergarten through eighth grade. Wilk has been with the department for five years as Facilities Coordinator, responsible for scheduling events at city rental buildings. Steven Chavarria, the former Sports Coordinator, resigned on October 8. For the time being Wilk is managing and coordinating the rentals of the Rec. Department facilities and overseeing youth sports. Applications for the Facilities Coordinator position closed November 5. When a new person is hired, Wilk will be able to focus his attention solely on the elementary and middle school sports teams. Wilk has a degree in Kinesiology (exercise science) from Cal State East Bay where he mainly focused on nutrition and wellness. After graduating, he worked at the Cal State Athletic Department for five years as the Athletic Equipment Manager. There he facilitated the operation of games on campus, and ran summer camp programs, which serves him well in his responsibilities for the sports programs at Piedmont. “I am definitely looking forward to the change and the challenge. It is more a lateral move. I am still a Recreation Coordinator, just moving into a different assignment with sports. It will be great to expand my knowledge, and take a lot of the skills and education I learned at Cal State John Wilk takes over the position of Sports Coordinator at Piedmont Recreation Department with responsibility for teams from kindergarten through eighth grade. and apply it to the sports program here,” Wilk explained Wilk was a competitive cyclist in the past, and continues to ride, but just for fun. “Cycling was the thing that pushed me to go to school to study exercise science,” he said. “I think one of my favorite programs here is track and cross country. This is one of our largest teams. We typically have around 70 athletes. Our coaches are great and have been very welcoming to students and athletes of all abilities.” Wilk is also very excited about the K-8 basketball programs. “Coming out of Covid we still have close to 500 kids signed up to participate in the basketball programs. It is definitely a big undertaking but is really fun once it gets going. It’s going to be exciting to see kids playing in the gyms again.” Piedmont is unique with a city agency operating what customarily would be a school program. For more than 30 years all K-8 sports programs have been operated by the Recreation Department. This dates to a time when Recreation Director Mark Delventhal went to Middle School Principal John Morrison and offered to help the school by managing its sports programs for students in grades 6-8, including securing coaches, officials, and having uniforms for the athletes. Wilk currently shares these responsibilities with Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns while doing double duty as the Facilities Coordinator.
articles.title: John Wilk is Rec. Department’s new Sports Coordinator

articles.text: The Oakland-Fukuoka Sister City Association will host a culinary event on December 8 featuring Roux 40’s Chef Lala Harrison and Josh Hammerling of Hammerling Wines. The event celebrates the 60-year anniversary of the sister city organization. It will be held via Zoom. Harrison and Hammerling will feature their food and wine pairings for guests. Those who purchase tickets to the event will be invited to pick up a prepared meal that serves two, and can be finished at home under the guidance of Chef Harrison. Harrison’s gluten-free meal will include Blackened Chicken, Charred Scallion Chili Oil, Garlic Collard Greens, and Citrus Candied Yams. The dish can be prepared within 30 minutes. All elements are prepped or pre-cooked to reduce cooking time. The chef will demonstrate step-by-step how to prepare the meal. Hammerling will speak about his experience with sparkling and cabernet wines. Those signing up can select between two of his vintages: a Cabernet Pfeffer or a Sunflower Sutra. The event takes place on Wednesday, December 8, from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The pickup location is at Copper Spoon on Broadway in Oakland the day before. The deadline to reserve a meal is December 1. To reserve your spot, visit https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ ofsca-east-bay-culinary-adventure-chef-lala-harrison-hammerling-wines-tickets-202553802877.
articles.title: Oakland Sister City Dec. 8 culinary event features Chef Lala Harrison

articles.text: Editor: Congratulations on almost a quarter century of publishing the local paper. It’s an impressive accomplishment. articles.text: The rain had come and gone, and Wednesday, November 10, was a beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group to explore more Piedmont streets. Another strong turnout of 25 walkers arrived at the Exedra: Sherry Jacobs, Noemi Alvarado, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Emma Sangil, Charlene Louie, Monica Calliste, Dena Belinkoff, Jim Kellogg, Priscilla Wanerus, Alicia Rivera, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Pat McMahon, Lois Price, Hellen Dong, Quincy Dong, Stella Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Carole Lyons, Wenny Young, Tami DeSellier, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. The group was joined by Jill and Ron Day from England who were making a long-delayed visit with their son, daughter-in-law, and two granddaughters in Piedmont. The chosen location last week was Rose Avenue and Nace Avenue and nearby streets on the southwest edge of Piedmont at the Oakland border. This part of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days, shortly after its founding in 1907. Nace, Howard, and Lake were are built around 1908. The oldest houses on Nace are the “Gibson House” (46 Nace), built in 1910, and the “Govan House” (18 Nace) built in 1911. Pat Keller, a walker, said her home on Nace was built in 1914. The walkers crossed Oakland Avenue to Latham Street, Piedmont’s only street named Street. Most others are Avenue or Road or Drive. Continuing on Greenbank Avenue they arrived at Rose Avenue, where they admired the beautiful, old, gingerbread Victorian homes, one with a rooster weathervane. The homes are beautifully maintained, colorful, and rival those in San Francisco. At the end of Rose they came to Kingston Avenue, and then past Beach School on Lake, and then up to Nace, one of the city’s L-shaped streets. As luck would have it, David Yam was coming out of his house, the “Gibson house’ on Nace. Warren Gibson, whose family had lived in the house it for 70 years, was a woodworking teacher at Oakland Tech and had done incredible detail work inside the house. The catalpa tree the Gibsons planted in the 1920s, nearly 100 years ago, is now huge. The walkers returned via Cambridge Way, which has two large palm trees, then up Greenbank to San Carlos and Magnolia. When the walkers arrived at the Exedra they invited their new English friends, the Days, to join future Wednesday walks while they are in town. The day was a four-mile exploration with new and old friends, and some unexpected Piedmont history. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, November 17, 2021 Walking on Wednesday A group with Walking on Wednesdays stands by a 100-year old catalpa tree on Nace Avenue on November 10. Wednesday Walkers explore Nace, Rose, Kingston By Dick Carter The rain had come and gone, and Wednesday, November 10, was a beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group to explore more Piedmont streets. Another strong turnout of 25 walkers arrived at the Exedra: Sherry Jacobs, Noemi Alvarado, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Emma Sangil, Charlene Louie, Monica Calliste, Dena Belinkoff, Jim Kellogg, Priscilla Wanerus, Alicia Rivera, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Pat McMahon, Lois Price, Hellen Dong, Quincy Dong, Stella Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Carole Lyons, Wenny Young, Tami DeSellier, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. The group was joined by Jill and Ron Day from England who were making a long-delayed visit with their son, daughter-in-law, and two granddaughters in Piedmont. The chosen location last week was Rose Avenue and Nace Avenue and nearby streets on the southwest edge of Piedmont at the Oakland border. This part of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days, shortly after its founding in 1907. Nace, Howard, and Lake were are built around 1908. The oldest houses on Nace are the “Gibson House” (46 Nace), built in 1910, and the “Govan House” (18 Nace) built in 1911. Pat Keller, a walker, said her home on Nace was built in 1914. The walkers crossed Oakland Avenue to Latham Street, Piedmont’s only street named Street. Most others are Avenue or Road or Drive. Continuing on Greenbank Avenue they arrived at Rose Avenue, where they admired the beautiful, old, gingerbread Victorian homes, one with a rooster weathervane. The homes are beautifully maintained, colorful, and rival those in San Francisco. At the end of Rose they came to Kingston Avenue, and then past Beach School on Lake, and then up to Nace, one of the city’s L-shaped streets. As luck would have it, David Yam was coming out of his house, the “Gibson house’ on Nace. Warren Gibson, whose family had lived in the house it for 70 years, was a woodworking teacher at Oakland Tech and had done incredible detail work inside the house. The catalpa tree the Gibsons planted in the 1920s, nearly 100 years ago, is now huge. The walkers returned via Cambridge Way, which has two large palm trees, then up Greenbank to San Carlos and Magnolia. When the walkers arrived at the Exedra they invited their new English friends, the Days, to join future Wednesday walks while they are in town. The day was a four-mile exploration with new and old friends, and some unexpected Piedmont history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Mitch Winters sister Elizabeth As a Troop 15 leader has written about Mitch, “he was a significant role model for many scouts.” Mitch was also part of the Piedmont Police Department’s Police Explorer’s Program, devoting approximately 350 hours/year to it. He helped with crowd and traffic safety at beloved town events like the Fourth of July parade and the Fallfest 5K run. Ultimately Mitch’s peers selected him as the Sergeant of the Explorers program. And he was part of the Piedmont Explorer team that went to the 2015 SWAT Tactical Competition in Chandler, AZ and, in a series of David-v.-Goliath-type upsets, placed first in 3 out of 11 events against better-funded teams from much bigger cities. This trip was when Mitch first started to fall in love with Arizona. With his parents’ permission, while still in high school, Mitch committed to the United States Marine Corps as an Infantryman. Mitch turned down admission to The Citadel because he wanted to start serving this country right away. He left for basic training two days after graduating from high school. In the Corps, he was deployed overseas for eight months, earned a meritorious promotion, won a National Defense Medal, was an Infantry Squad Leader, a Combat Marksmanship Coach, and a graduate of the brutal Marine Corps Water Survival School. In his off hours, he became a cross-fit enthusiast and a Brazilian Jiu Jitsu devotee—and he won his second tournament. He was honorably discharged from the Corps after four years of service. In June of this year, he graduated from the Mesa Arizona Policy Academy, full of joy, hope, and optimism—his natural state. He was so looking forward to being, as he put it, “out on the street.” As Phase 1 of a four-phase field training program, he was assigned to “Central Graves”—Central Mesa, the graveyard shift. Mesa is afflicted by the high crime rates that its two principal national gangs, MS-13 and the Aryan Brotherhood, inflict on it. Mitch was assigned a Field Training Officer (“FTO”) nicknamed “The Hunter”— someone who would proactively look for gang activity and get those gang members off the street. Mitch loved it. He thrived on it. He called us each week, in calls that would last an hour or more, to regale us with stories of the arrests that he had helped and the events on his shift. He loved Central Graves, and he admired and respected The Hunter. He could not wait to finish his field training program so that he could get “out on the street.” Something happened in Phase 2. On Friday, November 12, 2021—a date his family will never be able to forget, a date that will always be twenty-four hours of the blackest night—Mitch walked into his apartment bedroom, lay down on his bed, and shot himself. We had always known that Mitch had the ability to touch many different people in many different spheres of life. It’s only through his death that we have seen how true that was. We have had everyone from the son of a janitor to former United States Ambassadors reach out to tell us how much they admired Mitch and how sorry they are for our, their, and the country’s loss. And his (it turns out, quite extended) Marine family is bereft. Dozens of his former Marine buddies (a term Marines use to apply both to men and women) have reached out to us to convey their sorrow and share in our grief. To a person, they have told us that they loved Mitch. That he was a “great man”— although, being Marines, they salt up the language with words that a family newspaper can’t print. That he was a “natural leader” who “trained us well” and who “made us want to stand a little taller and straighter.” That, although it wasn’t his job to do so, Mitch was always making time to help his fellow Marines with their troubles and struggles, whether those were large or small. When I finally reached the Staff Sergeant who recruited Mitch into the Corps, and told him the news, the line went Mitch Winters by a Piedmont Police Department patrol car. silent for about 15 seconds. And then was filled with sobbing for about the next three minutes. He kept saying “I’m sorry, sir” (Marines call male civilians “sir”) but couldn’t contain the wellspring of grief that sprung from his core. He loved my son. He introduced my son to the Corps, which helped to turn Mitch into the very fine man that he was. I will always be in the Staff Sergeant’s debt. But in this call, I ended up consoling him. pages.text: Wednesday, November 17, 2021 25 Mitchell William Winters, raised in Piedmont and a graduate of the Piedmont schools, died on Friday, November 12, 2021, at the age of 23. He leaves behind a legacy of which anyone, of any age, would be justifiably proud. From the age of 8, all he ever wanted to do was serve this country, first in the United States Marine Corps and then as a police officer. He achieved both of those dreams—after starting early in his life to work towards them. While attending the Piedmont Schools, he developed a deep love for the Boy Scouts of America’s youth programs of character development and values-based leadership training. A member of Piedmont’s vaunted Troop 15, Mitch achieved various leadership positions, including as the Troop Representative to the Order of the Arrow. He also graduated from the Boy Scouts of America’s National Youth Leadership Training program and thereafter served on the Staff and as a Team Guide for that program. Ultimately, he earned the rank of Eagle Scout. His Eagle Scout project was informed and inspired by contact with the Oakland Police Department’s K-9 training facility; Mitch had seen the training officers eating lunch without a place to sit. So he built and installed a picnic table and benches for them. Mitch Winters Celebrating the great outdoors. Its Head of Security, legendary ex-Oakland gang and drug police officer John Gutierrez, gave Mitch his first law-enforcement-type job there as a Security Guard. If you knew Mitch and want to honor his memory, please come. (The Club has a dress code that, in the past, it has always enforced, so perhaps best to call ahead about it.) Dear friends of ours have set up a caring bridge, if you are so inclined, at https://www. caringbridge.org/public/mitchellwinters. Mitch has been uniformly and widely described to us as the last person anyone thought would kill himself. We thought that, too; his last words to us, the night before he died, were “I love you.” We love you, too, Mitch. As I’ve said to you and your sister since you were little, I love you like the stars above. By Vernon M. Winters, on behalf of the Winters family.

articles.text: As Piedmont continues to explore new housing programs, city staff is encouraging residents to send ideas, edits, and suggestions before the November 19 deadline. The new housing programs include draft design standards for multi-family housing, including apartment building, as well as new incentives for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), commonly known as “granny flats.” A community workshop was hosted by the city on October 21 detailing new housing programs and incentives. Staff used comments from that workshop to design a 58-page draft, which can be found by visiting https://piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx?portal Id=13659823&pageId=16745183. Suggestions and comments can be sent by email to piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov. You may also mail your comments to the Planning Division, City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. More information about the city’s housing plans and upcoming workshops and events can be found at www.piedmontishome. org.

articles.text: Speakers included Buffy Wicks, Jon Wizard, Andy Madeira A virtual community workshop entitled “Doing Our Part: Affordable Housing in Piedmont” organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) with the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) was held on November 9 and included a panel of expert speakers. “When you look at the housing crisis in California, the statistics are pretty alarming,” said Buffy Wicks, Piedmont representative in the State Assembly. In providing introductory remarks, she said, “We are 49 out of 50 [in the country] in homeownership, and fewest homes per population. There is a real shortage of homes at all income levels.” Wicks, who represents the 15th Assembly District, said that those who cannot afford properties or rentals in the Bay Area are forced to commute two or more hours from cities as far away as Stockton. “There are teachers in Oakland Unified School District that are Uber drivers on the side so they can afford housing. That is a big challenge. We’re creating a society of the haves and have-nots, and are squeezing out our middle class,” she said. Wicks described recent state legislation (Senate Bills 9 and 10) aimed at easing the burden of affordable home ownership, which would affect Piedmont and its housing stock. “One of the challenges for Piedmont is there isn’t a ton of vacant [land] waiting to be developed,” she said. “[The city] will have to get creative in terms of how you use these bills we’ve passed recently.” Jon Wizard, a member of the City Council in Seaside and Policy Director for YIMBY Law, offered background information on the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) and how it affects the state and Piedmont. He explained that cities are required to perform public outreach in the form of surveys, workshops, webinars, and advisory committees; most Bay Area cities and Los Angeles are currently at this stage of the Housing Element process. “Once [a city’s] planning staff gets feedback from the community, they need to work on creating the various policies that will shape the housing element, and the programs within those policies,” he said. “If a city does not have enough vacant land, then it must complete a re-zoning program.” Bay Area city housing elements are due in approximately 13 months, “about enough time to complete [the required] public outreach and create a draft plan,” Wizard said. Andy Madeira, CEO of East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation, described how the economic breakdown of the RHNA new housing unit goal will look. Madeira has been a Piedmont resident for 20 years and has worked in affordable housing for 30 years. “When we moved to Piedmont, it was pretty clear to me that Piedmont is a very homogenous city. It was, and still is, predominately white. I have to say that I’m ashamed I never questioned that, or asked why that was, or what I could do to change that,” he said. Madeira credited the PREC organization for shedding light on affordable housing issues in the community, and said that he hopes people will see that “we can develop a community [in Piedmont] that is welcoming to everyone.” The very low-income level and low-income level appropriate housing units that Piedmont must accommodate accounts for roughly 200 units combined, he explained. Very-low income is defined as an individual who makes less than $48,000 a year. A person earning less than $76,000 a year would be defined as low income. The average income of Piedmont residents is $101,794 a year, and the median household income in Piedmont is $212,222. Madeira used these statistics to explain that currently a verylow or low-income individual cannot afford to rent in Piedmont. He pointed to a sample size of 11 rentals in the city that ranged from $2,200 to $7,500. “Without subsidies, we won’t be able to get new housing units in Piedmont that are affordable. Affordable housing is really housing that is restricted to low income residents in exchange for receiving a variety of different subsidies,” he said. County Measure A-1 funds of $2 million is considered a subsidiary source for Piedmont. The November 9 workshop was initiated by the two organizations as the city updates its Housing Element. PREC member Sarah Karlinsky described it as a critical opportunity for Piedmont to address issues of racial segregation, and to build a more inclusive community. The participatory workshop allowed those who tuned in to join smaller groups to discuss their concerns and wishes regarding affordable housing in Piedmont.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Town Hall meeting on Monday, November 22 at 6:00 p.m. to provide an opportunity for Piedmont residents to learn more about Public Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Stations. The meeting will provide an opportunity for residents to ask questions about a funding opportunity and public EV charging in Piedmont. Following a short presentation about EV charging and the Alameda County Incentive Project, a panel will provide responses to questions submitted by attendees. Participants will ask their questions using the Q&A feature of Zoom. The moderator will group questions together and give them to the panel for a response. Members of the public can participate in the meeting in the following ways: • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/j/83233567482 • Telephone: Dial (669) 900-9128 and enter webinar/meeting number 840-0138-1498 On October 18 the city council approved the installation of four DC fast EV charging stations on Magnolia Avenue near the Exedra. They will be the first public chargers located in Piedmont and are anticipated to be operational by July 1, 2022. In addition, the City is exploring other locations for public charging stations. The City is seeking input from residents about their EV usage and preferences for EV charging. Residents are encouraged to complete an online EV community survey by November 26. “Public electric vehicle charging stations are intended to further support the adoption of electric vehicles in Piedmont,” said Alyssa Dykman, the City’s Sustainability Program Manager. “Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0 calls for the community to reduce its annual in-territory emissions from the transportation, building, solid waste, and water sectors by 40% below its 2005 baseline by 2030 and 80% by 2050. Emissions from CO2e from gas- and diesel-fueled vehicles are among the biggest obstacles to meeting these emissions reduction goals. In 2019, vehicles in Piedmont accounted for 49% of the community’s total emissions. The City has the chance to capitalize on the interest of EVs in Piedmont and further promote EV adoption through the development of EV infrastructure.” For more information contact Alyssa Dykman at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The City of Piedmont announced on November 9 that it is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee, established by City Council at its October 4 meeting. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on reviewing and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will use the experience of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall on or before Wednesday, December 8 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for the positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040.
articles.title: City seeks volunteers for Pool Bond Oversight Committee

articles.text: The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) is recommending booster shots of the COVID-19 vaccine for all people age 65 and older who received any of the three available vaccines. It also has recommended booster shots for older adults and certain groups who received Moderna, and all adults who received the Johnson and Johnson vaccine more than two months ago. “As family and friends make plans to gather in the coming months, we encourage everyone to get vaccinated as soon as possible,” ACPHD Public Information Officer Neetu Balram said. “Older adults and younger people with underlying conditions or certain other risk factors who received either Pfizer or Moderna more than six months ago can now get vaccine booster doses, and anyone who received Johnson & Johnson at least two months ago can also receive a booster.” Balram cites emerging evidence that suggests immunity from COVID-19 vaccination may wane over time. In October the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) authorized booster doses for people vaccinated with any of the three authorized COVID-19 vaccines and is highly recommending boosters for those over age 18 who received a Johnson and Johnson vaccine. Mixing and matching of booster is permitted by health officials, so recipients may choose a different vaccine for a booster than their original series. “COVID-19 vaccines have proven to be highly safe and effective, and booster doses will help ensure we get the greatest possible benefit,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Director. “I strongly recommend getting a booster if you are 65 or older, live in a long-term care setting, or have an underlying medical condition which places you at higher risk for infection and severe illness.” As of November 8, 16% of eligible residents in Alameda County are unvaccinated, or haven’t received their second dose of a two-dose series. Where to go Any eligible person seeking a booster shot can consult with their medical provider, or go to a chain pharmacy like CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid, Safeway, or Costco. A full list of vaccine-providing pharmacies in the area can be found at www. vaccines.gov. Some participating locations allow for walk-in appointments. Those who have not received any form of vaccination may create an appointment by visiting https://covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines.
articles.title: County recommends booster shots for 65 & older

articles.text: All-electric heating system will be costly, but will be explored Is a net-zero greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) community pool possible? The question was raised by residents at a virtual town hall meeting hosted by the League of Women Voters (LWV) on Thursday, November 4. Speakers at the event included Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Pool Project Manager George Sanen, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, and pool principal Architect Clarence Mamuyac. The majority of questions raised to the panel concerned whether the energy source used to heat the pools water will be net-zero carbon. Electrifying the building will be easy, Mamuyac said, but the real challenge is in heating the pools. “It takes a lot of power to heat the pools. The large rectangular pool will be somewhere between 70 and 80 degrees, and the smaller pool will stay at 85 degrees. It’s a big challenge,” Mamuyac said. pages.text: Volume 24, No. 4 Piedmont, California November 10, 2021 91¢ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont City seeks volunteers for Pool Bond Oversight Committee By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont announced on November 9 that it is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee, established by City Council at its October 4 meeting. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on reviewing and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will use the experience of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall on or before Wednesday, December 8 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for the positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. INSIDE Design, construction panel throws cold water on net-zero pool All-electric heating system will be costly, but will be explored By Allyson Aleksey Is a net-zero greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) community pool possible? The question was raised by residents at a virtual town hall meeting hosted by the League of Women Voters (LWV) on Thursday, November 4. Speakers at the event included Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Pool Project Manager George Sanen, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, and pool principal Architect Clarence Mamuyac. The majority of questions raised to the panel concerned whether the energy source used to heat the pools water will be net-zero carbon. Electrifying the building will be easy, Mamuyac said, but the real challenge is in heating the pools. “It takes a lot of power to heat the pools. The large rectangular pool will be somewhere between 70 and 80 degrees, and the smaller pool will stay at 85 degrees. It’s a big challenge,” Mamuyac said. Mamuyac’s firm, ELS Architecture & Urban Design, will also have to work with the city to see how it will schedule the use of the small pool, which will help gauge heating necessities and energy use. Pool covers saving on loss of evaporation and retaining water temperature are customary in the majority of aquatics facilities. It also has recommended booster shots for older adults and certain groups who received Moderna, and all adults who received the Johnson and Johnson vaccine more than two months ago. “As family and friends make plans to gather in the coming months, we encourage everyone to get vaccinated as soon as possible,” ACPHD Public Information Officer Neetu Balram said. “Older adults and younger people with underlying conditions or certain other risk factors who received either Pfizer or Moderna more than six months ago can now get vaccine booster doses, and anyone who received Johnson & Johnson at least two months ago can also receive a booster.” Balram cites emerging evidence that suggests immunity from COVID-19 vaccination may wane over time. In October the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) authorized booster doses for people vaccinated with any of the three authorized COVID-19 vaccines and is highly recommending boosters for those over age 18 who received a Johnson and Johnson vaccine. Mixing and matching of booster is permitted by health officials, so recipients may choose a different vaccine for a booster than their original series. “COVID-19 vaccines have proven to be highly safe and effective, and booster doses will help ensure we get the greatest possible benefit,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Director. “I strongly recommend getting a booster if you are 65 or older, live in a long-term care setting, or have an underlying medical condition which places you at higher risk for infection and severe illness.” As of November 8, 16% of eligible residents in Alameda County are unvaccinated, or haven’t received their second dose of a two-dose series. Where to go Any eligible person seeking a booster shot can consult with their medical provider, or go to a chain pharmacy like CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid, Safeway, or Costco. A full list of vaccine-providing pharmacies in the area can be found at www. vaccines.gov. Some participating locations allow for walk-in appointments. Those who have not received any form of vaccination may create an appointment by visiting https://covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines. articles.text: Non-traditional vice mayorship selection in 2020 prompts discussion Piedmont’s City Council may change from its traditional selection process for mayor and vice mayor following an unorthodox selection one year ago in November 2020. Councilmembers discussed options at a November 1 meeting. The only written policy regarding how the mayor and vice mayor are selected is found in the section 2.08 of the City Charter, which states, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and Vice-Mayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” For 30 years the city council has appointed the council member who has been re-elected for a second term as vice mayor and then mayor for two-year terms respectively. Additionally, seniority with city council would be the first qualifier of vice mayorship, and top votes received in an election as the second qualifier. This process has resulted in a twice-elected council member not having the opportunity to serve as vice mayor or mayor. Last year the role of Vice Mayor was dually assumed for the first time, with Tim Rood and Jen Cavenaugh designated as Vice Mayors in 2021-2022 and 2022- 2023 respectively. The City Council meeting on December 7, 2020 took an unorthodox turn when the council voted to split the position of vice mayor instead of it being a traditional two-year term. The city council voted to have Rood, a six-year member of the council, assume the title for one year followed by Cavenaugh for one year. Cavenaugh was the top vote-getter in 2016 and 2020, and Rood has seniority with six years on council. While it was ultimately decided by councilmembers that the vice mayorship would be “shared,” the decision was reached only after a lengthy discussion. The hiccup prompted groups like the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to author a letter to city council on December 11, 2020, pointing out a “lack of transparency and clarity” in the process. The groups called on city council to clearly write out rules and procedures and make them accessible to the public rather than “rely on institutional memory, or interpretation, to be passed along.” Moving forward At the November 1 meeting, Councilmember Conna McCarthy said that the traditional approach of “who gets the most votes is rather shallow.” In 2020, McCarthy, in response to the tradition of top vote-getting, said that a “vote for council is not a vote for mayor.” “I don’t see a groundswell of community dissatisfaction with the two-year rotation,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen offered. “But with respect to the key point of transparency, I would be an advocate of putting, in writing, what our customary practices have been for the past 30 years.” Andersen acknowledged that she was in favor last year of sticking to the traditional process, but added that it “leaves someone out. [It] doesn’t work with four-year terms and a five-year rotation.” Vice Mayor Tim Rood expressed gratitude to his colleagues for selecting him for the position following lengthy discussion in 2020. “I appreciate you having broken with tradition in allowing me to have this opportunity,” he said. To continue with a split-term option in these instances was floated among council, which Rood and Andersen favored. All councilmembers agreed that a written policy should be in place moving forward. Cavenaugh agreed that her preference would be to provide greater clarity. “Even though [this issue] only has come up a few times in the past 30 years, when it happens, it is meaningful. If there’s an opportunity to take our current system and improve upon it, whether that is sharing [the position] or greater clarity, I would be open to that,” she said. City Council directed City Administrator Sara Lillevand to compile a report by July 2022 that details options on how the city can establish a formal policy in writing.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously approved on November 1 a 3% salary increase for employees of the Public Works Department. The prior Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) expired in June 2021. The agreement for a pay raise will be in effect through June 30, 2025. Current and retired department employees also received modest increases to healthcare benefits. An update to bereavement leave now allows leave for purposes other than to attend funeral or memorial services. The total fiscal impact over the four-year period is $625,000. Educational incentives approved The council also approved educational incentives for all dispatchers who have obtained a Peace Officer’s Standards and Training Dispatcher Basic Certificate. Dispatchers who have completed educational training will receive an additional 2%. For new hires who have already completed certification, the 2% increase becomes effective upon completion of probation. Animal control officers who hold an AA degree or Law Enforcement Training Academy certification will be paid an additional 1%. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Animal control officers who hold an AA degree or Law Enforcement Training Academy certification will be paid an additional 1%. One strategy to achieve this is by accelerating the adoption of EVs and the growth of EV Charging Stations in Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: I read the clarification on the premium bond provisions in the city’s borrowing authority printed in the Piedmont Post on October 27. It notes that the city’s outside counsel assured staffers that the city has the authority to issue bonds at a premium dollar price, supported by an interest rate of up to 12%. Providing that response to the question posed in a letter previously printed in this paper is either naive or insincere, and in either case it is insulting. The premium proceeds amount to borrowing extra money which is repaid by committing the city to an above-market coupon, at least through the call date. The market yield for a Piedmont general obligation would be in the 3% area in today’s market; the 12% cap in the borrowing authority is standard boilerplate language designed to capture a range of market conditions over the long term, not to be a back door to borrowing as much as double the voter approved amount. The original letter to the Post was addressing the issue of the city borrowing even more than was originally and recently deemed necessary. When city employees quote lawyers to pretend to address a legitimate taxpayer question, while avoiding the substance of the question, we should all remind ourselves that tax paying Piedmont homeowners (not lawyers of staffers) are on the hook to pay this back.
articles.title: More comments about bond for community pool

articles.text: Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their chairs and music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce –- musically – the start of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. The big treat for runners (and spectators) this year will be the sign of eight symphony musicians from the Bay Area on hand to play music written for hunting horns 200 years ago. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a retired French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters various aspects of the hunt. However, over more than two centuries music was developed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see one with a very large circumference, called the trompe de chasse “Dauphine.” The trompe de chasse d’Orleans has a smaller circumference. The trompe de chasse Lorraine resembles an animal horn. But because they all are pitched in the key of D, they all have the same length of tubing – approximately 14 feet. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmpnt resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Piedmont resident Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, the mastermind. As the word spread among horn players, the group has grown to an ensemble of eight.
articles.title: Symphony musicians to provide fanfare for Turkey Trot

articles.text: The American Red Cross is encouraging blood donors of all blood types - especially type O - to make an appointment now. To encourage donations this month, people giving blood through November 23 will receive a $10 Amazon Gift Card by email. As the holidays approach and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns about a potential spike in flu cases this year, it’s important that those who are eligible, healthy and feeling well make an appointment to donate blood or platelets. The American Red Cross continues to address an ongoing emergency blood shortage, and donors are urged to give now to combat the lowest blood supply levels at this time of year in more than a decade. According to the CDC, flu cases reached an all-time low last year due to masking, physical distancing and shutdowns across the country, and many Americans may have reduced immunity this year. When seasonal illness increases, the number of healthy blood donors tends to decrease. Paired with winter weather, busy holiday schedules and ongoing COVID-19 concerns, the already-struggling blood supply could be further impacted throughout winter. There is no blood donation waiting period for those who have received a flu shot or a Moderna, Pfizer or Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine or booster, so long as donors are symptom-free. Donors are urged to schedule an appointment now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org or calling 1-800-733-2767. The nearest Red Cross blood bank is at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland. Tel. (800) 733-2767.
articles.title: Red Cross in need of donors of all blood types

articles.text: During an October 27 Piedmont School Board meeting, Supt. Randy Booker declared he was lifting the outdoor mask requirement for students, staff, visitors, volunteers, consultants and contractors who provide proof of full vaccination against Covid-19. The change went into effect November 1. The change was not an action item so no vote was needed. However, Booker reminded the board that they could advise him to delay his declaration. The board was split on the issue. “I was 100% on board with removing the mask mandate until I talked with the nurses [and Dr. Rutherford],” board member Megan Pillsbury said. Board member Veronica Thigpen also questioned the removal of masks for the vaccinated when outdoors and brought up the difficulty of determining who is unvaccinated on campus. Booker A healthy number of PHS students on Tuesday still wore masks outdoors after school on campus, but most students were happy to have photos taken without a mask. 11th graders Violet Lemley and Brianna Sotelo show their pearly whites on the PHS campus after school on Tuesday, November 9. stated that there are very few kids who are unvaccinated, so the district can identify them. Board Member Hilary Cooper led the charge for supporting the removal of masks. She suggested that the mask requirement should be lifted for elementary age students too, regardless of vaccination status. “I’m wondering [how] we tell a first grader, you don’t have to wear a mask at the park, but you have to wear one playing [during] recess,” she said. After a passionate discussion, School Board President Cory Smegal took the reins and made convincing points to stick with Booker’s decision. “We are asking our vaccinated kids to run the mile with a mask on. I think the way Randy has set up this policy where we relax the mandate for our vaccinated students is right on target,“ she said. The Post conferred with Piedmont’s Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF epidemiologist, on his stance. “I think it makes sense to me to wait, we are entering a surge in California, that is what people do not realize. This is right at the same time we entered the big winter surge last year,” he said. He was not adamant on the issue, however, saying that he thought it would be premature to lift masks for unvaccinated 5-11 year-old and that doing so for the vaccinated population on campus was “a close call.” Booker stated that 5-11 yearolds would have to wait until everyone is vaccinated on campus to unmask outdoors. “We will set a date,” he said. Middle School is grades 6-8, and the virtual event is 1-3:30 pm

articles.text: Piedmont students aged 5-11 became eligible to receive the Pfizer Covid-19 vaccine on November 3 following final approval from the Center for Disease Control. Piedmont School District’s vaccination requirements immediately went into effect for the newly eligible age group. This group of students will have until January 14 to present proof of full vaccination to attend school. Fully vaccinated is defined as being two weeks removed from the second dose. Accordingly student’s second dose should be administered by December 31. UCSF epidemiology and infectious disease expert, Dr. George Rutherford, recommends waiting four weeks in between shots for maximum efficacy. “When the [doses] are too close together the body doesn’t recognize it as a second stimulus, so it doesn’t mount as brisk of an immune response, which may have been some of the problems with Pfizer’s waning immunity,” Rutherford explained. The policy initially was going to require vaccination within eight weeks of CDC approval but was extended by two weeks, which will also allow families the option to wait longer than the minimum three weeks between shots. from scratch in finding appointments, we wanted to give a longer window of time. The policy gives Supt. Booker that authority in case of issues like limited vaccine supply, difficulty making appointments, etc.,” said Communication Director Brian Killgore. Only medical exemptions with accompanying doctor’s notes will be considered to avoid vaccination. This is the only exemption possible for students, teachers, volunteers and anyone working at or visiting schools in Piedmont. All families of 5-11 year-olds were contacted about the requirement by the district on Tuesday, November 2 as soon as the CDC Director approved the vaccine for 5-11 year-olds. “With the holidays approaching and knowing our age 5-11 students’ families are starting Deadline for proof of vaccination for age 12 and up is Nov. 17 Piedmont students aged 12 and older will have to present proof of full vaccination by November 17. Of the 1,222 age eligible students 95% have already presented documents providing proof of vaccination from COVID-19. “We have around 50 students remaining. We have reached out to families via email, text, letters, and are following up with phone calls,” said Killgore. Piedmont School District made the mandate for proof of vaccination on September 22, and mandated vaccinations October 17 for teachers and anyone working on or visiting campuses.

All families of 5-11 year-olds were contacted about the requirement by the district on Tuesday, November 2 as soon as the CDC Director approved the vaccine for 5-11 year-olds. “With the holidays approaching and knowing our age 5-11 students’ families are starting Deadline for proof of vaccination for age 12 and up is Nov. 17 Piedmont students aged 12 and older will have to present proof of full vaccination by November 17. Of the 1,222 age eligible students 95% have already presented documents providing proof of vaccination from COVID-19. “We have around 50 students remaining. We have reached out to families via email, text, letters, and are following up with phone calls,” said Killgore. Piedmont School District made the mandate for proof of vaccination on September 22, and mandated vaccinations October 17 for teachers and anyone working on or visiting campuses. A healthy number of PHS students on Tuesday still wore masks outdoors after school on campus, but most students were happy to have photos taken without a mask. 11th graders Violet Lemley and Brianna Sotelo show their pearly whites on the PHS campus after school on Tuesday, November 9. stated that there are very few kids who are unvaccinated, so the district can identify them. Board Member Hilary Cooper led the charge for supporting the removal of masks. She suggested that the mask requirement should be lifted for elementary age students too, regardless of vaccination status. “I’m wondering [how] we tell a first grader, you don’t have to wear a mask at the park, but you have to wear one playing [during] recess,” she said. After a passionate discussion, School Board President Cory Smegal took the reins and made convincing points to stick with Booker’s decision. “We are asking our vaccinated kids to run the mile with a mask on. I think the way Randy has set up this policy where we relax the mandate for our vaccinated students is right on target,“ she said. The Post conferred with Piedmont’s Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF epidemiologist, on his stance. “I think it makes sense to me to wait, we are entering a surge in California, that is what people do not realize. This is right at the same time we entered the big winter surge last year,” he said. He was not adamant on the issue, however, saying that he thought it would be premature to lift masks for unvaccinated 5-11 year-old and that doing so for the vaccinated population on campus was “a close call.” Booker stated that 5-11 yearolds would have to wait until everyone is vaccinated on campus to unmask outdoors. “We will set a date,” he said. articles.text: I recently had the privilege of interviewing Barney Saltzberg for my Creative Parenting Podcast. He is the author of Beautiful Oops, which Bay Area Children’s Theatre adapted into a musical a few years ago. At one point in the interview, he casually said, “If you can’t draw a straight line, just draw a squiggly one.” And this has really stuck with me as such a critical viewpoint for parents as we raise our kids. I’m thinking of the straight line as the typical path – the one that is often thought of as “right”, and the squiggly one as the creative path, the non-traditional creative approach. How often do we try our hardest to “draw the straight line” as parents?! For instance, I am not great at tracking “the stuff” of kid rearing... the jackets, the permission slips. And I spend a lot of my time forcing myself to try to do it RIGHT! But what if I should be “drawing the squiggly line” and coming up with creative alternatives so that I don’t have to do something I’m just not that good at? Example: lining our front entryway with bins for kids to drop stuff in and then creating a nighttime ritual around “stuff sorting” while playing one of our favorite songs. Or making “stuff tracking” into a game, where my kids get a stone in a jar every What should success look like? time they find something without asking me for help? Fill the jar, get ice cream sundaes for dinner! Once we parents embrace that squiggly line, how can we apply the same practice to our kids? Allow them to accept that there are some things they do really well and other things that might require more creativity. The more we can give our kids the same freedom we give ourselves to not be perfect at everything, the easier it will be for them to love their strengths and their challenge zones. I think about my son who found the assignments in his art class very challenging but was thrilled when his teacher gave him permission to doodle whenever he needed to. The teacher liked the doodles so much that she accepted them as his art assignment. That’s truly the squiggly line in action. Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. Listen to her interview with Barney Saltzberg this week on her Creative Parenting podcast (Apple, Spotify, Google, Amazon, Stitcher or wherever you listen): https:// podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ creative-parenting-with-nina-meehan/id158060599
articles.title: Straight line vs. squiggly line

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir performs at Oakland Museum After a nearly two-year hiatus, the Piedmont East Bay Children Choir, a beloved local institution, finally returned to performing live on Saturday, October 30. It was a monumental event, given that the last two years of choir concerts were singers’ recorded voices mixed together and uploaded to YouTube. We can all agree nothing is the same when you’re sitting in a zoom meeting for over an hour. Looking back at the virtual choir season, every Tuesday and Thursday we would get on the Zoom call, camera off, zone out for two hours and log off. It was extremely hard to focus when nothing was happening besides someone talking through a computer. I still don’t understand how I remembered all the songs just by looking at the music and hearing the piano. This fall, when virtual rehearsals ended, it felt strange – but wonderful – to be within reach of each other. We had to get used to our voices again because on Zoom we never heard what we sounded like together. Because of the ever-looming threat of COVID-19, we have to wear special masks while singing that make us all look like ducks. I’m about four feet away from all of the people in my choir, so half the time I don’t know what people 15 feet away from me sound like. And the sound we make comes out muffled because of the masks, which means that we have to run through specific sections multiple times when rehearsing. Each time we sing the section, it sounds different. But I’ll take that any day over sitting in front of the computer screen. We’ve had enough of that. After rehearsing in person for two months the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was ready for their first in-person concert in two years on October 30. It was the PEBCC Benefactor Gala to help raise money for the choi, the biggest event of the year, and was held at the newly created outdoor gardens at the Oakland Museum of California. Leading up to the concert, the senior levels of the choir had worked extremely hard to make sure the songs would be immaculate. Then there was the logistical part, where every part of the seating, food, and auction had to be tailored to perfection. Everybody at the PEBCC had an important job. The Gala started at 6 p.m., but the singers had to be there at 4 p.m., meaning a five-hour affair for the performers. It made me realize how much I missed being part of a live concert, when everybody is exhilarated and anxious, having fun with friends and waiting for their time on stage. After arriving, we went to the green room (dressing and rehearsal area) in the museum’s theater. It was modern, very airy and filled with light. The acoustics were perfect. We warmed up with singing drills, then ran through our songs until it was time for us to go on stage for a sound check. We returned to the green room for dinner. Pizza has never tasted so good. In addition to performing, members of the Ensemble got to wait on the tables and socialize with the benefactors. We worked in teams of five, forming a circle around tables and waiting for a guest to raise the slip of paper with the menu choice from the buffet. Being a waitress was hectic getting everyone’s orders in and bringing them back quickly. After we finished, all Ensemble kids headed to their tables in the back of the pavilion and sat down to watch Ancora perform their three songs. In the middle of the singing a fat rat ran right under our legs. Since there was a live performance, we couldn’t yell or scream, so we all had to stifle our shouts and not laugh too loudly about it. I have never seen a rat run as fast as that one did. Turned out it had a friend that watched us from above the garden stairs before a brave volunteer mother scared it away with a newspaper. When Ancora finished its performance to a long round of applause, the auction began. I did hear some prices that were way beyond my budget. After a final warm-up, we walked onstage. The lights were bright, the wind was cold, the exhaustion was there, and yet everyone was ready to sing. We sang three pieces, Hymn to Freedom, a piece with the message that no one is free until everyone is; Agnus Dei, a plea for mercy; and Bolo Bolo Sab Milo Bolo, a song about the god Shiva, written by Eric Tuan the choir’s Artistic Director I had never been more exhilarated. No matter how much I may have complained to my friends and family over the past year and a half, I had missed being a part of a choir. I could hear our sound during the performance: so strong, so full of emotion. For the first time in two years I felt like I was part of something bigger than one person, a choir and a community. I can’t wait to have more concerts, tours, and summer camps. Make no mistake, the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is back. Larissa Edel, a freshman at Bentley School, has been a member of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir for nine years.
articles.title: The return of live singing – with an audience

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, November 10, 2021 Why do the schools need this campaign? The gap between Piedmont School District’s per-child education costs and what the district will receive from state and local sources is $2,140. The cost to educate each student is $19,000 per year. The amount the district receives from state and federal sources is $11,354. The amount the district receives from local sources, including the parcel tax is $5,506. Let’s do the math: that only adds up to $16,860, leaving a funding gap of $2,140 per student. Each year the community meets the challenge by contributing to the Giving Campaign, helping the school district maintain its position as one of the highest-ranked school districts in the state of California. The funding problem starts at the top: California has one of the lowest per-child school funding rates in the United States and one of the highest costs of living. The state sadly ranks between 41st and 46th out of the 50 states in terms of per-student spending. California’s public schools also rank among the lowest in the entire country in terms of teacher/pupil ratio, reading and math scores, and college readiness. But because Piedmont is so deeply committed to supporting our children and schools, the district has managed to buck those state trends. Support from the community has helped build a school system that consistently delivers small class sizes, high reading and math scores, and strong college preparedness. Over the past 30 years, the Piedmont community, including the 60% of Piedmont residents who don’t have children in schools, have repeatedly voted to approve local school parcel taxes, funding essential services to maintain excellence in our schools and keep Piedmont property values high. A question that often comes up is: “Why aren’t our schools fully funded by this parcel tax?” Piedmont’s school parcel tax supplies 25% of the funds for the schools, but that’s not enough to completely close the gap, especially given ever-rising costs. The additional support that the PUSD receives from the Giving Campaign is essential to maintain the schools’ educational excellence. Without the Giving Campaign and other fundraisers Piedmont’s schools would struggle to continue providing small class sizes, elective and AP classes, music and art programs, librarians, counselors, class aides, and other specialists. Those student resources help give children the stellar educational experience that they deserve. To learn more about the Giving Campaign and to make a donation, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate. Each time we sing the section, it sounds different. But I’ll take that any day over sitting in front of the computer screen. We’ve had enough of that. After rehearsing in person for two months the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was ready for their first in-person concert in two years on October 30. It was the PEBCC Benefactor Gala to help raise money for the choi, the biggest event of the year, and was held at the newly created outdoor gardens at the Oakland Museum of California. Leading up to the concert, the senior levels of the choir had worked extremely hard to make sure the songs would be immaculate. Then there was the logistical part, where every part of the seating, food, and auction had to be tailored to perfection. Everybody at the PEBCC had an important job. The Gala started at 6 p.m., but the singers had to be there at 4 p.m., meaning a five-hour affair for the performers. It made me realize how much I missed being part of a live concert, when everybody is exhilarated and anxious, having fun with friends and waiting for their time on stage. After arriving, we went to the green room (dressing and rehearsal area) in the museum’s theater. It was modern, very airy and filled with light. The acoustics were perfect. We warmed up with singing drills, then ran through our songs until it was time for us to go on stage for a sound check. We returned to the green room for dinner. Pizza has never tasted so good. In addition to performing, members of the Ensemble got to wait on the tables and socialize with the benefactors. We worked in teams of five, forming a circle around tables and waiting for a guest to raise the slip of paper with the menu choice from the buffet. Being a waitress was hectic getting everyone’s orders in and bringing them back quickly. After we finished, all Ensemble kids headed to their tables in the back of the pavilion and sat down to watch Ancora perform their three songs. In the middle of the singing a fat rat ran right under our legs. Since there was a live performance, we couldn’t yell or scream, so we all had to stifle our shouts and not laugh too loudly about it. I have never seen a rat run as fast as that one did. Turned out it had a friend that watched us from above the garden stairs before a brave volunteer mother scared it away with a newspaper. When Ancora finished its Advertise Here! performance to a long round of applause, the auction began. I did hear some prices that were With the... Piedmont Post way beyond my budget. After a final warm-up, we walked onstage. The lights were bright, the wind was cold, the exhaustion was there, and yet everyone For more information on placing an ad call... 626-2468 or email: nancy@cmc-ads.com was ready to sing. We sang three pieces, Hymn to Freedom, a piece with the message that no one is free until everyone is; Agnus Dei, a plea for mercy; and Bolo Bolo Sab Milo Bolo, a song about the god Shiva, written by Eric Tuan the choir’s Artistic Director I had never been more exhilarated. No matter how much I may have complained to my friends and family over the past year and a half, I had missed being a part of a choir. I could hear our sound during the performance: so strong, so full of emotion. For the first time in two years I felt like I was part of something bigger than one person, a choir and a community. I can’t wait to have more concerts, tours, and summer camps. Make no mistake, the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is back. Larissa Edel, a freshman at Bentley School, has been a member of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir for nine years. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Over Halloween weekend local FIRST Robotics team 8033, Highlander Robotics, competed with their robot Whirlpool in their first in-person tournament since their inception in 2019. Chezy Champs is an annual three-day invitational hosted by Bellarmine College Prep in San Jose and has historically featured world class teams. This year was no different. Of the 39 teams invited, 26 were former World Champions. Teams traveled from as far away as Israel to compete against friends and rivals in what some saw as a stand in for the cancelled world championships in 2020 and 2021. In the crowded field, the rookie Highlanders turned heads. “I have been going to robotics competitions for six years. This was a whole new level and by far the best event I have ever attended! Top teams wanted to meet the bold new team from Piedmont running swerve drive and to see their unique climber,” said team manager, Helen Potter. The robot’s climbing mechanism was designed and built by Alex Ware, Alyssa Angsupanich, and Basia Young working with Mechanical mentor Klaus Zietlow. It features a wheel-driven cable track with carbon fiber hook and a ratcheting winch with paracord and was responsible for several of the team’s wins later in the tournament. Their team placed 15th of 39 after 10 qualifying rounds with a 7-3 record and advanced to the playoffs. In the playoffs they were eliminated by the top-seeded alliance from Israel, the eventual winner of the tournament. The Highlanders were recognized in the awards ceremony as the Most Improved Team. New recruits, Matteo Scano and Vaughn Khouri, performed well as the driver and mechanism operators. Alex Ware and Reece Beck along with mentor Frank Zhao expertly repaired and serviced their robot Whirlpool in the pits between matches. New software team members, Lewy Reece Beck, Alex Ware, Arun Brahma, Peter Stokes, Avery Chan in the Highlander pit. Whirlpool, the Highlander Robotics robot. Highlander team members in the stands. Seiden and Charlie Clowes, working with software mentor Kevin Clark, were able to solve software issues on the climber mechanism early in the qualification rounds which was critical for the Highlanders strong match performance. Jasper Tripp, scouting lead, led a team of students that gathered data on the opponents and alliance partners which provided critical information for each match. Team captain Charlie Lambert kept the team focused and worked closely with alliance partners to optimize performance and point contribution in each match. In the FIRST Robotics CompeWhirlpool (8033) outgains two other robots in the Chezy Champs competition.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 10, 2021 11 Highlander Robotics Continued from page 10 tition, teams of high schoolers are presented a 3 vs. 3 game in early January and challenged to build a robot from scratch and compete in that format in six weeks. Teams are fielded from throughout the U.S. and the world. Highlander Robotics was founded to compete in FRC in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert. During their first season in 2020, a founding team of 11 established basic skills and built a robot, named Nessie, to compete in the game Infinite Recharge which is centered around picking up and shooting dodge balls into targets before reaching an endgame where 125- pound robots grab a pull-up bar and lift themselves off the ground. The season was cancelled in response to COVID one week before their first competition. In 2021, the FRC format was adapted for an at-home virtual challenge and robots from the previous year were allowed. The Highlanders, now with 18 students for the new season, chose to build a more ambitious new robot, Whirlpool. It features a swerve drivetrain, the ability to shoot targets high in the air, and a mechanism that allowed the robot to hook a bar and lift itself off the ground. The team designed and built it in small groups in the Lambert garage and tested their software in Piedmont Middle School’s Morrison gym. In the Infinite Recharge At-Home competition, Whirlpool scored well in skills challenges and earned the team the Rookie Game Changer Award. By the fall this year, the Highlanders had grown to 27 students with a new leadership team after six seniors graduated last Spring. With hopes of being invited to Chezy Champs in the Fall, the team spent September and October training new recruits and preparing Whirlpool to compete. The new season begins on January 8, 2022 and the Highlanders will design and build a new robot to compete in the new challenge at UC Davis and San Jose State in March and April 2022. articles.text: Piedmont faces No. 2 Marin Academy today in Larkspur The No. 3 ranked Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team got the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs started with a 7-3 win over No. 6 Terra Linda in the quarterfinals on Saturday, November 13 at Carondelet in Concord after receiving a firstround bye. “We’ve figured out that the best way for us to win games is to play really solid defense and not give up any counter-attack goals,” said coach John Savage. It was another strong defensive outing for the Highlanders forcing long shots towards PHS goalie Dariush Kashani. “That was the plan, to double team and help set and force shots from the perimeter. We wanted to force shots from their less experienced guys,” said Savage. The match featured Declan Linnane leading the offense with a 3-goal hat trick. The team’s seven goals came from three players, Linnane (3), Antonio Rivera (3) and Shane Miller. “Declan played really well. He’s starting to pick his spots effectively and realize that he has the speed to counter-attack. Offensively, he’s a facilitator and a driver. Because the other team is focused on our primary scoring options, Declan will have opportunities if he puts himself in the right position. He definitely did that on Saturday,” said Savage. 7-3 win over No. 6 Terra Linda Terra Linda opened the game with a goal at the end of the first quarter, but Piedmont powered back in the second quarter to jump ahead 3-2 before halftime. The Highlanders tacked on two unanswered goals in the third for a 5-2 advantage, and added two goals in the fourth for the 7-3 final. In the second quarter, nearly three minutes ran off the clock by the time Piedmont drew an exclusion and sent in a goal 25 seconds later from Antonio Rivera to tie it 1-1. Terra Linda’s Ben Shafer scored on their next possession. But Linnane scored the first of three goals with 2:58 remaining to tie it at 2-2. With 1:55 left in the half, Piedmont drew another exclusion to gain a 6-on-5 opportunity, Shane Miller scored after 13 seconds for a 3-2 lead at the half. Defense also reigned supreme in the third quarter with nearly half the quarter running off before Linnane scored with 3:39 remaining, 4-2. Rivera sent in Piedmont’s next goal with 2:21 left, 5-2. Piedmont successfully killed a penalty when Terra Linda drew an exclusion on Miller with 1:43 left. In the fourth, TL’s Daniel Buckley scored 36 seconds in, 5-3.
