articles.text: It was a rough way to end the season-finale at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Friday, November 5, as the Highlander were shutout 35-0 by the Monarchs. The team ended its season with 2-7 overall record and 2-4 in league. PHS trailed 7-0 at the end of the first period, 14-0 at halftime, and 28-0 at the end of the third quarter. Despite the Highlanders’ struggles this season, Piedmont fought valiantly with a depleted roster that fluctuated between 15-19 available players throughout the season. “The kids did not quit. They hung in mentally with those small roster numbers. At any given time they could have walked away, but they didn’t. That’s a testament of the kids. Generally when numbers are low, morale goes down. But they understood what we were in for and pushed forward,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Johnson had high praise of seniors Ethan Feldstein, Mason Kimball, and Nico Defazio for their toughness this fall. “Ethan and Mason were threeyear varsity players and understood what it took. They led by example, Ethan played fearlessly through a shoulder and finger injury, and all types of aches and bruises. He showed what it took to maintain a level of excellence through the pain. Nico Defazio he hung in there through pain, had finger surgery, and wanted to come back immediately. He fought through it and came back for the finale,” said Johnson. Despite the loss, a bright spot was the school’s quarterback of the future, freshman Markos Lagios, getting the start. He rushed for nearly 90 yards and also passed for nearly 100 yards. “What I love about him is that he’s very mature for only being 15. He’s never played tackle football and we knew things were going to move faster for him. We wanted to get him the experience of seeing the speed of varsity football,” said Johnson. Lagios is characterized by his speed and strong arm – a common trait of the modern quarterback. Although he faces critiques of being “undersized,” Johnson is confident that Lagios has loads of potential. “To lead an offense, you have to lead by example and out-work everybody else. I know he’s ready for it. We’re looking for him to learn how to read defenses this offseason and we’ll get that time in. I’ve told him so many quarterbacks have been undersized and it doesn’t matter; he has the tools to get it done,” said Johnson. Looking ahead, the Highlanders will return some vital players to the lineup, including brothers Bautista and Matteo Costa, who at running back and linebacker will be back as seniors. Defensive lineman Bailey Cain and receiver/ defensive back Ryan McConathy will also be senior leaders. “The Costa brothers will be a major focal-point, same with Bailey Cain and Ryan McConathy. Those are going to be the guys we focus on and will be major points of what we do next season. They will all be great leaders for the team,” said Johnson. Bautista Costa is seen as a key player on next year’s team. Photos by Mike McConathy Piedmont wraps up its season after falling to Mt. Eden last Friday. Pictured is Matteo Costa tackling the Monarchs’ quarterback. Piedmont started freshman quarterback Markos Lagios (4) runs against Mt. Eden.

articles.text: The Piedmont tennis team traveled to Chabot College in Hayward for the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6. No. 1 singles player Bridgette McEfee reached the singles finals, and Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany placed fourth in the doubles bracket. “We would have liked two second-place finishes, but it’s still a good result. Bridgette did really well to reach the finals,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. McEfee entered as the No. 3 seed and received a first-round bye. She defeated Alameda’s Nisha Johnson 6-1, 6-2 in the quarterfinals on Friday, then followed with a gritty 6-4, 7-6 (7-5) semifinal win on Saturday, upsetting No. 2 Maya Curry of Berkeley. Facing O’Dowd’s talented No. 1 ranked sophomore Polina Marakhtanova in the finals, McEfee lost 6-0, 6-2. “Against Maya Curry, we split Staff Photo Jim Landes (left), Corey Reich, Bridgette McEfee, and Neil Rothenberg gather for a photo after McEfee’s second-place finish in singles in the WACC Championship Tournament. the last two matches and they both went to three-sets. I went into this match thinking I had to absorb the ball because I wasn’t going to beat her off groundstrokes and winners. So I was going for consistency, playing my Photo by Brian Mahany Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany placed fourth in the doubles ladder. best, and keeping up my energy,” said McEfee. McEfee’s consistency got the best of her Berkeley counterpart. It came through in the second set with a late comeback after trailing 5-4, gaining a game as the server before stealing another game as the returner. McEfee held match point at 6-5, but Curry tied as the returner 6-6 to force a seven-point tiebreaker. In the breaker, the two players traded games until reaching 5-5, when McEfee went ahead on another long rally, 6-5. With match point as the returner, McEfee sent a hard backhand to the feet of Curry after the Yellowjackets’ starter began to approach the net. Curry was unable to make solid contact on the ball, and it was over. “I just focused on keeping things consistent, trying out some new shots. I got a little tired in the second set; she started hitting really well and the tiebreak was stressful, but it was fun,” said McEfee after her big win. In the finals, McEfee squared off with Marahtanova for the third time this season, resulting in the No. 1 seed from Bishop O’Dowd claiming a 6-0. 6-2 win and championship banner. McEfee marks the second-straight Piedmont singles starter to reach the finals after Makenna Thiel won last spring’s championship. In doubles, Becker and Mahany earned the No. 2 seed after a strong regular season. The two defeated Ariana Alharazy and Elliott Schraag of Berkeley 7-5, 6-1 in the quarterfinals on Friday, but fell to O’Dowd’s No. 3 ranked Piper Bunkers and Maya Mehta in three sets, 4-6, 7-5, 6-4. “You have to give the O’Dowd girls credit, they played better and better over the course of the match. We strategically made some mistakes by letting O’Dowd get too many volleys to win the point. We had beaten them twice in close matches [earlier in the season] and knew it was going to be a tough one,” said Landes. Playing for 3rd place on Saturday, the Highlanders were upset by Chan and Fong of Castro Valley, the No. 4 seed, 6-1, 6-4. Singles player Anne Jumper lost in a narrow three-set opening round 3-6, 6-2, 6-3 on Friday. She fell 9-7 in the seven-point consolation ladder. articles.text: Big seasons ahead for JoJo Murphy & A.J. Harris Staff Photos Coach Ben Spencer talks over the upcoming boys’ basketball season. As the fall season winds down, all eyes turn to Binks Rawlings Gym for the return of basketball. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team returns after being moved up to Division 3 (larger enrollment schools) n the North Coast Section. The team finishing last spring’s shortened schedule with a 11-5 record playing some of the best schools in the Bay Area. Coach Ben Spencer’s newborn son, Jordan, arrived just in time for the ramp-up to the regular season. The squad had a scrimmage with Marin Academy last Saturday, November 6 in the Rawlings Gym and will have a scrimmage game with Freedom of Oakland this Saturday, November 13 at 12 p.m. The Highlanders play a NCS Foundation game on November 22 against Granada before the start of the regular season on November 26 with St. Ignatius in San Francisco. The Highlanders head into the season with JoJo Murphy fresh off a Bay Area Basketball Player of the Year award from WestCoastPreps.com. The offense will undoubtedly be built around him, but Spencer keyed on areas he thinks Murphy has improved. “JoJo is a stud. He’s a D1-caliber player. He’s worked on his defense all summer, and I think that will be his biggest jump. He’s really committed to defense. We JoJo Murphy returns as a senior leader. He led Piedmont in scoring last season.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Thoughtsicle.com Tyson Lake is the only surface body of water in Piedmont. It is estimated to have 3 million gallons of water, and was the site of drowning victims in 1951 and 1952. With Halloween having come and gone, here’s some spooky history that took place in Piedmont many years ago. Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences on La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind Hampton Field. The location is not public property but is the only body of water in Piedmont. It’s not a lake for fishing and is possibly better known for two drowning tragedies that took place in the 1950s. On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune reported that the Alameda County coroner’s jury recommended that Tyson Lake, an unused reservoir, be drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year-old James Richards four days earlier. But nearly one year to the day of the first accident, a second young man drowned. On July 10, 1952 19-year old Donald Stracner drowned while swimming with two companions. John Haubner, a former Piedmont Police Officer and a Navy diver in World War 2, was called on to retrieve Stacner’s body. “As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life,” the Tribune wrote. On August 8, 1952, the City of Piedmont urged the 20 homeowners surrounding the lake to erect a fence around the lake to prevent future drownings. Photos courtesy of HistoryofPiedmont.com A clipping of a 1952 Oakland Tribune article of Piedmont PD’s search for Donald Stracner. Photo courtesy of Thoughtsicle.com Tyson Lake isn’t known for its great fishing, but some have been known to reel out a carp.
articles.title: The tragic history of Piedmont’s Tyson Lake

articles.text: Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on November 20. Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 20 at 4:00 p.m. under the sponsorship of the Kodály Foundation for Music Education. The program will include works by Grieg, Brahms, Schubert, Debussy, De Greeve, and Indonesian composer Ananda Sukarlan. Suandrianna graduated in 2016 with a Bachelor of Music in Piano Performance at the Universitas Pelita Harapan in Jakarta. She received the Roger L. Keyes Award as the Outstanding Graduate Student in Piano from Baylor University School of Music in Waco, Texas, and earned a double Master’s in Performance (piano and organ) in 2020. Donations (general $20; student/senior $10) may be made at the door. The concert will be performed without intermission (75 minutes). Masks and proof of vaccination are required. A reception for the artist will follow, hosted by the Kodály Foundation for Music Education. For more information, visit www. kodalyfoundation.org or call 415- 606-9887. articles.text: Oakland Symphony’s opening concert of the 2021-2022 season is on Friday, November 19, and features pianist Lara Downes performing Florence Price’s Piano Concerto. The program also includes William Grant Still’s In Memoriam: The Colored Soldiers Who Died for Democracy, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3 (Eroica). Downes is among the foremost American pianists of her generation, a trailblazer on and off-stage whose musical roadmap seeks inspiration from the legacies of history, family, and collective memory. Downes’ playing has been called “ravishing” by Fanfare Magazine, “luscious, moody and dreamy” by the New York Times, and “addicting” by the Huffington Post. As a chart-topping recording artist, a powerfully charismatic performer, a curator and tastemaker, Downes is recognized as a cultural visionary on the national arts scene. Her forays into the broad landscape of American music have created a series of acclaimed recordings, including America Again, selected by NPR as one of “10 Albums that Saved 2016,” and hailed as “a balm for a country riven by disunion” by the Boston Globe. Her recent Sony Classical debut release For Lenny debuted in the Billboard Top 20 and was awarded the 2017 Classical Recording Foundation Award. In 2020, Downes celebrated the Year of the Woman with world premieres of newly discovered works by Florence Price and Margaret Bonds, and large-scale commissions from Paola Prestini and Clarice Assad, in collaboration with the Chicago Symphony and the Louisville Orchestra. Oakland Symphony will be led by guest conductor Mei-Ann Photo by Ken Carl Oakland Symphony will be led by guest conductor Mei-Ann Chen at the November 19 concert. Pianist Lara Downes will perform with the Oakland Symphony on November 19. Chen at the November 19 concert. A pre-concert talk from the stage will be given by John Kendall Bailey at 7:05 p.m. “Our season is presenting guest conductors who were connected to Michael as colleagues, as those he influenced, and those who influenced him,” said Symphony Executive Director Mieko Hatano. “In accepting the engagement, each spoke to the singular values of the Oakland Symphony as an orchestra that is recognized nationally as an authentic voice of social justice through music. These conductors all built their Oakland Symphony programs upon those values. We look forward to welcoming each of them on the podium during our Memorial Season.” To purchase tickets for the November 19 concert, and for more information, visit www. OaklandSymphony.org. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California will present an exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, beginning this Saturday, November 13. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of her ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. The exhibition will be on display through June 2022. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” Edith Heath Photo courtesy of University of California, Berkeley A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To purchase tickets and learn more about the exhibition, visit www.museumca.org.
articles.title: Oakland Museum opens Edith Heath exhibit on Saturday

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production of “Father/Daughter” will premiere live this Friday, November 12, and will be available to stream December 7-12. Written by playwright Kait Kerrigan and directed by M. Graham Smith, the play is a contemporary romance featuring two actors playing two pairs of lovers, detailing how parents and children can impact romantic lives. The play is a recipient of the Edgerton Foundation New Play Award, which allows productions extra time for development and rehearsal through a monetary grant. Kerrigan, an award-winning playwright and lyricist, is best-known for We Have to Hold Hands and Mad Ones. “Kait Kerrigan’s writing is insightful, audacious, and liable to make you either laugh or cry when you least expect it,” said Aurora Artistic Director Josh Costello. Playwright Kait Kerrigan Aurora Theatre will host a post-event discussion with the playwright on Friday, November 19, and Tuesday, November 23, and also on December 1 and 9. Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams will moderate the discussion, and may be joined by actors, directors, or other community members. To purchase tickets for live performances, or streaming access, visit https://www. auroratheatre.org/fatherdaughter. The theater is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley.
articles.title: Aurora opens this Friday with Father/Daughter

articles.text: Piedmont resident Don George, a widely respect travel writer and currently Editor at Large for National Geographic Travel, will offer a book talk with illustrations at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 13, at 4:00 p.m. He served as Travel Editor at the San Francisco Examiner and Chronicle for 15 years, and was Travel Editor at Salon, and Lonely Planet. It is his first appearance before a hometown audience. “This is something I have looked forward to doing for a number of years,” he said. He will read selected passages from some of his 14 books, including The Way of Wanderlust, his most recent anthology, How to be a Travel Writer, and By the Seat of My Pants. Don George is the author of the award-winning anthology The Way of Wanderlust: The Best Travel Writing of Don George, and of How to Be a Travel Writer, the best-selling travel writing guide in the world. His most recent book is an ebook entitled Wanderlust in the Time of Coronavirus: Dispatches from a Year of Traveling Close to Home. He is also the editor of 10 acclaimed literary anthologies, including A Moveable Feast, The Kindness of Strangers, and An Innocent Abroad. He has visited more than 90 countries and has written more than a thousand articles for print and online publications. He has been honored 18 times in the Society of American Travel Writers’ annual Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism competition. In addition to his writing and editing, Don has taught travel writing at the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism and the San Jose State University MFA Program in Creative Writing. He has spoken about his writings and Photo by Rob Yelland Travel writer Don George will discuss his favorite destinations in a book talk at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, November 13. Among the 14 published books he has edited or written, he will draw principally from The Way of Wanderlust, a travel anthology. Getting a close look at elephants in Africa. When in Paris, the first stop is the Eiffel Tower. travels at corporations around the world, including the New York Times and Google. articles.text: Berkeley Marina Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, will present a new exhibit, The Other Side of the Fence: Considering Green and the Power of Color, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit is dedicated in loving memory of the artist’s mother. Bonnie Drewes Stehr, who recently died. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November 13 to 21. A reception will be held on Friday evening, November 12. To attend the reception, RSVP to Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Red is hot, blue is cold, and yellow was known to make Van Gogh smile. While our reaction to color is affected greatly by personal preference, there is no denying that color has the ability to make one feel while eliciting a tangible reaction. In this exhibit Stehr explores the power of color by focusing on the impact of green. In 1140, stained glass at Notre Dame de Chartres showing Christ on the cross has the crucifix depicted in a green color, despite the fact that we know the cross was made of wood and was likely a shade of brown. Of course, green is associated with life ... rolling green hills in Spring, a lush forest, or a perfectly manicured baseball field ... all images that can elicit feelings of growth, vitality, and renewal. The cross depicted as green refers to the renewal that one’s soul can experience due to the sacrifice of Jesus on that cross. We encounter green in our daily lives in various shades. There is the brilliant green of a lawn encountered in morning light. There is the neutralized green of an oak tree that can almost appear warm under the light of early evening. Furthermore, the greens one perceives in a foreground change greatly when viewing them at a distance. The exhibit will include 30 new paintings in which the color green has an important role in the impact of the painting. Stehr will address the chemistry of green as he discusses how he mixes green to achieve the various effects. Also being exhibited are 45 paintings from previous exhibitions.

articles.text: Thomas Hardy wrote Far From the Madding Crowd in 1874 during the height of the Victorian era. It was a time when women deferred to the wishes of men and were considered property to be acquired and then ignored. Men, in contrast, offered women safe harbor and financial security. Hardy’s story has proved to be resilient and some might say timeless if not prescient. It is in great part because Hardy created in the character of Bathsheba Everdene as an atypical woman who is resiliently independent, desiring to live on her own terms and not those dictated by a husband. She declares to a suitor that she wishes to be no man’s property. The film, starring Carey Mulligan as Bathsheba, is not only beautifully photographed, but Mulligan shines as she conveys the emotions of a woman who inherits a large farm and the title of mistress of all she surveys. She is determined to “astonish” all who now work for her and make a success of the farm. She is not a dilettante but a woman who wishes to live on her own terms in a society where women are cloistered by custom and social mores. For all of her sturdy values and willingness to work hard in the fields, she is also a woman of emotions and passions. Hardy brings this to the fore when Bathsheba finds herself desired by three men, each vastly different. One is the farm’s shepherd, Gabriel Oak (Matthias Schoenaerts), a quiet man who has no station in life but is ever willing to step into the breach when needed. The second is a wealthy gentleman farmer, William Boldwood (Michael Sheen), whose vast holdings run parallel to Bathsheba’s farm. Impulsively, she sent him a Valentine’s Day card and the result was more than she bargained for. The third is a soldier, Sgt. Francis Troy (Tom Sturridge), bedecked in scarlet and gleaming helmet. He is someone who stirs her emotions that prove to be reckless and far removed from her practical and grounded approach to all other aspects of life. Suddenly this 19th century woman begins to lose her moorings and is confronted with a series of choices that most women of that era could never have imagined. Her vulnerability stems from a confused heart, not from a lack of financial independence. She is, in effect, the female equivalent of William Boldwood, who also makes a life changing decision. How Bathsheba sorts out this existential moment makes for a genuinely fine narrative, delivered by an excellent cast. As a period film, Far From the Madding Crowd is compelling and solidly engaging. Tangentially, the Brits adapted Hardy’s novel in 1967. Directed by John Schlesinger, the film starred Julie Christie, Alan Bates, Peter Finch and Terence Stamp. At the time it was considered definitive (almost three hours), as well as a tour de force portrayal by Christie whose startling beauty gave the film a far different look than this recent incarnation. Mulligan is in many ways a more interesting casting choice, her independence and allure drawn from her convictions and not overshadowed by her appearance. Far From the Madding Crowd. Starring Carey Mulligan, Mathias Schoenaerts, Michael Sheen. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13.

By Chris Honore’ For so many reasons, Up in the Air is a marvelous movie: stylish, intelligent, poignant and consistently comedic. The fact that this underlying reality, which is haunting, doesn’t overpower the film is testimony to the brilliance of writer-director Jason Reitman, and the superb acting ensemble, led by George Clooney. Clooney portrays Ryan Bingham, a debonair corporate assassin who travels nonstop, from city to city, firing people. It’s a job that the companies themselves are loathe to do. And so, he sits across a table and explains to long-time employees that they are being “let go,” as he prefers to say, instead of “you’re fired.” Bingham embraces his life in the air. He has elegantly turned his entrance to and exit from airports into an art form. He packs with studied efficiency, breezes through lines, swipes his cards, flashes his ID and is soon ensconced on the next flight, happily on his way to the next series of firings. He brags that he spends 322 days on the road and is miserable the other 43 days. He has no home to speak of – his apartment looks like an impersonal hotel room – and no connections to anyone, though he has a sister. He turns the idea of the lonely crowd on its head and his solitary life into an enthusiastic preference absent even a hint of angst. What is so superb about the film is that Bingham is an executioner and the audience is completely beguiled by his smile and intelligence and wit. He never pauses to unpack his emotions or reflect on the impact of his task and for a good part of the film neither does the audience. But then two women enter his life, one a businesswoman, Alex (Vera Farmiga), and Natalie (Melanie Lyskey), a new hire at his company. Alex he meets in a hotel lounge. Natalie is sent on the road with him to learn the ropes, so to speak. Both challenge his view of life, his contented detachment, and his elaborate rationales for his choices. Incrementally, the audience begins to sense that Bingham’s carefully manicured existence may not be as tightly compacted as first assumed. Though the film focuses all but exclusively on Bingham, so likable, so nicely constructed, and perhaps so starkly alone, the real tragedy resides with those he fires. Reitman includes snapshots of non-actors who have been recently let go, asking them to look into the camera and share what it means to loose their jobs after a decade or more. We watch as their faces crumble and they run the gauntlet of emotions and we can all but hear a door slamming shut. They are the subtext this film. For the most part disguised but also ever-present. Up in the Air is wonderfully written and acted, a quilt of themes, surprising and enjoyable in every way. Up in the Air. Starring George Clooney, Vera Farmiga and Melanie Lynskey. articles.text: A scene from Surf’s Up. Indeed, Surf’s Up is a fun, family-oriented, computer-animated tale about a teenage rockhopper penguin named Cody Maverick (Shia LaBeouf) who has always dreamed of being a world-class surfer ever since he met, some years ago, the legendary wave rider Big Z/Geek Topanga. Hence, he can often be found riding waves offshore near the town of Shiverpool, where he lives with his mother Edna (Dana Belben) and his brother Glen (Brian Posehn). One day a reality film crew arrives to make a documentary film about surfing. And so the feature becomes a faux documentary (perhaps a parody) in which the surfers talk in dude speak into the camera. Along with the film crew is Mikey Abramowitz (Mario Cantone), a talent scout, who is looking for possible entrants to compete in the Big Z Memorial surfing contest, to be held on the Hawaiian-style island of Pen-Gu. Cody jumps at the chance to enter and soon is off to the island. Along the way he befriends Chicken Joe (Jon Heder), a gnarly, good-natured caricature of a serious denizen of the surf world. Almost immediately upon arriving on the island, Cody meets a lovely lifeguard, Lani Allikai (Zooey Deschanel), a gentoo penguin, who rescues him from the surf and takes him to meet her uncle, Geek (Jeff Bridges), who helps Cody shape a new surfboard in preparation for the contest. He even helps train him, all while injecting some life lessons, reminding the teen that surfing is about having fun as well as winning. Cody’s main rival for the championship is Tank “The Shredder” Evans (Diederich Bader), a dude who has won the annual contest for almost a decade. Cody wants to win, especially to impress Lani. The event is run by a scheming rodent voiced by James Wood. Surf’s Up is a wonderful feature, steeped in surfing culture and lingo, with a lush backdrop, lots of imaginative characters, a gorgeous blue ocean, plus some great action scenes. Kids will be thoroughly entertained. Surf’s Up. Directed by Ash Brannon and Chris Buck. With Voices of Shia LaBeouf, Jeff Bridges, and Zooey Deschanel. Sony computer animation. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Surf’s Up a kid’s delight

articles.text: Wall-E, an animated collaboration between Pixar animation studios and Disney, debuted in theaters in 2008. It was a huge hit then as it should be now with a new generation of youngsters. Kids will be enamored with this small, irresistible tin box named WALL-E (Ben Burtt), who has binoculars for eyes that are not only functional, but capable of a panoply of emotive expressions. We watch him scoot around the dusty, dystopian remains of an uninhabited, litter-strewn earth on tractor-like wheels. Apparently, he was left behind to collect and compact the detritus of the longago departed humans. The name WALL-E is actually an acronym for Waste Allocation Load Lifter-Earth Class, which captures his day-in and day-out job. The year is 2700, and the planet has long ago been abandoned by its residents, who now live on a massive cruise ship-like space station called Axiom, which is run by a big box corporation, Buy N’ Large, and managed by robots who service the denizens’ every need. The humans move about in large hover recliners, have grown fat and lazy, wanting only to consume and watch their individual screens while drinking milkshakes. Meanwhile, back on earth, it becomes clear that WALL-E feels deeply his isolation and loneliness, made evident by the way he peruses the memorabilia left behind. He has a place of his own where he keeps old light bulbs, hubcaps, a Zippo lighter, and one of his favorite items, a Rubik’s cube. He often spends time in his digs, accompanied only by a tenacious cockroach, watching old Gene Kelly videos. To his surprise, an unmanned probe is sent to earth from Axiom named EVE (Elissa Knight), an Extra-terrestrial Vegetation Evaluator. She is sleekly designed, looks like an iPod, and beeps. Her purpose is to determine if there is any hope of the humans returning to the rust-colored planet and reestablishing any kind of organic life. Of course, from the get-go, WALL-E is smitten with EVE, and gives her some seedlings and a small plant he has found in his travels. EVE, having discovered what she was looking for, lifts off for Axiom. Naturally, WALL-E follows her, and thus begins the manic second half of the story that asks the questions whether EVE and WALL-E will end up together, and will the lazy humans decide to return to earth (a violation of the A113 “never return directive”) and begin the process of transforming the urban desolation they created centuries before back into something that resembles the once blue planet. Kids will definitely tune-in to find out. WALL-E. Directed by Andrew Straton. Pixar animation studios. With voices of Ben Burtt, Elissa Knight, Jeff Garvin. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated G. A scene from Surf’s Up. By Chris Honoré Indeed, Surf’s Up is a fun, family-oriented, computer-animated tale about a teenage rockhopper penguin named Cody Maverick (Shia LaBeouf) who has always dreamed of being a world-class surfer ever since he met, some years ago, the legendary wave rider Big Z/Geek Topanga. Hence, he can often be found riding waves offshore near the town of Shiverpool, where he lives with his mother Edna (Dana Belben) and his brother Glen (Brian Posehn). One day a reality film crew arrives to make a documentary film about surfing. And so the feature becomes a faux documentary (perhaps a parody) in which the surfers talk in dude speak into the camera. Along with the film crew is Mikey Abramowitz (Mario Cantone), a talent scout, who is looking for possible entrants to compete in the Big Z Memorial surfing contest, to be held on the Hawaiian-style island of Pen-Gu. Cody jumps at the chance to enter and soon is off to the island. Along the way he befriends Chicken Joe (Jon Heder), a gnarly, good-natured caricature of a serious denizen of the surf world. Almost immediately upon arriving on the island, Cody meets a lovely lifeguard, Lani Allikai (Zooey Deschanel), a gentoo penguin, who rescues him from the surf and takes him to meet her uncle, Geek (Jeff Bridges), who helps Cody shape a new surfboard in preparation for the contest. He even helps train him, all while injecting some life lessons, reminding the teen that surfing is about having fun as well as winning. Cody’s main rival for the championship is Tank “The Shredder” Evans (Diederich Bader), a dude who has won the annual contest for almost a decade. Cody wants to win, especially to impress Lani. The event is run by a scheming rodent voiced by James Wood. Surf’s Up is a wonderful feature, steeped in surfing culture and lingo, with a lush backdrop, lots of imaginative characters, a gorgeous blue ocean, plus some great action scenes. Kids will be thoroughly entertained. Surf’s Up. Directed by Ash Brannon and Chris Buck. With Voices of Shia LaBeouf, Jeff Bridges, and Zooey Deschanel. Sony computer animation. 1 hr., 25 min. articles.text: Part 32 in a biweekly series As we have discussed in previous columns, the scope of design in our built environment covers a huge range, encompassing everything from large city and regional planning all the way down to things like the entry hardware on doorways – and everything in between. In the last column we reviewed the concept of “massing” which can be considered the macro scale of building design. This week we move to the other end of the spectrum, architectural detailing which is building design at the micro scale. The combination of form and function, art and engineering that defines architecture is very evident in building detailing. Not only do the waterproofing details have to keep the water out, they also must fit into the aesthetic and must look nice. The famous modernist architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe is often credited with first stating the familiar maxim: “God is in the details”, underscoring their importance in no uncertain terms. As a visually supportive component they can enhance and reinforce an overall design concept or, if not thought through, compromise or even undermine it. All buildings contain a multitude of systems that include structural, plumbing, electrical, and HVAC (heating, ventilating and air conditioning) to name just a few. These numerous different systems must be coordinated and designed to accommodate their spatial and functional needs. The oversized outrigger beams on this brown shingle house is also an aesthetic consideration, adding interest and texture to the building (but not necessarily structurally required).

articles.text: Te-Ping Chen presented her collection of short stories Land of Big Numbers to the First Mondays Reading Group on November 1. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group held a zoom meeting on November 1 to discuss Land of Big Numbers written by Te-Ping Chen. Through an invitation by group member Albert Chen, a cousin of the author, Chen was invited to speak with the group on November 1 and she accepted. This special discussion drew a strong showing of 16 regular readers, and first-time reader Betsy Lim. Te-Ping Chen was a correspondent in the Wall Street Journal’s Beijing bureau for four years from 2014 to 2018. All but two of the 10 stories in her book are set inside China. There are countless, potential stories within this land, but Chen’s Land of Big Numbers offers a window into ordinary life in China. The stories are based on her experiences and understanding of the Chinese people and society that come from her reporting and a fertile imagination. Story examples include a young woman from the countryside who finds work in a Shanghai flower shop and daydreams about the lives of her well-off customers; a farmer who seeks to build an airplane from metal scraps; a delicious fruit that is deemed dangerous by the authorities; and a chef who tries and fails to understand his twin sister’s political activism. Another story examines how people may trade away their free will in exchange for comforts provided by the state. Land of Big Numbers received very positive critical review. The members of the group liked it and had many questions for Chen. Before the author joined the zoom call, Albert Chen provided some background on his younger cousin, who grew up in Oakland, attended Head Royce and then Brown University. She received a Fulbright Scholarship to study Chinese in rural China, and then a job with the Wall Street Journal in Hong Kong. To Albert’s consternation, she was transferred from Hong Kong to Beijing, far more dangerous, and reported from there for four years. The group was impressed with her writing. Her stories and the voices in them were different and timeless. They provided insight in portraying an authoritarian society and culture. Her stories are a collection of realism, allegory, magical realism, and fables. The tone in some of the stories is dystopian using it to convey what everyday peoples’ lives are like in China today. Some readers found the stories of life in repressive China to be depressing. Others liked the short story format but wanted to know more about the characters and what happened to them. Chen leaves her readers wanting more, a device used by good writers of short stories. When Chen joined the zoom call with the reading group, she provided more information about herself. As a reporter she spent her days collecting stories about life in China and included the richness in the lives of people in her stories in the book. The Communist state provides a degree of wellbeing for people, so most of them find their life acceptable and satisfying. Their lives may be comfortable, but it does come at a “dark fairy tale” cost to their personal freedom. Chen said that state control is only a fraction of the experience in China, but it is quite real. The older generation may have more of a challenge with this new China because their early communist lives were more idealistic. Younger people are enjoying the country’s new, higher standard of living, and new, zany lifestyles. However, Chen left the First Mondays readers with a sense of hope in her last story, a story about people in China who value freedom and want to live free. Chen is now the Wall Street Journal’s reporter in Philadelphia. She lives there with her husband and their young child and is working on a novel. The readers were impressed that this delightful, young woman, whose verbal communication is as eloquent and fluid as in her written words, is able to manage her several worlds so fully and effectively. Everyone is looking forward to the publication of her new book and reading it. Before ending the November discussion, the group confirmed that its selection of December is Michael Lewis’ non-fiction, The Premonition: A Pandemic Story. The January selection will be Hamnet, a novel by Maggie O’Farrell. Alternating fiction and non-fiction, the group chose The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown, a 2013 New York Times bestseller, for their February book. The next discussion will be Monday, December 6, and will start at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting, the group will meet in person at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. Michael Lewis’ non-fiction, The Premonition: A Pandemic Story is the December selection.

articles.text: Long-time Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick have announced the release of their newly published children’s book, Ripley’s World, available for purchase starting November 15. Written by Connie and illustrated by Mark, the story is about the adventures of their late rescue-cat Ripley and her many neighborhood animal friends. It features titular character Ripley, a feline who the author describes as a “tiny, feisty, funny, calico kitty with a big imagination.” Ripley’s story is bolstered by her many real-life friends in Piedmont: raccoon twins, baby possums, and a squirrel that plays tag. Also featured are Ripley’s German Shepard sisters, Kapo and Pele, and Hariel, the upsidedown goldfish. The couple adopted Ripley from East Bay SPCA – the runt of a litter of kittens abandoned at a construction site in Oakland. “When we took her home, she fit right in the palm of my hand, this little teeny thing,” Connie said. “Well, she ended up ruling the house and living for a good 18 years. She was a pistol - what she didn’t have physically, she absolutely made up in her energetics. She was tough!” Both Connie and Mark affectionately refer to all their animals as “family” rather than pets. Connie recalled that Ripley got along well with her German Shepard sisters Pele and the younger Kapo, both search-and-research dogs, but quickly added that “Pele would always defer to Ripley.” Even Hariel, their Oranda goldfish, lived upside-down for a decade due to a swim bladder defect. His depiction in the story gives a message of resilience; the couple explained that Hariel is an important character in the book because, like the real-life goldfish, disability does not get in the way of a happy and healthy life. The story arc of a blended family also plays a big role in Ripley’s World. “What constitutes a family? For us, Ripley, Kapo, Pele, and Ripley’s World officially comes out on November 15. Authors Connie and Mark Herrick with Kapo. Hariel - that’s our family. They aren’t our pets. People can define their families however they want, and families can have very diverse personalities,” Connie explained. The onset of the global pandemic forced many of us to shelter-in-place for the majority of 2020. The couple looked at that time as an opportunity to bring Ripley’s adventures to life in a published story, something they had discussed for years prior to its completion. “Our friends would always ask about Ripley,” Connie said. “As these stories came together, about nine years ago, I started writing them down. With the onset of the pandemic, [Mark and I] had worked together to bring them to life in illustration and narrative.” The publishing process took approximately nine months, explained Connie, who admitted that having a book published “isn’t for the faint of heart.” The couple chose to self-publish, which allowed them to maintain the integrity of the art and text. An important factor to consider was the inlay of Mark’s watercolor illustrations. Watercolor, the artists’ preferred medium, may not maintain its original color integrity and resolution when printed. It is also an unforgiving medium to work with in the editing process, Mark explained. “The colors you get, the luminosity of the colors, and how it flows and blends really captivates me,” he said. “But with watercolor – if you make a mistake, that’s it, the painting is done; you can’t fix it.” “[Mark and I] edit the pages and illustrations back and forth,” Connie said. “We weave the whole thing together, and he’s as much a part of the writing process as I am. Part of my job, in addition to writing, was art direction – and I’m very protective of his art and how it’s presented.” Although the couple enlisted the help of some friends for proofreading and graphic design, the couple mostly kept the book a secret until it was finished. “It was hard keeping it a secret,” Mark admitted. “It’s been super fun to work on something like this with my partner; it was a very organic process.” Now with a second book already in the works, the process begins again, starting with a storyboard and a sketch. Ripley’s Missing Locket is due to come out in 2022, with Ripley’s Vet Visit to be released the following year. The current book is formally available for purchase on November 15. A signed and personalized copy can be purchased at https:// www.ripleyandfriendz.com/shop. Ripley’s Store, which includes personalized items from the children’s book, donates 100% of its profits to support animal adoption, wildlife preservation and children’s literacy.
articles.title: Piedmont couple writes, illustrates children’s book, Ripley’s World

articles.text: Eye to Eye founder discusses his student mentorship program David Flink, a new Piedmont resident and founder of Eye to Eye, has been named a 2021 CNN Hero for his work in launching and maintaining a unique mentorship program. The company has grown from a college service project in 1998 to what is now a national program used in 150 schools in 22 states across the country and impacting more than 1,350 students each week. The program pairs college-aged and high school-aged mentors with younger students who experience learning differences that may adversely impact their successes in school. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, November 10, 2021 Piedmont couple writes, illustrates children’s book, Ripley’s World By Allyson Aleksey Long-time Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick have announced the release of their newly published children’s book, Ripley’s World, available for purchase starting November 15. Written by Connie and illustrated by Mark, the story is about the adventures of their late rescue-cat Ripley and her many neighborhood animal friends. It features titular character Ripley, a feline who the author describes as a “tiny, feisty, funny, calico kitty with a big imagination.” Ripley’s story is bolstered by her many real-life friends in Piedmont: raccoon twins, baby possums, and a squirrel that plays tag. Also featured are Ripley’s German Shepard sisters, Kapo and Pele, and Hariel, the upsidedown goldfish. The couple adopted Ripley from East Bay SPCA – the runt of a litter of kittens abandoned at a construction site in Oakland. “When we took her home, she fit right in the palm of my hand, this little teeny thing,” Connie said. “Well, she ended up ruling the house and living for a good 18 years. She was a pistol - what she didn’t have physically, she absolutely made up in her energetics. She was tough!” Both Connie and Mark affectionately refer to all their animals as “family” rather than pets. Connie recalled that Ripley got along well with her German Shepard sisters Pele and the younger Kapo, both search-and-research dogs, but quickly added that “Pele would always defer to Ripley.” Even Hariel, their Oranda goldfish, lived upside-down for a decade due to a swim bladder defect. His depiction in the story gives a message of resilience; the couple explained that Hariel is an important character in the book because, like the real-life goldfish, disability does not get in the way of a happy and healthy life. The story arc of a blended family also plays a big role in Ripley’s World. “What constitutes a family? For us, Ripley, Kapo, Pele, and Ripley’s World officially comes out on November 15. Authors Connie and Mark Herrick with Kapo. Hariel - that’s our family. They aren’t our pets. People can define their families however they want, and families can have very diverse personalities,” Connie explained. The onset of the global pandemic forced many of us to shelter-in-place for the majority of 2020. The couple looked at that time as an opportunity to bring Ripley’s adventures to life in a published story, something they had discussed for years prior to its completion. “Our friends would always ask about Ripley,” Connie said. “As these stories came together, about nine years ago, I started writing them down. With the onset of the pandemic, [Mark and I] had worked together to bring them to life in illustration and narrative.” The publishing process took approximately nine months, explained Connie, who admitted that having a book published “isn’t for the faint of heart.” The couple chose to self-publish, which allowed them to maintain the integrity of the art and text. An important factor to consider was the inlay of Mark’s watercolor illustrations. Watercolor, the artists’ preferred medium, may not maintain its original color integrity and resolution when printed. It is also an unforgiving medium to work with in the editing process, Mark explained. “The colors you get, the luminosity of the colors, and how it flows and blends really captivates me,” he said. “But with watercolor – if you make a mistake, that’s it, the painting is done; you can’t fix it.” “[Mark and I] edit the pages and illustrations back and forth,” Connie said. “We weave the whole thing together, and he’s as much a part of the writing process as I am. Part of my job, in addition to writing, was art direction – and I’m very protective of his art and how it’s presented.” Although the couple enlisted the help of some friends for proofreading and graphic design, the couple mostly kept the book a secret until it was finished. “It was hard keeping it a secret,” Mark admitted. “It’s been super fun to work on something like this with my partner; it was a very organic process.” Now with a second book already in the works, the process begins again, starting with a storyboard and a sketch. Ripley’s Missing Locket is due to come out in 2022, with Ripley’s Vet Visit to be released the following year. The current book is formally available for purchase on November 15. A signed and personalized copy can be purchased at https:// www.ripleyandfriendz.com/shop. Ripley’s Store, which includes personalized items from the children’s book, donates 100% of its profits to support animal adoption, wildlife preservation and children’s literacy. articles.text: Wednesday, November 3, was a morning of surprises for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. On a picture perfect, sunny morning, a turnout of 27 walkers was on hand to enjoy the day. The walkers were: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Alan Goldhammer, Elise Collins with K-9 best friend Lia, Jim Kellogg, Rhonda Ferrero, Mike Henn, Charlene Louie, Harriette Louie, Helen Dong, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Quincy Dong, SiowFang Tan, Kat Gustafson, Pat Keller, Stella Houston, Bob Gustafson, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Sherry Jacobs, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Priscilla Wanerus, Noemi Alvarado, Shirley Nakao, Dave DeRoche, and Dick Carter. The group was happy to welcome first time walker Pat McMahon. An excellent article by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society in a recent issue of the Piedmont Post told the surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm at the end of the 19th century. Gail told her readers that at that time there were only three kinds of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed that silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are the food for silk worms, and built a twostory, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” It is worth noting that the trees and this history were the inspiration for the name of today’s Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont. an additional seven acres were obtained, and about 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves, which the women harvested, chopped, and fed to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. At the Silk Farm the cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 200 to 300 feet long. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. But the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. Because of this history, Littlewood Avenue was chosen as the day’s destination. The group descended down Littlewood to where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees were once planted. The walkers were a little surprised to see no evidence of the trees, or their history. At the dead-end of Littlewood they saw a red London telephone booth on a private driveway. The homeowner, Michael Plitkins, greeted the walkers and invited them in and see what he has created. It was another surprise. Michael has a company that creates unique structures and virtual soundscapes. He bought the house in 2014 and transformed the area at the front of it into an incredible tropical garden with a swimming pool, water slide, and pool house. Jungle sound effects enhance this imaginary other world. This Littlewood Avenue side trip to Michael’s tropical wonderland had certainly not been planned, and it was time for the walkers to retrace their steps back to the Exedra. It had been a morning full of surprises. The Walking on Wednesday group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome by registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. Glowfari features hundreds of life-size glowing animal lanterns throughout the Zoo. It will include some new light fixtures for the event’s return this year. articles.text: The Tuesday after Thanksgiving has become known as Giving Tuesday, when people are encouraged to donate to charitable organizations. If you’d like to take part in this special day, you’ll want to maximize the effectiveness and benefits of your charitable gifts. So, consider these questions: Is the charity reputable? Does it use its resources Most charitable organizations are honest and dedicated to helping their specific causes. But sometimes there are a few “bad apples” in the bunch. These groups aren’t necessarily fraudulent (though some are), but they may spend an inordinate amount of their donations on administrative expenses, rather than directing this money to where it’s most needed. Fortunately, you don’t have to guess about the trustworthiness or the efficiency of a particular group, because you can To make sure that a charity is an actual charity – one that is tax-exempt and listed as a 501(c) (3) organization – you can go to www.irs.gov, the website of the Internal Revenue Service, and hit the “Charities & Nonprofits” link. An organization called Charity Navigator (www.charitynavigator.org) tracks charitable groups’ financial health and accountability, including how much is spent on administrative and fundraising costs. Generally speaking, a charitable group that dedicates more than about 30% to 35% of its total costs to administration and fundraising expenses might be considered somewhat inefficient, though you’d want to evaluate each charity individually, since extenuating circumstances can occur. Keep in mind, though, that smaller charities may not have the same resources as a national organization to provide the reporting necessary for Charity Navigator. Will my employer match my contribution? You can make your charitable gift go a lot further if your employer matches it. Typically, companies match donations at a 1:1 ratio, but some will match at 2:1 or even higher. Check with your human resources department about your company’s policy on charitable matches. • Are my charitable gifts tax deductible? An organization called Charity Navigator (www.charitynavigator.org) tracks charitable groups’ financial health and accountability, including how much is spent on administrative and fundraising costs. Generally speaking, a charitable group that dedicates more than about 30% to 35% of its total costs to administration and fundraising expenses might be considered somewhat inefficient, though you’d want to evaluate each charity individually, since extenuating circumstances can occur. pages.text: Wednesday, November 10, 2021 27 Shopping local at the White Building By Laura Martin Bovard You may have already heard, this year we have even more reasons for shopping locally. One is the ongoing issues with shipping, due to containerized freight sitting on ships that cannot dock. Others include is how our earth benefits when we choose locally-sourced, how our community benefits when we support local small businesses, and how our souls benefit when we support local artists. The building my firm is lucky to call home is The White Building, a registered historic structure in downtown Oakland, on the corner of 15th and Webster. Not only is it an architectural landmark, but also the current owners, Vida and Saied Karmooz, are lovely human beings. As landlords they attract just the best people. A number of new businesses have moved in downstairs in recent months, and I hope you will drop by our block and shop with them. One of the wonderful new tenants has already “made their mark,” painting vintage-style window signs for the other tenants. The warm, gracious and talented couple behind Memory Signs and Joseph Rivas and Napang Boonpaung. They specialize in a specific sign painting technique, an art form that they learned from their mentor, ‘Doc’ Guthrie, and proudly carry forward in a world that is ever-changing. Their shop on 15th Street is also a base of operations for Meng’s pop-up-houseplant purveyor: Memory Plants. To further augment beauty-present, Saint Flora offers not only bright and bold unique floral arrangements, but also gifts and home goods – all with a generous helping of love and spiritual resourcing. The colors of Tosh’s arrangement are as vibrant and full of joy as the woman herself. Even just getting a glimpse of her front window is enough to give your heart a lift. Once inside, Tosh might just pause the transaction and hand you a card to read, with words on it that will touch your heart and possibly bring you to tears for the moment of grace that it invites. Up the block Dream Farm Commons. a haven for creativity, hosts rotating, thought-provoking gallery shows featuring local artists whose works initiate conversations that promote positive social change. Curated through the consensus of a team of six artist-owners, the installations highlight themes of “radical imagination, art-making, social change, and creative production.” And on the other end of the building, 8Ball Oakland is a soulful skate shop, which similarly features art just under one’s feet – on the boards, as well as all the necessary tools of the skate-trade, and cool, branded merch. This place is also a collaborative, run by a group of friends who are skaters and artists – a labor of love, creativity, and commerce. When we patronize these businesses, we share in the positive social impact they are having on Oakland. I write often in this column about buying local for my clients, and for myself. May we all follow through on the promise in the messaging, “Doing well by doing good.” Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors. com Facade of the White Building. articles.text: Alameda County began rolling back indoor masking requirements on Monday, November 1, joining San Francisco, Sonoma, Marin and Contra Costa Counties in easing COVID-19 restrictions. Under the new Health Order, businesses, organizations, or hosts must verify that all patrons, employees, and attendees are fully vaccinated before allowing people to participate without face coverings inside their facilities of 100 or less capacity. On October 7, public health officials from all eight Bay Area counties announced that indoor mask mandates would be lifted if each county met certain case rate and vaccination criteria among its population. In order to lift its indoor masking requirement, Alameda County must have 80% of its population fully-vaccinated and Alameda County Health Officers must deem COVID-19 hospitalizations as “low and stable.” The county anticipated a mid-December date for lifting restrictions but announced on October 28 that COVID-19 cases and hospitalizations are on the decline. “I n A la me d a Cou nt y, COVID-related hospitalizations are down to 89 from a summer high of 238 in August. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has reached an agreement with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) to install four single-port fast Electric Vehicle (EV) charging stations on Magnolia Avenue near the Exedra Plaza. The City Council approved the appropriation of $75,000 from the General Fund to facilitate the costs at an October 18 meeting. This approved location is a shift from the proposed four charging stations next to the Rec. Tennis courts on Bonita Avenue as discussed by City Council on June 21. The original proposed 10-year agreement would have allowed EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. Council members discussed whether the location was appropriate and whether the one-hour charging limit could be extended but delayed a vote. The council delayed a vote again on July 19. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit told council members that staff had requested to pull the agenda item and return to city council for consideration. “Progress is being made with East Bay Community Energy in addressing the concerns that council expressed in the past. Our preference is to bring a fully-baked plan that we feel is going as far as we can go with East Bay Energy, but it’s just not ready yet,” Benoit said on July 19. The plan presented to council at its October 18 meeting was approved unanimously. “Other than the location and increased time allotment [to charge] from 60 minutes to 90 minutes, the terms of agreement were unchanged from June,” confirmed City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Electric vehicles may charge at a port for 90 minutes; following that time-frame, the driver will incur a time-based fee. The Piedmont Police Department will enforce parking spots and regulations in the same manner as other restricted parking spots in the city, Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers confirmed. In addition to the four designated EV charging parking spots, one space is included to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales added that following the June meeting, the city staff worked with EBCE to find the best site for EV chargers. “EBCE and city staff identified the Magnolia Avenue location as the most ideal location for a variety of reasons,” he noted. Piedmont Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman, who has heralded EV charging station implementation in the city for nearly a year, told council members that the approval is an important milestone for the city’s climate action goals. “Climate Action Plan is very much on the minds of city council, staff, and residents alike. One of the main areas the city must target in emissions reductions is in the area of transportation,” Dykman said. articles.text: An all-day meeting on Tuesday, November 2 by an advisory panel of medical and public health experts at the Center for Disease Control (CDC) resulted in unanimous agreement to approve BioNTech and Pfizer Inc.’s COVID-19 vaccine for children aged 5-11. Within hours, the CDC director Dr. Rochelle Walensky, gave final approval, and kids in the U.S. can start receiving the vaccine today, Wednesday November 3. Piedmont School District vaccine policy requires parents to provide the district with proof of their child’s vaccination within eight weeks of emergency approval. As of press time the district had not announced an official date for 5-11 year olds to provide proof of full vaccination. The district was one of the first in the nation to mandate the vaccine for students 12 and up on September 22, and also led the way with a mandate for teachers on October 17. Weekly testing and statements of personal or religious belief against the vaccine are not valid alternatives for teachers or students. Only doctors’ notes will be considered. There is some wiggle room once the district sets a start date for the eight week period if vaccine rollout proves to be difficult. “If supply of the vaccine in the Bay Area becomes an issue, the Policy also gives the Superintendent authority to adjust the deadline as necessary,” said PUSD’s Director of Communications Brian Killgore. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont Public Works Department and City Council. Editor: My neighborhood at Rose and Linda Aves and the streets surrounding Beach School have lots of beautiful street trees. Every year in this season, they drop their leaves. Every year the City sends its very expensive street sweeping vehicle to clean the gutters and keep the leaves out of our storm drains. This year, like in years past, only about 1/3 of the gutters are cleaned. Why? Because cars are parked on street-cleaning day. They fill the streets for two reasons: 1) There are no signs saying No Parking on street cleaning mornings 2) There is no enforcement of the No Parking advisory. Sometimes a resident will voluntarily post signs in front of his house, and once in a while a police officer will ticket offending parkers. They seem to do that only if: 1) The resident calls the City 72 hours in advance 2) The resident calls the City on street cleaning day to report a violation 3) A police dispatcher determines that proper 72-hours notice was given. This so-called “parking enforcement” only applies to the residence of the active volunteer. As a result of this overburdened, ridiculous process, the City’s expensive street sweeping vehicle wastes fuel and depreciation costs by just driving around, not sweeping, because of cars parked where the leaves have accumulated. This can easily be solved. 1) The City should post permanent signs identifying the No Parking days. 2) The City should police the scheduled streets on sweeping days and enforce the No Parking signs. 3) The street sweeping vehicle driver should call into headquarters to report the location of offending vehicles. With all due respect, please implement a responsible, systematic policy for assuring that our streets are cleaned and city resources are used effectively. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and ELS Architecture and Urban Design kicked off a series of community workshops on Tuesday, November 2. ELS was chosen by the city council to design a new Piedmont Community Pool complex. Two sessions were held on Tuesday – in the early afternoon and evening – allowing residents to learn about the process that the firm and city will use over the next three years. ELS staff were available to answer questions about programming potential, project size and scope, budget, and timeline. The new pool is slated to open in 2-1/2 years, in summer 2024. The first workshop served as an opportunity for residents to share thoughts and aspirations about the project. It also marked an opportunity for the firm to gather information from Piedmonters to refine the final design Clarence Mamuyac, principal at ELS Architects, describes plans for public meetings to discuss the city’s new aquatic complex. Residents gather for the first community workshop about the planned new pool. The gathering was held in the Veterans Hall yesterday at 1 p.m. concept. Project goals include, at minimum, two pools and a twostory support building envisioned in the 2016 conceptual plan. ELS and the City is targeting winter 2022 for design concept completion - that is also the target date for construction to begin. “We need more information, more input, that’s what this [first workshop] is about,” said Clarence Mamuyac, the design firm’s principal architect. “We’ll gather information from this session, and then on November 16, we will present ideas and will deputize everyone who shows up that day as architects. [Residents] will help us critique those ideas.” Mamuyac told the crowd that, at the final scheduled workshop, December 14, the preferred direction will be presented. “Let me say at the onset, it’s not going to satisfy everybody,” he told the audience. “But we will hear you, we will try our best to come up with solutions that fit most needs.” ELS will move forward with developing a draft program and concept directions for presentation, comment, and critique from the public. The next workshop is on Tuesday, November 16, from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Following the presentation, attendees will be invited to join a design team for a 20-minute charrette.
articles.title: Community workshop for new pool hosted by ELS and city on Nov. 2

articles.text: The League of Women Voters Piedmont will host a town hall tomorrow, November 4, at 4 p.m. to discuss the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The virtual town hall will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging aquatic facility. The current pool closed indefinitely on September 8, 2020; the new community pool is set to be completed in summer 2024. This event will include brief presentations from the city’s team which will be followed by an audience question-and-answer segment moderated by League of Women Voters Piedmont President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers are Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register for free at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded, and you can watch it live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel.
articles.title: LWV to host town hall on Piedmont Pool Nov. 4

pages.text: Wednesday, November 3, 2021 3 Community workshop for new pool hosted by ELS and city on Nov. 2 By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont and ELS Architecture and Urban Design kicked off a series of community workshops on Tuesday, November 2. ELS was chosen by the city council to design a new Piedmont Community Pool complex. Two sessions were held on Tuesday – in the early afternoon and evening – allowing residents to learn about the process that the firm and city will use over the next three years. ELS staff were available to answer questions about programming potential, project size and scope, budget, and timeline. The new pool is slated to open in 2-1/2 years, in summer 2024. The first workshop served as an opportunity for residents to share thoughts and aspirations about the project. It also marked an opportunity for the firm to gather information from Piedmonters to refine the final design Clarence Mamuyac, principal at ELS Architects, describes plans for public meetings to discuss the city’s new aquatic complex. Residents gather for the first community workshop about the planned new pool. The gathering was held in the Veterans Hall yesterday at 1 p.m. concept. Project goals include, at minimum, two pools and a twostory support building envisioned in the 2016 conceptual plan. ELS and the City is targeting winter 2022 for design concept completion - that is also the target date for construction to begin. “We need more information, more input, that’s what this [first workshop] is about,” said Clarence Mamuyac, the design firm’s principal architect. “We’ll gather information from this session, and then on November 16, we will present ideas and will deputize everyone who shows up that day as architects. [Residents] will help us critique those ideas.” Mamuyac told the crowd that, at the final scheduled workshop, December 14, the preferred direction will be presented. “Let me say at the onset, it’s not going to satisfy everybody,” he told the audience. “But we will hear you, we will try our best to come up with solutions that fit most needs.” ELS will move forward with developing a draft program and concept directions for presentation, comment, and critique from the public. The next workshop is on Tuesday, November 16, from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Following the presentation, attendees will be invited to join a design team for a 20-minute charrette. LWV to host town hall on Piedmont Pool Nov. 4 By Allyson Aleksey The League of Women Voters Piedmont will host a town hall tomorrow, November 4, at 4 p.m. to discuss the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The virtual town hall will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging aquatic facility. The current pool closed indefinitely on September 8, 2020; the new community pool is set to be completed in summer 2024. This event will include brief presentations from the city’s team which will be followed by an audience question-and-answer segment moderated by League of Women Voters Piedmont President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers are Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register for free at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded, and you can watch it live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel. The fun begins early on Thursday, November 25 at the Exedra, located at the intersection of Magnolia and Highland Avenues. articles.text: The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will be hosting a community workshop, “Doing Our Part: Bringing Affordable Housing to Piedmont,” cosponsored by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) on Tuesday, November 9. The upcoming workshop is part of PREC’s ongoing community engagement and education outreach supporting equitable and affordable housing in Piedmont. The workshop will address the Housing Element and the city’s General Plan update. Residents are invited to attend and participate, and a panel of speakers will discuss how the city can meet its housing goals mandated by the state, and the importance of creating affordable housing. The panel will also address how the housing element process can help the Piedmont community achieve greater racial and economic diversity. Speakers include Assembly member Buffy Wicks, Seaside City Council member Jon Wizard, and CEO of the East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation (EBALDC) Andy Madeira. The event is moderated by PREC member Sarah Karlinsky. The workshop will be held on Zoom and begins at 7 p.m. Register for the event at https://www.piedmontracialequity.org/. articles.text: This Halloween was one for the ages, as kids at Havens School arrived on campus October 29 for a parade first thing in the morning. Since Halloween was largely canceled last year due to Covid-19, it looked like costumes received extra effort this year. Harry Potter costumes were prominent, as were the ever-popular witch and princess getups. This year an influx of doctor and nurse costumes took center stage. The modern-day heroes were well represented by kids thankful to be in school and to be safe and healthy. Fourth grader Connor Khouri spreads his batwings wide, casting a large shadow at the Havens Halloween parade. Havens student Maddie Frazier, dressed as a witch, with kindergarten teacher Lydia Adams in a rainbow costume. Havens first grader Luke Carnazzo’s teacher Amy WooLee found out that Luke would be dressed as Mickey Mouse, so she surprised him by dressing as Minnie Mouse. Havens students filed onto campus from the Highland Ave entrance on October 29 dressed in their best Halloween costumes.

articles.text: In a multi-year budget update provided to the Piedmont School Board on October 13, it was revealed that though the current budget has a $1.6 million surplus, the school district is likely facing a shortfall of $1.4 million in both the 2022-23 and 2023-24 school years. The update stated that the two largest factors affecting the budget are declining student enrollment and personnel salaries. The most significant change is the reduced Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF) funding due to Piedmont’s declining enrollment. The current school year had 2,348 students, 145 fewer than last year. “While this does not impact funding this year, it continues to create a financial challenge in the years ahead,” wrote School Superintendent Randy Booker in a report to the school board. With 47 fewer students than expected this year, the impact on the 2022- 23 budget is $570.000 less in LCFF funding in 2022-23 and $415,000 less in 2023-24. Other expenditures contributing to the $1,400,000 shortfall include: • Books & Supplies- $531,000 2021-22 2022-23 2023-24 Original GAP based on 6/23/21 Budget Measure H Rev Adj -1,400,000 -1,400,000 131,966 131,966 131,966 State Unemployment Ins Adj 192,000 45 Day Rev Lottery Revenue Adjust 75,600 73,765 73,028 UA Undesignated Balance 948,205 Enrollment Proj LCFF Adjust -570,000 -415,000 Oct Update Salary & Benefit Adjust 427,000 427,000 427,000 Total Adjustments (excl Meas H) 1,642,805 -69,235 85,028 Balance Avail (from Prior Year) 0 1,642,805 173,570 Remaining Gap (if negative) 1,642,805 173,570 -1,141,402 Piedmont School District’s Finance Director Ruth Alahydoian gave an update on the school budget on October 13. • New Play-Surfaces at Elementary Schools- $112,000 • New Air-Conditioning Systems at Beach School- $610,000 • Heating and Air Conditioning System- $107,000 • Wi-Fi infrastructure throughout PUSD- $180,000 Some of these expenses were already factored into this year’s budget. The greatest change in the positive direction for the current year’s budget comes from a reduction in salaries and benefits for teachers and classified staff due to a number of long-time teachers retiring earlier this year and being replaced by less tenured faculty members. The district saved $427,000 in salaries and benefits. As currently predicted, the district’s current $1.6 million surplus will drop to $173,000 after the 2022-23 school year and a $1,140,000 deficit after 2023-24.
