articles.text: Let your kids play in the rain. As a Californian we all know how important rain (and snow) are to our very existence. It is something we need in order for trees to grow, crops yield, and to make sure water flows freely from the tap. We take these things for granted until they are limited. and then we value them. As a proponent of outdoor play and its importance to the growth of children’s bodies and brains, I am doubly supportive of playing outdoors in the rain. Rain gives children an opportunity to engage in a different type of play – especially in California where rain is inconsistent, at best. What a treat it is to play outside in the rain. For children there are many benefits for this change up in outdoor adventure: • Shift in the senses Everything is different when it’s raining. The dimension of sight, smell, touch and sound are all changed when it’s raining. Exploring the outdoors in the rain gives children an opportunity to try out their motor skills in a different environment. A wet and slippery world is very different (and fun). Taking a rain walk and observing together the shift in all the senses is an exploration worth taking. • Boost in creativity The rainy landscape brings the world into a new view. Sand and mud turn into molding clay, surfaces are slippery – sometimes dangerous, sometimes fun. All of this changes the normal outdoor play spots into spaces where imaginations can run free. Playing in what was a grassy field might now be a lake with a sea serpent. • Staying Active the family outdoor experience, we expand the opportunity to get kids moving. Keeping kids active means less adverse health outcomes over time. It may be messy, but it is fun. • Navigating Nature Playing outdoors is of course important for many reasons, but embracing the outdoors in all weather, including rainy, wet days helps children deepen their connection with nature, perhaps creating lifelong attitudes and behaviors. Winter is coming. I feel like there may be rain in the forecast. Get your raincoat and boots and have an adventure on a rainy day. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling.
articles.title: Rain is wonderful

By Kymberly Miller As a Californian we all know how important rain (and snow) are to our very existence. It is something we need in order for trees to grow, crops yield, and to make sure water flows freely from the tap. We take these things for granted until they are limited. and then we value them. As a proponent of outdoor play and its importance to the growth of children’s bodies and brains, I am doubly supportive of playing outdoors in the rain. Rain gives children an opportunity to engage in a different type of play – especially in California where rain is inconsistent, at best. What a treat it is to play outside in the rain. For children there are many benefits for this change up in outdoor adventure: • Shift in the senses Everything is different when it’s raining. The dimension of sight, smell, touch and sound are all changed when it’s raining. Exploring the outdoors in the rain gives children an opportunity to try out their motor skills in a different environment. A wet and slippery world is very different (and fun). Taking a rain walk and observing together the shift in all the senses is an exploration worth taking. • Boost in creativity The rainy landscape brings the world into a new view. Sand and mud turn into molding clay, surfaces are slippery – sometimes dangerous, sometimes fun. All of this changes the normal outdoor play spots into spaces where imaginations can run free. Playing in what was a grassy field might now be a lake with a sea serpent. • Staying Active By adding rain-play into the family outdoor experience, we expand the opportunity to get kids moving. Keeping kids active means less adverse health outcomes over time. It may be messy, but it is fun. • Navigating Nature Playing outdoors is of course important for many reasons, but embracing the outdoors in all weather, including rainy, wet days helps children deepen their connection with nature, perhaps creating lifelong attitudes and behaviors. Winter is coming. I feel like there may be rain in the forecast. Get your raincoat and boots and have an adventure on a rainy day. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling. School Site Reps: Rita Fabi, Emily Harrold, Tonya Antonucci, Jill Saper, Amelie Kappes, Christine Wente von Metzsch, Colleen Allan, and Kat Di Piazza. We are co-chairing the Giving Campaign this year because we want to ensure Piedmont schools continue to provide an excellent education for all of our children. Between our two families, we have five children who attend the Piedmont schools at all levels, from elementary to high school. The past year and a half have been rough for all of us, but we are so happy that the kids are back in school and re-engaging with their teachers, their fellow students, and their activities. PUSD has done a great job re-opening our schools this fall and they need our support more than ever. During the pandemic, like everyone we know, we thought about our options. After careful consideration, we recommitted to the Piedmont schools. They offer a well-rounded, comprehensive curriculum in a safe, welcoming, community-oriented environment. The Piedmont teachers and staff are dedicated to ensuring that every child has the opportunity to thrive. In order to help our schools and our students succeed, we need to support them financially. The reality is that our government does not provide sufficient funds for our public schools. The gap between what our schools receive from state and federal funding and other local sources and what they need to maintain our existing programs is $2,140 per student. We are asking every family in the district to participate in the Giving Campaign by donating the amount that is right for your family. Piedmont deeply values community and education. Donating to the Giving Campaign is a way to demonstrate our collective values, as well as our appreciation for the role that our schools play in our children’s lives. At least for our two families, we have never appreciated our schools more. This is why the theme of our campaign this year is Forward Together. Please join us in donating to the Giving Campaign and thank you for your support of our schools. –Colleen Allan and Christine Wente von Metzsch Co-Chairs, The Giving Campaign Giving Campaign Committee members strategize about participation.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Nº 43, in a biweekly series Parisians are flocking to an art collection from Russia that introduced French avant-garde art to the sleepy giant of a nation. Russian brothers Mikhail and Ivan Morozov were early adopters of French post-impressionism, which at the time was panned by critics and gallerists as too radical, poorly conceived, amateurish, and badly drawn with slapdash brushstrokes. The works were deemed offensive. The deepest cut was that neither the Louvre nor the National Gallery was buying any. These emerging ar tists included Henri Matisse, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Alfred Sisley, Edgar Degas, Paul Cézanne, Vincent Van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, and Pablo Picasso – names all familiar now. At the end of the 19th century, the Morozov clan was one of the richest families in Russia, industry titans with an intense interest in art and philanthropy. Their ancestry was unusual: they were peasant serfs, and their wealth was rooted from great-grandfather Savva, born into servitude. He was ambitious, trained as a textile worker and used his wife’s Mikhail Morozov (1870 – 1903) by Valentin Serov, 1902 Ivan Morozov (1871 – 1921), by Valentin Serov, 1903 Vavara Morozov (1848 – 1917) by Valentin Serov, 1884 Fondation Louis-Vuitton, designed by American architect Frank Gehry, completed in 2014. dowry to set up his own sewing room. Starting with silk ribbons, Savva parlayed textiles into multiple factories and established a multi-generational dynasty. He boldly imported textile machinery from England, defying the French embargo, and he profited from the shortage of textiles wrought by Napoleon’s scorchedearth destruction of industry around Moscow. serfdom by buying his family’s freedom for the colossal sum of 17,000 rubles, today’s equivalent of $397,000. It’s a story of grit, perseverance, and shrewdness by a family climbing from abject poverty into a life of material wealth. But their world tragically collapsed when their assets, business empire, and then their home was seized by the new Soviet state in the overthrow of bourgeois society. The premiere of Louis-Vuitton Foundation’s The Morozov Collection: Icons of Modern Art culls 200 works from their lifetime collections. The exhibition is the logical sequel to The Shchukin Collection: Icons of Modern Art of 2017, where Morozov colleague Sergei Shchukin’s reputation was rehabilitated as a trailblazer when he was bringing Paris art to Moscow. The Morozov and Shchukin families both inherited their fortunes from textiles. The families were close, but rivals, competing to buy from the same Paris art dealers. Shchukin created a benevolent pathway to bring art to the Russian public, filling the walls of his palatial home with nouveau art that stunned and excited the senses, created controversy and debate. Many of Shchukin’s contemporaries were in awe at the notion of public art, as Russia had none. The Morozov brothers were like-minded, and welcomed the public. The third generation Morozov sons, Mikhail and Ivan. were born into a rarefied life where they devotedly pursued the arts, unlike Shchukin who didn’t begin collecting art until age 40. The Morozov brothers also benefitted from a much broader education than Shchukin, and as teenagers they entered apprenticeships with influential Russian painters Valentin Serov and Konstantin Korovin, family-portrait painters already ensconced in the varying Morozov households. Mikhail and Ivan, one year younger, flourished in art, literaView of La Défense, a major business district about two miles west of the Paris city limits. ture, theater, and ballet, core pursuits encouraged by their mother Varvara, a literate, philanthropic presence in their lives. Her sons learned to paint plein air, developing an adoration of landscapes. Varvara was the industrialist in the family, a Morozov textile heiress alongside her five brothers, each a participant in the Morozov empire. Mikhail graduated in history and linguistics and wrote a comedy for the stage. Ivan painted well as a hobby, and he was sent to Zurich to study chemistry and learn new dye techniques; but both men preferred the arts to managing the factories they inherited. Mikhail traveled frequently to Paris and amassed 39 Western paintings and 44 Russian. When Mikhail died suddenly at age 33 in 1903, Ivan who had been heading up the family business stepped into his brother’s role. He too traveled to Paris, often buying from his brother’s preferred art dealers, Ambroise Vollard and Paul Durand-Ruel. Ivan Morozov proved to be an eager buyer, acquiring Picasso’s Two Acrobats, Renoir’s La Rêverie, and Monet’s A Corner of the Garden at Montgeron. pages.text: Wednesday, November 3, 2021 11 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from page 10 conceptualized with artists Pierre Bonnard and Maurice Denis who became his personal favorites, to adorn his Moscow mansion. Denis painted grand pastel panels with mythological themes for his patron’s Concert room, which was reconstructed for the current exhibit in Paris. Mikhail’s wife, pursuant to his will, transferred his collection to the highly respected Tretyakov Gallery founded by philanthropist Pavel Tretyakov who had provisioned the gallery and gifted it in 1892 to the City of Moscow. The Tretyakov and all Soviet museums were nationalized, and today the state museum is dedicated entirely to Russian art and artists. In her book Morozov: The Story of a Family and a Lost Collection, Natalya Semenova states that Ivan was in denial about staying in Moscow; and within their home they were progressively confined to fewer rooms, until eviction. The family escaped to Switzerland and ultimately lived in Karlsbad, West Germany where Ivan died of heart failure. Initially, art collectors believed that nationalizing the treasures would preserve the works in perpetuity, and it appeared to be so under Lenin. But Stalin hard-liners censored works that they deemed would fail to glorify the state. Attempts were made to destroy works that some anonymous official deemed frivolous or vulgar. Yet, heroes stepped in. According to Natalya, they hid the art or shipped pieces stealthily to safe locations. “Access to the art Morozov collected [was] obstructed or downright forbidden for nearly half a century.” See Americans in Paris on page 32 “Fruits et Bronze,” by Henri Matisse, 1909 “Le Coin du Jardin à Montgeron,” by Claude Monet, 1876 “La Rêverie” Jeanne Samary in a Low-Necked Dress, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1877 “La Glace du Cabinet de Toilette,” by Pierre Bonnard, 1908 Dave Perez… ...a uality guy He was a friend, neighbor, and the ultimate car whisperer — fixing Piedmonters’ cars since 1979. articles.text: Highlanders upset #1 Berkeley 12-8; beat Alameda 6-5 in semifinals A the scorekeeper’s clock struck zero at poolside, Piedmont water polo coach John Savage shot his arms above his head, screaming exuberantly. His team had just defeated Berkeley 12-8 to win the championship of the Western Alameda County Conference for the first time. The victory last Saturday, October 30 at the Encinal pool in Alameda, was Piedmont’s first league title after getting close a number of times in the past __ years. “I’ve been coaching for nine years and played for four years when at the school before college. I don’t think we’ve ever won, I know it hasn’t happened in my time,” Savage said. “The boys did an incredible job. It was a whole team effort; every single person on this team played a role. I am incredibly proud of them.” Savage helped lead the school to third-place finishes in 2021 and 2019, and his teams were in the finals in 2018 and 2014. Piedmont entered the WACC Tournament this fall as the No. 3 seeded team, but upset No. 2 Alameda 6-5 in the semifinals on Thursday, October 28. Berkeley entered as the two-time defending champions. Notably, Piedmont’s accomplishment was done without any superstars. In prior years it benefitted from the skill of Max Wagener, now at the University of Redlands, Henry Saunders, now at USC, Patrick Conn, currently playing for the University of Toronto. “This is a very complete team. Staff Photos Goalie Dariush Kashani makes a monumental save on a penalty shot by Alameda in the semifinals. Antonio Rivera scored five goals against Berkeley and two in the finals against Alameda, including the game-winner. Piedmont coach John Savage (right) celebrates his water polo team’s first league title. I can trust anyone in the water with the ball,” said Savage. “They knew what they are doing, and they can attack, attack, attack. Today, our defense was set up to attack Berkeley’s best player, Chase [McFarland], an incredible athlete,” “In my freshman year, we had a really good squad with Patrick and Henry, and they really set the foundation for us to compete year-in and year-out,” added senior captain Antonio Rivera. “We’ve kept that legacy going by setting a new high. We’ve had a lot of close games where our defense has had to stick it out, and that’s what happened these last two games. We’ve stuck with the system and its working,” The Yellowjackets entered the match after defeating Bishop O’Dowd 25-22 in the semifinals, not exactly a defensive showcase. Piedmont won a tight 6-5 victory in the other semifinal against Alameda. But in the championship game with Berkeley, Piedmont’s defense took over the game, making nine steals. “Our plan was to force the shot from anywhere but Chase. We were planning for him to go up, try to draw a foul, and shoot. That’s exactly what happened. I played with Chase for nine months, he’s a great player and it’s always an honor to go against him,” said Piedmont’s star goalie Dariush Kashani. Championship Game Recap Piedmont opened with a 2-0 advantage but trailed 3-2 after the first period. Then its defense came to life, shutting out Berkeley while scoring four goals for a 6-2 lead at halftime. They kept a three-goal advantage, 9-6 going in the fourth quarter, and closed out the win at 12-8. Rivera scored first with a penalty shot 40 seconds in. After a few trades of possession, Murray Davis scored with 2:47 left after drawing a man-advantage, 2-0. Shane Miller had a goal, three assists, and two steals in the championship win over Berkeley.
articles.title: PHS wins first WACC Championship in school history

articles.text: Water Polo Dariush Kashani is a junior goalie on Piedmont’s water polo team who helped the school win its first WACC League Championship on Saturday, October 30. He recorded nine saves and a steal in Piedmont’s 12-8 title victory over Berkeley. He also had a critical penalty save in the semifinals against Alameda on Thursday, October 28 in Piedmont’s 6-5 victory. He was the Piedmont Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2020.

articles.text: Fun Rides scheduled for Nov. 7, Nov. 14 The Piedmont High School’s Mountain Bike Team is staying active by hosting three Fun Rides. The first was on Sunday, October 31 in Chabot Regional Park. The team welcomed freshmen riders, practiced skills and played games, including Bike Soccer, kicking a ball while on their bikes, similar to polo, but without horses and mallets. The team plans two more Fun Rides, Sunday, November 7, and Sunday, November 14. The rides are open to all teenagers. Piedmont MTB is a Piedmont High club team that uses local trails and competes in the larger Bay Area. The team competes with other high school teams in the Spring. For more information see www. piedmontmtb.com. High school students can learn more by e-mailing piedmontbiking@gmail.com. Piedmont junior Artun Duransoy gets off a kick during Piedmont Mountain Bike team’s game of bike soccer on October 31 PHS freshman Leo Hurwitz looks for an attempt on ball. Piedmont MTB is set to host more Fun Rides on Nov. 7 and Nov. 14. Their regular season is in the Spring.

articles.text: Bautista Costa runs for 136 yards, two touchdowns Piedmont’s football team was victorious 12-6 over Kennedy on Friday, October 29 under the lights of Witter Field. A season-finale win over Mt. Eden would qualify the team for the Div. 4 North Coast Section playoffs. “It was a big win, I’m excited that we were able to pull it out. We made some mental mistakes, but we brought it to them in the end. Mt. Eden has a big front-four and five. If we win, we’ll be able to petition for NCS and we might see Encinal again,” said PHS coach Jerome Johnson. Bautista Costa had his biggest game of the season with 136 rushing yards on 25 carries, a touchdown, and a 9-yard pass reception for a TD. With senior receiver Nico Defazio out of the lineup, Costa showed his talent as a running back. “Without Nico, we were going to run the ball more often and I knew I had to prepare for that in practice. They were my first touchdowns,” said Costa quietly. With the narrow victory, Piedmont’s defense again came up big, forcing nine tackles for loss from seven different players, plus five quarterback sacks from four players. In addition, four players forced Kennedy fumbles came away with recoveries. “We’ve been told to strip the ball whenever we can, so we get forced fumbles. It’s worked out well. We’re confident in our D-Line and knew we could put pressure on their quarterback,” said senior lineman Mason Kimball, who had a blocked extra point attempt. Game Recap The first quarter ended in a 0-0 deadlock, while Kennedy, but Kennedy inched ahead 6-0 by halftime.. Piedmont tied it 6-6 in the third quarter before pulling ahead 12-6 with 5:43 left in the game. The first quarter ended with back-and-forth possession after Piedmont worked into the Titans’ red zone, but a 15-yard penalty pushed them back to their own 31, and ultimately turned over on downs at the end of the first. Kennedy drove to Piedmont’s 29 on the ensuing possession when Ethan Feldstein sacked the quarterback for a 10-yard loss. Keita Clear came away with a sack on a 4th- and-7 on the Piedmont 41. The Highlanders wound up punting to the 2-yard line with 5:21 left in the second period, and forced Kennedy into a 3rd-and-11. But Kennedy’s QB took a snap from shotgun in the back of the end zone and found an open receiver on a crossing route resulting in a 99-yard touchdown three minutes before halftime. Kennedy’s PAT kick was blocked by Kimball. Trailing 6-0, Piedmont gave Kennedy supreme field position, punting to their own 38. articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team blew away the Titans of Kennedy High in Richmond last Friday, October 29 at Witter Field. The 42-0 victory was a crowd-pleaser for the final home game of the season. Kennedy’s first defensive drive was stopped cold by Cash Elmquist, and turned into Sam Shelby breaking several tackles on a long touchdown run. After another defensive stop, Shelby scored again on a pass reception. The Scots powered into the end zone on a trick-play using center Logan McGilloway for a 2-point conversion. Piedmont recovered a fumble deep in Kennedy’s territory on the next possession, leading to Shelby’s third touchdown, bringing the score to 22-0. Running back Tommy Ashton scored Piedmont’s fourth touchdown for a commanding 28-0 lead. On the kickoff, Henry Smith plowed tackled the Kennedy receiver deep in Titans’ territory to force a fumble, which he recovered. Shafer Dando then turned upfield to score a touchdown for a 35-0 lead following Shelby’s extra point. Piedmont’s Nick King had an acrobatic sack on the Kennedy quarterback leading to another turnover. Piedmont quarterback Markos Lagios connected with receiver William Ferreira on a deep pass to the 1-yard line, and Smith drove across the goal line for Piedmont’s final touchdown, 42-0. Piedmont defensive lineman Arman Kazemi recorded two sacks on Kennedy’s last series. NEXT UP Piedmont plays Mt. Eden in Hayward this Friday, November 5 at 4:30 p.m. for its final game of the season. Photo by Chuck Wolf Receiver Sam Shelby scored had three touchdowns in Piedmont’s big 42-0 shutout of Kennedy.
articles.title: JV Scots shut out Kennedy

articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team finished its regular season last week, falling to Bishop O’Dowd 5-2 on Tuesday, October 26 at home, but defeating rival Berkeley 5-2 on the road on Thursday, October 29. “We had a really strong day against Berkeley, another solid outing from the doubles lineups,” said coach Jim Landes. The squad finishes its season 17-8, and the loss to O’Dowd snapped an eight-match winning streak. The victory over Berkeley solidified Piedmont’s second-place finish in the WACC’s Foothill Division behind O’Dowd. The Highlanders now prepare for the WACC Singles and Doubles Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6 at Chabot College in Hayward. The North Coast Section team championships follow on November 9-13 5-2 win over Berkeley In Piedmont’s 5-2 win against Berkeley. The Highlanders swept all three doubles matches and won two of four singles matches. In doubles, the No. 1 duo of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany won in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. They are likely to receive a high seeding in the upcoming doubles tournament at Chabot College. The No. 2 tandem of Rose Siemers and Mara LaForte won a close first set and an easier second set, 7-6 (7-3), 6-3. At No. 3 Cecilia Defazio and Emma Eisemon won in straight sets, 6-0, 6-4. No. 1 singles player Bridgette McEfee won a three-set battle and built a strong lead in the super breaker, 6-4, 2-6, 10-5. Also winning was No. 4 Anika Gilliland in straight sets, 6-2, 6-3. No 2 Anne Jumper lost in singles, 7-5, 6-0, and Michaela Bini lost 6-4, 6-3 at No. 3 singles. 5-2 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont fell to O’Dowd in the final home match of the season last Tuesday, October 26. Piedmont’s eight seniors were honored at the match for Senior Day; Becker, Mahany, McEfee, Siemers, Audrey Frankel, Ava Heirsh, Elise Young, and Sofia Ferraro. Photos by Brian Mahany Audrey Mahany (front) volleys in a point against Bishop O’Dowd. She and Amanda Becker (back) won 6-2, 4-6, 10-8 in a tense victory over the Dragons. They also won 6-4, 6-4 against Berkeley. Bridgette McEfee won in three sets against Berkeley, 6-4, 2-6, 10-5. The Dragons swept all four singles matches and won a doubles match. Becker and Mahany at No. 1 doubles won in three sets, 6-2, 4-6, 10-8. At No. 3, Eisemon and Defazio got the job done, but were taken to three sets, 4-6, 7-5, 6-4. Audrey Frankel and LaForte at No. 2 doubles, lost 6-2, 6-3. In singles, McEfee lost to O’Dowd’s college prospect Polina Marakhtanova, 6-0, 6-1. Jumper fell 6-3, 6-1 at No. 2; Bini lost 6-4, 7-5 at No. 3; and Gilliland lost 6-1, 6-3. NEXT UP Piedmont (17-8) heads to the WACC Individual Tournament (Singles and Doubles) at Chabot College in Hayward on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6. Matches start at 9:00 a.m. Cecilia Defazio (back) and Emma Eisemon won 6-0, 6-4 against Berkeley and won in three sets in a match with O’Dowd.

articles.text: The Head of The Charles Regatta crosses under six historic bridges on the Charles River, and historically attracts hundreds of thousands of spectators from all over the world. The Oakland Strokes returned to the prestigious Head of the Charles Regatta in Cambridge, Massachusetts the weekend of October 22-24. Piedmont High senior Max Cole was in the Strokes’ varsity 8 boat, which 11th of 80 boats. Also competing from Piedmont High was senior Amelie Tristram in the Strokes’ Varsity 4 boat. The Head of The Charles is among the largest rowing events in the U.S. for youth and collegiate rowers, annually attracting hundreds of teams from around the world. Cole characterized the event as a moment he’s been waiting for since reading about the Head of the Charles when he was a freshman. “When the Head of The Charles came around, it was wild. There are an estimated 250,000 spectators; miles of tents everywhere selling and promoting products, college teams, all sorts of stuff. This is one of the biggest races in the world, Olympians have raced here,” said Cole, a PHS senior. “It’s well over 1,000 boats with races over three days, its nonstop. The bridges over the Charles River are crowded with people and even on the sides of the river, there are people everywhere. It really hit me on race day that I was about to compete in this event I’ve been dreaming about since my freshman year,” he added. The event was canceled in 2020 due to the global pandemic. Crew, as a whole, sustained a troublesome year and a half that featured little to no racing for some student-athletes. It made this year’s Head of Charles that much more special. “Last year, we weren’t allowed to practice in groups of more than eight, and mostly did singles… The last serious race before this was February of my sophomore year. You step out of the plane to Boston and it dawns on you, ‘Holy cow, I’m racing in one of the most prestigious races ever,’” said Cole. “The Charles is a very windy river. The coxes who steer the boat are very competitive and won’t yield if you’re going faster than them, so a boat actually crashed into us and forced us into a wide turn. Maybe we would’ve gained a few spots if that hadn’t happened, but I’m still happy with how we raced,” said Cole. Also competing from Piedmont were Ryan Tripp who helped Dartmouth finish fourth in the Men’s Lightweight Eight, and Andrew Stoddard, now at MIT.
articles.title: Piedmont rowers compete at Head of The Charles Regatta

articles.text: Photos by Ernie Tai Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Founder Susie Rahl (left), founding Artistic Director Bob Geary, Executive Director Keri Butkevich, and Artistic Director Eric Tuan. One hundred fifty supporters of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir gathered on Saturday evening, October 30, for the 2021 Benefit & Concert, “Harvest Moon Rising” (also known as the Singing Moon). Held outside on the lush grounds of the Oakland Museum of California, it was the first opportunity in almost two years for Choir parents and patrons to see one another, have an al fresco dinner, and enjoy choral music. The two choirs that performed – Ancora and Ensemble – last sang in person in January 2020, so the evening was a true homecoming. Strict COVID-19 measures were followed – all attendees were asked to access the Clear to Go! App, upload their vaccination cards (or a negative test), and answer a few questions. Those who were cleared received a QR code to show the event organizers on arrival. We were directed to wear our masks whenever we weren’t eating or drinking. And, eat and drink we did. The Benefit started with passed hors d’oeuvres as everyone was arriving, followed by a bountiful dinner buffet. For this writer there was some anxiety in the proximity of everyone again, but everyone observed the masks-on request. We were welcomed by the Choir’s Executive Director Keri Butkevich, Board of Directors President Poppea Dorsam, Benefit Co-Chair Roshmi Mukherji, Artistic Director Eric Tuan, and Benefit Sponsor Paul Swenson (who read a heartfelt poem he’d written when his daughter Lucy graduated from the Choir). The coming season will be the Choir’s 40th. It wouldn’t be a Benefit without choir performances. Two advanced choirs sang, Ancora and Ensemble. Ancora started with Cancion de Otono (Autumn Song) “Where do you come from, my love, And then where are you going? Return to the place where you came from, Keep going to where you are heading, my love.” They ended the set with Deep River, the popular spiritual from the early 20th century: “Oh, don’t you want to go to that Gospel-feast? That Promised Land, where all is peace? A live auction followed. Enthusiastic auctioneer Sharon Mor coaxed higher-and-higher bids from the audience, starting with an original choral composition by Artistic Director Eric Tuan, then two dinners hosted by James Bell and Foster Goldstrom. As night was falling, we used our phone’s flashlight to illuminate our raised bidding paddles. Ensemble followed, regaling us with Oscar Peterson’s Hymn to Freedom: “When every one joins in our song And together singing harmony That’s when we’ll be free.” The group ended with Bolo Bolo Sab Mil Bolo, a Hindu devotional: “Let us all chant together He carries a trident And sounds the drum. Let us all beat drums.” A second round of fund-raising, Fund A Need, will provide needed funding, including underwriting a choir at a Title 1 school. It appeared that virtually every attendee donated some amount, starting at $10,000 and going to $50. The last round was spirited with the “Last Man Standing” receiving a classical guitar emblazoned with artwork by choir members. It was both a fun and a productive evening, and literally a breath of fresh air as we all start to get back to normal. Ernie Tai is a PEBCC alumni parent, a former board member, and a super fan. A capacity crowd of 150 supporters of PEBCC enjoyed dinner outside at Oakland Museum of California for the choir’s benefit and concert on Saturday, October 30. articles.text: Photo by David Schroeder Mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz will sing the lead role as Dido in Opera San Jose’s production of Dido and Aeneas. Opera San Jose returns to live performances with Henry Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas at the California Theatre beginning November 13. Dido and Aeneas is an opera in a prologue and three acts, with a libretto by Nahum Tate. The production is directed by Joseph Marcheso, and features mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz as Dido and baritone Efrain Solis as Aeneas. Soprano Maya Kherani stars as Belina and award winning bass-baritone Nathan Stark is the Sorcerer. Running time is 60 minutes with no intermission. The season launched with a streaming production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri. Dido and Aeneas will be followed by productions of Bizet’s Carmen in February, and Bernstein’s West Side Story in April. “This season we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” General Director Khori Dastoor said in describing the company’s 2021- 22 season. Proof of vaccination is required to attend this event, and masks are required for all attendees at the California Theatre. Evening performances will begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees will be at 2 p.m. For more information on COVID protocols and to obtain tickets to upcoming live performances, visit https://www. operasj.org/subscriptions/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose’s Dido and Aeneas opens November 13

articles.text: 2021-22 season dedicated to the late Michael Morgan O a k l a n d S y m p h o n y announced that its 2021-2022 concert season will be dedicated to its late conductor and artistic director, Michael Morgan. Morgan served as Oakland Symphony’s Music Director and Conductor for more than 30 years before he passed away on August 20, 2021. “It would be very hard to overstate the impact that Michael Morgan has had on not only the Oakland Symphony, but the entire Orchestra field,” said James Hasler, President of the Oakland Symphony Board of Trustees. “For more than 30 years he championed the role of the Oakland Symphony as a community builder – bringing us all together through dedication to education, celebration of the full range of music in our community, and leadership in collaborating with other local arts organizations. We miss him very much and we will find comfort in his spirit that will be with us forever.” The memorial season runs performing Florence Price Piano Concerto. The program also includes William Grant Still’s The Colored Soldiers Who Died for Democracy, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3 (Eroica). As an added feature, a pre-concert talk from the stage will be given by John Kendall Bailey at 7:05 p.m. “Our season is presenting guest conductors who were connected to Michael as colleagues, as those he influenced, and those who influenced him,” said Symphony Executive Director Mieko Hatano. “In accepting the engagement, each spoke to the singular values of the Oakland Symphony as an orchestra that is recognized nationally as an authentic voice of social justice through music. These conductors all built their Oakland Symphony programs upon those values. We look forward to welcoming each of them on the podium during our Memorial Season.” To purchase tickets for the November 19 concert, and for more information, visit www. OaklandSymphony.org Pianist Lara Downes will perform with the Oakland Symphony on November 19. from November 19 this year to May 20, 2022 and will continue with performances at the Paramount Theatre. The season opens on Friday, November 19 at 8 p.m. with a concert led by guest conductor Mei-Ann Chen and featuring pianist Lara Downed

articles.text: Oakland Ballet, directed by Graham Lustig, is offering two performances of its popular Luna Mexicana in honor of Dia de Los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, on Friday and Saturday, November 5 and 6 at the Paramount Theatre. Luna Mexicana is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food - orchestrated as a celebration of family and loved ones. Prior to the performances, visit the Paramount Theatre lobby to see the ofrendas created by local artists. The shows will be performed at 7:30 p.m. on Friday, and 2 p.m. on Saturday. Each show is 90 minutes with no intermission. Doors will open 60 minutes in advance. To purchase tickets and for more information, visit https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/ luna-mexicana/.

articles.text: HG Wells’ The Time Machine is a magical book. The reader’s imagination takes flight. It costs the traveler nothing because our imagination is without limit. There are magical places around the world. Take your pick. The shrouded mystery of Machu Picchu, musical Vienna, the opulence of Venice, history frozen in time in Pompeii. Great as these are, there are wonders close to home. Old Sacramento is one of them, and it’s less than two hours away. The entire area has witnessed a rebirth that is extraordinary. The level of excitement is high, but the downside is the incredible noise pollution. Tourists are delighted at every turn, but the noise from the street is deafening. Take yourself back in time for dinner on the refurbished paddle-wheeler Delta King. You can really have some fun here if you “dress for dinner” and make a big entrance into the oak-paneled dining room. Not far from old town is the Crocker Art Gallery. They used to present concerts in the old days before Covid. Let’s hope the concerts will resume. It’s worth the drive. At the opposite end of Old Town is the railroad museum, a Time Machine of unique stature. All the docents bring history to life. They even have “the Gold Spike.” Learn how the Transcontinental railroad was built; combining the political genius of Abraham Lincoln, some incredible graft and corruption, the triumph over racial prejudice, manifest destiny, and much more. There is considerable romance to train travel. Get into the mood by listening to the whimsical humor of Rossini’s The Little Pleasure Train and the flights of fantasy in Jaume Torrent’s Journey to a Magic World. Torrent promises to play it the next time he is in Piedmont. Two composers were able to capture the actual sounds of trains in music. Heitor Villa-Lobos did it in his Little Train of the Caipira. Arthur Honegger did it in his Pacific 231, which should be seen in the 1949 movie with vintage trains. For lighter fare I recommend Roy Clark singing Folsom Prison Blues or Hank Williams singing his own Ramblin’ Man. All aboard! One of the posters in Old Town Sacramento urging Californians to vote the California way. It reminds me of the way they used to vote in Chicago – vote early and often.
articles.title: Destination: fantasy

articles.text: The Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, has opened an exhibit entitled Color into Line: Pastels from the Renaissance to the Present, which will be on display through February 13, 2022. Color into Line displays 80 masterpieces created with pastels from the Renaissance era to modern day. Featured artists include Edgar Degas, muralist Diego Rivera, John Altoon, Wayne Thiebaud and Joan Mitchell, as well as rarely-displayed artworks. The exhibition draws from the archival works of the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts, as well as selected loans from local private collections. Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/pastels. articles.title: Color Into Line exhibition at Legion of Honor now on display

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) will present an exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, beginning November 13. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. The exhibition will be on display through June 2022. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” explained Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo courtesy of UC Berkeley Edith Heath, founder of Heath Ceramics

articles.text: UC Berkeley’s Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) currently is showcasing the work of celebrated Japanese cinematographer Kazuo Miyagawa in a series that continues through November 28. Miyagawa (1908-1999) is the visual stylist behind classic films directed by Akira Kurosawa, Kenji Mizoguchi, and Koa Ichikawa, among others. The best examples of his stylistic work and videography will be shown, several of which are in the film archive’s collection. Rashomon, Sansho the Bailiff, and Ugetsu will be shown, as well as other scope-format masterpieces. “Longtime BAMPFA filmgoers may remember Miyagawa’s March 1981 visit, a time [when] he was still actively making films and spoke about his development as a young filmmaker,” said Susan Oxtoby, Director of Film and Senior Film Curator. “A firm believer in filmmaking as a collaborative art form, Miyagawa felt it worked best when a director allowed space for a cinematographer or actors to bring their own creativity to the interpretation of the script.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets for screenings, visit https://bampfa.org/program/ kazuo-miyagawa-cinematographer-and-visual-stylist.
articles.title: Pacific Film Archive screening films on Kazuo Miyagawa through Nov 28

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, November 3, 2021 The Musical Gourmet Oakland Ballet Dia de los Muertos performance this Friday and Saturday The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Ballet, directed by Graham Lustig, is offering two performances of its popular Luna Mexicana in honor of Dia de Los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, on Friday and Saturday, November 5 and 6 at the Paramount Theatre. Luna Mexicana is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food - orchestrated as a celebration of family and loved ones. Prior to the performances, visit the Paramount Theatre lobby to see the ofrendas created by local artists. The shows will be performed at 7:30 p.m. on Friday, and 2 p.m. on Saturday. Each show is 90 minutes with no intermission. Doors will open 60 minutes in advance. To purchase tickets and for more information, visit https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/ luna-mexicana/. Oakland Ballet opens its 2020-2021 season with Luna Mexicana, celebrating Dia de Los Muertos. Color Into Line exhibition at Legion of Honor now on display By Allyson Aleksey The Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, has opened an exhibit entitled Color into Line: Pastels from the Renaissance to the Present, which will be on display through February 13, 2022. Color into Line displays 80 masterpieces created with pastels from the Renaissance era to modern day. Featured artists include Edgar Degas, muralist Diego Rivera, John Altoon, Wayne Thiebaud and Joan Mitchell, as well as rarely-displayed artworks. The exhibition draws from the archival works of the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts, as well as selected loans from local private collections. Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/pastels. Destination: fantasy By Joseph Gold HG Wells’ The Time Machine is a magical book. The reader’s imagination takes flight. It costs the traveler nothing because our imagination is without limit. There are magical places around the world. Take your pick. The shrouded mystery of Machu Picchu, musical Vienna, the opulence of Venice, history frozen in time in Pompeii. Great as these are, there are wonders close to home. Old Sacramento is one of them, and it’s less than two hours away. The entire area has witnessed a rebirth that is extraordinary. The level of excitement is high, but the downside is the incredible noise pollution. Tourists are delighted at every turn, but the noise from the street is deafening. Take yourself back in time for dinner on the refurbished paddle-wheeler Delta King. You can really have some fun here if you “dress for dinner” and make a big entrance into the oak-paneled dining room. Not far from old town is the Crocker Art Gallery. They used to present concerts in the old days before Covid. Let’s hope the concerts will resume. It’s worth the drive. At the opposite end of Old Town is the railroad museum, a Time Machine of unique stature. All the docents bring history to life. They even have “the Gold Spike.” Learn how the Transcontinental railroad was built; combining the political genius of Abraham Lincoln, some incredible graft and corruption, the triumph over racial prejudice, manifest destiny, and much more. There is considerable romance to train travel. Get into the mood by listening to the whimsical humor of Rossini’s The Little Pleasure Train and the flights of fantasy in Jaume Torrent’s Journey to a Magic World. Torrent promises to play it the next time he is in Piedmont. Two composers were able to capture the actual sounds of trains in music. Heitor Villa-Lobos did it in his Little Train of the Caipira. Arthur Honegger did it in his Pacific 231, which should be seen in the 1949 movie with vintage trains. For lighter fare I recommend Roy Clark singing Folsom Prison Blues or Hank Williams singing his own Ramblin’ Man. All aboard! articles.text: Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 20 at 4:00 p.m. under the sponsorship of the Kodály Foundation for Music Education. The program will include works by Grieg, Brahms, Schubert, Debussy, De Greeve, and Indonesian composer Ananda Sukarlan. Suandrianna graduated in 2016 with a Bachelor of Music in Piano Performance at the Universitas Pelita Harapan in Jakarta. She received the Roger L. Keyes Award as the Outstanding Graduate Student in Piano from Baylor University School of Music in Waco, Texas, and earned a double Master’s in Performance (piano and organ) in 2020. Donations (general $20; student/senior $10) may be made at the door. The concert will be performed without intermission (75 minutes). Masks and proof of vaccination are required. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Guy Orban founded Kiss That Frog 25 years ago as a Berkeley-based wholesale distributor of fine French goods. The company’s biannual warehouse sale, now called Le Marché Pop Up, has been a staple in the Berkeley community for well over a decade, drawing hundreds to its doors every spring and fall. Due to COVID-19 the sale was moved online last year. The virtual event was a raging success, and will remain as an online sale. “To reconnect digitally was a beautiful surprise. It gave us all the chance to say hello again in a different form,” explained Orban. “To share our enthusiasm with our friends from out of town was wonderful.” From November 12-14 this month, Le Marché is back with another virtual warehouse sale. Shoppers will be pleased to know that new and exclusive products will be offered in addition to the usual popular items. articles.text: Covid-19 restrictions, a group of Piedmont Seniors recently went to Palo Alto to visit several sites. The first was the Rodin sculpture exhibit on the Stanford Campus, adjacent to the iconic Cantor Center for the Arts. If you can’t visit the actual Rodin Museum in Paris, this exhibit is the next best thing, and it’s here in our backyard. Rodin’s goal was to convey complex emotions and diverse psychological states. Even 100 years after Rodin’s death, he continues to be recognized for his definitive sculptures of the human form. One of the most widely recognized of August Rodin’s sculptures is The Gates of Hell (see photo). The seniors then stopped at the relatively new Anderson Museum next to the Cantor Museum for a fascinating look at modern American art. This collection is one of the most outstanding private collections of modern and contemporary American art assembled in a single exhibit. The artwork is a gift from the Anderson family who built a collection over the last 50 years. Admission is free but advance tickets are required. The seniors continued their day to see the beautiful Elizabeth Gamble Gardens in Palo Alto and enjoy a delightful luncheon in the middle of the gardens. The Gamble mission statement is “to maintain our historical house and garden as an oasis of beauty and tranquility, providing a community resource of horticulture, inspiration, and enjoyment”. Since the house became a public property in 1985, a volunThe Piedmont Seniors recently visited the “Gates of Hell” sculpture by August Rodin at Stanford University. Pictured are (front) Janet Epstein (left), Diane Frost, Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska; (back) James Ayotte, Fred Pemberton, Gregory Jurin, Sandra Curan, Tanya Hu, Larry Hu, and Irene Westler. teer group in excess of 300 has completely restored the gardens, paths, and irrigation, and lighting has been added, along with a gazebo, which has become a popular spot for outdoor weddings and celebrations. The property was originally owned by the Gambles of the Proctor and Gamble family. After lunch, the Seniors were treated to a private tour of the century-old Gamble House, which is situated prominently on the property. The Piedmont Seniors look forward to exploring other parts of the Bay Area in upcoming months. If interested in joining the group for future excursions and meetings, contact coordinator Janet Epstein at 510-420-3070, or e-mail jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Mary and Bill Geong attend a ceremonial gala in Washington D.C. honoring Chinese American World War II veterans. Piedmont resident Bill Geong received the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of his father who served the nation during World War II. A ceremonial gala was held in Washington D.C. on September 30 honoring Chinese American World War II veterans and their families. The medal is a bronze duplicate of the Congressional Gold Medal awarded to veterans in recognition of their service. It is estimated that 20,000 Chinese Americans served in the Armed Forces during World War II, and that 40% of those who served were not citizens due to laws that denied citizenship to persons of Chinese descent. In December 2018 a bill was signed recognizing the military services of Chinese Americans despite facing discrimination in the country they served. “It was a bitter-sweet moment for us because, my father-in-law missed the occasion by a year,” said Mary Geong, wife of Bill Geong. “The Japanese American World War II veterans were awarded this honor [years prior] and the Filipinos who fought alongside American GIs in World War II were honored in 2017. It is fitting that the Chinese American veterans finally received recognition for their services in 2018,” she said. In 2019, the Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation honoring Chinese American veterans. The proclamation was presented to members of the Piedmont Asian American Club on April 1, 2019. “Although small in numbers, Chinese Americans made important contributions to the World War II effort,” explained Geong. “They are widely acknowledged for their role in the 14th Air Force, widely known as the Flying Tigers. Additionally, many Chinese American women served in the Women’s Army Corps, the Army Air Forces, and the United States Naval Reserve Women’s Reserve. Some became pilots, air traffic controllers, flight trainers, weather forecasters, occupational therapists, and nurses.” The obverse design depicts Chinese American servicemen and a nurse, representing the service branches in World War II. pages.text: Wednesday, November 3, 2021 23 Resident Bill Geong accepts Congressional Medal at DC gala Mary and Bill Geong attend a ceremonial gala in Washington D.C. honoring Chinese American World War II veterans. By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont resident Bill Geong received the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of his father who served the nation during World War II. A ceremonial gala was held in Washington D.C. on September 30 honoring Chinese American World War II veterans and their families. The medal is a bronze duplicate of the Congressional Gold Medal awarded to veterans in recognition of their service. It is estimated that 20,000 Chinese Americans served in the Armed Forces during World War II, and that 40% of those who served were not citizens due to laws that denied citizenship to persons of Chinese descent. In December 2018 a bill was signed recognizing the military services of Chinese Americans despite facing discrimination in the country they served. “It was a bitter-sweet moment for us because, my father-in-law missed the occasion by a year,” said Mary Geong, wife of Bill Geong. “The Japanese American World War II veterans were awarded this honor [years prior] and the Filipinos who fought alongside American GIs in World War II were honored in 2017. It is fitting that the Chinese American veterans finally received recognition for their services in 2018,” she said. In 2019, the Piedmont City Council issued a proclamation honoring Chinese American veterans. The proclamation was presented to members of the Piedmont Asian American Club on April 1, 2019. “Although small in numbers, Chinese Americans made important contributions to the World War II effort,” explained Geong. “They are widely acknowledged for their role in the 14th Air Force, widely known as the Flying Tigers. Additionally, many Chinese American women served in the Women’s Army Corps, the Army Air Forces, and the United States Naval Reserve Women’s Reserve. Some became pilots, air traffic controllers, flight trainers, weather forecasters, occupational therapists, and nurses.” The obverse design depicts Chinese American servicemen and a nurse, representing the service branches in World War II. The reverse design features an Iowa class battleship, an M4 Sherman tank, and a P-40 Warhawk from the Flying Tigers in front of an American flag from the 1940s. The U.S. Mint produced one 24-carat gold medal, valued at $70,000, which is permanently displayed in the Smithsonian National History Museum. articles.text: A large group of walkers received a guided tour of Millionaires’ Row at Mountain View Cemetery last Wednessday, October 27. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a special Halloween week tour of the Mountain View Cemetery on Wednesday, October 27. A strong turnout of 40 participants met in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum and were led on a guided tour by long-time cemetery docent Jane Leroe, a 75-year old groundbreaking trial attorney. Jane explained that in the early 1860s a group of leading local businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and also the 13th mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, created the cemetery under the California Rural Cemetery Act of 1859. His group bought 200 acres of fields far from the center of Oakland for the cemetery so that it would always be in a rural setting. Mountain View was established in 1863 and 26 acres were added later. A total of 170,000 people are buried there with space for an equal number in future years. It was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park and much of UC Berkeley and Stanford University. The association that the founders formed still operates the cemetery today. Many of California’s most important historical figures are buried at Mountain View. Including Hearst Castle architect Julia Morgan, Alexander and Josephine Dunsmuir of Dunsmuir House, Anthony Chabot of Chabot Observatory, railroad tycoon Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli of Ghirardelli Chocolate, Oakland mayor Samuel Crockett, and the “Black Dahlia” Elizabeth Short. One of the cemetery’s main attractions is “Millionaires’ Row,” a section where the most grand, elaborate crypts stand, housing some of California’s most famous and wealthy residents. It is located at the peak of a hill with an expansive view of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. Jane noted that these businessmen came to California around 1850, and were the men who sold the miners the things they needed. At the time the cemetery was created, Egyptian archeological discoveries were being made by the western world, and everything Egyptian was the rage. The cemetery’s Egyptian obelisks and pyramids reflect that popularity. There are two tiers of Millionaires’ Row. The lower tier was for the wealthy, and the upper tier was for the really wealthy. The tomb of Samuel Merritt is Jane’s favorite because of all the beneficial things he did and created for the area. Locals realized it was Merritt who was responsible for the lake in the middle of Oakland, so they simply referred to it as “Lake Merritt.” The walkers were then told the history of Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli, “Borax” Smith, Charles Doe of UC Berkeley Library fame, and many others. The walkers found Jane to be an animated storyteller, providing candor and humor to give life to these long dead people. Before leaving, Jane told a final story of the Grand Army of the Republic soldiers’ graveyard. They were Civil War Union veterans who died in California, or whose bodies were moved to Mountain View. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: • Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Quick, simple, and bursting • 4 eggs, extra-large with flavor describes this soup • Flat-leaf parsley for garnish perfectly. You may have most of the ingredients on hand, and it only takes about 30 minutes to prepare. Along with garlic, Spanish pimentón de la vera dulce is the flavor forward ingredient here. It originates from the Extremadura/La Vera region of Spain, where the mild, red peppers are dried over oak fire. It adds a warm, smokey note to everything from soup and stews to dry-rubs and even breading/ coating mixes. It’s in frequent use in my kitchen, but I still store it in the refrigerator to ensure it retains its bright flavor. Given that this soup is of modest nature, it is easy to embellish. Add minced red bell pepper whilst sautéing the onions and garlic and add a diced tomato when you add the broth. But take care to not embellish so much that the garlicy-ness becomes muted. Spanish-Style Garlic Bread Soup Adapted from The New Spanish Table by Anya von Bremzen Serves 4 Ingredients • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus additional as needed • 1/2 medium yellow onion, finely diced • 12 cloves garlic, about 1/4 cup, minced. Set aside 1 tablespoon of the garlic to use in the 2nd addition of garlic to the soup • 2 ounces Serrano ham, finely diced. Substitute with prosciutto. • 6 ounces bread, cut into 1-inch cubes. Use batard, round loaf, or baguette. Dayold bread is ideal. • 2 teaspoons sweet, smoked Spanish paprika, pimentón de la vera dulce • 4 cups chicken broth or stock Instructions 1. Heat the olive oil in a heavy 4-quart saucepan over low heat. Add the onions and most of the garlic (reserving the 1 tablespoon to add later), and ham, stirring until the onion becomes translucent and the garlic is very fragrant, about 4 – 5 minutes. Do not let the onion or garlic take on any browning. 2. Add the cubes of bread and stir to coat the bread evenly with the oil, about 2 - 3 minutes. Add a bit more oil if needed. 3. Remove the pan from the heat and sprinkle in the paprika. Stir to coat the cubes of bread evenly. Return the pan to the burner and add the chicken stock. Increase the heat to medium and simmer for about 5 minutes. You want to bread to expand but retain its shape. Add the reserved 1 tablespoon of minced garlic and cook another minute or so. Taste and adjust seasoning. 4. To poach the eggs: Crack one egg into a small ramekin. Make a small well in the simmering soup and carefully pour out the egg into the prepared well. Repeat with remaining three eggs then cover the saucepan. Let the eggs poach in the simmering soup undisturbed for about 5 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks reach the desired consistency. (I prefer the yolks to be slightly runny, which when stirred into the soup add a velvety texture.) 5. Carefully ladle the soup into serving bowls, adding the poached egg last so it floats on top. Garnish with parsley and serve immediately. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: Spanish-Style Garlic Bread Soup

articles.text: An American White pelican with large fishhooks lodged into its throat and fishing line encircling its neck and bill succumbed to injuries on October 31, despite being rescued from Lake Merritt on Wednesday and treated by the Oakland Zoo. After receiving fluids, and food at the Zoo’s Veterinarian hospital the pelican, nicknamed Merritt, was transferred to the International Bird Rescue where she passed away. Using two kayaks and a small motorboat to reach and then catch the pelican, Oakland Zoo’s VP of Animal Care, Colleen Kinzley, and Zoological Manager Andrea Dougall, brought the bird to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital for treatment. Upon arrival at the Zoo, veterinary staff examined the bird, administered fluids, conducted a blood draw, and checked the injured area on the neck. From initial observations, they determined that the fishing tackle had prevented the bird from being able to eat or drink for weeks, and was suffering from dehydration, starvation, and possible anemia. The staff fed Merritt smelt and capelin fish and had early hopes for her recovery. Her death serves as a vivid reminder of the dangers of fishing items left in Lake Merritt and in all waterways. “Untold numbers of birds, turtles and other wildlife are affected by this solvable issue. Proper disposal of fishing line is crucial, and every citizen can help by picking up any fishing items found in nature,” said Amy Gotliffe, Vice President of Conservation at Oakland Zoo. An American White pelican, named Merritt, was ensnared by multiple barbed hooks on a fishing lure. Between 2002 and 2015, a study by the Audubon Society reported that California-based International Bird Rescue treated at least 2,957 birds for injuries caused by fishing gear. The Oakland Zoo urges guests and the public to join them in Taking Action for Wildlife by changing fishing habits to help save birds and other marine life like Merritt the pelican. When fishing, never leave behind lures, hooks, fishing lines, or bait. Dispose of any gear properly in boxes or similar enclosed receptacle within designated disposal areas or at home. A well-known limerick written by Dixon Lanier Merritt, editor of The Tennessean, is often attributed to humorist and poet Ogden Nash: A wonderful bird is the pelican. His bill can hold more than his belican. He can hold in his beak Enough food for a week, But I’m damned if I see how the helican. Oakland Zoo Animal Care Staffer Ann Marie Bisagno comforts the rescued pelican in Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital.
articles.title: Snared Lake Merritt pelican dies despite emergency care

articles.text: Chabot Space and Science Center, located in the Oakland hills, will reopen its doors to the public on November 12 for the first time in nearly 20 months. The reopening weekend will feature extended hours, special events and talks and the unveiling of their new exhibit the NASA Ames Visitor Center. Reopening weekend hours Friday, November 12: 5:00 – 10:00 p.m. Saturday, November 13: 10:00 a.m. – 10:00 p.m. Sunday, November 14: 10:00 a.m. – 5:00 p.m. Special events Schedule 7:00 p.m. Friday, NASA Partnerships; Talk by Bruce Pittman Learn about Space Portal, how the NASA partnerships work and expand to successful partnerships such as SpaceX. 11:00 a.m. Saturday: “Suited for Space” with astronaut Yvonne Cagle. Cagle will tell her exciting astronaut personal narrative illuminating the enthralling journey launching dreams into aspiration, action, and exploration. 2:00 p.m. Saturday: NASA Women STEM Host Dr. Debbie Senesky will lead a discussion about how early STEM education led female scientists to careers with NASA. Dr. Natasha Batalha will share her research work at NASA Ames exploring exoplanets and brown dwarfs. Dr. Huy Tran will discuss her immigrant story coming from Vietnam to America, and her work at NASA Ames leading Chabot Space & Science Center will reopen on Friday, November 12. A young scientist examines a rover made in the new NASA Ames exhibition at Chabot Space and Science Center. the aeronautics department. Lead Bioinformatics Scientist Amanda Saravia-Butler will share her successes with NASA Ames’ GeneLab. Physical Scientist Marilyn Vasquez will speak about her role as Supervisor of Earth Science Project and Office Director at NASA Ames. 1:00 p.m. Sunday: STEM Pathways to Aerospace Meet a panel of former Galaxy Explorers who began their careers at Chabot Space & Science Center. These aerospace engineers represent space agencies such as SpaceX, Nordstrom, Joby, and Lockheed Martin. Chabot Space & Science Center is located at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in Oakland. your Snared Lake Merritt pelican dies despite emergency care by Oakland Zoo By Jay Russell An American White pelican with large fishhooks lodged into its throat and fishing line encircling its neck and bill succumbed to injuries on October 31, despite being rescued from Lake Merritt on Wednesday and treated by the Oakland Zoo. After receiving fluids, and food at the Zoo’s Veterinarian hospital the pelican, nicknamed Merritt, was transferred to the International Bird Rescue where she passed away. Using two kayaks and a small motorboat to reach and then catch the pelican, Oakland Zoo’s VP of Animal Care, Colleen Kinzley, and Zoological Manager Andrea Dougall, brought the bird to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital for treatment. Upon arrival at the Zoo, veterinary staff examined the bird, administered fluids, conducted a blood draw, and checked the injured area on the neck. From initial observations, they determined that the fishing tackle had prevented the bird from being able to eat or drink for weeks, and was suffering from dehydration, starvation, and possible anemia. The staff fed Merritt smelt and capelin fish and had early hopes for her recovery. Her death serves as a vivid reminder of the dangers of fishing items left in Lake Merritt and in all waterways. “Untold numbers of birds, turtles and other wildlife are affected by this solvable issue. Proper disposal of fishing line is crucial, and every citizen can help by picking up any fishing items found in nature,” said Amy Gotliffe, Vice President of Conservation at Oakland Zoo. An American White pelican, named Merritt, was ensnared by multiple barbed hooks on a fishing lure. Between 2002 and 2015, a study by the Audubon Society reported that California-based International Bird Rescue treated at least 2,957 birds for injuries caused by fishing gear. The Oakland Zoo urges guests and the public to join them in Taking Action for Wildlife by changing fishing habits to help save birds and other marine life like Merritt the pelican. When fishing, never leave behind lures, hooks, fishing lines, or bait. Dispose of any gear properly in boxes or similar enclosed receptacle within designated disposal areas or at home. A well-known limerick written by Dixon Lanier Merritt, editor of The Tennessean, is often attributed to humorist and poet Ogden Nash: A wonderful bird is the pelican. His bill can hold more than his belican. He can hold in his beak Enough food for a week, But I’m damned if I see how the helican. Oakland Zoo Animal Care Staffer Ann Marie Bisagno comforts the rescued pelican in Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Bob Fisher died on November 30, 2020 at the age of 91. Born Robert Sheldon Fisher in Riverside, CA, he gained an appreciation for classical music at a young age thanks to a grade school teacher and listening to radio broadcasts of the Metropolitan Opera in New York City on Saturdays. As a child he also developed a life-long love of trains and was an avid model railroader throughout his life. He enjoyed multi-generational trips to the Redwood Valley Railway in Berkeley’s Tilden Park with his sons, grandsons and great-grandsons, and on occasion with all four. As a philosophy major at the University of California at Berkeley, he began attending performances of San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera, something he enjoyed until his last years. Bob was a long-time board member of the Wagner Society of Northern California, and went with them to Bayreuth, Germany to see Wagner’s Ring cycle. He was editor of the Wagner Society’s quarterly newsletter for over 20 years, and transformed it into a well-respected scholarly journal, Leitmotive, with international subscribers. Bob’s musical knowledge and passion for opera was appreciated by his many friends at both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera. A highlight of his year was speaking with Maestro Herbert Blomstedt backstage during Blomstedt’s annual conducting trip to San Francisco. Bob was also a long time board member of The College Preparatory School in Oakland, ranked in 2007 by the Wall Street Journal as the sixth best high school in the United States. While chairman of the board of trustees, he led the acquisition of a new site and the construction of a new campus, which opened in 1983 and doubled the student capacity. All three of Bob’s sons graduated from College Prep. Bob was a fixture at the annual Piedmont Fourth of July parade and could frequently be seen at Piedmont High School sports events cheering on his local grandsons. He loved to treat his grandsons to baseball games, the opera and the symphony. Bob built and lived in his delightful, cozy Piedmont home for over 40 years. He was loved and respected by friends and neighbors for his charm, intelligence and kindness. Bob Fisher is survived by sons Benjamin (Margaret), Thomas (Marina), and Seeger, as well as six grandsons, Winston, Matthew (Emily), Myles (Lindsay), Benjamin Jr. (Grace), Edward, and Mitchell. He is additionally survived by three great-grandchildren, Dennis, Robert and Clara. He is predeceased by sisters Olive Steinen and Jean Bohr. A memorial will be held on November 6, 2021 at 1:15 p.m. at Mountain View Cemetery, 5000 Piedmont Avenue, Oakland. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Salvation Army or San Francisco Symphony. Bob Fisher died on November 30, 2020 at age 91. After graduating from UC Berkeley in 1951, Bob married Ann Gordon Clise of Seattle. Their three sons, Ben, Tom and Seeger, all grew up in Berkeley along with a succession of wellloved golden retrievers. Bob was a 2nd Lieutenant in the U.S. Army in the Korean War from 1952 to 1953. After returning home, he opened Berkeley’s first high-fidelity store, The Audio Shop. In 1955 he started a new business, Fisher Berkeley Corporation, which manufactured nurse-call and doctor-locator communication systems for hospitals nationally and internationally. He served as the chief executive officer for over 40 years before selling the business in 1998 upon his retirement. Bob’s loyalty to his employees was demonstrated annually through a carefully selected Christmas present, given to each of his employees in Berkeley, meticulously wrapped by Bob and his family.
articles.title: Piedmont resident Bob Fisher dies at age 91

articles.text: Bonnie Stehr, who truly valued family and friendships above all else, passed away on October 11, 2021 at the age of 78. Bonnie took great pride in the accomplishments of her family, creating memories through a lifetime of summers at Lake Tahoe. She enjoyed every opportunity she had with her vast directory of friends that spanned classmates, business associates, and community members. She possessed a wonderful, endearing, and fun-loving spirit. She was always enthusiastic and eager to contribute, support and assist. She was an exemplary mother, grandmother, sibling and friend. Born in San Francisco, she was the daughter of Fred and Jean Drewes. She grew up in Piedmont and attended Piedmont High School. She went on to graduate from U.C. Berkeley where she was a proud alumnus and active member of the Pi Beta Phi sorority. Bonnie married her high school sweetheart, Jim, and eventually settled in Piedmont. A renowned cook, Bonnie leveraged her culinary skills to form Bonnie’s Cooking. Following her divorce from Jim, Bonnie embarked on an extremely successful 30-year career as an Account Manager with healthcare benefits company Sitzmann, Morris and Lavis. Following her retirement, she settled in her townhome in Hiller Highlands where she hosted or participated in numerous warm gatherings that included her multitude of friends and family. She thoroughly enjoyed travel, Cal and Stanford sports, and reveled in Town and Country Club events. Regardless of the activity, Bonnie had the ability to maintain a tremendous degree of positive energy that had a tangible effect on many. Her boundless Bonnie Stehr died on October 11, 2021 at age 78. capacity for love had her always willing to open her heart to others. She will be deeply missed by many. Bonnie is survived by her sons, Jim (wife Danya) and Michael (wife Maryanne), her 3 brothers, Michael (wife Barbara), John (wife Susette) and Doug, and her five grandchildren, Bennett, Clayton, Emily, Peter and Jack.
articles.title: Piedmont super mom Bonnie Stehr dies unexpectedly on October 11

articles.text: But the Yellowjackets stormed to the lead with a goal by Luke Childs at 2:35 and a pair of goals by McFarland. The second quarter was action packed. Shane Miller quickly tied the game in 28 seconds, 3-3. Piedmont retained the lead when Miller found Declan Linnane for a goal at 5:57. Berkeley had a man-advantage opportunity at 5:30 but Kashani helped kill the 30-second penalty with a critical save at close range. McFarland then had a shot hit the side post on the ensuing possession, and Kashani had another save with four minutes to spare. With 3:49 before halftime, Davis extended Piedmont’s lead to 5-3. Kashani helped kill another penalty with a save at 2:10 and turned it into another goal when Miller found Rivera for a 6-meter shot goal with 1:37 left in the half. Kashani had another save with 27 seconds to go. In the third quarter, Berkeley’s McFarland netted a goal after two minutes of play and the Jackets’ Jacob Wilson made it 6-5 on a breakaway goal at 4:36. But that was the closest the Yellowjackets would get. Miller was able to push in a goal at close range with 4:06 in the third, 7-5, followed by Krumins landing a rocket-shot with 1:16 left. Rivera then scored on a counter-attack with 57 seconds left, 9-5. McFarland made it 9-6 with 15 seconds. In the fourth, McFarland inched Berkeley closer by converting a penalty shot after 30 seconds of action, 9-7. After a failed Jackets’ man-advantage with five minutes left, Piedmont drew a foul of its own, and another Miller to Rivera combination resulted in a goal with 4:15 remaining and a 10-7 lead. Berkeley scored its last goal with 3:13 left by way of a push-in by Samuele Gabriel. It took Piedmont just 19 seconds to respond with Rivera launching in a goal from 7 meters out with 2:54 left, 11-8. After another save by Kashani, Piedmont gained a kick-out penalty and took just 10 seconds to score after Rivera sent a pass over the defense to George Stein for the game’s final goal at 2:22. In the remaining time, Piedmont made sure to keep its defense back and double-teamed McFarland. It resulted in saves by Kashani with 1:30 left and 30 seconds. Final stats: Rivera scored five goals and had three steals. Davis and Krumins each had two goals, and Krumins had a steal. Miller, Linnane, and Stein each had individual goals. Miller also had three assists and a steal. Kashani had nine saves and one steal. 6-5 semifinals win over Alameda The Highlanders and Hornets were tied 2-2 at the end of the first quarter, and PHS held a 4-3 led at halftime. Piedmont extended the lead to 5-4 in the third, and Rivera scored the game-winner with 3:10 left in the game. The victory avenged a 9-5 loss to the Hornets on October 5 while playing without its leading scorer, Rivera. Krumins scored the game’s first goal after 56 seconds. Miller made the game 2-2 by scoring with 2:34 left in the first quarter. In the second period, Piedmont went ahead when Stein scored with 1:41 prior to halftime. Alameda tied 20 seconds later, but Rivera quickly put PHS back in the lead, 4-3 with 1:09 to go. The game was tied 4-4 in the third quarter when Miller scored with 11 seconds to go, 5-4. In the fourth period Alameda tied it at 5-5 after gaining a penalty with 3:22 left. But the Hornets’ joy was short-lived when Rivera sent in a laser shot after just 11 seconds. Scorers include Miller and Rivera each with two goals, Krumins and Stein had one. NEXT UP: NCS Playoffs Piedmont (18-5) automatically qualifies for the Div. 2 North Coast Section playoffs. It was given the No. 3 seed and has bye in the first round. The Highlanders will face the winner of No. 6 Terra Linda vs. No. 11 Marin Catholic on Saturday, November 6. Sophomore Peter Krumins had two goals against Berkeley.
