articles.text: The 34th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade, organized by merchants on Piedmont Avenue, returned this year to a large crowd of families dressed for the occasion on Saturday morning, October 30. This year, due to countywide restrictions from the COVID pandemic, all activities took place outdoors. The Avenue was closed for about three hours for a costume parade and trick-ortreating. With Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson as Grand Marshal, the parade was led by bagpiper Fred Payne, beginning at Pet Food Express on Piedmont Avenue and Montell Street. Piedmont Avenue Elementary School’s trunk-or-treat supported the parent-teacher association and Friends of Piedmont Library organized an arts and crafts table for young parade attendees at Key Route Plaza. One of the highlights of the event was the pet costume contest, hosted by Pet Food Express, which awarded gift card prizes for best dressed dog. Valerie Ow Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers, participated as a judge at the event. “I have loved dogs my entire life and always used to dress up my Jack Russell, Rosie, for all of her 19 years. It was enjoyable to search for the cutest, most clever and fun Halloween costumes for pets in our area,” she said. “The experience is pure joy, to see our community come alive with Dog Costume Contest judges at Pet Food Express with the winner, a Whippet in his “Ruff Seas” costume. smiles, costumes, pets and merriment is just icing on the cake.” The parade on Piedmont Avenue has been a tradition for decades, and is uniquely special to the merchants. “The parade builds so much community and goodwill. It shows that together our small businesses support and appreciate our loyal clients and customers,” Ow Lee said. “Families were eager to be outside, dress up in silly costumes and trick-or-treat for candy. They surely missed the Halloween and pumpkin fun last year. We provided a safe and fun community venue on Piedmont Ave - it was so well received, and people can’t wait to attend next year.” Larson echoed Ow Lee’s sentiments when reflecting on the parade’s resonance with merchants and neighbors of Piedmont Avenue. “I think the parade is a great thing for Piedmont Avenue and a great way to connect with the community,” Larson said. The parade was started in 1986 by a number of merchants who wanted to give kids a safe place to trick-or-treat. Richard Stone, the late owner of Continental Hearing and a member of the Lions’ Club, used the opportunity to raise money for Children’s Hospital and the Lions Center for the Blind in Oakland. Photo by Isadora Delibertis A little ladybug trick-or-treats at the Nathan and Co. gift shop on Piedmont Avenue. Brian Goehry and Abby Refer of Wine on Piedmont are dressed as Dom Perignon and white wine grapes.
articles.title: Great turnout at Piedmont Ave. Halloween Parade

articles.text: In the late 1950s when Khrushchev denounced Stalin, there was a softening to the West and the forbidden modern art masterpieces began to emerge. Moscow’s Pushkin Museum and Leningrad’s (St. Petersburg) Hermitage took over one of the greatest collections of modern masters in the world. Natalya Semenova curated both the Shchukin exhibition and the Morozov exhibition She began with very little media, only two portraits and a photograph, plus access to interview a Morozov great-grandson living in Paris. She spent five years piecing together the Morozov story by digging into French and Russian archives, bills of sale, jottings and notes, memoirs, and letters. The Morozov family has received no compensation for their lost art. Already a blockbuster, the Morozov exhibit starts at the galleries below ground, and zigzags to all four levels. On the day we attended, the crowds overflowed, and the queues were long, as it was a Saturday. The exhibit runs through February 22. Louis-Vuitton Foundation’s ultra-modern cultural center with its warren of galleries, terraces, and outlooks, rises from the thickly vegetated Bois du Boulogne, a winged splendor of translucent glass against massive, exposed wood and steel beams. The views are spectacular. Madame Forsyth and Michael Mathews, the Piedmont Post’s Americans in Paris, are enjoying autumn in Paris during a typically rainy season. Sure-footed boots and a brawly are recommended. Send comments to: pkf.empower@gmail.com. “La Mer aux Saintes-Maries”, by Vincent Van Gogh, 1888

articles.text: Getting out of town during Ski Week in February this year, Anastasia Edel and her youngest daughter, Larissa, headed to England, where they encountered Cirara, a major 3-day storm. Undaunted, they read the Piedmont Post outside the Brighton Royal Pavilion in Brighton. It was only weeks before the virus shutdown in the U.S. when life was good. articles.text: The League of Women Voters Piedmont will host a town hall on Thursday, November 4 to discuss the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The virtual town hall will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging aquatic facility. The current pool closed indefinitely on September 8, 2020; the new community pool is set to be completed in summer 2024. This event will include brief presentations from the city’s team which will be followed by an audience question-and-answer segment moderated by League of Women Voters Piedmont President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers are Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register for free at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded, and you can watch it live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel.
articles.title: LWV to host town hall on Piedmont Pool November 4

articles.text: A cyclone over the Pacific Ocean merged with a category 5 atmospheric river last weekend and brought a deluge of water, mudslides, and debris across the Bay Area. No flooding occurred in Piedmont, but the city did lose three trees in the williwaw. A bomb cyclone (bombogenesis) is defined by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) as a midlatitude cyclone that rapidly intensifies, and can happen when a cold air mass collides with a warm air mass; an atmospheric river, classified in severity similar to the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, is defined by NOAA as a flowing column of condensed water vapor in the atmosphere responsible for producing significant levels of rain. The two weather phenomena merged last weekend and brought with it cancellations, evacuations, and general blight and damage. Two crew members of the Piedmont Public Works Department stayed overnight at the Corporation Yard on Saturday, October 24, in preparation of the storm surge. Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich explained that an extra street sweeper was added in on Saturday and Sunday to help with “hot-spots” in town that are more prone to flooding or debris collection. On Sunday, the Bay Area saw an unforeseen amount of rain. The National Weather Service called preliminary rainfall totals “staggering,” and said that Sunday was the “fourth-wettest day ever” in San Francisco in terms of rainfall. articles.text: On Tuesday October 26, a Food and Drug Administration Advisory Committee met to discuss the emergency approval of BioNTech and Pfizer’s COVID- 19 vaccine for children 5-11 years old. The committee recommended that the FDA approve the vaccine for the age group. Formal FDA approval would mean that Piedmont students ages 5-11 would need to show proof of vaccination within eight weeks to attend school. The FDA is not required to follow the advice of its committee, but typically does. A final decision by the FDA on whether or not to allow emergency approval for children 5-11 is expected within a week. In its meeting on September 22, the Piedmont School Board mandated COVID-19 vaccination for all eligible students as a requirement for attending classes. Currently, students age 12 and up must provide proof of vaccination by Wednesday, November 17th. If the FDA approves the new age group, PUSD’s policy requires parents to provide the district with proof of vaccination within eight weeks, with the only caveat being a medical exemption. (Full vaccination is achieved two weeks after the second dose). Dr. George Rutherford, a UCSF epidemiologist and infectious disease expert, recommends waiting at least four weeks between the first and second shots. “I would try to stretch out the time between the first and second doses a little longer than three weeks; I would try four. The farther you can stretch it out the greater will be the protection that is provided. That is one of the reasons we are having problems with waning immunities because it was a three-week gap initially,” Rutherford explained. On Friday October 22 the FDA said that Pfizer’s case study of 2,268 elementary age students produced an efficacy rate of 90.7% against symptomatic infection seven days after their second shot. This efficacy results from a smaller dose than that given to people 12 and up receive, 10 micrograms instead of 30 micrograms. The most common side effects for this group occurred after the second dose and included pain at the injection site, fatigue, and headache. The FDA says no serious adverse events associated with the vaccine occurred in the study. Rutherford does not see any reason to be cautious and wait for kids to get the vaccine. “I think we are in a good position with this,” he said. “I think it’s hugely Piedmont resident and epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford was the Piedmont Post’s Citizen of the Year in 2020. important for children to be vaccinated for their own health. It’s tremendously helpful for the overall effort to stop the damage from Covid.” Piedmont has the highest vaccination rate of any city in Alameda County by a large margin. As of October 13, 97.5% of Piedmonters eligible (age 12 and older) are fully vaccinated according to the Alameda County Public Health Department (Covid-19.acgov.org/data.page?). For information on receiving a $50 incentive from Alameda County for each Pfizer shot, see: Covid-19.acgov.org/vaccine-incentives.page?.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has requested a second extension of the Measure A-1 application deadline. City Council made the request, which will be reviewed by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors. If granted, the city would have until December 31, 2023 to produce a project application that describes how it will use its $2.2 million allocation in county funds to develop affordable housing programs. In presenting the agenda item to the city council at an October 18 meeting, City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that the efforts of city staff, the Planning Commission, the city’s ad-hoc Measure A-1 subcommittee, and residents led to the recommendation for another extension of the county’s deadline. The city earlier received an extension of the deadline from December 31, 2021 to December 2022. “As we [discussed] for more than a year with how to best approach our 6th cycle housing element update, one that is so substantially different than anything we’ve been asked to tackle in the past, we continue to learn and wrap our heads around this process,” Lillevand said. She added that the recommendation to request an extension “makes for the most efficient and effective use of the city’s time and resources.” On September 13, the Planning Commission determined that the development of a multifamily affordable housing project on cityowned land would have a greater chance of attracting a developer, but that related zoning code revisions and CEQA-reviews would not be completed within the constraints of the current deadline the county set for applications. Piedmont’s application for the use of Measure A-1 funds is currently set at December 31, 2022, and, according to an accompanying staff report, a one-year extension would “align Measure A-1 efforts with [the city’s] Housing Element update timeline.” While the city council members present were in favor of an extension, concerns with how to approach the deadline extension were expressed. “This is absolutely the right approach, it’s clear that we’ve demonstrated that we’ve spent a lot of time thinking about A-1,” said council member Jen Cavenaugh, but added, “I’m not sure we’ve made the case in our argument, and why one more year isn’t sufficient.” Conna McCarthy questioned the probability of a second extension approval. Planning Director Kevin Jackson responded “that there was no indication it’s a slam-dunk, but that [the city] has a good case.” The city considered Measure A-1 funds as a potential source of funding for new incentives for constructions of accessory dwelling units (ADUs) that are rent-restricted for low and verylow income residents. However, residents and city staff have expressed interest in exploring other possibilities. “I’m very pleased that staff has embraced the notion of pivoting away from an ADU-centric philosophy of increasing our housing. We’re really looking to explore more creative opportunities,” Mayor Teddy Gray King said. “We are experiencing a time in Piedmont where we truly have an organized, vocal, passionate group of Piedmonters who want to explore those opportunities.” Lillevand noted that, upon city council’s approval of the extension, the city would “dive into preliminary site assessment of city-owned properties.” Residents speak up Deborah Leland, Chair of the Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee, offered her support of the extension, and added that the city government should utilize the acreage it owns in Piedmont when exploring lots for fair housing. “I’m in support of moving away from using Measure A-1 for ADU (accessory dwelling unit) financing, and instead seeking the time necessary to pursue using those funds for affordable rental housing,” she said. “The city... is by far the largest landowner in Piedmont, owning 64 acres of land. Taking a close look at cityowned property is both reasonable and necessary,” she said. Irene Cheng, speaking on behalf of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign [PREC], spoke in support of building multi-family affordable housing in the city. “We believe strongly that creating affordable housing is a necessary step to building a more diverse and inclusive community that I know we’d all like to see,” Cheng said. “We support the proposal for an extension, which will allow the city to come up with a viable plan for multifamily affordable housing and will let us do the community engagement work that is essential to the process.” PREC, in partnership with the League of Women Voters, will host a community workshop focused on fair and affordable housing via Zoom on November 9 at 7 p.m. Resident Andy Maderia, CEO of East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation and a scheduled guest speaker at that meeting, pointed out that Alameda County voters approved Measure A-1 five years ago. He also referenced Measure UU, the bond to build a new community pool, and asked city council to “bring the zeal and sense of time and necessity to the building of affordable housing in Piedmont [similar to building] the pool.” “I think the second extension is needed, but I hope that we don’t wait that long [2023]. I hope we... don’t separate the housing element process from the process of identifying a public site for affordable housing,” he said. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Elected officials and community leaders from throughout Alameda County were invited to attend an event at Temple Beth Abraham in Oakland on Monday, October 25, for an event called “Hineni: Here I Am” aimed at bringing awareness to rising antisemitism. Program speakers included Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf, State Senators Steve Glazer and Bob Wieckowski, State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, Berkeley Mayor Jesse Arreguin, Oakland Schools Superintendent Dr. Kyla Johnson-Trammell, and Carl Chan from Oakland Chinatown Chamber of Commerce. “Hineni” in Hebrew translates to “Here I am,” and is the name of a prayer of preparation and humility, chanted by the cantor on Rosh Hashanah. It is also an integral prayer recited at Yom Kippur services. The Jewish Community Relations Council (JCRC), a public affairs organization working on behalf of the Bay Area Jewish community, organized the event and launched a website in July calling on residents and local leaders to share personal experiences about antisemitism. The website, https://hereiamstories. org/, invites members of all communities to learn about anti-bias organizations and how to respond to antisemitism. Temple Beth Abraham Rabbi Mark Bloom described Monday’s event as “a gathering of communal leaders standing with the Jewish people against anti-Semitism in response to the significant increase in anti-Semitism over the past year.” Piedmont was represented at the event by Mayor Teddy Gray King, School Superintendent Randall Booker and Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers. There were 170 people in attendance for the outdoor event, a mix of leaders of the Jewish Community and civic leaders from across the East Bay, including Oakland’s Police Chief, Mayors and City Council Members from Oakland, Piedmont, Berkeley, Alameda, Walnut Creek, Emeryville, Fremont, and Hayward. The speakers included Rabbi Jacqueline Mates-Muchin of Temple Sinai; Melissa Chapman, CEO of the Jewish Community Center of the East Bay; Danny Grossman, CEO of the Jewish Community Federation; and Tyler Gregory, Executive Director of the Jewish Community Relations Council. “The event was very successful in making us in the Jewish community feel much less alone as well as in bringing the diversity of the broader East Bay community together,” said Rabbi Bloom.
articles.title: East Bay leaders rally against antisemitism

articles.text: The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will be hosting a community workshop, “Doing Our Part: Bringing Affordable Housing to Piedmont,” cosponsored by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) on Tuesday, November 9. articles.text: In responding to a resident requesting clarification about the use of “premium bonds” for the construction of a community pool under the provisions of Measure UU, City Clerk John Tulloch explained: “I am writing in response to your inquiry pertaining to the use of Premium Bonds for Measure UU. The City forwarded your request for legal analysis to the City’s Bond Counsel. They provided a response that I am sharing and paraphrasing below. “The legal authority for the City to issue General Obligation Bonds, whether at par, premium or discount, is embedded in the California Constitution and codes, the City Charter, and related ordinances and resolutions of the City Council. For example, California Government Code Section 53508.7 provides, ‘The bonds shall be sold at a public or private sale and at a price at, above, or below par, as the legislative body determines.’ “As approved by the voters in Measure UU, the City has the legal authority to sell bonds in a principal (par) amount that does not exceed $19.5 million and at an interest rate that does not exceed 12%. Accordingly, the City may sell the bonds in a principal amount of up to $19.5 million. In addition, subject to the 12% interest rate cap, the City may sell the bonds at a price above par, thereby generating additional proceeds in the form of original issue premium. “At the time Measure UU was being considered by City Council, given then-current interest rates, it was anticipated that the sale of bonds in the principal amount of $19.5 million may yield more than $23.0 million in proceeds, with the difference being the payment of an original issue premium by investors in the City’s bonds. The amount of original issue premium paid by investors will depend upon market conditions at the time of sale of the bonds. The bonds will be priced so the median rate paid by the taxpayers is consistent with the Tax Rate Statement included in the Measure UU documents.”

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Western Neighborhoods Project The Museum at The Cliff held an opening party on October 23. Spearheaded by the Western Neighborhoods Project, the pop-up aims to promote the rich history of the building and Sutro Baths as the National Park Service searches for a new, long-term tenant. A temporary pop-up museum has opened at the former Cliff House gift shop, and now is open to the general public until midThe Cliff House restaurant, housed in a historic building perched above the cliffs just north of Ocean Beach in San Francisco, closed last year due to leasing issues with the National Park Service (NPS) and dining closures brought on by the pandemic. The Cliff House’s main draw since 1863 had been the magnificent Pacific Ocean views. Though the NPS has said it is “committed to maintaining the iconic building,” the long-term future of the space is unknown. On February 2, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed a resolution urging the NPS to find an immediate vendor for the space while it searches for a long-term tenant. On Saturday, October 23, the Western Neighborhoods Project, a nonprofit based in the Inner Richmond district and dedicated to preserving San Francisco history, opened a temporary museum open to the public inside the former Cliff House gift shop. The pop-up museum is in partnership with Art Conservation and The Great Highway gallery, with support from the Golden Gate National Recreation Area’s Park Archives and Records Center. Some artifacts likely to be on display are swimsuits from the Sutro Baths, an 1890’s stool belonging to Adolph Sutro, a luncheon menu from President Teddy Roosevelt’s visit to the restaurant in 1903, and many more. “I’m so proud of [the] efforts to preserve many of the historical artifacts that create this wonderful museum while the National Park Service searches for a new vendor for the Cliff House,” said San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, who serves District 1, where Cliff House is located. The museum will be open to the public from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. through April 2022.
articles.title: New pop-up museum housed at San Francisco’s Cliff House

articles.text: Kim Hunter displays a handful of new Giving Campaign lawn signs. Each year in early November, a hardworking crew of Giving Campaign elves fans out across Piedmont to deliver purple lawn signs promoting the school district’s largest annual fundraiser. After this year’s November 1st deadline, families who have contributed to The Giving Campaign will see a sign magically appear on their lawn, signaling the household’s support for Piedmont schools and its students. “We want to encourage all families to donate to help us reach our goal of at least $3 million, which the school district is counting on to keep our budget and programs whole next year,” said Giving Campaign co-chair Christine Wente von Metzsch. “The Giving Campaign is the largest annual fundraiser for our schools, and we rely on contributions from all families in our district in order to keep our class sizes small and our educational programs strong,” added co-chair Colleen Allan. Each year, the funding gap increases between what Piedmont schools receive from government sources and local taxes and what it takes to maintain the quality of education in Piedmont schools. For the 2022-2023 school year, that gap amounts to $2,140 for each student in the district. Last year Piedmont Education Foundation granted over $2.7 million to the school district, funds that are hard at work in classrooms. Sixty-four percent of that amount helps the district achieve a low student-teacher ratio with A fresh lawn sign surrounded by colorful flowers. small class sizes. Health and wellness, including elementary counselors, athletics, and the middle and high school Wellness Center, accounts for 15% of the grant, and another 15% is earmarked for student support, including paraprofessionals, classroom aides, and intervention specialists. The remaining 6% funds PUSD’s libraries, art and music, and instructional technology, including Chromebooks. To participate in the Giving Campaign and help fund our students and schools, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org/ donate/ Delivery of lawn signs is done the old-fashioned way.

articles.text: School Board to discuss H1 Bond budget at tonight’s meeting Members of the Piedmont School Board will receive an update at tonight’s meeting on both the cost and timeline overruns of the STEAM classroom building and the theater building still in construction. The meeting, October 27, will be at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall. Voters approved up to $66 million for school construction based upon the H1 public Bond. It was intended to cover all costs for the two buildings, and have some money for additional projects. According to the school district, unforeseen and added costs “contributed roughly $6.5 million to bond program costs.” The increased cost now puts the total for the two buildings at $70.3 million. Financing options will be discussed during the meeting. The school board’s background document includes the following: • California’s Division of State Architect (DSA) mandating changes which added significant quantities of structural steel and concrete. • Required overtime labor to ensure STEAM completion for the start of the 2020-21 school year. (Overtime was later discontinued when Covid canceled in-person classes, and urgency to reopen.) • Discovery and replacement of deteriorating underground utilities for all existing high school buildings and discovery and repair of a dangerous underground void beneath the PHS breezeway. • Pandemic-related costs including a full-time health and safety officer at the STEAM and theater construction sites, and additional shifts for fewer workers and Covid spacing. • Relocation and upgrade of the District internet server room, including new servers, switches, and battery storage. • Necessary shoring for the theater foundation and an unexpected new concrete driveway. • Costs of theatrical lighting fixtures and controls that were discontinued due to Covid-19. “The District worked with Overaa [Construction, the general contractor] and its subcontractors to offset more than half of these costs without compromising the life cycle of the buildings or educational programs... The District [also] deferred certain features including: solar panels; furnishings, fixtures, and equipment for the black box theater; and other items that can be added later when additional funding becomes available,” wrote School Superintendent Randy Booker. “Value engineering” and deferment of features offset some of the added costs, but there is still a shortfall of up to $2.9 million. That amount does not include deferred items, including the theater’s orchestral shell, acoustical panels, and solar panels. Last year, Piedmont students began a fundraising campaign to pay for the missing solar panels on the classroom building. The board will discuss ways to pay for the overages at tomorrow’s meeting. A background document lists a $4-6 million state bond they could receive but which is contingent upon a state election item. “The timing of receipt is uncertain because it depends on the approval of a statewide school construction bond measure,” Booker stated. The full document can be viewed at Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/Attachment.aspx?S=36030373&AID=1 79483&MID=9077. Options to cover costs until possibly receiving money from the state will be discussed at future meetings. “The options include a no-interest loan of up to $1.8 million from the Piedmont Education Foundation, and financing from Overaa for the full amount of anticipated State funds for a term of up to three years,” Booker stated in the document. Members of the community can attend the meeting in person at 7:00 p.m., or view on Zoom. To register, click on https://us06web. zoom.us/j/86434103152. Piedmont City Hall is located at 120 Vista Avenue.
articles.title: School STEAM building, theater both over budget

articles.text: Studying for the SAT does not have to be a daunting or painful task. Here are some helpful tips to help make the text more palatable and to improve scores. Get competitive. Seeing progress is important. Taking practice tests that give an actual score can invigorate that competitive spirit. While there are many great online resources for practice tests and studying, it is important to familiarize yourself with the format of the test which will be on paper. Most students have not taken a test that lasts over an hour, so get ready for the SAT – a three-hour test with one 10-minute break and one five-minute break. Make sure to “practice like you play,” by sitting down and simulating the long haul. If your test is scheduled for 9:00 a.m. on a Saturday, taking a practice test at the same time and day will add routine and comfort to the actual morning of the test. Another important part of using the same tools and materials is to practice with the correct calculator. Most calculators are allowed in the exam room except Get SAT studying in early, instead of trying to cram Start with one hour each weekend. for the TI-92 graphing calculator because it has a QWERTY keyboard and cell phone calculators which are not allowed. Take the time to practice on a real calculator, the same one you will use on the test and ditch the phone. Know where all the buttons are on your calculator so it is like second nature. For the Reading Comprehension sections, here’s a tip for getting through those questions in a timely manner and without sacrificing scores. The key is to have a strategy which will get through the story while only reading it once. There are two types of reading comprehension questions. Some are line or paragraph “spot-specific”, for example one of these may look like “in line 13 what does this phrase mean?” The other kind is based upon reading the entire text. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: The Piedmont High cross country program traveled to Cordova High School near Sacramento on Saturday, October 23 for the Postal Nationals, a 3,200- meter event. Schools throughout the country upload their two-mile times into a database. The course at Cordova High is 3200 meters, comparable to a 2-mile race in track. Piedmont’s boys’ team finished 6th among 52 California schools, and the girls placed 8th in a field of 27 teams. “The two-mile event is a nationwide competition with teams posting their best 3,200- meter times for comparison across the country. We were lucky to be invited to a live rendition of the full race experience at Cordova High. It was a thrill to watch 3,200 racing, it felt much shorter than our traditional 3-mile events for cross country,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. The Highlanders also ran a 5K event at Oyster Bay in San Leandro two days earlier, Wednesday, October 21. Piedmont’s boys’ team was fastest among 10 schools, and the girls finished 3rd among nine teams. Jack Stein led the way for Piedmont in both events, finishing the Postal Nationals with a time of 9:54.27 to finish fifth in a crowded field of 123 runners. He won the League Center Meet on Thursday with a time of 16:25.99. As for the girls, sophomore breakout performer Josephine Oesterer also led both events, clocking an 11:44.23 at Postal Nationals to finish 14th of 99 runners at Cordova while winning the WACC 5K at Oyster Bay with a time of 19:27.81 against 66 runners. Postal Nationals recap On an overcast Saturday in Rancho Cordova, Piedmont’s boys’ team placed sixth, with Jesuit, Trabuco Hills, McClatchy, Dana Hills, and Sacred Heart as the top five. Stein led Piedmont with an overall fifth-place finish in a field of 153 runners, followed closely by super sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse in ninth with a time of 10:03.02. Junior Christian Taylor crossed the finish line five seconds later for 11th place, and Parker Long placed 14th in 10:16.69. Piedmont’s boys’ team continued to display strong pack running (5th, 9th, 11th, 14th). The girls’ team placed 8th out of 27 schools, led by Josie Oesterer with a 14th place overall finish in 11:44.23. Sophomore Jamie Schwarz was 19th in 11:52.33 in a field of 99. Mara Lovric placed 32nd in 12:38.07, Violet Lemley finished 49th in 13:17.57, and senior Molly McWeeny came in 59th, 13:34.03. articles.text: Consolation game with Lick tomorrow at 6 p.m. The girls’ water polo team was shut out 6-0 by Bishop O’Dowd in the opening round of the WACC Championship Tournament yesterday at Encinal High in Alameda. The squad will play in the consolation bracket tomorrow, Thursday, October 28, against Lick-Wilmerding. It was a defensive battle from the get-go after the Dragons opened with a 2-0 lead and led 3-0 by halftime. O’Dowd added one more in the third quarter, and finished with a pair of goals in the final quarter for the 6-0 win. Pied mont defeated the Lick-Wilmerding 19-7 on September 22, so there is reason for optimism. On Tuesday, O’Dowd’s Maddie Porras scored after three and a half minutes in the first quarter. The defensive battle continued until 20 seconds were left when the Dragons’ Diana Garcia-Becerra scored, 2-0. In the second quarter, the Highlanders were able to draw an ejection with 5:21 on the clock but the squad was unable to convert its opportunity. BOD’s Harper Casey-Housand scored their goal with 3:25 left in the half. In the third quarter, O’Dowd’s Fiona Corbetta scored after two minutes. As for the fourth quarter, the Dragons scored with in a 6-on-5 advantage with 3:39 on the clock. Piedmont also drew a player-advantage with 2:58 on the clock, but were unable to get a shot into the net. O’Dowd’s Casey-Housand scored with 1:15 left in the game. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-10) heads to the Encinal pool tomorrow, October 28, for a consolation match in the league tournament against Lick-Wilmerding at 6:00 p.m. Annika Nilsson eyes down a pass. Frankie Broening puts up a shot with the Dragons’ defender draped on her arm.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Homecoming football game with Bishop O’Dowd was exciting for the first half on Friday night, October 22, when the Highlanders led O’Dowd 8-7. The second half, however, was a completely different story, and the Dragons rebounded to win 31-8. Piedmont’s depleted varsity roster of 17 players did what it could, but the wear and tear on the starters – with most on the roster playing both offense and defense – began to show. Trailing O’Dowd by one touchdown heading into the last quarter, 14-8, the Dragons ran away for a 31-8 win. The halftime lead against O’Dowd – a perennial football powerhouse in Oakland – was the first in at least five years. “I’ll be looking at the film to see why we gave up the edge,” said coach Jerome Johnson. “On offense, we couldn’t get better field position. Once again, we had some mental mistakes, and it reflects on the score.” Piedmont defensive lineman Mason Kimball had a big day with one QB sack, three tackles for loss, and two forced fumbles. “Mason Kimball is our anchor and our rock. He is our inside rusher and he keeps pressure and pushes the pocket. He and Ethan Feldstein set the tone on the inside,” said Johnson. The defense fought valiantly to achieve eight tackles for loss, four sacks, two interceptions, two fumble recoveries, and three forced fumbles. Game Recap PHS opened the game with an onside kick attempt and forced a turnover on downs at their own 49 yard line by stopping BOD’s receiver short of a first down on a 4th down. After a Piedmont-punt, O’Dowd retained possession at the 50 and drove to Piedmont’s 25-yard line. Bailey Cain recorded a sack for a loss of six yards to force 3rd-and-15. Defensive back Ryan McConathy then knocked a pass down to make it fourth down. An incompletion on fourth down gave Piedmont possession again. The two sides traded possession once more to end the first quarter in a 0-0 deadlock. PHS opened the second quarter at its 19 yard line and began to move. A Dragon defensive back got his hand on the ball to force a fumble at the BOD 45-yard line. On its next play, a long pass over the top of the defense connected for a 55 yard touchdown pass and a 7-0 lead for O’Dowd. But Piedmont came firing back with wide receiver Defazio taking a 62-yard catch and run to the BOD six yard line. At the two-yard line, the offense called a designed stretch run for quarterback Adhi Bornstein. He was met by a swarm of defenders who knocked the ball loose at the twoyard line and a fumble recovery. On O’Dowd’s next possession, Ryan McConathy was able to strip the ball loose from the Dragon running back at the five yard line. The ball was scooped up at the goal line by O’Dowd, but Lucas Bernales and Battista Costa tackled him in the end zone for a safety, making the score 7-2. On a 4th down, Piedmont was unable to make a first down at O’Dowd’s 41-yard line, and the Dragons worked the ball to Piedmont’s 45/ They attempted another bomb down the sideline, but this time the ball was intercepted by Defazio in the end zone and returned to the 31. From there, PHS drove to the BOD 49, but was stopped on 4th-and-9 with 33 seconds left in the half. The Dragons tried two pass plays that ended in Piedmont’s favor. The first play resulted in Kimball blitzing the quarterback for an eight-yard loss, a fumble but recovery by the Dragons. On 2nd-and-18 with time expiring, the Dragons looked deep again, but Kimball made his second consecutive sack and forced fumble. This time, the ball was scooped up by Cain for a 35-yard touchdown run, and an 8-7 Piedmont lead at halftime. In the second half, PHS turned the ball over on an interception at the BOD 42. The Dragons turned it into a 22 yard touchdown carry and 14-8 lead with 10:47 left in the third quarter. Photo by Mark Aikawa Defensive lineman Bailey Cain had a scoop and score for the Highlanders, enabling Piedmont to an 8-7 lead at halftime. Staff Photo Ryan McConathy reaches to poke the ball out for a forced fumble against Bishop O’Dowd.

This time, the ball was scooped up by Cain for a 35-yard touchdown run, and an 8-7 Piedmont lead at halftime. In the second half, PHS turned the ball over on an interception at the BOD 42. articles.text: Playing at the Metro Links Golf Course near the Oakland Airport, Piedmont’s golf team placed third in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with a combined score of 473 strokes. Alameda won its 17th consecutive league title with a score of 387, and O’Dowd was second with 422. Other teams competing included San Lorenzo (519), Arroyo (524), Berkeley (542) and Castro Valley (544). Team scores represented the total of the top five golfers on each team. For Piedmont, junior Aryana Fisher finished as the school’s low medalist with an 18-hole round of an 87. Freshman Mei Assalian shot a 92, senior Dabney Warner followed with a 94, junior Rahimeen Shah shot a 99, and junior Krysta Tsukahara had a 101. “Every season we want to get a little smarter and a little stronger. We’ll be excited to get back to work next season,” said Piedmont coach Howard Oliver. Fisher was Piedmont’s low medalist this season on several occasions. She scored a 36 at Monarch Bay on September 30, and led at Sequoyah Country Club on September 16 with a 49. For Assalian, the freshman, her impressive debut season included scores of 40 on September 30 at San Leandro’s Monarch Bay, second behind Fisher. She also shot a round of 47 at the Metro Links on September 21. PHS finished its season with an 8-4 overall record. Oliver and Piedmont golf returns this spring with the boys’ team. articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team wrapped up its season on Thursday, October 21 at Binks Rawlings Gym with a nail-biting 3-2 loss to Berkeley, 22-25, 25-18, 25-12, 21-25, 16-14. “Even though we got the loss, it felt like a win,” said coach Leslie Blakely. “We got into a five-set match after they swept us 3-0 earlier in the season. We played really well and showed good energy and that fight that we have. I’m super proud of them.” The Highlanders honored the five seniors on the roster prior to Thursday’s game, including Ruby Shaffer, Sofia Croley, Ari Talwatte, Sophie Nevis, and Amelia Wire. “It was an emotional game. It could’ve gone better over the last couple of points, but it was a great game to end on. These girls are going to do so well, I can’t wait to see them lead,” said Shaffer, a captain on the team. Although the squad finished with a 3-12 record, the team fought valiantly in front of a roaring crowd to the finish. The squad has some talented underclassmen in important roles, including Bree DeYoung, Lila Town, Sadie Town, Eden Lorin, Tara Kothari, Izzy Grimmer, and Bauer Peterson. “It makes me so happy to see how much of an impact you can make as a senior. You can empower other players and make the team stronger as a community. Next year the girls are going to be so strong; they have already built that tight-knit connection. I’m really sad to leave and stop playing with my close friends, but it’s nice to end on this note,” said Talwatte. Volleyball will return to Binks Rawlings Gym in the spring a boys’ team, also coached by Blakely. Game Recap The Highlanders opened with a triumphant 25-22 win in the first game, but fell 25-18 in the second and 25-12 in the third. Piedmont won the fourth game 25-21, and forced an extra point in the fifth, but Berkeley closed it out with a narrow 16-14 victory in the fifth set. Berkeley’s new head coach is Alison West, the former coach at Piedmont who helped lead PHS to the North Coast Section playoffs. West’s final year in Piedmont was the last time the Highlanders reached the postseason. In the first game, Berkeley opened to a 5-1 lead, but Piedmont eventually powered ahead 9-8 with five straight points when trailing 8-4. While down 19-16, PHS’ Nevis smacked down two spikes along with an offensive error from BHS to tie 19-19. After back and forth scoring, PHS tied at 22-22 then gained three straight points to win due to offensive errors by the Jackets, 25-22 Piedmont. But the Highlanders couldn’t find similar fluidity in the second game, falling 25-18 after allowing seven straight points to open. Berkeley held Game Point at 24-13; PHS rallied five straight points to 24-18, but an offensive error was the end of it, 25-18. In the third, the two sides traded points until Berkeley held a 9-6 lead—then it was all Jackets, going on to score the next nine of 10 points to jump ahead 18-7. They closed out strong, 25-12. In the fourth set, Piedmont did well to limit rallies and jumped out to a 6-2 lead to start. Berkeley was able to tie at 13-13, but PHS gained five straight points to go ahead 18-13. DeYoung closed the game with a powerful spike into the Jackets’ midcourt, 25-21. In the fifth and final game, Piedmont opened with a 6-1 lead with help of two spikes by Shaffer and an ace by Wire. Two aces by Lila Town to make it 10-6, but Berkeley was able to eventually tie at 12-12 and gain match point at 14-12. A service error by Berkeley made it 14-13, while Nevis sent in an ace to tie it at 14-14. However, a pair of offensive errors helped Berkeley finish things with a win, 16-14. Final stats: Shaffer with eight kills and three aces; Wire had six kills and an ace; Nevis had six spikes and an ace; Talwatte had six spikes and an ace; DeYoung had five spikes; Sadie Town and her sister Lila each had two aces. Ruby Shaffer goes up for a spike. She had eight on the night. Senior Ari Talwatte had six kills and an ace.
articles.title: Volleyball ends season with 3-2 loss to Berkeley

articles.text: Belmont-based First Generation Swim Foundation has launched a scholarship program for free swim lessons for Bay Area kids who are the first in their family to learn how to swim. Families may complete the online application at www.firstswimmer.org/apply for English or www.firstswimmer.org/apply-inspanish for Spanish. Ten scholarships will be awarded to local children ages four to 16. With 20 percent of all drowning victims age 15 or younger, Zane Tanabe started a foundation to combat this danger. He noticed that many of the parents of his teammates on the swim and water polo teams didn’t know how to swim. “Swimming saves lives, and no one has taught first generation swimmers these skills. My hope is that this foundation will give them the chance to learn,” said Tanabe. First Generation Swim Foundation is a 501c3 nonprofit organization with the mission of preventing under-resourced Bay Area kids from drowning by giving free swim lessons to those who are the first in their family to learn to swim. Zane Tanabe, the founder of First Generation Swim Foundation, is a Belmont resident and sophomore at Sacred Heart Preparatory, where hs is a varsity swimmer and water polo player.
articles.title: Swim scholarships available for Bay Area kids

articles.text: An art exhibition entitled Suspended Matter will open at Berkeley Art Center on October 30. The exhibition will be on display through January 15, 2022. Suspended Matter features the work of artists Julia Goodman, Asma Kazmi, Laura Arminda Kingsley, and Jenifer K. Wofford, and is curated by Patricia Cariño Valdez. Through various mediums including sculpture, video, photography, and paintings, the artists consider connections between humanity and the domestic objects that shape our environments and surroundings. The name of the exhibition is a riff off the scientific definition of a “disruption in the environment,” such as erosion or flooding. “The works in Suspended Matter contemplate how we interact with others and our surroundings,” said Carino Valdez. “From the reconstitution of familiar fabrics into abstract shapes as seen in Goodman’s sculptures to a close examination of domestic objects that we interact within Kazmi’s work, the artists recognize the shifting interactions with our values, beliefs, and the everyday objects that we keep. The otherworldly sci-fi videos by Kingsley and Wofford’s depictions of solitude and isolation remind us of the constant revaluation of our existence and our resilience in relation to the past and present.” Berkeley Art Center is located at 1275 Walnut Street in North Berkeley. For more information call (510) 644-6893.
articles.title: Suspended Matter exhibit at Berkeley Art Center opens Oct. 30

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre will reopen on November 12 with a live production of Wintertime by Charles Mee and directed by Les Waters. It will be performed until December 19. Berkeley Rep welcomes back Mee and Les Waters who have teamed up in the past to bring Fetes de la Nuit and Big Love to the stage. Wintertime is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family who arrive at their summer house in the winter woods for supposedly secret rendezvous—and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” The cast stars James Carpenter as Frank, Sharon Lockwood as Hilda, and includes Carmen Berkeley as Ariel, Nora El Samahy as Mariam, and Sarah Nina Hayon as Jaqueline. Tickets are now on sale. Berkeley Rep requires all audience members to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification, and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre at 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wintertime/ to purchase tickets. Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Addison Street.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep reopens Nov. 12 with Wintertime

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, will present an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum of Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition opened on October 20 and will be on display through February 27. It is the premier museum solo exhibition for Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo and includes more than 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artist’s paintings that show his calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working between Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. The text by American sociologist, civil rights activist, and author W.E.B Du Bois inspires the exhibition title which aims to be a study of “Black life behind the veil of race.” The Museum of the African Diaspora is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibition/amoako-boafosoul-of-black-folks/. articles.text: Jayden Lee (Leon Jones, right) and his mom, Crystal (Velina Brown) play a game in The Great Khan, now playing at San Francisco Playhouse on Post Street. San Francisco Playhouse will present The Great Khan on stage now through November 13. The show is written by Michael Gene Sullivan, the prolific writer of shows for the long-running San Francisco Mime Troupe. The Great Khan will be directed by Darryl Jones, and stars Velina Brown (Crystal), Leon Jones (Jayden) and Jamella Cross (Ant). The story follows protagonist Jayden, an African American teenage boy who saves a girl, Ant, from sexual assault. Following the incident, Jayden and his mother are forced to move to keep him safe from the boys who attacked Ant. Both Ant and Jayden try to figure out how to define themselves in a culture that insists on seeing them as forever dangerous. The Great Khan is in a rolling world premiere through the National New Play Network. Tickets are available with a seating chart with fixed social distancing. Masks will be required during the performance. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required for all audience members. Visit www.sfplayhouse.org to purchase tickets.

The exhibition will be on display through January 15, 2022. Suspended Matter features the work of artists Julia Goodman, Asma Kazmi, Laura Arminda Kingsley, and Jenifer K. Wofford, and is curated by Patricia Cariño Valdez. Through various mediums including sculpture, video, photography, and paintings, the artists consider connections between humanity and the domestic objects that shape our environments and surroundings. The name of the exhibition is a riff off the scientific definition of a “disruption in the environment,” such as erosion or flooding. “The works in Suspended Matter contemplate how we interact with others and our surBerkeley Rep reopens Nov. 12 with Wintertime By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Repertory Theatre will reopen on November 12 with a live production of Wintertime by Charles Mee and directed by Les Waters. It will be performed until December 19. Berkeley Rep welcomes back Mee and Les Waters who have teamed up in the past to bring Fetes de la Nuit and Big Love to the stage. Wintertime is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family who arrive at their summer house in the winter woods for supposedly secret rendezvous—and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” The cast stars James Carpenter as Frank, Sharon Lockwood as Hilda, and includes Carmen Berkeley as Ariel, Nora El Samahy as Mariam, and Sarah Nina Hayon as Jaqueline. Tickets are now on sale. Berkeley Rep requires all audience members to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification, and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre at 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wintertime/ to purchase tickets. roundings,” said Carino Valdez. “From the reconstitution of familiar fabrics into abstract shapes as seen in Goodman’s sculptures to a close examination of domestic objects that we interact within Kazmi’s work, the artists recognize the shifting interactions with our values, beliefs, and the everyday objects that we keep. The otherworldly sci-fi videos by Kingsley and Wofford’s depictions of solitude and isolation remind us of the constant revaluation of our existence and our resilience in relation to the past and present.” Berkeley Art Center is located at 1275 Walnut Street in North Berkeley. Soul of Black Folks exhibit at MoAD on view through Feb. 2022 By Allyson Aleksey The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, will present an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum of Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition opened on October 20 and will be on display through February 27. It is the premier museum solo exhibition for Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo and includes more than 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artist’s paintings that show his calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working between Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. The text by American sociologist, civil rights activist, and author W.E.B Du Bois inspires the exhibition title which aims to be a study of “Black life behind the veil of race.” The Museum of the African Diaspora is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse will present The Great Khan on stage now through November 13. The show is written by Michael Gene Sullivan, the prolific writer of shows for the long-running San Francisco Mime Troupe. The Great Khan will be directed by Darryl Jones, and stars Velina Brown (Crystal), Leon Jones (Jayden) and Jamella Cross (Ant). The story follows protagonist Jayden, an African American teenage boy who saves a girl, Ant, from sexual assault. Following the incident, Jayden and his mother are forced to move to keep him safe from the boys who attacked Ant. Both Ant and Jayden try to figure out how to define themselves in a culture that insists on seeing them as forever dangerous. The Great Khan is in a rolling world premiere through the National New Play Network. Tickets are available with a seating chart with fixed social distancing. Masks will be required during the performance. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required for all audience members. Visit www.sfplayhouse.org to purchase tickets. articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes singer-songwriter Angelique Kidjo as the organization’s first season-long artist-in-residence. She will perform her unique take on the Talking Head’s 1980 album Remain in Light this Friday, October 29 at Zellerbach Hall. “One of the great pleasures this season is welcoming Angélique Kidjo, who hasn’t appeared here in nearly a decade, back to Berkeley as our first season-long artist-in-residence,” said Jeremy Geffen, Cal Performances’ artistic director. “Having been a presenter, collaborator and fan of her work for years, I know firsthand of her passion, conviction, and boundless curiosity. She brings inextinguishable energy to bear in both her performances and her community outreach work.” Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and was recently named one of Time Magazine’s “100 most influential people of 2021” for her work in the arts and as a cultural ambassador. The artist, who fled a dictatorship in her home country of Benin, draws from her personal experiences when creating music. Kidjo’s latest recording, Mother Nature, was released earlier this year and incorporates West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. “Angélique draws from her personal experiences a deep sense Photo courtesy of Cultural Services of the French Embassy Angelique Kidjo of conviction as well as profound passion for exploring the breadth and depth of the human experience—qualities that make her the perfect partner for our season-long Illuminations programming,” said Geffen. “And most importantly, she comes to our campus hoping to learn as much as to share.” “By inviting her to meet with faculty and students, Cal Performances reinforces and supports the university’s values of cultivating and sustaining a diverse, equitable, informed, and inclusive and accessible community.” The concert begins at 8 p.m. Tickets range from $36 to $96. Half-price tickets are available for UC Berkeley students. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, at calperformances. org, and at the door. Proof of a COVID-19 vaccination is required for audience members. Close To Home Favorite & McCaulous.com Classic Pajamas & Gowns Made of High Quality 100% Cotton Brushed Flannel

articles.text: Art installations, pre-concert activities; post-concert auction, cocktail reception, & dinner San Francisco Symphony celebrates its annual Dia de Los Muertos event featuring traditional Latin American music and culture, an array of guest artists, and family-friendly festivities on Saturday, November 6. Enluis Montes Olivar will serve as conductor for this special event. Members of the San Francisco Symphony will be joined by violinist Alexander Barantschik, vocalist Flor Amargo, and the Casa Circulo Cultural collective. The program includes music by Arturo Marquez, Astor Piazzolla, and Jose Pablo Moncayo Garcia. The event begins at 2 p.m., and a post-concert Dia de Los Muertos reception and dinner will be held. The Day of the Dead, celebrated on November 1 and 2, originated in Mexico. The multi-day holiday celebrates family and friends gathering to pay respects to loved ones who have died. San Francisco Symphony has celebrated the holiday with an annual concert featuring traditional song and dance. Symphony requires proof of full vaccination for all patrons above the age of 12 to enter Davies Symphony Hall. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2021-22/Dia-de-losMuertos. articles.text: Oakland Ballet opens its season with Luna Mexicana, celebrating Dia de Los Muertos. Oakland Ballet will perform a special event entitled “Luna Mexicana” in honor of Dia de Los Muertos (Day of the Dead) on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6, at the Paramount Theatre. “Luna Mexicana” is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for the holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food - orchestrated as a celebration of family and loved ones. Prior to the event, visit the Paramount Theatre lobby to view the ofrendas created by local artists. The dance performance will be 90 minutes with no intermission. Friday night’s performance is at 7:30 p.m., and the Saturday performance is a 2 p.m. matinee. Doors will open 60 minutes in advance. For tickets and more information, visit https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/ luna-mexicana/.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Orchestra rehearsing in Piedmont Center for the Arts. What is that sound? Headlights shining on the glistening street. Newspapers delivered in double plastic rain jackets. Dogs wiggling for a purpose. Hopefully, the road to normalcy is around the corner. In baseball, the game was called on account of rain. That was a good thing for our Piedmont Chamber Orchestra. Musicians from as far away as Sacramento dodged the raindrops and assembled in the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday. What was originally announced as a concert on the lawn became an open rehearsal indoors. The musicians outnumbered the listeners. It was kind of like a command performance for Queen Victoria. The good news is that the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is in good shape. The repertoire was set with a Franz Schubert overture, a Gabriel Fauré Suite and Beethoven’s favorite Symphony No. 8. Maybe they will do me the honor to play my newest arrangement. All the orchestra needs now is to set a concert date. articles.text: Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on November 20. Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 20 at 4:00 p.m. under the sponsorship of the Kodály Foundation for Music Education. The program will include works by Grieg, Brahms, Schubert, Debussy, De Greeve, and Indonesian composer Ananda Sukarlan. Suandrianna graduated in 2016 with a Bachelor of Music in Piano Performance at the Universitas Pelita Harapan in Jakarta. She received the Roger L. Keyes Award as the Outstanding Graduate Student in Piano from Baylor University School of Music in Waco, Texas, and earned a double Master’s in Performance (piano and organ) in 2020. Donations (general $20; student/senior $10) may be made at the door. The concert will be performed without intermission (75 minutes). Masks and proof of vaccination are required. A reception for the artist will follow, hosted by the Kodály Foundation for Music Education. For more information, visit www. kodalyfoundation.org or call 415- 606-9887.

articles.text: Notable twentieth century classical music theorist Heinrich Schenker and leading developer of bebop Charlie Parker both used core melody. Schenkerian analysis expresses the harmonic and melodic essence of a piece of music. While building a library of Parker phrases, I was listening to the head melody (the main thematic section) at seventy percent speed, to transcribe his performance on “Confirmation” and “Moose the Moochie.” I noticed he was playing the essential notes in each phrase with more dynamic accent. These “core melody” tones can be memorized as a melodic framework and elaborated differently each time you improvise. Now, in addition to an analysis of his melodic design, I could be cued by his louder notes. Use the link below to see and hear my use of Charlie Parker’s core melody concept and other attributes of his playing to create improvisations in his style: www.guitarimprov.com/ParkersCoreMelody.pdf Parker’s “dual melody” design is an imitation of two-voice counterpoint on one instrument. Play one or more notes of a melody in the high range of pitch, beginning a second melody with one or more notes in the low range, then alternate between the two ranges. In his “V” design, the melodic line goes up/down or down/up with a quick, ornate melodic figure at the peak or valley. You can read more in this excerpt from the Melodic Cells chapter of Guitar Improv: www. guitarimprov.com/zz-Charlie_ Parker_Design.pdf In his late teens, Parker practiced 12 hours daily, building his chops on his axe in a remote woodshed. He made this claim in a 1954 interview with Paul Desmond. Many people exaggerate in such claims, but judging by his playing, it seems true. Bandleader Jay McShann recalled that when their touring car ran over a chicken, Parker asked to go back and pick it up and cook it for dinner. From then on, his nickname was “Yardbird” (a.k.a. Bird). In 1939, Parker was looking for something new. In his words, “I was working over “Cherokee” and as I did, I found that by using the higher intervals of a chord as a melody line and backing them with appropriately related changes, I could play the thing I’d been hearing. I came alive.” He’s referring to the ninths, elevenths and thirteenths, which he featured the rest of his life. The high note in the first phrase of Duke Ellington’s “In a Sentimental Mood” is an eleventh. Jamming after hours at Monroe’s Uptown House and Minton’s Playhouse in Harlem in 1939-1941, Parker developed a new concept of melody and chord progression in his association with trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie and pianist Thelonius Monk. They took their contemporary Art Tatum’s reharmonization of chord progression into more dissonant territory. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www. guitarimprov.com

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, October 27, 2021 The Musical Gourmet Thoughts on a rainy day read in the newspapers.“ I took The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet his advice and read a review of one of our most prominent local orchestras. Apparently not content to play beautifully, they stooped to cheap theatrics. At one point in the music, the conductor had the violins “leap to their feet.” My teacher, Jascha Heifetz, set high standards for himself and high standards for his art. He was famous for saying: “If I play badly, I deserve to be hissed.“ I wonder what he would say about the concert in question, with violins leaping to their feet, Indeed! Wouldn’t it be better that the orchestra had played brilliantly and the audience leapt to its feet in sincere appreciation for an excellent performance? The food part of Musical Gourmet There is a new Thai restaurant on Piedmont Avenue, Pla Daek restaurant (4133 Piedmont Avenue) which has been open just three months. Of special interest is that it features regional Thai cuisine. The restaurant is beautifully decorated with museum quality murals on the wall. The dishes are beautifully elegant, as is the service. My wife and I shared a fresh roll ($10) which was delicious and came with two sauces. We also got the famous Pad Thai with shrimp for $16. For quality, size of portions, decor and service, this is one of the top Thai restaurants in the area. A bonus to our readers One last thought. If you want to see stupendous vaudeville fiddling, check out the videos of vaudeville violinist extraordinaire Wilbur (Willie) Hall. There are no cheap theatrics here… just jaw-dropping virtuosity. articles.text: Local artist Michael Stehr will present a new exhibit, The Other Side of the Fence: Considering Green and the Power of Color, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit is dedicated in loving memory of the artist’s mother, Bonnie Drewes Stehr, who recently died. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November 13 to 21. A reception will be held on Friday evening, November 12. To attend the reception, RSVP to Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Red is hot, blue is cold, and yellow was known to make Van Gogh smile. While our reaction to color is affected greatly by personal preference, there is no denying that color has the ability to make one feel while eliciting a tangible reaction. In this exhibit Stehr explores the power of color by focusing on the impact of green. In 1140, stained glass at Notre Dame de Chartres showing Christ on the cross has the crucifix depicted in a green color, despite the fact that we know the cross was made of wood and was likely a shade of brown. Of course, green is associated with life ... rolling green hills in Spring, a lush forest, or a perfectly manicured baseball field ... all images that can elicit feelings of growth, vitality, and renewal. The cross depicted as green refers to the renewal that one’s soul can experience due to the sacrifice of Jesus on that cross. We encounter green in our daily lives in various shades. There is the brilliant green of a lawn encountered in morning light. There is the neutralized green of an oak tree that can almost appear warm under the light of early evening. Furthermore, the greens one perceives in a foreground change greatly viewing them at a distance. The exhibit will include 30 new paintings in which the color green has an important role in the impact of the painting. Stehr will address the chemistry of green as he discusses how he mixes green to achieve the various effects. Also being exhibited are 45 paintings from previous exhibitions. articles.text: Piedmont resident Don George, a widely respected travel writer and current Editor at Large for National Geographic Travel, will offer a book talk with illustrations at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 13, at 4:00 p.m. He served as Travel Editor at the San Francisco Examiner and Chronicle for 15 years, and was Travel Editor at Salon, and Lonely Planet. It is his first appearance before a hometown audience. “This is something I have looked forward to doing for a number of years,” he said. He will read selected passages from some of his 14 books, including The Way of Wanderlust, his most recent anthology, How to be a Travel Writer, and By the Seat of My Pants There is no admission fee for the event, and books will be available for purchase. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Don George (right) at Machu Picchu, the 15th-century Inca ruins in southern Peru.
articles.title: Celebrated travel writer Don George to speak at PCA Nov. 13

Saturday, November 20, 4 p.m. Jessica Suandrianna, pianist The Kodály Foundation for Music Education presents young Indonesian pianist Jessica Suandrianna currently on tour. Michael Stehr exhibit opens in Nov. at Center for the Arts Local artist Michael Stehr will present a new exhibit, The Other Side of the Fence: Considering Green and the Power of Color, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit is dedicated in loving memory of the artist’s mother, Bonnie Drewes Stehr, who recently died. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November 13 to 21. A reception will be held on Friday evening, November 12. To attend the reception, RSVP to Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Red is hot, blue is cold, and yellow was known to make Van Gogh smile. While our reaction to color is affected greatly by personal preference, there is no denying that color has the ability to make one feel while eliciting a tangible reaction. In this exhibit Stehr explores the power of color by focusing on the impact of green. In 1140, stained glass at Notre Dame de Chartres showing Christ on the cross has the crucifix depicted in a green color, despite the fact that we know the cross was made of wood and was likely a shade of brown. Of course, green is associated with life ... rolling green hills in Spring, a lush forest, or a perfectly manicured baseball field ... all images that can elicit feelings of growth, vitality, and renewal. articles.text: Chris Evans as Captain America. Review by Chris Honore’ Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel Comics. Summer blockbusters recently have been defined by the superhero: Thor, X-Men: First Class, Green Lantern, and not to forget Transformers. Plus Harry Potter, a superhero to be sure. Ask Voldermort. Now comes Marvel’s Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans ala CGI), is desperate to join the army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), but can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off to fight not just the Nazis, but a ratcheted up version of the evil doers, an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), who also possess some serious weaponry. This first Captain America is an origin film (beginning in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by CGI. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth, justice, and VE-day, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Sequel to follow. Captain America: The First Avenger. Directed by Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Friends With Benefits is not your grandfather’s movie. In the 1939 film, Gone With the Wind, Vivien Leigh asks Clark Gable, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?” He turns and says, “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn.” That singular word, “damn,” evoked gasps from audiences and represented a sea change in movies. And it was the beginning of a gradual loosening of film censorship regarding not only language but the interaction between men and women (physical and verbal). Until the late 1950s, Ozzie and Harriet slept in separate beds and everyone had a robe handy. Decorum and restraint ruled. But that was then and this is now, and romantic comedies such as Friends With Benefits definitely represent another sea change in terms of language and physical contact. True, “FWB” has outstanding portrayals by Mila Kunis as Jamie, young NYC based headhunter, and Justin Timberlake as Dylan, online art director from LA, who arrives in New York for an interview with GQ magazine. And true the exploration of benefits is taken to the edge of that well-worn envelope and beyond. “FWB” is randy and profane and funny, even if it’s a runaway cliché. You know the drill: cool guy and hot girl like each other and swear they can be friends even if they have sex. Neither is looking for a commitment. They have tons of chemistry, hangout well, text, and even find themselves in the middle of a Manhattan flash mob, doing what flash mobs do. It’s all kinda cool. But not to forget: benefits signify benefits. No matter the steam on the windows and their amazing mutual attraction. What Jamie and Dylan refuse to acknowledge is what everyone in the audience already knows: they’re in love. Denial (or sustained dissembling when confronted) is not a river in India, but in rom-coms of this ilk it’s a familiar refuge. The tension is nicely developed and drawn out, compounded by Jamie’s conviction that she’s damaged in some vague way and Dylan’s certainty that he’s emotionally unavailable. Both have been told this during past breakups. As romantic comedies go, and there have been a spate of them in the last several years, “FWB” is the exception: it’s really good. The writing is sharp, the pacing is engaging, and both Jamie and Dylan are smart and interesting, especially Jamie. Kunis is wonderful, and if she is an example of the young, metro woman who is confident and fearless, in a funny, quick, and intelligent way, that’s all to the good. Friends With Benefits is light years from It Happened One Night, the 1934 movie with Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert, and way better than anything that has appeared recently, including No Strings Attached a good example. Friends With Benefits. Directed by Will Gluck. Starring Mila Kunis, Justin Timberlake, Patricia Clarkson, Richard Jenkins and Jemma Elfman. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R
articles.title: Friends With Benefits a surprisingly good romantic comedy

articles.text: Part 31 in a semi-weekly series The important concept of architectural building massing refers to the overall general form, shape, size and orientation of a structure, apart from the more detailed considerations like fenestration, detailing, or textures, all of which enter a little bit later in the design process. Generally, after the decision on architectural style, I would say that overall building massing becomes the most important consideration of any architectural design. It is so important because it forms the “infrastructure” of the whole aesthetic – of all the subsequent design decisions that follow. It is at the apex of the design hierarchy—what is first observable and evident when approaching a building. This concept extends to adjacencies as well as buildings themselves, that is to say, the building massing certainly should respond to neighboring buildings, significant landscaping and geographical features as well. It is for these reasons that regulations and guidelines, including in Piedmont, often make reference to “massing” as an important part of the neighborhood and city aesthetic. Closely associated with massing is composition. Although the two architectural design terms are sometimes used interchangeably, in my experience massing refers more to the overall three-dimensional form, while composition refers to the arrangement of additional elements within and supportive of the basic massing. Massing is an integral part of, and in many cases defines architectural styles. For example, low, strongly horizontal massing is a chief characteristic of Ranch style homes. Steeply sloped gable roof buildings of 2.5 to 3 floors is a common massing characteristic of virtually all Tudor homes as we have discussed in previous columns. But, like most everything else associated with the design of the built environment (or all art for that matter), there are really no hard and fast absolutes. Wonderful exceptions exist to all rules, regulations and Photos by Will Adams Architectural massing can be judged by how well a building responds to its surrounding site. This ski lodge derives its main form from the surrounding sloping mountains and uneven terrain upon which it sits, and its 4.5 floors that match the ridge height to the neighboring pine trees. The composition (position and sizes) of the secondary sloping roofs are used to support the overall building massing concept.
