articles.text: Photo by Julie Reichle Photography Cancer League board members prepare for the Annual Holly Ball. Pictured are: (front) Kelly Winniford (left), Lucy Ridgway, Kate Osler, Rachelle Hebrard; (2nd row) Jenna Caldwell, Barbara Dickason, Kristen Dixon, Laura Woo; (3rd row) Deborah Odendorf, Kia Conn, Janet Nunan, Rebecca Heywood, Jacque Jumper; (top row) Teresa Baum, Camilla Soghikian, Karen Ellis, and Alison Avagliano. The Cancer League has announced that the 48th annual Holly Ball will be held in person on Friday, December 3 at the Claremont Country Club. It is the organization’s largest fundraiser of the year. This year’s theme, A Medieval Knight, will give people a longawaited chance to mingle with friends and support breakthrough cancer research while experiencing the world of Knights, Royals and even Jesters. The black-tie event will commence with a cocktail reception followed by a seated dinner, raffle, live auction and dancing into the night. One hundred percent of profits from Holly Ball are used to support the Cancer League’s mission to fund cancer research, early detection, education and patient care. “COVID-19 has had many unintended consequences in the fight against cancer,” said Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair. “Cancers have gone undiagnosed, research has been suspended and many clinics are working at diminished capacities. These roadblocks have given us even more motivation to get research back on track by making this year’s Holly Ball a smashing success.” Cancer research is normally funded by large nonprofit organizations that require a significant proof of concept. But getting the funding required to develop this initial data set can be challenging, leading cutting-edge ideas struggling to get noticed. Just like technology startups, these research startups need seed funding to get off the ground. Funds raised at the annual Holly Ball event help The Cancer League find and fund these breakthrough research projects, accelerating us all towards the cure. “The Cancer League has been seeding bold, new research at UCSF for over 20 years,” confirmed Alan Ashworth, President at UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. “These projects have gone on to earn funding from hugely competitive sources so they can yield meaningful changes in how we treat cancer with investigational therapies and clinical trials.” Donations and sponsorships are welcome at any level. Sponsorships at the $1000 level and above will be invited to a Sponsor Party on November 11th. This year’s sponsors include the David & Susan Martin Foundation, Mr. Gary Kovacs, John Muir Health/ UCSF Health, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Jenna & Jack Caldwell, The Grubb Company, Celine & Alastair MacTaggart, and Camilla & Shahan Soghikian. To make a donation or learn more about The Cancer League, visit the website at www.thecancerleagueinc.org. About The Cancer League The Cancer League is a San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit that funds groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages. Since its inception in 1973, The Cancer League has raised and donated over $5 million toward the fight against cancer. The organization has an average yearly allocations budget of over $300,000 and an average grant size between $10,000-50,000. The Cancer League is a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization.

articles.text: As we enter the fall and winter months, Piedmonters prepare for shorter, darker, and colder days in varying ways. Many of us, including a vast majority of the population of the Northern Hemisphere, bring out cold-weather clothing and spend time preparing for holiday celebrations. For the Southwestern United States, the fall months include long-awaited rain after months-long dry spells. California relies heavily on the precipitation of these wet months to replenish our water supply in the forms of surface water and groundwater. In Northern California, the vast majority of our water originates as snow in the Sierra Nevada region and feeds into a network of surface water sources. In the Bay Area, 60% of the water supply is sourced from the Sierra Nevada snowpack. Of the annual water supplied to the San Francisco Bay Delta, 40% comes from the Sierra snowmelt. Piedmont’s water, supplied by the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD), comes from the Mokelumne River watershed and is collected in the Pardee Reservoir in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Throughout the winter, the accumulation of water in the snowpack of the Sierra Nevada Mountains is crucial. The snowpack can increase our surface water storage by over 70% by acting like a natural reservoir during the colder months. When water is stored in the mountain snowpack, the delayed rate of release allows this water to slowly melt and accumulate in man-made surface reservoirs as temperatures rise. During our warmer months, precipitation levels fall and water demand is high, but the water stored in the mountain snowpack alleviates seasonal fluctuations in rainfall. However, as global temperatures rise, less water falls as snow in the Sierra Nevada, resulting in decreased snowpack. According to the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Report released in August, the global temperature is expected to reach or exceed 1.5°C of warming above pre-industrial levels in the early 2030s in all emissions scenarios considered. As climate change progresses, Northern Californians will experience high year-to-year variability of precipitation in the form of “booms and busts”, or very wet periods followed by very dry periods. These “whiplash” events will swing our local ecosystem through extreme conditions, with the largest individual storms becoming more intense, accompanied by more frequent extremely dry precipitation periods. One of the results of these changes is greater intensity and persistence of drought, which has ranging impacts here in California including those on agriculture, drinking water, ecosystems, energy, industry, and recreation. Namely, nearly 70% of California’s existing area of wine production may be vulnerable under climate change by mid-century. Meanwhile, decreasing snowpack in the Sierra Nevada’s will threaten the industry and recreation of the area throughout the winter season. Similarly, California’s Forest land, which comprises roughly one-third of the state’s total land area, is threatened by heat and drought, including increased fire frequency and intensity, and new threats such as changing wildlife and insect populations. In Piedmont, residents can not only take overarching measures to combat climate change, such as actions to reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions, but also to prepare for and increase resilience to drought. Piedmont Connect’s recent event series, “Living with Drought”, highlighted water conserving techniques and presented case-studies on healthy, ecofriendly, water-efficient homes and gardens. One such action, highlighted by the organization’s garden tours, includes adapting gardens and yards to reduce water use and transition away from invasive and water intensive landscaping. Other resources include the Piedmont Climate Challenge and EBMUD. The Piedmont Climate Challenge highlights water-wise changes including mindful lifestyle changes as well as home appliance upgrades to maximize water efficiency. Similarly, the EBMUD website includes a section on Conservation and Rebates, which features the WaterSmart Gardener resource, the WaterSmart Calculator, and information on rebates, programs, and tools that will help residents and businesses increase water efficiency. Annie Wensley is the City of Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.

One hundred percent of profits from Holly Ball are used to support the Cancer League’s mission to fund cancer research, early detection, education and patient care. “COVID-19 has had many unintended consequences in the fight against cancer,” said Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair. “Cancers have gone undiagnosed, research has been suspended and many clinics are working at diminished capacities. These roadblocks have given us even more motivation to get research back on track by making this year’s Holly Ball a smashing success.” Cancer research is normally funded by large nonprofit organizations that require a significant proof of concept. But getting the funding required to develop this initial data set can be challenging, leading cutting-edge ideas struggling to get noticed. Just like technology startups, these research startups need seed funding to get off the ground. Funds raised at the annual Holly Ball event help The Cancer League find and fund these breakthrough research projects, accelerating us all towards the cure. “The Cancer League has been seeding bold, new research at UCSF for over 20 years,” confirmed Alan Ashworth, President at UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. “These projects have gone on to earn funding from hugely competitive sources so they can yield meaningful changes in how we treat cancer with investigational therapies and clinical trials.” Donations and sponsorships are welcome at any level. Sponsorships at the $1000 level and above will be invited to a Sponsor Party on November 11th. This year’s sponsors include the David & Susan Martin Foundation, Mr. Gary Kovacs, John Muir Health/ UCSF Health, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Jenna & Jack Caldwell, The Grubb Company, Celine & Alastair MacTaggart, and Camilla & Shahan Soghikian. To make a donation or learn more about The Cancer League, visit the website at www.thecancerleagueinc.org. About The Cancer League The Cancer League is a San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit that funds groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages. Since its inception in 1973, The Cancer League has raised and donated over $5 million toward the fight against cancer. The organization has an average yearly allocations budget of over $300,000 and an average grant size between $10,000-50,000. The Cancer League is a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: In spite of the threat of rain, 17 fearless members of Walking on Wednesdays group and two K-9 best friends were at the Exedra on Wednesday, October 20 for their weekly stroll through town. Though overcast, not a drop of rain fell on the walkers during their pre-Halloween walk. One of the many things the walkers enjoy about Halloween is the creative decorations on homes. A house at Hampton and Glen Alpine had some especially fun decorations. A home on Lexford Road built in a storyteller architectural style that is unusual, and it seemed appropriate to see it at this time of year. The group had not been on Hampton, Lexford and Huntleigh Roads for a couple of years, so that part of town was selected as the destination. The walkers went up Lincoln Avenue so they could see the decorations on a home in the first block of Crocker which had a large set of skeletons and skulls in the front yard. At King Avenue, a house almost looked like the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch there were so many pumpkins in front. Continuing on Hampton they saw a free library in front of one house. At the corner of Hampton and Glen Alpine they saw two sets of animated characters that included Scooby-Doo and the Flintstones. Crossing La Salle Avenue, they passed through the two large columns marking the entrance to the St. James Woods neighborhood that was developed in the early 20th century. Its streets are still clearly defined by the brown terracotta tiles inlaid in the sidewalks. The walkers went up Lexford to a large, storybook style home built early last century, on a large lot with cobblestones arranged around the front yard. The house’s exterior is made almost entirely of bricks and it has a slate roof. There is even a turret on the middle of the house that gives the look of a castle or fort. A sign at the front door proclaims, “The Roster Crows, but the Hen Delivers.” They also enjoyed the ghosts, skeletons, and other Halloween decorations all around the yard. On the walk they observed lovely gardens with cedar trees, azalea bushes, and fall colors. At the top of street, just before the intersection with La Salle, a large set of skeletons, reclining in garden chairs, watched the walkers go by. None of the walkers had ever visited La Salle Court, a culde-sac, and they couldn’t resist one more new street. Up a fairly steep hill at the top is another large, impressive home with a swimming pool in front. As the group started down the hill, they noticed an abstract statue in a yard that appeared to be a man with broken chains in his outstretched hands. They decided this was Marley’s Ghost, Scrooge’s former business partner in Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol. It was about a 3-mile walk in less than two hours and was time to return to their starting point at the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group, sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: accepted practice. It is often difficult to itemize exactly what makes for good building massing and the related composition. I suppose it is a combination of style awareness and a common-sense response to surrounding site conditions—all the while providing for the multitude of functional requirements of construction and servicing that the building must accommodate. I think that good architects combine continuing aesthetic consideration, professional experience and past trial and error efforts to arrive at successful architectural massing and composition. In the end, the measure of success is simple: does it work? And does it look good? Next: Architectural Detailing Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Some think this 9-unit multi-family Piedmont complex might have been designed by the famous modernist architect Irving Gill. It is wonderfully laid out with an inner courtyard with beautiful bay views, and private unit entries. However, I think the building massing is lacking; it would have looked better with another story (and more detail attention to the street side). It is interesting that a bigger building (and additional units) can sometimes improve the building aesthetic and urban design. This beautiful Piedmont house employs a reoccurring massing motif often used by astute architects: an L shaped plan introduces a street facing gable to relieve the long ridge and eave of the main roof. The massing of the deck and porch cover (accentuated by the planting) provides the same relief.
articles.title: Walking Piedmont

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board stated at its October 13 meeting that all teachers, staff, contractors, consultants, volunteers and visitors to schools must show proof of vaccination no later than December 9. Negative Covid tests are no longer an option. The board’s decision does not provide for personal belief or religious belief exemptions; only medical exemptions will be considered. An earlier draft of the resolution included an option to submit a personal belief statement for not being vaccinated. However, the board was adamant that since no such clause is valid in the student’s mandate, that the teacher and staff mandate should not have the opt-out clause either. Supt. Randy Booker explained the controversy behind the requirement for teachers and staff to be vaccinated. “This [resolution] was a bit trickier to develop [than the one for students] because we do not have an existing staff immunization policy. No one does. It doesn’t really exist,” Booker told school board members. Board member Amal Smith Everyone on Piedmont school campuses must provide proof of Covid-19 vaccination by December 9.
articles.title: School board requires vaccination for everyone at Piedmont schools

articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade, a treasured public event since 1986, returns this year after last year’s hiatus due COVID-19 and related restrictions. The 34th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade will take place on Saturday, October 30, starting at 11:00 a.m. at the corner of Montell Street and Piedmont Avenue. The event is family-friendly and geared to youth, organized by the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association. Come in costume and stop by the shops along Piedmont Avenue for trick-or-treating opportunities. Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson has been named the Grand Marshal for the third year. “I had a wonderful time [those two years], mostly scaring children,” joked Larson, who dressed in tails, a top hat, a sash and a monster mask to lead the parade. “I think this is a great thing for Piedmont Avenue and a great way to connect with the community,” said Larson. Larson has spent the better part of his life making sure Piedmont Avenue is a vital, vibrant destination for Piedmont and Oakland residents. The annual pet costume contest, held concurrently with the parade, is at 12:30 p.m. at Pet Food Express. The Piedmont Avenue Elementary School PTA is sponsoring events on the school playground from 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., including “trunk-ortreating.” Parents must accompany their children to this free event. The event will be held outdoors, but masks and face-coverings are encouraged per county guidelines.
articles.title: Piedmont Ave. Halloween Parade returns on Sat., October 30

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Lisa Wise Consulting will host a virtual event tomorrow, October 21, entitled “New Fair Housing Programs Community Workshop/ The Zoom meeting will start at 5:30 pm, to include a discussion of new goals for multifamily housing and ADU incentives. New California laws, such as SB35 and SB 330, require cities to apply standards that are objective and “knowable in advance” to applications for multifamily housing developments, such as apartment buildings. Discretionary design review or conditional use permits are no longer allowed. Last year, the City and LWC began to prepare objective design standards for future multifamily housing developments, including the citywide Fair Housing Survey conducted in March 2021 and presentations to the Housing Advisory Committee in May and June 2021. The results of this work will be described to the Piedmont community on October 21, 2021. State laws, including AB 671, require cities to develop incentives for the creation of accessory dwelling units (ADUs) that can be offered at affordable rents to residents with very low, low, and moderate incomes. The October 21 event will also include a discussion of possible new ADU incentives. New incentives would generally be available to homeowners who choose to rent their new ADUs at very low or low rents for a period of 10 years. articles.text: A homecoming for Piedmont architect who proposed new pool 20 years ago Piedmont’s City Council unanimously selected ELS Architecture and Urban Design as the architect of record for the Piedmont Community Pool Project during a Monday, October 18 meeting. A total of eight firms submitted proposals, and each was reviewed independently by a swath of city staff, including City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Mayor Teddy Gray King, Community Pool Advisory Committee Chair Steve Roland, Pool Project Manager George Sanen, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Planning Director Kevin Jackson, and Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit. Councilmember Betsy Andersen and Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman were added to the review team to form a 10-person panel. Clarence Mamuyac, principal at ELS architecture in Berkeley. Three architecture firms, ELS, HED and WRNS Studio, were determined by the panel to be the most highly qualified. Individual interviews were held with the finalists on September 27. The selection of ELS Architecture and Urban Design was unanimous. The core design team will be led by the firm’s president and CEO, Clarence Mamuyac, a longtime resident of Piedmont who proposed a new community pool 20 years ago. articles.text: The genesis of Piedmont’s ban, and the results 30 years later Piedmont and a few other cities in the Bay Area have served as a case study for a statewide ban on gas-powered leaf blowers and other lawn-mowing equipment. Assembly Bill 1346, signed by Gov. Newsom on October 9, declared that small, off-road engines (SOREs), primarily used in lawn and garden equipment, emit high levels of air pollutants including oxides of nitrogen and reactive organic gases. The new law was introduced by Assemblymembers Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park) and Lorena Gonzalez (D-San Diego) in response to projections that smog-forming pollution from gas-powered lawn equipment will surpass that from passenger cars this year. Zero-emission equivalents to all SORE equipment, like leaf-blowers and lawn-mowers, are available; cities like Palo Alto, Lomita, and Piedmont all created policy to ban the use of gas-powered lawn equipment in favor of cleaner solutions. That was back in the 90’s; at the time, jurisdictions were attracted to the ban not just for environmental purposes, but also in the interest of noise reduction. Piedmont resident Tom Bowman can be credited with leading the way for a ban in the city as early as 1990. Bowman and friend Bill Jamieson decided they were tired of hearing the highpitched sound of gas-powered leaf blowers. Knowing that electric blowers were available and that gas-powered blowers were harming the environment, they wrote language for a city ordinance, put it on a ballot, and got wife, well, it looks like dad is finally getting his way in California,” he said, referencing a 1990 advertisement in The Piedmonter, “Vote Yes on Measure B,” authored by his father. The Campaign ad stated: “Surprised that a convenient gardening tool can put your health at risk? It does that, and more. There is no good reason for gas-powered leaf blowers to be used in Piedmont, except for the convenience of hired gardeners.” AB 1346 directs the California Air Resources Board to phase out the sale of SOREs across the state by 2024 and directs the board to identify and make available funding for commercial rebates to go toward the purchase of electric alternatives. “Piedmont has been leading the way with a ban on gasoline-powered leaf blowers since it approved by Piedmont voters on February 27, 1990. Piedmont was the first city in the East Bay to ban gas-powered leaf blowers. Bowman’s obituary in a 2018 edition of Piedmont Post read, “in his final days at home, Tom still bristled at the din of illegal leaf blowers used by his neighbors’ gardeners.” Bowman’s younger son, Jim Bowman, now a resident of Seattle, acknowledged how pleased his father would be of the statewide ban in California. “I chuckled, and said to my

articles.text: On October 7, public health officials from all eight Bay Area counties announced that indoor mask mandates may be lifted if case rate and vaccination criteria are met. Alameda County Public Health Department estimates that this could occur in mid to late-December. In order to lift the indoor mask requirement, Alameda County must have 80% of its population fully-vaccinated and Alameda County Health Officers must deem COVID-19 hospitalizations as “low and stable.” As of October 18, 83% of Alameda County’s residents were fully vaccinated. The mandate may be lifted by mid-December, assuming that “at least some 5 to 11-year-old residents are fully vaccinated after December 10.” Hospitalization rates must continue to decline in the county, and the public health agency warned that a late fall or early winter surge could slow progress. According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 90% of ICU beds at Kaiser Hospital in Oakland are occupied, and at least 70% of ICU beds at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital are occupied as of October 18. On the same day, Alameda County entered the “moderate,” or “yellow” level of community transmission according to the Center for Disease Control tracker, meaning that COVID-19 community transmission is no longer considered “widespread.” Meeting the yellow level of community transmission is another benchmark that public health officials consider when lifting indoor mask mandates. Most Bay Area jurisdictions re-instated their indoor mask mandates in August, following a summer surge in COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. “Masks and vaccines together have protected residents of Alameda County and the Bay Area during the summer wave,” confirmed Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Officer. “While we expect COVID-19 and flu to circulate this winter, with more people well-protected from severe illness by vaccination we will be able to loosen mask requirements safely.” Marin County is currently the closest Bay Area county to discontinuing the mask mandate. Marin County Public Health Director Dr. Matt Willis said the earliest date the indoor mask mandate could end is November 3. Marin County’s population is at least 80% vaccinated as of October 18, and its hospitalization rate, or number of occupied hospital beds, is lower than Alameda County’s. As of October 18, 87% of ICU beds at Kaiser Foundation Hospital in San Rafael are occupied, and 55% of ICU beds at Marin Health Medical Center in Greenbrae are occupied. For now, Alameda County’s Health Officer Order mandating masking indoors is still in effect. Regardless of vaccination status, residents must wear masks indoors at any public setting, business, government office, and workplaces unless actively eating or drinking. The county’s public health agency also strongly recommends that unvaccinated and not fully-vaccinated individuals wear a mask in outdoor, crowded settings. Staff Photo Alameda County may lift its mandate for masks to be worn at stadiums, businesses, malls, and other crowded indoor venues if it meets hospitalization and vaccination criteria.
articles.title: County to drop mask requirement by Dec. if vaccination, hospitalization criteria met

articles.text: The League of Women Voters will host a virtual town hall style meeting on Thursday, November 4, to describe plans and progress of the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The meeting will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging 3 pools. The current pools were closed permanently on September 8 one year ago. The new pool complex is scheduled to be completed prior to the summer of 2024. The Nov. 4 meeting will include brief presentations from the “city’s team”, to be followed by a question-and-answer session moderated by League of Women Voters President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers include Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register online at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded and can be viewed live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel.
articles.title: Town hall meeting Nov. 4 on Piedmont Pool to be virtual

These goals are aligned with measures in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, which aim to reduce emissions from high global warming potential gases, including those from gas-powered leaf blowers and lawn mowers.” Dykman added that California’s plan to prohibit the sale of new gas-powered leaf blowers, lawn mowers, and other off-road engines further reflects the state’s commitment to providing residents cleaner air and a healthier quality of life, as well as addressing the climate crisis. “The new ban also builds on the Governor’s Executive Order banning the sale of new gas-powered vehicles by 2035. Together, these laws will help accelerate the necessary shift towards electrification, an area Piedmont is familiar with based on its decades long gas-powered leaf blower ban and recently adopted reach codes,” she said. But there are even more sustainable solutions than what the recent legislation offers, said Piedmont Resident and Piedmont Connect member Margaret Ovenden. “I think the real solution is to stop getting rid of leaves in the first place,” she said. “We have this idea that they are messy and don’t belong in our outdoors environment, but having layers of leaves on the ground is actually important for our rapidly decreasing insect populations, as mulch for the soil, etc. Leaf blowing didn’t even become a thing until recent decades. Let the leaves lie where they fall!” “The night cleaning lady has been leaving us some great investment tips.”

articles.text: The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will host a virtual community workshop, “Doing Our Part: Bringing Affordable Housing to Piedmont,” on November 9 cosponsored by the League of Women Voters. The workshop is part of PREC’s ongoing community engagement and education outreach advocating equitable and affordable housing in Piedmont. The workshop will address the City’s Housing Element, part of its General Plan update. A panel of speakers will discuss how the city may be able to meet the state’s housing mandates and the importance of creating affordable housing. The panel will also address how the housing element process can help the Piedmont community achieve greater racial and economic diversity. Speakers include Assembly Buffy Wicks is Piedmont’s elected representative in the State Assembly member Buffy Wicks, Seaside City Council member Jon Wizard, and CEO of the East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation, Andy Madeira, a Piedmont resident. The event will be moderated by PREC member Sarah Karlinsky. The workshop will be held on Zoom and begins at 7 p.m. Register for the event at https://www. piedmontracialequity.org/.
articles.title: Buffy Wicks to speak at PREC workshop on affordable housing

articles.text: All staff members of the Piedmont Police Department will take part in anti-racism equity training over the course of several months following a resolution approved by the City Council last year. On August 2, 2020, city council approved a resolution unequivocally rejecting racism, and committed itself to “examining and owning our City’s history; engaging in community conversations about policing in Piedmont; and careful review of City policies, procedures, ordinances, values, goals, and missions through an anti-racism lens.” The Department has engaged in anti-bias policing practices, implicit bias, and procedural justice prior to the resolution’s adopting. The new training will be uniquely-tailored to the Department and community history, a press release from Piedmont Police Department stated. To achieve this goal, the Department has partnered with Cornelia Sylvester of Bay Area Coaching. Scan to book your estimate!

articles.text: Annie Wensley, Piedmont new Civic Sparks fellow. The City of Piedmont welcomed Annie Wensley as its new Civic Spark Climate Action Fellow on September 20. Wensley will work with the city’s Planning Department on climate action initiatives and other sustainability projects. Wensley graduated from Barnard College of Columbia University in New York City with a Bachelor’s degree in history, with concentrations in political science and women’s leadership studies. Prior to joining Piedmont, she worked as an Americorps Member with the National Park Service’s Student Conservation Association. Wensley was also an organizer for Kamala Harris for the People in 2019, where she recruited, trained and managed over 50 volunteers. Wensley said that the opportunities for public outreach on sustainability matters attracted her to her current position in Piedmont. One of the first tasks was to assist with the city’s free compost giveaway on September 18 at the Corporation Yard. The event was so successful the city is hosting another free giveaway this Saturday. “What I’m passionate about in regards to sustainability and environmental policy are community outreach and engagement, and climate action plan implementation,” she said. “Those two things really drew me to the city.” Wensley added that she wanted to work where there is a strong sense of community. Most recently, she and her family lived in University Place near Seattle. She chose to study at Barnard College in New York City because of its strong environmental policy program but was attracted to Piedmont because of its small size and sense of community. Wensley’s academic and professional background show a connection between environmental and social activism. “An important part of environmental movements is environmental justice, something we focused a lot on during our Civic Spark training. What drew me to [the Fellowship] is that it really focuses on capacity-building and what a Fellow can do in a year – not to just work on projects, but to help an agency like Piedmont’s local government gain the skills needed to move forward with [climate action] projects,” she said. The Civic Spark Fellowship is 11 months in which fellows serve an average of 40 hours per week. Each year, fellows work nationwide on over 100 capacity-building initiatives to help public agencies and local governments equip themselves with the resources to better respond to climate, water, housing, and mobility needs. “We are excited to have Annie on board and eager to continue to work towards our Climate Action goals,” said Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. The Civic Spark Fellowship is 11 months in which fellows serve an average of 40 hours per week. Each year, fellows work nationwide on over 100 capacity-building initiatives to help public agencies and local governments equip themselves with the resources to better respond to climate, water, housing, and mobility needs. “We are excited to have Annie on board and eager to continue to work towards our Climate Action goals,” said Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. modifications, these new plans can be used to quickly obtain Planning Division approvals and streamline the building permit plan review to construct a new ADU. articles.text: Piedmont after-school art instructor Karima Cammell currently has an exhibit, titled “High Water,” at Holton Studio Gallery, 2100 Fifth Street in Berkeley. The exhibit will be on view to the public through November 5, Tuesday through Saturday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Cammell is well known as founder of Castle in the Air on Fourth Street in Berkeley. After closing the store, she has turned to art fulltime. She also is children’s author and illustrator and teaches art classes for young students in Piedmont. Cammell recently returned from Florence, Italy where she studied ancient methods on how to gild glass with gold inlay, called traditional Florentine water gilding. Some of those works are included in the show. “I started pouring through every modern resource you could find and nobody had really seen how it was done in the modern era. I found 2000 years old samples from the Roman era where they sandwich gold between glass. I realized I just had to run experiments all night. If you get the temperature wrong the gold burns off and vanishes,” Cammell explained. For more information, see Holtonframes.com/gallery/highwater-new-works-by-karimacammell/. After-school art programs Cammell teaches art after school at all three elementary Cammell’s piece “Ark:1” uses pigments harvested directly from the earth mixed with egg tempera and 24kt gold on linden board. schools in Piedmont for the last three years. When Covid shut down many art class offerings in other school districts, Cammell continued to teach via Zoom in Piedmont and has returned to in-person classes this fall. With Castle in the Sky artist Ben Yates, Cammell teaches calligraphy, watercolor, and even miniature food sculpture. To see the after-school class offerings Piedmont parents can go to Homeroom.com and search Beach, Havens or Wildwood. Classes underway are: Mondays – Calligraphy at Beach Tuesdays – Watercolor at Havens and Mini-Food Art Sculpting at Wildwood Wednesdays – Watercolor at Beach Thursdays – Calligraphy at Havens Fridays – Watercolor at Wildwood Karima Cammell with some of her paintings.
articles.title: After-school art instructor Karima Cammell opens show in Berkeley

articles.text: The Piedmont Scout office announced this week that Ellen Maloney Ruhe has been named as its new District Executive with responsibility for working with council and unit volunteers to deliver Scout programs to the youth currently in Scouting. “I enjoy the people that non-profits attract,” said Maloney Ruhe. “They are motivated to help and uplift their peers, are inspired to do good work for a common goal, and value equality and diversity in the workplace. I’m looking forward to collaborating with and getting to know the volunteers involved with Piedmont BSA.” “It’s a challenge to find the right person for this position,” explained Scout Executive Kate Benson. “It requires someone who enjoys working with people, is organized, and really understands the mission of helping youth develop. We’re excited to bring Ellen on board.” Maloney Ruhe brings a depth of skills and experience, with a background in volunteer coordination, development, and theater management and production. She enjoys live theater, live music, museums, and stand-up comedy; she also collects comic books and is an avid reader in general. The Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America serves over 700 youth annually in programs built to develop character, fitness, citizenship and leadership Ellen Maloney Ruhe recently was hired as Piedmont Scout Council’s new District Executive. through outdoor adventures and fun activities. Cub Scouts serves boys and girls in grade school. Scouts BSA serves boys and girls in middle school and high school, and is most known for the Scouts who advance to the rank of Eagle. Venturing serves young men and women age 14-20, and has programs focusing on community service and high adventure. Exploring also serves young men and women age 14-20 with a local post chartered by the Piedmont Police Department. For more information about Scout programs, visit www.piedmontbsa.org, or call the Scout office at 510-547-4493.
articles.title: Piedmont Scouts name Ellen Maloney Ruhe as new District Executive

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: Troop 15 Scouts trekking toward Manzanita Point on Saturday morning. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 spent the weekend of October 16-17 camping out in 87,000-acre Henry Coe State Park, which straddles Santa Clara and Stanislaus Counties. The terrain is mostly rolling hills with oak, madrone and ponderosa pine “This event was an opportunity for scouts new to Troop 15 to get a taste of backpacking, visit with friends, learn some knots and go on a hike at night in the moonlight”, said Nate Woodley, a 5th-year scout. “We saw deer, ground squirrels, woodpeckers and a tarantula. We slept without tents, so we got to view the stars, planets and some meteors.” Each patrol cooked their meals using ingredients that require no refrigeration, although the use of fresh vegetables was encouraged. This prepares scouts for what they will cook daily on week-long backpacking trips offered every Three scouts rose at dawn on Sunday and hiked with their fishing gear a half mile to Bass Pond. “There was a wild boar on the other side of the pond, but it walked off when we approached”, said 6th-year scout Aidan Weiss. The Oak Branch Gang, Gianni Richmond (left), Ryan Wendel, Thalay Visessonchoke, and Thomas Ero, head back to camp after lunch. Panda Patrol members Zade McDonald (left), Enzo Dehlengiulio, Phoenix Ehrhart Mount, Ben Rogers and Ben Wilson greet the dawn. Troop 15 Scouts Christiane Zuber (left) and Willa Clendenning enjoy a lunch break along the trail. Abigail Taylor Collins (left), Samantha Taylor Collins and Willa Clendenning learn knot-tying from Assistant Scoutmaster Eric Downing. Life Scout Aidan Weiss displays a bass he caught using a lure as bait before releasing it back into drought-ravaged Bass Pond. A new scout got the notion to fashion a bow-and-arrow using a string and knife. Scouts form a circle after a night hike under the light of a waxing moon, Jupiter and Saturn, acknowledging whom and what they appreciated regarding the campout.

articles.text: The Piedmont boys’ water polo team easily won back-toback matches last week, defeating San Leandro 17-10 on Tuesday, October 12, and beating Alhambra 15-7 in Martinez on Friday, October 15. The pair of wins pushes their record to 14-3 as they head into the first round of the league tournament next Tuesday, October 26. The league finals will be played on Saturday, October 30. Sophomore Peter Krumins had a huge week with six goals against Alhambra and five against San Leandro. He continues to be a standout first-year varsity player. Senior captain Antonio Rivera, meanwhile, scored three goals and four assists against San Leandro and put in another two against Alhambra. 17-10 win vs. San Leandro Piedmont came out strong in the first quarter to lead 6-1 and jumped to a 10-6 by halftime. In the third quarter, the Highlanders’ defense held strong to extend the advantage 12-6. PHS added five goals in the fourth, 17-10. Griffin Stein scored the game’s opening goal after 30 seconds while Krumins got his first with 4:54 left in the opening period. A Rivera goal made it 3-1 with 3:26 on the clock, and Krumins scored on a penalty shot with 1:36 left. Rivera made it 5-1 with a minute left, while George Stein extended the lead to 6-1 with a heave with 2 seconds on the clock. But the Pirates stunned the Highlanders by powering back to tie the game at 6-6 with 2:47 left in the first half. Piedmont responded with four unanswered goals; Krumins rocketed one in with 2:40 to go, followed by George Stein’s second goal after 21 seconds, 8-6. Krumins added an insurance goal with 1:39 left, and Rivera closed out the first al scoring on a penalty shot with 34 seconds left. In the third quarter, Piedmont turned up the defensive pressure and allowed no goals by the Pirates, They took a 12-6 lead on goals by Rivera and Stein. In the fourth quarter, PHS scored five more goals, and allowed four by San Leandro. Declan Linnane scored after 20 seconds, and made the game 14-7 with 6:11 to go. Shane Miller scored with 5:24 remaining, then Rivera made it 16-8 with 4:59 on the clock. While Griffin Stein scored the final goal of the game, 17-10, with 30 seconds remaining. Final stats: Krumins scored five goals; Rivera had three goals, four assists, and two steals; George Stein had three goals and a steal; Griffin Stein had two goals; Linnane had two goals, one assist, and two steals. Miller had one goal. Photos by Nancy Brahm Peter Krumins scored six goals against Alhambra and five against San Leandro.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boy’ cross-country team ran away with a victory at the Rough Rider Invitational meet in Fresno last Saturday at Woodward Park, the course where the State meet is held in November. Jack Stein led the team with a sixth-place overall finish in a field of 234 runners. Piedmont’s team placed first of 27 teams in the Small School category. The girls were sixth of 17 teams. The Highlanders beat out predominantly Central Coast and Southern Section schools. Oakdale was second and Menlo, from the Central Coast Section, was third. Only one other North Coast Section school. Miramonte was eighth and will be a Division 4 opponent for PHS at the North Jack Stein placed sixth of 234 runners at the Rough Rider Invitational with a time of 16:40.2. Coast Section championships. Piedmont’s Jack Stein placed sixth of 234 runners with a time of 16:40.2. It marked his first time running the Woodward Park course since his sophomore year in 2019 at the Asics Clovis Invitational, improving his time by nearly three minutes from 19:36.2. Behind Stein, the Purple Train was rolling with sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse placing 11th with a time of 17:03.7. Showing strong pack running, junior Parker Long was 16th (17:23.1), senior Cooper Downing was 18th (17:26.7), and junior Christian Taylor was 20th (17:29.8). Long and Taylor dramatically improved their times since the 2019 Asics Invitational. Long lowered his time 1 minute, 30 seconds, and Taylor had a 5 minute, 30 second improvement. “The game plan was to stick together as much as possible in a large field for the overall win, and they got it done,” said a proud coach Jeanine Holmlund. articles.text: The Highlanders all matches against Mt. Eden last Tuesday, October 12 to win 7-0 at the Corey Reich Tennis Courts. The win improves the team’s record to 14-7 this season with three matches left on the schedule before the start of the WACC Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6. The girls’ tennis team was won six straight matches since narrowly losing 4-3 to Berkeley on September 23. Piedmont will wrap up its season against the Yellowjackets on October 28, a fitting finale at the Berkeley Tennis Club. “We’re rolling along. Everyone is playing sharp. Against Mt. Eden, we could move some players around and get people time. Laurel [Bentley] and Ruby [Guzdar] got their first starts and dominated,” said coach Jim Landes. Against the weaker team from Hayward, Michaela Bini was able to bump up from her usual No. 3 spot up to No. 1, and double-bagled her opponent 6-0, 6-0. “Michaela showed her usual consistently strong forehands,” said Landes. At No. 2 freshman Emma Eisemon continuing her impressive debut season o varsity with a 6-0, 6-1 win. Her usual teammate at doubles, sophomore Cecilia Defazio, won 6-0, 6-2, and at No. 4 singles, Sofia Ferraro won handily, 6-0, 6-1. “Emma is a young, talented player who is really good in front of the net. We’re excited about her future,” said Landes. In doubles, Mara LaForte and Anika Gilliland scorched the Monarchs’ top doubles team, 6-0 6-0. Photos by Brian Mahany Michael Bini won at No. 1 singles against Mt. Eden. “Anika has played better and better throughout the year. articles.text: Piedmont Homecoming game this Friday vs. O’Dowd Playing in Alameda on Friday, October 15, the Highlanders came up one touchdown short against the Encinal Jets, 34-28 loss. “It’s always the little things; maybe missing keys or some confusion in calling the correct play we sent in, or balls over the top just unable to knock them down. If we execute on those one or two little plays, they change the game. We are always right at the door, we just need to kick it open,” said Piedmont football coach Jerome Johnson. The Highlanders were able to keep the game deadlocked 14-14 at halftime, but allowed 20 points in the third quarter and trailed 34-21 heading into the last quarter. Piedmont’s final touchdown came with 1:38 left in the game, leading to an onside kick attempt to try to regain possession. Despite the loss, receiver Nico Defazio had another big game with 192 total yards of offense, 130 on pass receptions, including two touchdowns, and 62 yards rushing. Senior quarterback Adhi Bornstein completed 13 of 27 passes for three touchdowns. He was also intercepted three times in the second varsity start of his high school career. Playing cornerback on defense, he intercepted an Encinal pass. Game Recap Piedmont gave up a fumble on the opening possession at their own 35-yard line, resulting in a 65 yard touchdown run on Encinal’s first possession. But Piedmont responded quickly with a long offensive possession that ended with a 30-yard pass over the middle to Defazio in the end zone. He leaped over his defender to make the catch with seven minutes left in the first quarter. Piedmont’s defense did well to force a three-and-out on Encinal’s next possession and began at their own 44-yard line. However, a quarterback sack and fumble on the first play put the Jets in position to go ahead. PHS was able to force a 4th-and-10 for Encinal from the 28, but the Jets scored on a pass for a 14-7 lead with 3:14 left in the first quarter. Defazio returned the kickoff 20 yards to the PHS 48-yard line. The Highlanders worked the ball to the Jets’ 45 when Bornstein connected on a bomb to Ryan McConathy for the touchdown to tie Encinal 14-14. PHS forced a punt on Encinal’s next possession, but the Jets intercepted Piedmont at the Highlanders’ 32 yard line with 7:46 left in the second quarter. Piedmont’s defense stood stout, preventing Encinal from converting a 4th-and-6 at the 18-yard-line with 5:30 to go. The score remained tied at 14-14 at halftime. Nina Goldberg made an onside kick late in the game with Encinal on October 15. Photo by Mike McConathy Nico Defazio (8) reels in a touchdown reception against Encinal.

articles.text: The JV Highlanders had their strongest game of the season on Friday, October 15, crushing the Encinal Jets 39-6 in Alameda. Receiver Sam Shelby led the way with four touchdowns. Quarterback Marcos Lagios returned to the starting lineup after missing time. Encinal opened the game with a kickoff return for a touchdown, but it was its only score in the game. “It was nice to have Marcos back. We knew he was going to be ready, so we really wanted to let it rip. Encinal scored on the opening kickoff and that was it. We shut them down [after that],” said offensive coordinator Bradley Smet. Piedmont answered quickly on its first possession. Starting at the 30-yard line, the Scots scored on its first play from scrimmage by speedy receiver Sam Shelby, who scored on a 70-yard pass play. An extra point by Shelby made the score 7-6. On the Jets’ next possession, Piedmont’s Brandon Dicke recovered a fumble at Encinal’s 20-yard line, setting up running back Tommy Ashton for a shortyard touchdown run to put PHS ahead 13-6. Piedmont’s defense then forced a turnover on Encinal’s next possession when Cash Elmquist hurried the quarterback into an bad pass. Jordan Alemania intercepted the ball near the Jets’ end zone. It took just one play for quarterback Lagios to find Shelby on a touchdown pass and a 20-6 lead. Shelby scored twice more to guarantee a big win for the Scots. Piedmont‘s final points were scored with four minutes left in the game for the 39-6 final. NEXT UP Piedmont plays Bishop O’Dowd this Friday, October 22 at 4:30 p.m. at Witter Field for Piedmont’s Homecoming game. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team dominated with a 15-3 win at San Leandro last Tuesday, October 12. The team honored its three seniors on the roster after the match, Frankie Broening, F.K. Meagher, and Elizabeth Ethington. “I love these girls so much,” said coach Sarah Mooney, a Piedmont alum. “Our seniors are our emotional leaders and do so much for the team. Elizabeth is our rock,” she added. The Highlanders finished with 11 players scoring at least one goal. Ethington, the team’s goalie, had eight saves. “We played strong defense and passed the ball really well,” said Mooney. Annika Nillson quickly got Piedmont on the board on a 6-on-5 advantage 25 seconds into the match, following by Rosie Feldman netting one 18 seconds later for a 2-0 lead. Piedmont turned a steal by Madeline Payne for a goal by hole set Macie Gard after another 27 seconds on a feed by Odessa Dando, making it 3-0 after just a F.K. Meagher (5) sends a shot at San Leandro’s goal. Piedmont honored its three seniors on Oct. 12 at San Leandro, Frankie Broening (left), Elizabeth Ethington, and F.K. Meagher. minute and 10 seconds of action. Dando scored Piedmont’s next goal with 5:26 remaining, followed by Broening getting on the board after about 30 seconds. Ethington had a big save with 4:35 remaining with San Leandro holding a man-advantage, helping bring her team back to even strength. Feldman then scored with 3:10 remaining in the quarter After subbing into the game, Kate Meyes made it 7-0 with 0:57 remaining in first quarter after Anne Reardon made the assist. Meyes scored again, with 23 second left to go and an 8-0 lead to end the first quarter. In the second quarter, Sonja ten Grotenhuis scored with 5:28 to go after Meagher sent in a pass. Meagher then scored with 4:41 left in the half to make it 10-0. Reardon made it 11-0 after another 50 seconds on an assist from Broening. With 2:10 before halftime, Ethington stopped her second 6-on-5 opportunity for San Leandro by making another athletic save. However, the Pirates finally got on the board with 1:18 left, then scored again with 43 seconds on the clock. Reardon answered quickly for PHS with 20 seconds left, making it 12-2. In the third, Ethington stopped a penalty shot after a minute and 30 seconds, which led to Julia Montes leading a fast break down the pool for the 13-2 goal. After back and forth action, Payne made it 14-2 with 47 seconds left in the quarter on an assist from Dando. The fourth quarter had limited action with substitutes in the game. PHS scored its final goal with Broening with 1:02 remaining in the game. San Leandro put one in with 53 seconds left. Final stats: Feldman, Reardon, and Meyes each had two goals. Broening also had two goals and an assist. Individual goals were scored by Nillson, Gard, Dando, ten Grotenhuis, Meagher, Montes, and Payne. articles.text: Filoli terrace lights Filoli House and Garden in Woodside announced on October 6 a compensation structure based on the living wage for San Mateo County residents. Filoli’s new compensation plan for all employees, included in its 2019-2023 strategic plan, is based on a model created in 2004 by Dr. Amy Glasmeier of M.I.T. According to the calculations, the living wage in San Mateo County is $28 per hour for fulltime employees. Filoli, a nonprofit, cited the lack of a true, geographically-specific living wage information, and the fact that San Mateo County is the third most expensive place to live in America. “It’s an ethical imperative,” Filoli CEO Kara Newport said. “If we want to attract and retain a diverse staff reflective of our community, we have to pay a living wage. The Filoli experience is dependent on people, so the quality of employees matters.” Newport stated that Filoli cannot be equitable in practice without regional pay equity. In February, Filoli launched a Diversity, Equity, Accessibility and Inclusion (DEAI) Policy and Action Plan centered around the importance of investing in its employees. President of the Board David Wollenberg explained that Filoli has “a staff of over 60 people… and we want to keep them all.” The cost of living adjustment follows a series of benefits the nonprofit added in recent years, which included doubling the organization’s employee 401k match, adding additional holidays and personal time off, a sabbatical program, and education reimbursement.
articles.title: Filoli announces Living Wage Program for all full-time employees

articles.text: Concerts and other arts-related events will take place October The San Francisco Interna- 20-24. tional Arts Festival begins today at Fort Mason in San Francisco. The Festival’s mission is to embody the microcosm of the Bay Area’s vibrant artist community by providing multicultural performances. Guests may purchase a “create your own” festival pass that allows them to visit two to eight shows over the next five days. A range of artistic mediums will be represented, including dance, music, performance art, and theater; digital options and online passes are available as well. The festival’s lineup includes Mix’d Ingrdnts Dance Company, Sha Sha Higby, a pop-up theatre in the Great Meadow, a poetry showcase, Left Coast Chamber Ensemble, Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, among others. To see the full lineup and for tickets visit https://www.sfiaf.org/ calendar_sfiaf2021. San Francisco International Arts Festival begins today at Fort Mason.
articles.title: SF International Arts Festival begins today at Fort Mason for 5 days

articles.text: Legion of Honor, one of the two Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, opened an exhibit on October 9 entitled “Color into Line: Pastels from the Renaissance to the Present”. The exhibit will be on display through February 13, 2022. “Color into Line” displays 80 masterpieces from the Renaissance era and modern-day created with pastels. Featured artists include Edgar Degas, Diego Rivera, John Altoon, Wayne Thiebaud and Joan Mitchell, as well as rarely displayed artworks spanning from the Renaissance to present day. The exhibition draws from the Fine Arts Museums’ own holdings in the Achenbach San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum Foundation for Graphic Arts, as well as selected loans from local private collections. Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://legionof honor. famsf.org/exhibitions/pastels.
articles.title: Legion of Honor exhibition “Color Into Line” now on display

articles.text: Kazuo Miyagawa films to be shown Oct. 23 to Nov. 28 The Pacific Film Archive located on the UC Berkeley campus, will showcase the work of celebrated Japanese cinematographer Kazuo Miyagawa in a film series open to the public from October 23 to November 28. a young filmmaker,” recalled Susan Oxtoby, Director of Film and Senior Film Curator. “A firm believer in filmmaking as a collaborative art form, Miyagawa felt it worked best when a director allowed space for a cinematographer or actors to bring their own creativity to the interpretation of the script.” To purchase tickets for screenings and to see the list of films being offered, visit https:// bampfa.org/program/kazuo-miyagawa-cinematographer-and-visual-stylist. Miyagawa (1908-1999) is the visual stylist behind classics directed by Akira Kurosawa, Kenji Mizoguchi, and Koa Ichikawa, among others. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, October 20, 2021 Arts & Entertainment Filoli announces Living Wage Program for all full-time employees SF International Arts Festival begins today at Fort Mason for 5 days By Allyson Aleksey Concerts and other arts-related events will take place October The San Francisco Interna- 20-24. tional Arts Festival begins today at Fort Mason in San Francisco. The Festival’s mission is to embody the microcosm of the Bay Area’s vibrant artist community by providing multicultural performances. Guests may purchase a “create your own” festival pass that allows them to visit two to eight shows over the next five days. A range of artistic mediums will be represented, including dance, music, performance art, and theater; digital options and online passes are available as well. The festival’s lineup includes Mix’d Ingrdnts Dance Company, Sha Sha Higby, a pop-up theatre in the Great Meadow, a poetry showcase, Left Coast Chamber Ensemble, Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, among others. To see the full lineup and for tickets visit https://www.sfiaf.org/ calendar_sfiaf2021. Filoli terrace lights By Allyson Aleksey Filoli House and Garden in Woodside announced on October 6 a compensation structure based on the living wage for San Mateo County residents. Filoli’s new compensation plan for all employees, included in its 2019-2023 strategic plan, is based on a model created in 2004 by Dr. Amy Glasmeier of M.I.T. According to the calculations, the living wage in San Mateo County is $28 per hour for fulltime employees. Filoli, a nonprofit, cited the lack of a true, geographically-specific living wage information, and the fact that San Mateo County is the third most expensive place to live in America. “It’s an ethical imperative,” Filoli CEO Kara Newport said. “If we want to attract and retain a diverse staff reflective of our community, we have to pay a living wage. The Filoli experience is dependent on people, so the quality of employees matters.” Newport stated that Filoli cannot be equitable in practice without regional pay equity. In February, Filoli launched a Diversity, Equity, Accessibility and Inclusion (DEAI) Policy and Action Plan centered around the importance of investing in its employees. President of the Board David Wollenberg explained that Filoli has “a staff of over 60 people… and we want to keep them all.” The cost of living adjustment follows a series of benefits the nonprofit added in recent years, which included doubling the organization’s employee 401k match, adding additional holidays and personal time off, a sabbatical program, and education reimbursement. articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes Angelique Kidjo as the organization’s first season-long artist-in-residence. She will perform her unique take on the Talking Head’s 1980 album Remain in Light on Friday, October 29 at Zellerbach Hall. “One of the great pleasures this season is welcoming Angélique Kidjo, who hasn’t appeared here in nearly a decade, back to Berkeley as our first season-long artist-in-residence,” said Jeremy Geffen, Cal Performances Artistic Director. “Having been a presenter, collaborator and fan of her work for years, I know firsthand of her passion, conviction, and boundless curiosity. She brings inextinguishable energy—more so than most of her more junior colleagues, actually—to bear in both her performances and her community outreach work.” Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and was recently named one of Time Magazine’s “100 most influential people of 2021” for her work in the arts and as a cultural ambassador. The artist fled a dictatorship in her home country of Benin and draws from ,, her personal experiences when creating music. Kidjo’s latest recording, Mother Nature, was released earlier this year and incorporates West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. “Angélique draws from her personal experiences a deep sense of conviction as well as profound passion for exploring the breadth and depth of the human experience—qualities that make her the perfect partner for our season-long Illuminations programming. And most importantly, she comes to our campus hoping to learn as much as to share,” Geffen said. “By inviting her to meet with faculty and students, Cal Performances reinforces and supports the university’s values of cultivating and sustaining a diverse, equitable, informed, and inclusive and accessible community.” The concert begins at 8 p.m. on Friday, October 29 in Zellerbach Hall on the University of California campus. Tickets are $36 to $96. Half-price tickets are available for UC Berkeley students. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, at calperformances. org, and at the door. Proof of a COVID-19 vaccination is required for entry. Grammy Award-winner Angelique Kidjo returns to Cal Performances on October 29.

articles.text: San Leandro Players will present Ken Ludwig’s The Game’s Afoot; or Holmes for the Holidays on weekends from October 23 to November 21. The show will be directed by Bruce Kaplan. In December 1936 Broadway star William Gillette, admired the world over for his leading role in the play Sherlock Holmes, has invited his fellow cast members to his Connecticut home for a weekend of revelry. But when one of the guests is stabbed to death, the festivities in this isolated fun-palace of tricks and mirrors quickly turn dangerous, not to mention hilarious. Then it’s up to Gillette, assuming the persona of Holmes, to track down the killer before the next victim succumbs. The danger and hilarity are non-stop in this glittering whodunit set during the Christmas holidays. The cast includes Paul Pedersen, Rob Mueller, Laura Zimmerman, Kenneth Matis, Marsha Van Broek, Lisa Wang, Terry Guillory, and Piedmont resident Maya Rath. Performances are on Saturdays at 8 p.m. and Sundays at 2 p.m. from October 23 to November 21 at the San Leandro Museum and Auditorium, 320 West Estudillo Ave, San Leandro. Tickets are $20 General, and $15 for seniors and children under 12. For reservations call (510) 895- 2573, or order online at: www.

articles.text: Thomas (Blind Tom) Higgins was a prodigy. a virtuosic pianist, gifted composer, and one of the most in-demand musicians of his time in America. The most sensational career in recent memory began in 1958 when American pianist Van Cliburn won the first Tchaikovsky competition in Moscow. Remember that this was the height of the Cold War. The Russian judges did not know what to do, so they asked premier Nikita Khrushchev. All Khrushchev asked was: “Is he the best?” The judges said he was. Khrushchev said: “Give him first prize.” Another sensational career was begun when Leonard Bernstein substituted for an ailing conductor for a concert in Carnegie Hall. The rest, as they say, is history. Any violinist who won first prize at the Paris Conservatory was guaranteed an international career. Pablo de Sarasate was only one of many. And then there was the career of a pianist named Thomas Wiggins. His biography reads like the most sensational Hollywood movie. Thomas was born into slavery in 1849. He was also born blind. What I’m going to tell you might sound very strange, but his blindness turned out to be something of a blessing. Wiggins gained fame if not fortune as “Blind Tom”. Since he was born blind, he was unable to work in any capacity. He heard music in his youngest years and soon was playing the piano in an extraordinary manner. The little kid would hear any tune and play it back perfectly. Not long after this, he became the property of a certain General Bethune. The Civil War ended that situation, but the general envisioned a great financial future in “Blind Tom”. The general was a great promoter and marketed Blind Tom as the “genius of the age”. Remember that Blind Tom could play just about any tune he heard. The publicity ranged from genius to savant. It didn’t really matter to the general what the publicity said as long as he made money. And Blind Tom was a very marketable quantity. The amount of money he reportedly made was staggering. It also seems that the general, was an exploiter of the first order. How much money was passed on to Wiggins is debatable. One may assume that Tom was given a pittance. But how good was Blind Tom as a musician? They say that he composed some 7000 pieces, an unprecedented number. After listening to a few of his pieces, I discovered that they range from the exquisitely beautiful to bombastic. Once again, I ask you not to jump to conclusions. One of his compositions is entitled the “Battle of Manassas.” It is somewhat akin to Louis Moreau Gottschalk’s famous composition “The Union”. Blind Tom probably had never heard Gottschalk play the piano, and his composition is innovative in the extreme. Other people wrote battle music, so why not “The Battle of Manassas” by Blind Tom? It amazes me how he could even conceive a piece like this. How did he even learn about the sounds of battle? All of this was of great interest to me. I have never had the opportunity of hearing any music by this historical figure. But the ever-enterprising pianist Carl Blake performed two of Thomas Wiggins’ piano pieces on Sunday in San Francisco. He chose “Oliver Gallop” and “Reve Charmant”. Both pieces are thoroughly American and combine the pianistic panache of Gottschalk tempered with the melodic touch of Verdi. Carl Blake played these pieces with uncommon sensitivity and a beautiful tone. Maybe next time he will play “The Battle of Manassas”. To some Blind Tom was a heavily marketed curiosity; a savant of extraordinary dimensions who made a fortune for his exploiter… er …manager. I prefer to think of Thomas Wiggins as a fascinating talent. In many ways he was like the immortal jazz pianist Art Tatum, who was nearly blind. And that ain’t bad.
articles.title: Paths to fame

articles.text: Sound out the trumpets, Beethoven is back in operatown! They did right by Beethoven at the S.F. Opera, staging his only (and foresightedly heroic) opera Fidelio nearly a year after his 250th birthday, with Covid19 acting as the black-hat hold-up man at the War Memorial Opera House. If the performance was a bit spotty, no matter. The key word was revolutionary, his message of freedom and individuals bucking repression and suppression by corrupt authorities. And how revolutionary it was in 1805 to have a woman disguising herself as a man and prison guard to do the heroic deed, freeing the political prisoner Florestan, opera’s first great freedom fighter, at great personal risk. Their also being married leads to expressions of love and a grand public celebration in the finale’s music, foreshadowing the epic “Ode to Joy” still locked up for years in the mind and quill of the ill-fated composer Ludwig van Beethoven, who became stone deaf early on and left us at age 55. Given all the political prisoners around the world in today’s news, this opera is more than relevant. The opera showed the composer in transition, starting off with a traditional, low-key German Singspiel work (related to the mode of Mozart’s Magic Flute) and erupting in huge vocal outpourings and high drama of the future, with its passion bleeding into the rich score. It’s as if the last act were written some decades after the first. If you were expecting huge Wagnerian voices again in the two leads the other night, recall that when this opera appeared, Wagnerian voices were not yet cultivated and Richard Wagner himself not yet born. Slow starting, soprano Elsa van den Heever was effective and vibrantly hall-filling in the final scenes as Leonore, the opera’s main character (called Fidelio in her male guard’s disguise). The low male voices were admirable, from Greer Grimsley’s Pizarro to Soloman Howard’s Fernando to James Creswell’s Rocco. The best German of the night in the spoken passages came from Grimsley and Creswell. The supertitle translations softened the text, changing Rocco’s “Gold” aria dripping with greed to a mild discourse on the importance of money in this world. Tenor Russell Thomas’ Florestan fared best in the ensembles. He was hampered by his confinement, in a lower-depths dungeon, seated in a golden chair worthy for a monarch. Tilt! Overall, conductor Eun Sun Kim’s best moments came in leading the various trios and quartets by the principals as well as in holding together the massed crowds of the finale. Notable was how her orchestra brought out the surge within Pizarro’s arietta (act two, scene one), where similarities had you swearing that Beethoven was extremely familiar with the hell-scene finale of Mozart’s Don Giovanni. Kim’s keeping the orchestra and singers in sync worked intermittently. More control over the brass section and a bit more rehearsal would have been welcome. If you like contemporary production with modern structures, TVs and cell phones, this is your show, with the two-story rotating set by Alexander V. Nichols clearly the big attention-getter. Some corners had been cut out of pandemic necessity, where the warehouse-like structure hardly suggested a dungeon nor the depths for digging Florestan’s intended grave. Also cut in part was some of the dated dialogue, but uncut was the curiously bifurcated Beethoven score, a unique gem handed down, as Fidelio was his only such venture. Opera fans were already regretting the impending 2022 retirement of Choral Director Ian Robertson, who shaped the awe-inspired (Male) Prisoners Chorus in act one and the augmented fortissimo mixed chorus of the finale. Matthew Ozawa served as Stage Director. MUSIC NOTES Audiences were still euphoric about the resumption of an indoor opera season, after Tosca and Fidelio, both assembled under rather arduous conditions of pandemic which, among other things, inhibited importing foreign singers because of constantly varying Covid regulations everywhere… After Gustav Mahler’s innovation, countless theaters inserted the great “Leonore Overture No. 3” and played it between the last two scenes while stagehands laboriously converted from dungeon to open-air mass celebration. No such interpolation here, because the scene change is instantaneous (i.e., no curtain) with the rotating set…. The message of Fidelio is viewed as highly symbolic around the world; it was chosen to reopen major theaters in Vienna and Budapest in the past century after times of deprivation. Concurrent with the opera, reactivation has reopened the Ira Brilliant Center for Beethoven Studies at San Jose State University Wednesday to Friday afternoons. It has the largest music collection of Beethoven first editions anywhere outside of Germany. Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, in German with supertitle translations by San Francisco Opera. Two acts, one intermission, 2.5 hours. Performing October 14-30 at War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco. Masks and Vaxx required for all. For info: (415) 864-3330 or go online. www.sfopera.com
articles.title: Beethoven opera, held up

Their also being married leads to expressions of love and a grand public celebration in the finale’s music, foreshadowing the epic “Ode to Joy” still locked up for years in the mind and quill of the ill-fated composer Ludwig van Beethoven, who became stone deaf early on and left us at age 55. Given all the political prisoners around the world in today’s news, this opera is more than relevant. The opera showed the composer in transition, starting off with a traditional, low-key German Singspiel work (related to the mode of Mozart’s Magic Flute) and erupting in huge vocal outpourings and high drama of the future, with its passion bleeding into the rich score. It’s as if the last act were written some decades after the first. If you were expecting huge Wagnerian voices again in the two leads the other night, recall that when this opera appeared, Wagnerian voices were not yet cultivated and Richard Wagner himself not yet born. Slow starting, soprano Elsa van den Heever was effective and vibrantly hall-filling in the final Beethoven opera, held up scenes as Leonore, the opera’s main character (called Fidelio in her male guard’s disguise). The low male voices were admirable, from Greer Grimsley’s Pizarro to Soloman Howard’s Fernando to James Creswell’s Rocco. The best German of the night in the spoken passages came from Grimsley and Creswell. The supertitle translations softened the text, changing Rocco’s “Gold” aria dripping with greed to a mild discourse on the importance of money in this world. Tenor Russell Thomas’ Florestan fared best in the ensembles. He was hampered by his confinement, in a lower-depths dungeon, seated in a golden chair worthy for a monarch. Tilt! Overall, conductor Eun Sun Kim’s best moments came in leading the various trios and quartets by the principals as well as in holding together the massed crowds of the finale. Notable was how her orchestra brought out the surge within Pizarro’s arietta (act two, scene one), where similarities had you swearing that Beethoven was extremely familiar with the hell-scene finale of Mozart’s Don Giovanni. Kim’s keeping the orchestra and singers in sync worked intermittently. More control over the brass section and a bit more rehearsal would have been welcome. If you like contemporary production with modern structures, TVs and cell phones, this is your show, with the two-story rotating set by Alexander V. Nichols clearly the big attention-getter. Some corners had been cut out of pandemic necessity, where the warehouse-like structure hardly suggested a dungeon nor the depths for digging Florestan’s intended grave. Also cut in part was some of the dated dialogue, but uncut was the curiously bifurcated Beethoven score, a unique gem handed down, as Fidelio was his only such venture. Opera fans were already regretting the impending 2022 retirement of Choral Director Ian Robertson, who shaped the awe-inspired (Male) Prisoners Chorus in act one and the augmented fortissimo mixed chorus of the finale. Matthew Ozawa served as Stage Director. MUSIC NOTES Audiences were still euphoric about the resumption of an indoor opera season, after Tosca and Fidelio, both assembled under rather arduous conditions of pandemic which, among other things, inhibited importing foreign singers because of constantly varying Covid regulations everywhere… After Gustav Mahler’s innovation, countless theaters inserted the great “Leonore Overture No. 3” and played it between the last two scenes while stagehands laboriously converted from dungeon to open-air mass celebration. No such interpolation here, because the scene change is instantaneous (i.e., no curtain) with the rotating set…. The message of Fidelio is viewed as highly symbolic around the world; it was chosen to reopen major theaters in Vienna and Budapest in the past century after times of deprivation. Concurrent with the opera, reactivation has reopened the Ira Brilliant Center for Beethoven Studies at San Jose State University Wednesday to Friday afternoons. It has the largest music collection of Beethoven first editions anywhere outside of Germany. Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, in German with supertitle translations by San Francisco Opera. Two acts, one intermission, 2.5 hours. Performing October 14-30 at War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco. Masks and Vaxx required for all.
