articles.text: Lucas Hedges, Shia LaBeouf and Noah Jupe (front) star in Honey Boy. Honey Boy is a raw, gritty, semi-autobiographical film, written by Shia LaBeouf and revealing a period in his life when he was living in a seedy L.A. motel with his father, who he names James Lort (LaBeouf). His two alter-ego characters are 12-year-old Otis (Noah Jupe), a child actor, and the twenty-something, Otis (Chris Hedges) who has become a self-destructive movie star ordered into rehab by a judge. It’s in rehab, during sessions with a therapist, that Otis tells his story in a series of long flashbacks. The year is 1995. James is not so much a father as a man locked in perpetual battle with his own demons, while young Otis struggles to avoid becoming collateral damage. James – an alcoholic, ex-con, veteran, and former rodeo clown – riffs and rants and rages, his verbal abuse of Otis on occasion turns physical. Their interaction pretty much takes place in the confines of their motel room, usually before James takes Otis to the set on his motorcycle or in the evening when they have returned to their claustrophobic room. James is ostensibly managing Otis’ career as a child star acting in B-movies. And while Otis is on set, James attends AA meetings, veterans therapy groups, or plants rows of marijuana along a nearby freeway. Their dysfunctional relationship is that of father and son; however, it’s also one in which the son assumes the role of the reasonable adult and the father becomes the unreasonable child. There are times when Otis hates his father, the man who has exposed him to alcohol, weed, and cigarettes, seems to relish denigrating him while demeaning the size of his pre-adolescent penis. He meets and then tosses Otis’ Big Brother/mentor into the motel pool. He often rides off on his Harley, leaving Otis to spend long nights fending for himself. But then Otis also loves his father, craves his attention, and wants above all to be wrapped in his arms and protected. Regardless, James seems only intent on transferring to Otis – a lonely, precocious boy – the gnarled and twisted damage likely visited upon him. Honey Boy is not a vanity project by LaBeouf; rather, it’s a bleak, personal psychological dive into a complex relationship that haunts both father and son. If James is addicted to rage and chaos (now that he’s no longer drinking), Otis is addicted to his need to be loved by this tortured man. The performances of all three actors (LaBeouf, Jupe and Hedges) are astonishingly good, as is this strangely named film, Honey Boy. Honey Boy. Directed by Alma Har’el. Starring Shia LaBeouf, Lucas Hedges and Noah Jupe. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Honey Boy a gritty story with top-notch acting

articles.text: The White Ribbon, is a German film nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, and winner of the top prize (Palm d’Or) at Cannes. Directed by Michael Haneke (Cache).It is artful, superbly cast, and beautifully photographed in stark black and white. The year is 1913, on the cusp of World War I. The film opens with a lovely shot of farmers and villagers harvesting the summer wheat, followed by a celebration heralding the end of one season and the beginning of another. It’s tempting to romanticize this bucolic setting, a small town surrounded by the flat expanse of rural northern Germany, filled with hardworking people whose lives follow the rhythms of the land. But then Haneke grimly pulls back a curtain and reveals that behind this seemingly benign image is a bleak and cruel reality that is astonishing in its severity. There is no overt violence in the film except for a set piece in the first minutes when a doctor, riding home on his horse, is brought down by an all but invisible trip wire. At first the incident, called an accident, seems an aberration. But then other events take place of equal premeditation, testimony to the fact that a malevolent and mysterious perpetrator resides in the village. Though these chilling acts of violence are linchpins throughout the film, what is far more disturbing is the authoritarian, patriarchal cruelty leveled against the village’s children. The adults, charged with loving them, are so consistently perverse in their anger and punishments that it’s as if we’re watching and exorcism of their childhood innocence and innate empathy, carried out with an endemic ignorance and righteousness and malice that is disturbing to watch. The village Pastor, blinded by his own narrow Protestantism, in a particularly unsettling scene ties white ribbons around the arms of his children as reminders that they have violated his trust, betrayed their purity, and disappointed their parents. He will not remove the ribbons until they have demonstrated that they are pure once again. The ribbons torment the children and are reminders of the hypocrisy and heartlessness of those adults to whom the children look for protection and, yes, love. The f ilm also answers Haneke’s own question: is the heart of man inherently dark, absent any overriding humanity that will act as a counterbalance to evil? His answer is, in frame after frame, an unequivocal yes. He also asks the audience to extrapolate from the microcosm of this small village to the fascism that eventually gripped all of Germany in which millions were killed because of a reflexive response to the uber-fascist-father, Hitler, who turned Germany into a gnarled and pathological nation not dissimilar from the village nor the acts perpetrated against the children. To contemplate The White Ribbon is to feel both revulsion and admiration. Overly long (almost 2-1/2 hours), unrelentingly dour and forbidding, it is also unfailingly honest regarding the ability of one generation to do great harm to the next. For some, this film will be more than they want to endure. Others will watch in fascination while acknowledging that Haneke is a superb filmmaker. The White Ribbon. Starring Christian Friedel, Leonie Benesch, Urich Tukur and Ursina Lardi. Directed by Michael Haneke. 2 hrs., 24 min. Rated R.
articles.title: The White Ribbon an award-winning film from Germany

articles.text: The Incredibles, Pixar’s film about a family of superheroes. The Incredibles is a stylized, computer-generated action toon starring a family of under-the-radar superheroes. The patriarch of what will soon be a family of five is Mr. Incredible (Craig T. Nelson), a popular superhero, beloved by all for his rescues, foiled bank robberies, and suicide interventions. But despite his passion for what he does, the public grows weary of the collateral damage that occurs with each rescue. As a result, he and his new wife, Elastic Girl (Holly Hunter), are forced into what is called the Superhero Relocation Program, and are required to live normal lives, using the names Bob and Helen Parr. Flash forward 15 years. Bob is an insurance salesman, and he and Helen have three children – Dash (Spencer Fox), Violet (Sarah Vowell), and baby Jack Jack. As it turns out, Bob is growing increasingly dissatisfied with his mundane life. He yearns for the good old days when he was Mr. Incredible, and reminisces each day on the way to work while stuck in traffic with Lucius, aka Mr. Frozone (Samuel L. Jackson), while they listen to a police scanner. Both are tempted to help out the cops when they can. One day, a mysterious woman named Mirage (Elizabeth Pena) appears and makes them a job offer. Bob seizes the opportunity to return to his role as Mr. Incredible. He is convinced that like those days of yesteryear, he can make a difference. But he soon runs into an archenemy called Syndrome (Jason Lee). It doesn’t take long before Mr. Incredible’s whole family is involved in running battles and action chases with this nemesis. The Incredibles is one of Pixar’s best, a wonderful example of high-tech animation, lushly created backgrounds, slap-dash humor and jokes, with superhero costumes and signature masks. The kids will love it, as will the adults. The Incredibles, Computer animated. Directed and co-written by Brad Bird. With voices of Craig T. Nelson, Holly Hunter, Samuel L. Jackson. Pixar/Walt Disney. 1 hr., 55 min, Rated PG.
articles.title: The Incredibles – one of Pixar’s best

Meanwhile, Mumbles has a secret crush on the talented Gloria (Brittany Murphy), but doesn’t have the “heartsong” that is so necessary to find a companion. Happy Feet is charming and playful, making this rollicking tale of a unique penguin named Mumble (Elijah Wood) seem decidedly fresh. Apparently, every Emperor penguin sings a unique song called a “heartsong,” which is used to attract a mate. If the male’s song matches the female’s’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. Mumble soon becomes a young adult whose feet never stop moving; however it’s the elders, led by Noah (Hugo Weaving), Meanwhile, Mumble meets a group of mini-Mexican Adelie penguins, called “the Amigos,” whose leader is Ramon Lovelace (Robin Williams) who is willing to help Mumble court Gloria. Ramon sings “My Way” while Mumble lip-synchs. Naturally, Gloria falls for him. Soon all the young penguins are singing and tap dancing to “Boogie Wonderland.” Of course the elders are appalled. Mumble is ordered to stop, but refuses, and is exiled from the flock, and is blamed for what has been a lean fishing season. And thus Mumble’s adventure begins, one that takes him all the way to Australia where he ends up in a marine sanctuary where kids, one girl in particular, can stand and watch him swimming behind massive panes of glass pool. The girl taps on the glass and Mumble, with his beak, taps back, hoping to communicate with the humans. Event ually, Mumble is released from the sanctuary and finds his way home to his flock. It’s upon his return that he challenges the elders and prevails, and soon everyone is dancing and celebrating, most especially Mumble and Gloria and Ramon. Happy Feet. Directed by George Miller. With voices of Elijah Wood, Robin Williams, Brittany Murphy. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Happy Feet a wonderfully playful animated feature

Flash forward 15 years. Bob is an insurance salesman, and he and Helen have three children – Dash (Spencer Fox), Violet (Sarah Vowell), and baby Jack Jack. As it turns out, Bob is growing increasingly dissatisfied with his mundane life. He yearns for the good old days when he was Mr. Incredible, and reminisces each day on the way to work while stuck in traffic with Lucius, aka Mr. Frozone (Samuel L. Jackson), while they listen to a police scanner. Both are tempted to help out the cops when they can. One day, a mysterious woman named Mirage (Elizabeth Pena) appears and makes them a job offer. Bob seizes the opportunity to return to his role as Mr. Incredible. He is convinced that like those days of yesteryear, he can make a difference. But he soon runs into an archenemy called Syndrome (Jason Lee). It doesn’t take long before Mr. Incredible’s whole family is involved in running battles and action chases with this nemesis. The Incredibles is one of Pixar’s best, a wonderful example of high-tech animation, lushly created backgrounds, slap-dash humor and jokes, with superhero costumes and signature masks. The kids will love it, as will the adults. The Incredibles, Computer animated. Directed and co-written by Brad Bird. With voices of Craig T. Nelson, Holly Hunter, Samuel L. Jackson. It was a King Estate Pinot Gris and I remember thinking, “Damn, this is good! What is Pinot Gris? The state’s viticulture has come a long way since those ancient days. The Willamette Valley and areas around McMinnville have become the epicenter of wine growing and the two grapes that have become King and Queen are Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Oregonian vintners like to point out that their vineyards are on basically the same latitude as the great Pinot and Chardonnay vineyards in Burgundy France. California is too far south and its climate too “Mediterranean” to do justice to these two cold weather grapes, some Oregonians claim. It is true that to me the Pinots and Chardonnays from Oregon do seem to me to be more “Burgundian”. Christopher Winery in the Chehalem Mountains AVA in Willamette Valley in Oregon. The wines are hand crafted in small lots and sourced from a variety of vineyards in Willamette Valley. articles.text: Throughout the City of Piedmont, residents, businesses, and schools participate in three-container “source separated” waste collections. While Piedmonters are familiar with blue recycling, green organics, and black garbage carts, some residents may not understand why waste collection is separated in this way or how this method of collection advances Piedmont’s climate action goals. In particular, residents often have questions about organic waste. Organic waste is constituted of recovered products such as food scraps, green material, yard trimmings (landscape and pruning waste), untreated wood, and food-soiled paper products. When collected and processed on a significant scale, organic waste can be recycled into new products such as compost, mulch, biofuel, and electricity. In Piedmont organic waste is collected by Republic Services and converted into mulch and compost. While there are two significant methods of composting – backyard or home composting and commercial or industrial composting – the collection of green organic waste carts is part of the cycle of commercial and industrial composting. Industrial composting facilities are designed to effectively process large volumes of municipal and commercial organic waste. In turn, this compost can be sold back to landscapers, farmers, and plant nurseries in a circular, self-sustaining process. Not only can the product of large-scale composting advance California’s green economy, but with new regulations beginning in 2022, jurisdictions will begin procuring recycled organic material and making it available to residents. These new regulations, set forth in the California state legislation (Senate Bill 1383), were signed into law in 2016 in a statewide effort to reduce emissions of short-lived climate pollutants. The connection between compost and greenhouse gas emissions comes from the emission of methane gas from organic waste in landfills. Methane gas, which is a super pollutant that is over 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over the course of 20 years, is emitted when organic waste such as food scraps, wood, and paper decompose in landfills. As the single largest waste stream and the source of 20 percent of methane emissions in California, diverting organic waste to become compost can significantly reduce the state’s emissions. California’s new regulations support environmental initiatives at the core, while benefiting our communities and spaces and improving soil and air quality, all on both a state and local level. Piedmonters can benefit firsthand from the proper disposal of their own organic waste by collecting compost from the City’s free compost giveaway events. The City’s next compost giveaway is this Saturday, October 23 from 9:00am-12:00pm at the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. As Halloween celebrations draw closer, don’t forget to support the Piedmont community’s local schools at the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch at Coaches Field this year. Once your celebrations have wrapped up, remember that your pumpkins and food waste are compostable and placing them in the green organic waste bins will help reduce methane gas emissions for years to come. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s CivicSpark Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov. Photo courtesy of the City of Piedmont The city will host another free compost giveaway at the Corporation Yard following the success of the first giveaway last month.
articles.title: The Dirt on Compost

articles.text: State-of-the-art renovation includes new NASA Ames Visitor Center A rendering of the new NASA Ames Visitor Center at the Chabot Space & Science Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will reopen Friday, November 12 with a new NASA Ames Visitor Center, following more than 18 months of closure to complete construction on the largest project since 2000. “Chabot is kicking off an exciting next chapter to re-envision science education in partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, making visible the extraordinary people and legacy of discovery at NASA,” said Chabot Executive Director Adam Tobin. The NASA Experience will feature some fascinating items in space research and exploration, including spacesuits from the Mercury and Gemini missions, experimental heat shield technology, and a fan blade from the world’s largest wind tunnel. Many of these items have never been on display to the public. Visitors will get to step into the role of a NASA scientist by embarking on hands-on activities and connecting with NASA scientists in interactive stations. Guests will be able to design and build rovers, planes, and space robots for exploration, then test them in extraordinary environments inspired by labs at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will celebrate its reopening weekend with three days of festivities with extended hours to accommodate demand. Tickets will be limited, and visitors are encouraged to buy their timed tickets in advance. The weekend will include researchers and scientists from NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View, including astronaut Dr. Yvonne Cagle. Additionally, the weekend will include performances and workshops with community partners, a space-themed collaborative build zone, and robotics demonstrations by teen Galaxy Explorers. About Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and planet Earth. Chabot’s hours are 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Chabotspace.org 10000 Skyline Blvd, Oakland, (510) 336-7300.
articles.title: Chabot Space & Science Center to reopen Nov. 12

articles.text: Former Piedmonter Perenna Fleming dies on October 10. Perenna Pendrill Charles Fleming, a resident of Piedmont in the 1980s, died on October 10, 2021. The daughter of Sir John Pendrill Charles, K.C.V.O, MC, and Mary Pamela Waddell Dudley Charles, she was born on June 4, 1948 in London, England. Perenna grew up in London and graduated from Lawnside Academy and Sorbonne University in Paris. At age 19 she moved to Boston, Massachusetts and worked at the British Consulate, the Bull & Finch (“Cheers”) bar, and Apt Associates. She married Dr. Samuel Fleming in 1972. They moved to Laguna Beach, CA in 1982 and then to Piedmont in 1985. After raising two daughters, Perenna worked at the Institute for Contemporary Studies in San Francisco as Chief Operating Officer. She later created her own coaching business, a unique blend of executive coaching and spiritual healing. An avid traveler, Perenna visited all over the world including France, Cambodia, India, Italy, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. She was particularly fond of visiting her family and friends in England and Scotland. She joins her longtime partner Robert B. Hawkins Jr. (1941-2014), where they are undoubtedly hosting a dinner party. Perenna is survived by daughters Victoria Pendrill-Charles Fleming and Caroline Pendrill Caswell; sons-in-law Marshall Cale Gillespie and Jonathan Dwight Caswell; grandchildren Sienna Pendrill Gillespie, Kellan Jack Pendrill Gillespie and William Pendrill Caswell; sister Lady Lucinda Poole and stepsister Celia Ryan. A memorial service will be held at Piedmont Community Church on Sunday, November 7, at 2 p.m. In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to the Association for Frontotemporal Dementia at https://www.theaftd. org/support-aftds-mission/, and taking that trip you’ve been considering.
articles.title: Former Piedmont resident Perenna Fleming dies at 73

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group will have a special Halloween week tour of historic Mountain View Cemetery on Wednesday, October 27. The tour, which is scheduled for 10 a.m., will be led by longtime Mountain View docent Jane Leroe. The walkers last visited Mountain View in the spring but did not go to the famed “Millionaires’ Row,” a section where the most grand, elaborate crypts stand, housing some of the East Bay’s most famous inhabitants. It will be a focus of the October 27 visit. Parking inside Mountain View is available after signing in. Carpooling is suggested. Everyone is invited to join the Wednesday Walkers, and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov. Photo of Walking on Wednesdays group at Millionaires’ Row in Mountain View Cemetery in 2018.
articles.title: Wednesday Walkers to have guided tour of cemetery on Oct. 27

Chabot Space & Science Center to reopen Nov. 12 State-of-the-art renovation includes new NASA Ames Visitor Center A rendering of the new NASA Ames Visitor Center at the Chabot Space & Science Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will reopen Friday, November 12 with a new NASA Ames Visitor Center, following more than 18 months of closure to complete construction on the largest project since 2000. “Chabot is kicking off an exciting next chapter to re-envision science education in partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, making visible the extraordinary people and legacy of discovery at NASA,” said Chabot Executive Director Adam Tobin. The NASA Experience will feature some fascinating items in space research and exploration, including spacesuits from the Mercury and Gemini missions, experimental heat shield technology, and a fan blade from the world’s largest wind tunnel. Many of these items have never been on display to the public. Visitors will get to step into the role of a NASA scientist by embarking on hands-on activities and connecting with NASA scientists in interactive stations. Guests will be able to design and build rovers, planes, and space robots for exploration, then test them in extraordinary environments inspired by labs at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will celebrate its reopening weekend with three days of festivities with extended hours to accommodate demand. Tickets will be limited, and visitors are encouraged to buy their timed tickets in advance. The weekend will include researchers and scientists from NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View, including astronaut Dr. Yvonne Cagle. Additionally, the weekend will include performances and workshops with community partners, a space-themed collaborative build zone, and robotics demonstrations by teen Galaxy Explorers. About Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and planet Earth. Chabot’s hours are 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Chabotspace.org 10000 Skyline Blvd, Oakland, (510) 336-7300. Pictured are Albert Chen, Noemi Alvarado, Dorothy Shipp, Carol Bodnick, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Quincy Dong, Priscilla Wanerus, Carole Lyons, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Siow Fang Tan, Sherry Jacobs, Elise Collins with K-9 best friend Lia, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Larry Olsen, John Lenahan, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Kathy Marks, Pat Keller, Maulshree Solanki, and Dena Belinkoff. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered for its weekly walk on October 13 with 26 walkers and one K-9 best friend. The group was especially happy to welcome first-time walkers Kathy Marks, Pat Keller, Maulshree Solanki, and Dena Belinkoff. Priscilla Wanerus announced that Jane Leroe, a retired lawyer and longtime Mt. View Cemetery docent, would be leading a tour of the historic cemetery on October 27 – just in time for Halloween. As part of its goal of visiting every safe Piedmont street each year, the group decided to target the little-traveled streets below Wildwood School in the southwest section of Piedmont. They began on the one-way, lower part of Wildwood Avenue. The upper part of the same street is two ways, making Wildwood very unusual. The group came to the Four-W intersection of Wildwood, Winsor, Warfield Avenues, and Wallace Road. At Boulevard Way the walkers turned right and went down to Grand Avenue, crossing into Oakland. On the way they came upon a yard with an expansive, beautiful garden covered with cactus and other drought resistant plants, and a stately palm tree at the top of the yard. Near the bottom of Boulevard is an alley, the almost invisible Sylvan Way, where they a newly remodeled now modern home, and more Halloween decorations. The end of the block-long street presented a challenge, where it takes a 90-degree left turn to a very steep hill that ends on Wildwood Avenue. Wildwood quickly became Palm Drive, so named for the palm trees that early 19th Century Piedmont developer Frank C. Havens planted as the entrance to Piedmont Park. The group went up Wallace Road, a one-way street coming down, and passed the “Camel House” at the corner of Winsor, another home with a personal history. Turning left, they went down Winsor to Park View Avenue, which is at the base of Witter Field and another new street for the group where they saw many more ghosts, spiders, and skeletons on the homes. Park View ends at Magnolia Avenue, where the group turned right and went back uphill to their starting place at the Exedra. On the way they had one more opportunity to visit a seldom visited street, Larmer Court, a cul-desac with three homes. Does any other Piedmont street have fewer homes, they wondered. Even Cavendish Lane on the Oakland border near Park Boulevard has four Piedmont homes. It had been a fun, three-mile walk in less than 90 minutes; filled with seldom seen streets, unique homes and gardens, Halloween house decorations, social equity reminders, sounds of happy children, and good conversations with new and old Wednesday walking friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Playback Theatre with Martin Holtz is one of Stagebridge’s mainstay classes, offering two showcases during the Fall session. Stagebridge, the nation’s oldest Senior Theatre Company and located nearby in Oakland, is offering several online programs this Fall, and Playback Theatre students will be performing two digital showcases, on November 2 and 30. As a mainstay class in the Performing Arts Institute, Playback Theatre transforms stories into on-the-spot theatre pieces inspired by the life experiences of the audience members. The improvised pieces may be funny or sad, deep or playful, tragic, or life-affirming. “Since Playback Theater is based on what is going on with our lives, we get to feel connected to each person in the group,” said student Naomi Puro. “Learning to listen extra carefully to each person is a significant part of Playback, therefore each of our brains benefit from the work.” er’s skills with deep listening, emotional risk-taking, creative movement, and improvisational form, students honor each participant’s personal stories to extend the sense of digital community. “I’ve gained an ability to better express with words and feelings and how to better listen and observe [who is speaking],” said Piedmont resident Bob Cheatham. Even with social distancing, students can blend their needs for artistry, service, and ritual. Led by Martin Holtz, this class and art form depends on audience participation, even though some audience members may choose to just watch. This is a theater of empathy whose subject is the life experiences of the people attending the show. “Martin is the best Stagebridge instructor I’ve ever had in my ten years at Stagebridge,” said Sarah Strong. “He listens well, communicates well, his teaching is extraordinary, and he helps us to be more creative and better actors.” Holtz is a veteran of more than 30 years as a performer, award winning writer and artist-as-educator, in both South Florida and the San Francisco Bay Area. He is a trainer and creative consultant for the Center for Domestic Peace dealing with domestic violence, and a founding member of the Bay Area Playback Theatre. The Fall Playback Theatre showcases will be held Tuesday, November 2 at 3:30 p.m. and Tuesday, November 30 at the same time. To register, visit www.stagebridge.org/upcoming-events.

articles.text: We already know that staying physically active in your autumn years offers a variety of health benefits, like lessening chronic pain, delaying and preventing certain diseases, and helping you recover faster from an illness or injury. While physical exercise is important for a high quality of life, the connections we make with others, and the relationships we continue to build, also have a major impact on our overall wellness. I’ve learned that staying socially active is just as important as remaining physically active. According to the National Institute on Aging, as people get older they often find themselves spending more and more time at home alone. Research tells us that older people with an active lifestyle are less likely to develop certain diseases. Participating in hobbies, like taking an art class and other social and leisure pursuits, may lower the risk for developing health problems and can help to maintain one’s well-being. Other studies show how participating in creative arts, like music and dance, may help people age as well. For many, the primary reason for moving to an independent senior community is because they have acknowledged the need for a more active and engaged life. Here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, we have a huge calendar of social activities for our residents. Our free exercise classes such as Yoga, Zumba and Core Strengthening with our on-site personal trainers are not only great physical activities, but are a great way to socialize as well. Plus, we recently added a ballroom dance class and residents are refreshing their skills with the waltz, foxtrot and cha cha – and they are loving it! The Lake Merritt offers lots of programming inspired by our residents, as well as our weekly series of talks designed for older adults, Topics of Merritt. Residents attend these programs in person, and we invite the community to join us for free via Zoom. We are particularly excited about an upcoming program on November 4 at 3:30 p.m. Passions of a Dancer is an inspirational presentation by Stephanie Herman, a former Principal Ballerina. She shares her struggle to make her dreams come true and eventually dances worldwide with ballet legends such as Rudolf Nureyev and Mikhail Baryshnikov. To join us for this Zoom presentation, register online at: www.tinyurl. Pat Ross and Cynthia Ely demonstrate their ballroom dance form.

articles.text: Respite care is when a family caregiver is given a break – a rest or a respite – from their responsibilities caring for a loved one. This break might occur when another family member steps up for a time, or by hiring a professional caregiver to do some of the caregiving instead of the family. Many family caregivers are juggling work, caring for other family such as young children, plus a variety of tasks for someone who is physically or mentally unable to fully care for themselves due to age, illness, or disability. Sometimes it becomes too much, and in order to continue helping out at all, a break is needed. While home care is for the person who needs assistance, the respite is for the family of the client who is receiving the home care services. Why is respite care so important? The expression, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” sums up the critical need for respite care. Family caregivers can give too much of themselves in service to a loved one and damage their own health and wellbeing. When that happens, everyone needs care – medical care, home care, nursing care, you name it, depending on the circumstances. Even a weekly movie night out for a couple of hours, or a Sunday morning in church, during which time the person who needs care is tended to by another, can give someone back their own peace of mind and well-being. What does in-home care mean to you? If you are a family caregiver in need of a break, you might be wondering what a professional caregiver can step in and do in your place. A trained caregiver can be there to assist with daily bathing and grooming, become like a friend and companion to take walks and play games together, do a little light housekeeping during their visit, provide medication reminders, run some errands including those that the client may need to join, and more. Respite care is available for short and long-term care needs, whether someone is recovering from a surgery or developing additional symptoms after a diagnosis of a progressive illness. You may need respite care for a senior, or caring for a loved one of any age. Whether you seek out professional in-home care services or are asking friends and family to share the load, make sure you take breaks for yourself from time to time to maintain your wellness. Homewatch CareGivers is located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.

articles.text: A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, October 20, 2021 The History of Piedmont Piedmont’s silk farm – it’s all about mulberry leaves By Gail G. Lombardi High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” By 1885, the mulberry grove was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. The government stopped its appropriations in 1891, and the silk farm closed four years later. It was Piedmont’s only industry. Today, there are still Mulberrys in Piedmont. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. Their logo is a leaf with silkworm bites. Mulberry trees were also planted at the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Field in memory of the role they played in Piedmont’s early history. For more on Piedmont’s history and the Piedmont Historical Society, visit the website: Piedmonthistorical.org,. A wood rack with cocoons is at his feet, with more racks on the top shelf. The girls are preparing fresh silkworm trays with screens and mulberry leaves. The shelves behind them are filled with trays of silkworms and mulberry leaves. The machine at the right foreground chops mulberry leaves before they are fed to the silkworms. The sign reads “U.S. Experimental Silk Culture Station, Oakland Cal.”

articles.text: A carjacking occurred on Wednesday, October 13, at 7:50 p.m. in the area of Wildwood Avenue and Prospect Road. A resident seated in a vehicle was approached by approximately five suspects, one of whom was armed with a gun. The suspects ordered the victim out of the vehicle, stole additional items belonging to the victim, and fled the area in the victim’s vehicle. A witness called 911 and Piedmont officers responded to the scene. The suspects, male juveniles wearing dark hoodies, dark pants, and COVID face masks, were not located and are currently at large. The victim was not physically harmed. Detectives are currently conducting an investigation of this incident and working with regional law enforcement partners to identify commonalities with other similar incidents in other jurisdictions. Anyone with additional information about this incident is asked to contact Detective John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015 or Detective George Tucker at (510) 420-3013. While this type of crime is rare in Piedmont, the Police Department asks the public to be aware of their surroundings and report suspicious activity related to criminal conduct in a timely manner by calling 911 for emergencies and (510) 420-3000 for non-emergency situations.

A resident seated in a vehicle was approached by approximately five suspects, one of whom was armed with a gun. The suspects ordered the victim out of the vehicle, stole additional items belonging to the victim, and fled the area in the victim’s vehicle. A witness called 911 and Piedmont officers responded to the scene. The suspects, male juveniles wearing dark hoodies, dark pants, and COVID face masks, were not located and are currently at large. The victim was not physically harmed. Detectives are currently conducting an investigation of this incident and working with regional law enforcement partners to identify commonalities with other similar incidents in other jurisdictions. Anyone with additional information about this incident is asked to contact Detective John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015 or Detective George Tucker at (510) 420-3013. While this type of crime is rare in Piedmont, the Police Department asks the public to be aware of their surroundings and report suspicious activity related to criminal conduct in a timely manner by calling 911 for emergencies and (510) 420-3000 for non-emergency situations. articles.text: Staff photo Mom Julianna Monin with Evelina and younger sister Ceca examine the Giant Jack pumpkin to guess its weight. Evelina considered a large number and asked if it could possibly be 150 pounds. The Giant Jack is now on display at the Wildwood Dads’ Pumpkin Patch at Coaches’ Field. The Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch will be open daily through Saturday, October 30, with plenty of time for families to stock up prior to Halloween. The pumpkin patch has a big variety of 15 types of pumpkins and gourds. In addition to traditional carving pumpkins, the patch has some specialty pumpkins, like the Knucklehead, the “One too Many,” the American Tondo and the Polar Bear pumpkin (all white). New and popular this year are the other worldly Marina Di Chioggias, the tie-die colored Turks Turbans, and a ghost-shaped Yugoslavian Finger Fruit. “We have seen families come back twice with their kids. Some of that is motivated by not really having a Halloween last year so really everyone trying to make up for it,” said Wildwood Dad Randy Wells. The Giant Jack heavyweight pumpkin is the centerpiece. For $1 kids can guess the weight of the enormous pumpkin. The person with the closest guess will win the Giant Jack with free home delivery.

Back by popular demand, the City of Piedmont, in partnership with Republic Services, is holding a free compost giveaway for residents at the City’s Corporation Yard (next to Coaches Field on Moraga Avenue) on Saturday, October 23 from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Piedmont residents may pick up to one cubic yard of compost while supplies last. Preorders are not available. Bring shovels, gloves, containers, and proof of residency (driver’s license or current Republic Services bill) to pick up compost. Residents must bag and load the compost themselves. Residents are asked to wear masks or face coverings and follow the Alameda County Public Health Department’s COVID-19 guidance. While not required, it is strongly encouraged to fill out an online form to indicate your estimated pickup time on Saturday. The form can be found at https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FAIpQLSfd-w0Sz08FIuXz38E- 2kRntXClTl60awmIhUxPmU2IThe compost is made from yard trimmings and food waste collected in curbside organics collection services. Mixing compost with your soil adds nutrients to the soil, aids in water retention and pest control, and helps plants thrive The City is also proud to support the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch, which is next to the compost pickup area. Come by to grab your free compost and support Piedmont’s local schools. You can have your pumpkin, and compost it too. For more information contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420- 3058.

Reconciling is the verb the apostle Paul uses to describe what God is doing in the world. Paul uses many words – salvation, justification, redemption and reconciliation among them – to describe what God is doing in the world. articles.text: The Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail project has attracted a significant number of bids for a project of its modest size. The City’s proposed project to install a handrail and build steps on the hill between the Community Hall and Guilford Road has attracted an unusually large number of bids from contractors interested in doing the work, according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. A bid opening was held on October 6, with eight bidders showing interest in the project. “Contractors appear to be looking for work,” Gonzales noted at a Park Commission meeting on October 6. Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent agreed, adding that the city used an electronic virtual bid submittal, which may have boosted the response. “It’s wonderful to have eight bids. That means there is a lot of interest and that it is a competitive [process],” she said. “We had a Zoom bid opening, when usually our bid openings are in person.” Bids were received from HM Construction, Inc., Sposeto Engineering, Inc., FBD Vanguard Construction, Inc., Bay Construction Co., Wickman Development & Construction, Valentine Corporation, Kerex Engineering, Inc., and CF Contracting. The Highland-Guilford Steps are located on the southern entrance to the Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park and provide access to the Tea House. The existing configuration of the pedestrian pathway does not meet the City’s building code or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements for exterior steps. City Administrator Sara Lillevand told City Council at a September 7 meeting that city staff had received a report of a trip and fall that occurred on the stairs, elevating the project’s priority. The engineer’s estimate for the total cost of the project is $155,000. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club raised funds for the project with a combined donation of $55,000. The city will place emphasis on improving pedestrian safety, which includes reconfiguring colored concrete steps and landings with a nonslip finish; decorative handrails on both sides of the steps and landings; and replacing the sloped landing at the entrance off Highland Avenue with a small pedestrian plaza. Native shrub plantings around the plaza may include coffeeberry and Ribes Sanguineum, and a grove of native oaks will replace a dying, mature oak. Once the bidding process is finalized, City staff will bring a recommendation to City Council for review. The project will begin after City Council approves a contractor. “Any time there’s a bid opening, that is always exciting to me. Capital project delivery is one of the great things we do in Public Works,” Gonzales said.
articles.title: Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail Project attracts large number of bids

articles.text: The League of Women Voters hosted a town hall-style virtual meeting on October 5 to discuss Piedmont’s Housing Element and housing needs. Guest speakers included Rani Batra, Chair of Piedmont’s Housing Advisory Committee, Melissa Breach, Chief Operating Officer of California YIMBY (Yes In My Backyard), and Gloria Bruce, Executive Director of East Bay Housing Organizations. The discussion included a presentation on the state’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation. The Housing Element is a mandatory part of the Piedmont’s General Plan and, by State law, must be updated every eight years. The Element must address Piedmont’s immediate and longterm housing needs and set forth the City’s goals, policies, and actions to support increased housing. To help guide the process, the City convened a Housing Advisory Committee comprised of Piedmont citizens. In introductory remarks, Breach noted that California still has 25% of the homeless population in the U.S., while only having 12% of the nation’s population. California’s housing crisis is the catalyst for legislation that aims to increase the state’s housing stock and diminish its large homeless population. “The governor has already signed 37 housing bills, which is incredibly exciting,” Breach said. “Funds have been set aside for affordable housing. [It is] an unprecedented amount, but not nearly as much as we need.” YIMBY was the lead advocate on State Senate Bill 9, and the lead sponsor of SB 10, both signed by Gov. Newsom this year. The League of Women Voters endorsed both bills. SB 9 allows for duplexes and lot-splits in California, legislations Breach defined as “the bill that ended single-family zoning in California.” SB 10 allows for local governments to streamline and avoid red-tape requirements for new housing. Batra addressed the city’s process of meeting its goals of 587 new housing units in the upcoming Regional plan. “Our job is to identify land and sites to accommodate the RHNA. That doesn’t mean the city is responsible for building the housing itself, but [the city] needs to pave the way for that production to occur,” she said. Batra said the allocation represents “the magnitude of the challenge and opportunity, and the level of creativity and change that we may need to undertake to achieve this.” The city will invite the public to attend a Housing Element Community Workshop on December 2. California’s housing crisis is the catalyst for legislation that aims to increase the state’s housing stock and diminish its large homeless population. “The governor has already signed 37 housing bills, which is incredibly exciting,” Breach said. “Funds have been set aside for affordable housing. [It is] an unprecedented amount, but not nearly as much as we need.” YIMBY was the lead advocate on State Senate Bill 9, and the lead sponsor of SB 10, both signed by Gov. Newsom this year. The League of Women Voters endorsed both bills. SB 9 allows for duplexes and lot-splits in California, legislations Breach defined as “the bill that ended single-family zoning in California.” SB 10 allows for local governments to streamline and avoid red-tape requirements for new housing. Batra addressed the city’s process of meeting its goals of 587 new housing units in the upcoming Regional plan. “Our job is to identify land and sites to accommodate the RHNA. That doesn’t mean the city is responsible for building the housing itself, but [the city] needs to pave the way for that production to occur,” she said. Batra said the allocation represents “the magnitude of the challenge and opportunity, and the level of creativity and change that we may need to undertake to achieve this.” The city will invite the public to attend a Housing Element Community Workshop on December 2. articles.text: Governor Gavin Newsom’s California Comeback Plan includes a $15 billion investment in our climate -- with $3.9 billion going towards Zero-Emission Vehicles (ZEVs). This comes one year after the Governor’s Executive Order that 100 percent of in-state sales of new passenger cars and trucks will be zero-emission by 2035. What does this mean for Piedmonters and the city’s climate action goals? Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, adopted in 2018, outlines a target of 50% ZEV ownership by 2030. According to 2019 vehicle registration data, about 7% of vehicles registered in Piedmont are ZEVs. When ZEVs are charged using East Bay Community Energy’s Renewable 100 plan, vehicles can run on 100% California solar & wind energy rather than fossil fuels. Not only do electric vehicles benefit the environment and advance Piedmont and California’s climate action goals, but they also make sense economically. Tools like Plug In America’s PlugStar incentive search, the California Air Resources Board’s DriveClean incentive search, or Veloz’s Electric For All campaign Incentive assistant can help Piedmonters research and discover which incentives they qualify for. Some of these incentives include up to $7,500 in Federal Tax Credits, $4,500 from the California Clean Vehicle Rebate Project, $1,500 from the California Vehicle Retirement Consumer Assistance Program, $1,500 from the California Clean Fuel Reward, $9,500 from Bay Area Clean Cars for All, and preferred pricing from Drive Clean Bay Area’s EV Discount Campaign. Other incentives include an Alternative Fuel Infrastructure Tax Credit for those who purchase residential fueling equipment, EV use of HOV lanes, and clean air vehicle discounts on Bay Area Bridges. In addition to point-of-sale discounts, rebates, and incentives, EVs are known for their capacity to save money over time. Energy.gov uses a tool called the eGallon, showing how much cheaper it is to drive on electricity, while FuelEconomy.gov provides a tool to directly compare fuel costs between vehicles, and PG&E provides an EV Savings Calculator which calculates the cost of specific electric vehicles to own over 5 years, including the cost of the vehicle, electricity vs gasoline, maintenance, and insurance. As part of Piedmont’s climate action goals, the City is having important conversations around EV Charging Stations in the Civic Center Area and Fleet Electrification. Piedmont would be following in the footsteps of the state of Washington and Bay Area cities like Fremont, San Francisco, and Sacramento which have made progress in purchasing EVs as part of a municipal fleet electrification process. While Piedmonters can currently add a Level 2 charging system to their home through a streamlined permit process, adding public charging stations in the City could provide an incentive to adopt electric vehicles by providing additional opportunities to charge them quickly. While ZEVs are just one step towards meeting Piedmont and California’s climate action goals, investing in an electric vehicle is an important step to investing in our climate and our future. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: A plug for Zero Emission Vehicles

articles.text: In the last three weeks Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign has held three events demonstrating the depth and breadth of support for Piedmont schools. Parties celebrating new community members, major donors, and Piedmont schools’ alumni brought together a large number of supporters. On September 20, the Education Foundation hosted an event outside Piedmont Community Hall to welcome new families to town. Giving Campaign donor Xenia Meyer moved here with her family a year and a half ago. “The community here is so welcoming to newcomers,” she said. “The whole ethos of ‘it takes a village’ is something I really feel here.” Cortney and Ben Allen hosted an event in their backyard on Sheridan Avenue on September 29 to celebrate families providing significant levels of support for Piedmont schools. “It was so nice to gather in person and have great conversations with parents,” said hostess Cortney Allen. “It was a beautiful night with a wonderful group of community members,” On Thursday, October 7, Alicia and Jim Kalamas on Bellevue Avenue hosted the newly formed Alumni Committee with 80 Piedmont alumni. More than 400 Piedmont residents are alumni of the schools and have returned to raise their own families here. With a total of $1.4 million raised thus far, the Giving Campaign is almost halfway to this year’s goal of raising $3 million to support students and the schools. The funds raised by the Giving Campaign will help close the gap between what the schools receive from state, federal, and local taxes and what it costs to provide an excellent education. The gap is approximately $2,140 per student. Giving Campaign funds help preserve small class sizes, elective and AP classes, music and art programs, librarians, counselors, class aides, and other specialists. The Ed Foundation accepts pledges with monthly payments, by credit card or through online bill pay, as well as gifts of stock and from Donor Advised Funds. PEF’s tax ID is 94-6426176, checks can be made payable to Piedmont Education Foundation and sent to 401 Highland Avenue, and credit card contributions can be made by phone at 653-1816 or online at PiedmontEdFoundation. Photo by Picture Happy Photo The Kalamas family hosted a Giving Campaign event in their backyard on October 7. Pictured are Alicia Gruber Kalamas (left), Ashley Stevanovic, Sarah Meyjes, Peter Wagener, Jill Saper, and Amelie Kappes. org/donate .
articles.title: Trio of Giving Campaign events in last 3 weeks

articles.text: East Bay families will have two weekends to enjoy Halloween-themed festivities at Children’s Fairyland this year – October 22-24 and October 29-31 with two daily sessions each weekend. Decked-out Fairyland sets like the ghost town formerly known as Old West Junction and rides including the “Creepy Crawly” are just a few of the many seasonal surprises. At the end of each session, visitors are welcome to march in a physically-distanced Monster Mash parade, and kids get a special prize at the exit. Costumes are encouraged. Tickets need to be reserved in advance. A limited number of timed-entry tickets will be available to ensure physically-distanced events. Fairyland is open from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tickets are available at: https:// childrensfairyland.brushfire.com/ fairyland/513430.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School Choir (formerly A Capella), directed by Jorell Chavez, will present a new event, a Fall Vocal Showcase, on Thursday, October 21st at 7:00 p.m. in the middle school multi-purpose room. The program of music includes Compositions by Sara Bareilles, Jacob Naverud, English songwriter Adele, and selections from the musicals Into the Woods and Waitress the Musical. Chavez became choir director in August of 2020 but did not meet students in person until Spring of 2021. His music backg rou nd includes a Bachelor’s degree in Voice/ Choral Conducting and French from San Francisco State. He studied voice for two and half years at the Conservatoire Frédéric Chopin in Paris, France. Currently he is pursuing his Master’s degree in Choral Conducting at San Jose State University. A $5.00 suggested donation for adults will be requested at the door. Admission for students is free. For more information, contact Jan D’Annunzio at jdannunzio@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: On October 1 California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared the COVID-19 vaccination mandatory for all students K-12 to attend classes in person. The Piedmont school board had already mandated COVID- 19 vaccination on September 22 for all eligible students (age 12 and up). Piedmont’s policy states that students eligible for the vaccine, (12 years old by September 22) must provide proof of full COVID vaccination no later than Wednesday, November 17 or they will be excluded from campus education and referred to independent study. We encourage other states to follow our lead to keep our kids safe and prevent the spread of COVID-19,” he added. Essentially Piedmont’s policy remains in effect and is not effected directly by the mandate. However, the district’s policy has room for adjustment, “In anticipation of younger students becoming eligible for the COVID vaccine in the coming weeks, we will adjust the policy as needed,” wrote Booker. If vaccine supplies are limited once new age group become eligible, PUSD can amend the eight-week window for full vaccination (full vaccination is two shots, plus two weeks removed). As of October 7, 87% of Piedmont’s age-eligible students have already submitted their proof of vaccination ahead of the November 17 deadline.

articles.text: Fall is a time for transitions. School is underway, but as the darkness comes earlier and the air gets colder, it seems like something shifts in our family life. We are spending less time playing outdoors, more time looking for indoor activities, and the routine of day to day becomes our guiding force. I find this shift fascinating because it always takes me by surprise – at least a little bit. I wake up one day and realize that summer is over, even though I have known this for weeks. Obviously, the holidays coming up are part of this transition, but I’m interested in spending more time thinking about the “in between” – the days when it’s not about costumes and trick or treating, but remembering the cleats on the way to soccer practice. It’s not about the big family meal with turkey, but the grilled cheese sandwiches on a Tuesday. Not the days with tons of presents, but packages that bring a new fleece to keep warm on the walk to school in the morning. How do we make sure that the “in between” days have opportunities for growth and excitement in our family? It’s so easy to get caught in the routine of daily tasks. I’d like to propose that this time of year is the perfect opportunity to use creativity to imagine with your family what is possible. What does exquisite look like for your family life? In the book Play – How it Shapes the Brain, Opens the Imagination, and Invigorates the Soul, Dr. Stuart Brown and Christopher Vaughan write eloquently about the importance Using creativity to make the most of “in-between” days. of Creative Play. “Creative Play takes our minds to places we have never been, pioneering new paths that the real world can follow.” (pg. 93) How can we use Creative Play to dream with our kids? Here is one idea, but I bet you can put on your creative hats and come up with tons more! Family Vision Board In the olden days, we used to make vision boards with these things called magazines, but your children likely have never experienced an actual magazine. So, for the purposes of this activity, ye old internet and a printer will work just fine. Get a big piece of poster board and divide it into four sections. Label each section: Daily Life, Play Together, Play Apart, Big Dreams. Before you start, help everyone get in a playful mindset by playing a silly game like twister or Hokie Pokie or Freeze Dance. Now, with laptop available, start asking your kids and all adults in the house, “What would our days look like if our daily life was truly exquisite?” Let everyone throw ideas out there and then google images that match the ideas. Print them out and paste them on the board. Repeat with: “How do we all want to play together?” “How do we want to play individually? “What big dreams do we have that may feel out of reach right now, but might be fun or exciting some day for our family?” I hope you enjoy the “in between” days and use all of that creative energy to make every day enjoyable...and a few of them memorable! Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. articles.text: In my 13 years as a math tutor I have come to discover the key to math is to humanize it. The world of numbers can be bland, droll, distant, but certain strategies, tricks and hacks can help bring math to life, to give it a personality. With just a slightly different perspective and the right equipment, math can evolve from being a powerful but confusing “tool” to a powerful “ally.” First acquire the proper instruments, supplies and gadgets at the start of the year. This is something that is really a prerequisite for anyone other than a math genius able to compute every calculation in his head. Get a calculator or two. Buying two identical calculators, one for home and one for class, can help guarantee you use the same calculator every time. Get to know all the functions and buttons and soon enough it will be muscle memory. I recommend moving to a graphing calculator as soon as possible. It takes a while to learn, so using it early in 9th grade or even middle school will ensure four or more years of experience. Don’t bother trying to get familiar with the calculator on a phone, as you will not be able to use that on tests. I recommend using a pencil when doing math at all levels, because there will be plenty of opportunities to erase (unless you can do the New York Times crossword flawlessly in one take). Also utilize color pencils. This will help make things stand out and gets the left side of the brain involved. In algebra, just having two extra colors can be useful to circle like terms or keep track of negative signs. And by all means use paper. If using graphs, graph paper is a must. Doing math with a keyboard is nearly impossible, as Using a chalk board at home can help reveal the big picture in math by providing plenty of space. there is no key for tangent, square root, or pi. Just write it down. Keep it neat, take your time, space things out, use a whole page. Furthermore, use a large white board or a chalk board at home to easily show the material. Math doesn’t have to be small, elusive or confusing. It’s more fun when it’s big, bold and basic. Use a ruler, and make those graphs pristine. Use a protractor or trace a cup, and get those circles perfect. Taking neat notes with careful penmanship and staying organized gives every student an advantage and is usually all a struggling math student needs. Make sure to buy the actual textbook. I recommend investing in the instructor’s copy of the book. Believe it or not, some math teachers are not experts on the subject matter, and the teachers’ editions include methods to help teachers explain the material. (The answers to homework are in the back of every book, so this is not cheating.) If you have your own book, feel free to underline, circle or write questions next to problems.

articles.text: Artist Karima Cammell founded and teaches “Castle in the Air” after-school art classes for Piedmont kids at all three elementary schools. When not teaching youngsters, she paints. Her current exhibit, “High Water,” is on view at Holton Studio Gallery. 2100 Fifth Street, in Berkeley until October 30. The show opened with a reception on October 9 and includes Cammell’s thought-provoking paintings. Her art scans the shore, finding a world both on fire and drowning beneath waves of social, political, and climate change. Cammell is well known for being the founder of beloved Fourth Street shop Castle in the Air in Berkeley but since closing the store has pivoted to being a full-time artist. She also continues her work as a children’s author and illustrator and runs the ever popular art classes for Piedmont youth. Along with artist Ben Yates, Cammell teaches classes ranging in subjects from calligraphy to watercolor to miniature food sculpture. “Our after-school program is great fun,” Cammell said. “We teach kids calligraphy, watercolors, simple bookbinding and illumination. We operate on the value that art is a gift, and it makes our work infinitely rewarding.” To see the after-school class offerings, see Homeroom.com. Classes are open now and will return in the Winter and Spring of 2022. To learn more about the show, see Castleintheair. biz/highwater. After school art instructor at Piedmont elementary schools Karima Cammell has a gallery showing of her paintings now in Berkeley.
articles.title: After-school art instructor Karima Cammell’s exhibit now open in Berkeley

When not teaching youngsters, she paints. Her current exhibit, “High Water,” is on view at Holton Studio Gallery. 2100 Fifth Street, in Berkeley until October 30. The show opened with a reception on October 9 and includes Cammell’s thought-provoking paintings. Her art scans the shore, finding a world both on fire and drowning beneath waves of social, political, and climate change. Cammell is well known for being the founder of beloved Fourth Street shop Castle in the Air in Berkeley but since closing the store has pivoted to being a full-time artist. She also continues her work as a children’s author and illustrator and runs the ever popular art classes for Piedmont youth. Along with artist Ben Yates, Cammell teaches classes ranging in subjects from calligraphy to watercolor to miniature food sculpture. “Our after-school program is great fun,” Cammell said. “We teach kids calligraphy, watercolors, simple bookbinding and illumination. We operate on the value that art is a gift, and it makes our work infinitely rewarding.” To see the after-school class offerings, see Homeroom.com. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. Black Hills with Cedar, 1942, Georgia O’Keefe A Romantic Drama: the Film, “Eiffel” Michael and I both love films, especially on the big screen, which is why Lost in Frenchlation is recommended when living abroad. We saw Eiffel at a private, funky movie room, Club de l’Étoile Cinema on Rue Troyon near Place Charles de Gaulle. The bonus view was seeing the Arc de Triomphe under night lights for the last wrapping-removal from the Christo project. The film recreated convincingly the high-wire action playing out under the tower of a muddy, dangerous project, a quagmire showing frighteningly primitive engineering feats (1886-1889). The viewer already likely knows that a French competition for a monument to promote the Paris World’s Fair was afoot, and Gustave Eiffel won. The construction hit troubled waters, and public opinion turned against Eiffel who was the face of the “metal folly.” Parisians genuinely feared it would topple and come crashing down on them. A romantic plotline that people believe is the lore for the tower’s sweeping, cursive “A” shape is an homage to Adrienne, his teenage lover. It is best to not examine the legend too closely for fact. Just expect a beautiful young heroine to fall in love with Eiffel, leave him, then find him, but he loses her, gets her back, their plan goes awry, she leaves him, and so on. The heart pangs, but it will work out, so enjoy. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews returned to Paris after a productive time back in Piedmont during late summer. articles.text: The Piedmont tennis team won its last two league matches, edging past Alameda 4-3 on Thursday, October 7 and swept Arroyo of San Lorenzo 7-0 two days earlier on Tuesday, October 5. Both matches were played on the road. Their victory over Alameda was significant, a resounding response to a 6-1 loss to the Hornets one month earlier. “We had to pull out all the stops for this match,” noted coach Jim Landes. “They trounced us 6-1 a month ago. This time, our doubles teams were sharp, and all three won in straight sets.” Piedmont’s 4-3 team victory was the result of the three doubles teams winning, and a key victory at No. 4 singles by Anika Gilliland, 7-6 (7-3), 6-2. It was Gilliland’s fifth consecutive win. “Anika clinched our victory in two tough sets. She has been playing better every week and mixed up her shots as usual, with good forehands, serves, drop shots and lobs. She threw in some strong backhands as well,” said Landes. In doubles, Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany continued their dominant performance in league with a 6-1, 6-1 win at No. 1. It was their sixth win this season. At No. 2, Mara LaForte and Audrey Frankel won 6-3, 6-3, while Ceclia Defazio and Emma Eisemon at No. 3 doubles comStaff Photo Anika Gilliland won 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 at No. 4 singles to clinch Piedmont’s 4-3 win over Alameda bined for a gritty win in two sets, 7-6 (7-3), 6-2. It marked their sixth win as a doubles team. “Cecilia and Emma had to play a tiebreak in the first set but won it handily. They are really starting to gel as a team, with both of them more aggressive at the net,” said Landes of the firstyear varsity combination. At singles, Bridgette McEfee lost 6-2, 6-3 at No. 1, Anne Jumper lost in three sets at No. 2 by scores of 4-6, 6-2, 6-2. At No. 3 singles Michaela Bini powered through a tense 3-set match before losing, 6-7 (8-6), 6-2, 10-8. 7-0 sweep of Arroyo Playing Arroyo in San Lorenzo, Piedmont won all seven matches in straight sets. At No. 1 singles, Jumper won 6-2, 6-1, and Bini won by the same scores at No. 2. Mahany scored her opponent at No. 3 singles, 6-1, 6-0, and at No. 4, Audrey Frankel won easily, 6-1, 6-2. Photo by Brian Mahany Amanda Becker (left) and Audrey Mahany dominated Alameda’s doubles team, 6-1, 6-1.

articles.text: Piedmont’s JV Scots traveled to Berkeley High on Friday, October 8 to face the Yellowjackets on their Homecoming night. While the game ended in a 20-10 loss, there were some bright spots for Piedmont. articles.text: 5 runners set personal records The Piedmont boys’ team dominated a league cross-country race with 10 schools and held at Hayward High on Wednesday, October 6, with its five principal runners all recording personal best times. In team scores, the Highlanders far outpaced the competition, easily defeating Berkeley (2nd) and Castro Valley (3rd). The course at Hayward will be the site of both the League and North Coast Section Championships in November. Jack Stein was the overall winner in a field of 79 runners. His time of 15:37.5 was 17 seconds faster than his last race. His time is five seconds shy of Reece Proctor’s winning time in 2018, a PHS record. Continuing his breakout season was sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse in second with a time of 16:03.57; a 23-second improvement from a race on September 15. Junior Parker Long placed fifth in 16:16.65, a 26-second improvement, and classmate Christian Taylor, in seventh, clocked a time of 16:20.1. Only six second back was sophomore Julien Lee in 11th overall. “We’re at mid-season. The time is flying by and our runners are flying with fast times,” said PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. “It’s exciting to see them doing well and improving.” Girls Results The girls’ team finished fourth out of nine teams behind Berkeley. 1. Alameda 2. Castro Valley 3. Berkeley 4. Piedmont Sophomore Josephine Oesterer continued her strong season with a 3rd place finish in a field of 63 runners in 19:07.54. “Josie’s been having quite the season. She’s really working hard,” said Holmlund. Sophomore Jamie Schwarz was fourth in 19:30.6. a 31-second improvement. Piedmont’s next runners were senior Mara Lovric in 24th (21:01.05), junior Violet Lemley in 25th, and senior Molly McWeeny in 43rd. NEXT UP Pied mont’s cross-cou ntry team will compete in the Roughrider Invitational at Woodward Park in Fresno this Friday, October 15 at 1:30 p.m. It is the home course of the CIF State Championship meet. articles.text: Six miles of hiking on Hayward Plunge and Greenbelt trails Halloween is right around the corner, so what better time to delve into the spooky and haunted. Growing up around Hayward, the gruesome legend of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park is a well-known story, which provides an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class of students up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night, when the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or crying, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in white garb when he was a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be protected by thickets of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand.
