pages.text: Wednesday, October 13, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON The haunted Hayward Plunge Trail Six miles of hiking on Hayward Plunge and Greenbelt trails By Jonathan Comeaux Halloween is right around the corner, so what better time to delve into the spooky and haunted. Growing up around Hayward, the gruesome legend of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park is a well-known story, which provides an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class of students up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night, when the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or crying, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in white garb when he was a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be protected by thickets of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for Staff Photos A spillway along Ward Creek on the Hayward Plunge Trail, a notoriously haunted park in the East Bay. Eucalyptus trees tower overhead. Travel up the stairs and stay next to Ward Creek to continue on the Hayward Plunge Trail. The trail is popular for mountain bikers. With quick ascents and declines. another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree line, and you’ll have the option to head back down, or turn right and walk down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail where you’ll be reunited with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles, we only passed 29 people at noon on a Sunday. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought the feeling that eyes were always following. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive. The hilly trail provides over 1,100 feet in elevation gain in six miles. Hikers will cross numerous bridges on the hike. A view of the Greenbelt Trail alongside Ward Creek, which connects with the Hayward Plunge Trail. The trail is wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers.

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival at the Gardens of Lake Merritt. Autumn Lights Festival, an artfilled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Gardens at Lake Merritt, returns this year for three nights, October 14-16. The festival draws more than 10,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt. This year it celebrates its 10th anniversary. Visitors will experience 60 locally produced illuminated art displays throughout Oakland’s seven-acre municipal gardens. There will also be a kids’ “fun zone,” art market, food court, and a beer and wine garden. All festival attendees must provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID test to enter. Masks are required, and per-night capacity is reduced. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/ autumn-lights-festival-2020/.
articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt this week

articles.text: Concerts are free to attend, no RSVP required The Oakland Museum of California has announced a new, free program series open to the public in October entitled “Lunchtime Sessions: Music, Dance, and Storytelling in the Garden” beginning this Saturday, October 16 at noon. The museum reopened in June after 15 months of closure due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This series will be the museum’s first in-person program held in the newly renovated gardens which were recently completed as part of a multi-year $85 million comprehensive campaign. “Lunchtime Sessions” will feature local artists and performers spanning multiple genres. The renovated gardens include an outdoor stage with built-in sound equipment, offering a collaborative space for performers. Visitors are encouraged to bring their own blankets to sit on the lawn, and food and beverages may be purchased from the museum’s new café, Town Fare. Guests may also bring their own food to events. This Saturday, October 16, Awesome Orchestra Collective will kick off the series. The Bay Area-based collective was founded in the spring of 2013 by conductor David Moschler, the Music Director of Berkeley-based Youth Musical Theater Company. Over 2000 local musicians have played in the Orchestra. “Lunchtime Sessions” are free and open to the public, tickets and reservations will not be required to attend. However, due to countywide restrictions, capacity may be limited. Visit https://museumca.org for more information. Oakland Museum of California
articles.title: Oakland Museum to launch outdoor programs

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Father/Daughter will premiere starting November 12 for one month and will be available to stream December 7 through 12. Father/Daughter, by playwright Kait Kerrigan and directed by M. Graham Smith, is a contemporary romance featuring two actors playing two pairs of lovers. The structurally incentive play details how parents and children can impact romantic lives. Father/Daughter is the recipient of the Edgerton Foundation New Play Award, which allows productions time for development and rehearsal through a monetary grant. Kerrigan, an award-winning playwright and lyricist, is best-known for We Have to Hold Hands and Mad Ones. “Kait Kerrigan’s writing is insightful, audacious, and liable to make you either laugh or cry when you least expect it,” said Artistic Director Josh Costello. To purchase tickets for live performances, or for streaming access, visit https://www. auroratheatre.org/fatherdaughter Photo by David Allen The play Father/Daughter by Kait Kerrigan will open at Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley on November 12. ®
articles.title: Aurora Theatre opens Nov. 12 with Father/Daughter

articles.text: Michael Morgan Oakland Symphony will honor the late Michael Morgan, its conductor for 30 years, with an all-star memorial concert at the Paramount Theater on Tuesday, October 19, at 6:30 p.m. Artists from across the Bay Area and throughout the U.S. will join in celebrating the life and legacy of Maestro Morgan. The San Francisco Conservatory of Music, San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, Mads Tolling, Zachary Gordon, and many more will be present. Morgan was also music director of the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra and artistic director of Festival Opera in Walnut Creek. As a guest conductor, he appeared with most of the country’s major orchestras including the New York Philharmonic, New York City Opera, Photo by Liz Hafalia, San Francisco Chronicle San Francisco Opera, and more. Morgan passed away on August 20 at age 63. The concert is free to the public, but you must RSVP before Tuesday, October 19. Proof of vaccination is required to enter the Paramount Theatre. Masks must be worn while seated. Children under 12 are not permitted to attend. RSVP by visiting https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/event/ we-remember-michael/.
articles.title: Michael Morgan memorial concert at Paramount October 19

articles.text: San Francisco Conservatory of Music (SFCM) will present a baroque orchestral performance on Halloween, October 31, at 2 p.m. The concert will be held at the Caroline H. Hume Concert Hall and will be live-streamed. Pieces from some of the most iconic baroque composers will be performed, including the music of Antonio Vivaldi, Arcangelo Corelli, Henry Purcell, Andre Cardinal Destouches and Johann Sebastian Bach. Special guests include dancer Jennifer Meller, baroque oboist Marc Schachman, and soprano Jayne Diliberto. Corey Jamason and Elisabeth Reed serve as co-directors for the baroque ensemble. The Conservatory’s baroque ensemble performs music of the 17th and 18th centuries in both orchestral and chamber settings. Nearly all instruments and voice types can participate in this genre. Many pieces have been performed by the ensemble in the recent past, including Handel’s Ode for St. Cecelia, Semele, Serse, Rinaldo, Giulio Cesare, Ariodante, Rodelinda, Atalanta, Agrippina, Alcina, Monteverdi’s L’incoronazione di Poppea, Purcell’s The Fairy Queen and Charpentier’s Les arts florrisants. The ensemble has also participated in the premieres of new works by composition faculty members Mason Bates and Elinor Armer. Tickets for the in-person or livestream may be purchased at https://sfcm.edu/performance-calendar/event/sfcm-baroque-orchestra. Proof of vaccination is required to enter SF Conservatory.
articles.title: SF Conservatory hosts concert of baroque music on Oct. 31

articles.text: The film The Revenant is an extraordinary film: intense, unrelenting, gorgeous to behold and unflinching in its realism. The year is 1823. It’s mid-winter in Montana and South Dakota. A group of men, working for The Rocky Mountain Fur Company, are just completing six months of trapping, preparing pelts and readying their riverboat for a return trip to their base camp, a roughly constructed fort downstream. The trip will be long and arduous. The forest is quiet, wind stirs high in the trees when suddenly a man, in mid-sentence, is shot in the throat by an arrow. The group is set upon by Arikara warriors, and the trappers must fight a desperate and brutal battle as they attempt to get to the boat and escape. Among the few survivors are Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his son, Hawk (Forrest Goodluck), who is part Pawnee. During one of their stops along the way Glass is attacked by a grizzly sow, protecting her cubs. It is one of the most heart-stopping scenes in the film, a mauling that leaves Glass close to death. The party makes the decision to leave behind three men, including Hawk, to bury Glass when he dies (they are certain he is near death) and then make the journey on their own to the fort. His son is killed by one of the trappers, but Glass, still alive, is thrown into a shallow grave and partially buried. Through sheer will, he eventually emerges, discovers the body of his dead son, A scene from Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu’s The Revenant. Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible, John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – which will take your breath away – and the crucible of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (Birdman), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so, the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. The acting is superb; it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they endured as they went through a long and grueling shoot. They, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, were recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The Revenant. Directed by Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Tom Hardy, Domhall Gleeson. 2 hrs., 36 min. Rated R.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Revenant – top marks for cinematography and acting

articles.text: Nicholas Hoult protrays J.R.R. Tolkien in Tolkien. There are three narrative threads that run through Tolkien, a lush production told under the umbrella of what is loosely referred to as a biopic. At the outset, the film tells the story of a band of four young brothers, mates at an English prep school, who spend hours in each other’s company while insisting that art can and will change the world. There is Geoffrey (Anthony Boyle), Christopher (Tom Glynn-Carney), Robert (Patrick Gibson) and, of course, Tolkien (Nicholas Hoult), who is more formally known as John Ronald Reuel (J.R.R.). While their friendship is interesting and perhaps an accurate portrayal, there is also a restrained, cerebral quality to their interactions. Something is missing. Perhaps an intensity. The second thread is the meeting of Tolkien and Edith Bratt. Their encounter initially takes place in a rooming house for foster children, she as a companion to the wealthy owner of the home. He is brought there when, at 12-years-old, his mother unexpectedly dies of diabetes. His lodging is arranged by his mentor and guardian, Father Frances (Colin Meaney), who promises to assist the boy as best he can. Gradually, over a period of years, Edith and Tolkien are drawn to one another and their connection grows. But their attraction and relationship is described, like so much of this story, with caution. They are young, and there are embers waiting to be fanned. The third thread, and one that is ripe with graphic details and information, is the rich imagination of Tolkien. He fills the walls of his rooms with his drawings. He keeps notebooks filled with his stories. And he demonstrates a passion for language. In one remarkable scene he sits in a restaurant with Edith and they have a conversation about a phrase, much loved by Tolkien, “cellar door.” Of all the exposition in the film, there is something captivating in this moment. Eventually, he meets a university professor, a scholar of philology, who points the way. Unfortunately, it is Tolkien’s imagination that seems too quickly to be passed over. In scenes that are filled with his drawings, the camera never pauses to reveal in close-up the intricacies of his fabulist talent and the richness of a world beyond. Behold, there are dragons, gnarled trees, characters. Unexpectedly, it becomes evident that the story is a series of long flashbacks, revealed from the point of view of Tolkien, an army officer trapped in one of the unspeakable warren trenches of WWI and struggling to survive. So harrowing are the scenes of war, so overwhelming with danger and perpetual carnage, Tolkien retreats into memory or fantasy. The Germans with flamethrowers become dragons bellowing long streams of fire; tanks are knights on horseback riding slowly through a wasted killing field; black, wispy battlefield smoke becomes ominous and threatening. Actually, Tolkien’s experience in that hellish war, more specifically the Battle of the Somme, could not only have been the fulcrum for this film, but it could have been the gateway to the years ahead when he actually imagined and then crafted The Hobbit and later The Lord of the Rings, which taken together represent some of the most imaginative writing of the 20th century. Regrettably, Tolkien ends just as J.R.R. sits down at his desk and gazes out a window at a bucolic field in the distance and writes just two words: The Hobbit. Tolkien. Directed by Dome Karukoski. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Lily Collins, Colm Meaney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Tolkien a fascinating history of JRR Tolkien

The Germans with flamethrowers become dragons bellowing long streams of fire; tanks are knights on horseback riding slowly through a wasted killing field; black, wispy battlefield smoke becomes ominous and threatening. Actually, Tolkien’s experience in that hellish war, more specifically the Battle of the Somme, could not only have been the fulcrum for this film, but it could have been the gateway to the years ahead when he actually imagined and then crafted The Hobbit and later The Lord of the Rings, which taken together represent some of the most imaginative writing of the 20th century. Regrettably, Tolkien ends just as J.R.R. sits down at his desk and gazes out a window at a bucolic field in the distance and writes just two words: The Hobbit. Tolkien. Directed by Dome Karukoski. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Lily Collins, Colm Meaney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu’s The Revenant. Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible, John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – which will take your breath away – and the crucible of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (Birdman), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so, the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. The acting is superb; it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they endured as they went through a long and grueling shoot. They, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, were recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The Revenant. Directed by Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Tom Hardy, Domhall Gleeson. 2 hrs., 36 min. Rated R. ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: Chicken Run, from the creators of Wallace & Gromit, is an immensely fun, entertaining feature that will capture the imaginations of youngsters from the get-go. It’s also an amazing technical achievement, created by some 40 animators, working with stop-motion claymation, real props, three dimensional sets, with a cast of chickens with perky dialogue and personalities to match. The story is set on a bleak chicken farm in Yorkshire, England, run by a cranky (bordering on sadistic) commandant, Mrs. Tweedy (Miranda Richardson). She rants and screeches about the lack of egg production and is working on a Rube Goldberg plan to turn all the chickens into pot pies if things don’t pick up. Among the chickens is Ginger (Julia Sawahla), a spunky prize hen, who is not about to simply give in to Mrs. Tweedy, unlike her complacent peers. Early on, she tries to dig a tunnel under the wire fence using a kitchen fork and is caught by Mrs. Tweedy’s guard dogs and put into solitary confinement. All seems lost, the chickens’ fate all but sealed, when Rocky, a Rhode Island circus rooster, who can fly, and is a Yank to boot, shows up. Brash, overly confident, he convinces the hens that he can teach them to fly as well. Of course, Rocky also falls for Ginger, and as a result the two begin to hatch a plan for a prison-break. Surprisingly Rocky does need some convincing. Meanwhile, Mrs. Tweedy’s potpie contraption is coming together, egg production is declining, and both Rocky and Ginger realize that time is of the essence – all the hens have all been put on double rations in order to fatten them up. Chicken Run a fun ride, full of humor, pranks, dances, all with a backstop of a lively song, Flip, Flop, and Fly. For comic relief there are two wily rats (Timothy Spall and Phil Daniels), and Babs (Jane Horrocks) who is the always knitting. Considering that this feature is Claymation, the facial expressions of the hens are extraordinary, painstakingly formed with exceptional attention to detail. The story also pays obvious homage to all those films featuring the likes of the Great Escape, and Stalag 17; the chicken coop occupied by Ginger et.al is referred to as Coop 17. Chicken Run is delightful and the kids will enjoy it to the max. Chicken Run. Directed by Peter Lord and Nick Park. Stop-motion Claymation. With voices of Mel Gibson, Julia Sawahla, Miranda Richardson. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated G. A scene from Aardman Animastions’ Chicken Run.

articles.text: Kids will love Wallace & Gromit, an Oscar-winning franchise of 30-minute shorts, plus one feature. The first short was A Grand Day, followed by The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave, and A Matter of Loaf and Death. The Curse of the Were-Rabbit was the Aardman studio’s first Claymation feature film. The stars of the franchise are, of course, Wallace (Peter Sallis), a suburban Brit with a pearshaped head and wide, ear-to-ear smile, and his faithful, industrious, ever-silent Beagle (graduate of the Dogwart Academy). They live together in a house filled with labor saving inventions and Rube Goldberg-like contraptions, invented by Wallace, whose day jobs include window cleaner, and baker. In Were-Rabbit, he is the owner of the Anti-Pesto Services, a pest control company. His current responsibility is to keep the village gardens free of vegetable-eating rabbits. He, of course, has an invention just for this purpose, a vacuum that sucks up the rabbits, which he keeps in his basement. All of this is in preparation for the Town’s annual vegetable growing competition, the winning prize being a golden carrot. One evening, using his invention, Wallace captures a rabbit who is eating Lady Tottington’s (Helena Bonham Carter) vegies. Unfortunately, his contraption has a miscalculation, and he creates a gigantic Were-Rabbit that is ravenous for vegetables, and is chomping its way through garden after village garden, something that will surely upset the coming vegie growing contest. Hearing of this garden emergency, Lord Victor Quartermaine (Ralph Fiennes) volunteers to hunt down the culprit with his rifle and shoot it; however, lady Tottington objects, and convinces the town folk to allow Wallace and his Anti-Pesto Services to take care of the problem. The mystery that Wallace must solve is who or what is this Were-Rabbit? It’s a puzzle that takes Wallace and Gromit on an adventure. Wallace even discovers giant muddy footprints that lead into his own house. And even Gromit, who is highly intelligent, can’t figure out the source of the footprints. There are lots of surprises and chases, and even threats by Quartermaine to kill the Were-Rabbit with a golden bullet. Things get more than a bit chaotic, at one point involving an airborne dogfight between Gromit and Q.’s dog, Phillip. There’s a bit of romance-lite thrown in (Wallace and Lady T. have some chemistry). It’s all daffy fun, wonderfully creative, involving lots of pratfalls and puns. Youngsters will be smitten. Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. Directed by Nick Park. Claymation by Aardman Animations. With voices of Peter Sallis, Ralph Fiennes, Helena Bonham-Carter. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated G.
articles.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit

articles.text: Pianist Adrien Zarragoza Solano Symphony music director and conductor Semyon Lohss is an inspiration. He is all for the music and the results show it. Under his direction the orchestra plays with razor sharp precision and with great attention to dynamics. The orchestra was featured in Schubert‘s 6th Symphony. It was a very Viennese interpretation, and the quick tempos kept the orchestra on its toes. Many years ago, friends of mine who played in the San Francisco Symphony under Pierre Monteux said that he inspired the orchestra to play above their abilities. That’s what Semyon Lohss does. We have a great composer in our midst. You probably don’t know his name as a prominent musician. His credentials are impressive. Among them are that he was a violinist in the Amsterdam Philharmonic and Director of the youth program with the San Francisco Symphony. He is now a State Farm insurance agent, but Frank Bliss is a great composer. Frank’s newest work is a four-movement symphony based on the business cycle. What a novel concept that is. He adapted one of the movements as a memorial to a friend. I heard this version in Frank’s arrangement for violin and harp with Frank playing the violin part. The sincere sentiment of the music brought the audience to tears. I hope that one of our local orchestras will play Frank’s entire symphony. articles.text: Piedmont has the possibility of becoming a world destination. First, we should adopt Munich as our sister city. Now that I have got your attention… Munich, Germany hosts the world’s largest folk festival – the Oktober Bierfest. For the second year in a row, this gigantic festival was canceled. Piedmont made up for it… More specifically the Piedmont Center for the Arts. You don’t have to fly to Germany or even speak German. Admission to the 9th annual Piedmont Beer Festival was $10 per person and included a custom pilsner glass with the Center’s logo. For an additional five dollars you could get an authentic German meal of grilled Bratwurst, warm potato salad and warm red cabbage, all courtesy of Piedmont Grocery. To say this is a popular event is putting it mildly. Approximately 150 beer connoisseurs and German food lovers enjoyed themselves immensely. This year the celebrity judges included Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery’s Dave Larson. Fire chief Dave Brannigan was on hand to check the results. That was on Friday. Next year, let’s have a German-style oompah band. And now some musical notes... On the local music scene, the Prometheus Symphony played a virtual concert. Their programs are always interesting, and we look forward to live concerts in the near future. The Solano Symphony is another fine local orchestra. They opened their 35th season on Sunday with a very exciting concert. Adrien Zarragoza was the featured soloist in Beethoven’s Piano Concerto #3. This young pianist is a talent to watch. He has a blazing temperament which was perfect for the Beethoven concerto. In many ways Zaragoza reminds me of a young Vladimir Horowitz. His technique is facile; he can thunder with the best of pianists, and then in an instant caress the keys in the most gentle manner. As I said, he is a talent to watch. Solano Symphony music director and conductor Semyon Lohss

articles.text: Virtual livestream performance tomorrow San Francisco Opera will present Beethoven’s Fidelio beginning October 14. The opera company will also offer the first three performances to livestream, marking the first livestream in the company’s history. Fidelio, originally titled Leonore, is Beethoven’s only opera. The libretto tells the story of Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named “Fidelio,” who rescues her husband Florestan from a political prison. The opera marries the themes of personal sacrifice, heroism, and triumph with Beethoven’s own political outlook. The performance by San Francisco Opera is a modern-day ref lection of incarceration. Director Matthew Ozawa presents this brand-new production of Fidelio, starring Elza van den Heever, Russell Thomas and Greer Grimsley. articles.text: Book lovers with the First Mondays Reading Group included Alicia Rivera, Ken Young, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, Nancy Henn, Swee Ling Chen, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long The First Monday Reading Group met 14 strong at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on October 4. a lovely, warm day. The early fall, “secret summer” day and beautiful location and refreshments may have been incentives for readers come for the discussion, but the expectation of an interesting discussion of the group’s October book, the best-seller Nomadland, was an even stronger motivation. Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century is a 2017 nonfiction book by American journalist Jessica Bruder. This is her account of older Americans who, after the recession from 2007 to 2009, have adopted transient lifestyles going from one place to another around the United States in search of low-paying, seasonal jobs. The book was adapted to the 2020 film of the same name, starring Frances McDormand, which won the Academy Award for that year’s Best Picture. Bruder expanded a cover story for Harper’s magazine into Nomadland. Her nomads, many of whom are senior citizens, don’t think of themselves as “homeless.” Instead, they refer to themselves as “houseless.” They feel they are no longer burdened by mortgage payments, repairs, and other house expenses. However, most of them did not become “houseless” by choice; many lost their houses because of mortgage fraud, job loss, health care debt, divorce, alcoholism, and additional factors. They sleep in their cars, trucks, or campers and try to make the best of their situations. The author traveled with some of the houseless for years while researching and writing her book. She built her novel around a senior citizen named Linda May. She and her fellow travelers found physically demanding, low-wage jobs in North Dakota sugar beet fields, California campgrounds, and an Amazon distribution center in Texas. These seniors created community wherever they were; offering tips for overcoming common troubles, sharing food, repairing vehicles, helping each other through depression, and sharing information about potential employers. The readers felt that the book was helpful in making people more conscious of the hardships that lower income, older adults face in America. These are not people that Piedmonters usually see in their daily experiences. The severity of what some seniors in our nation experience was a cause for not only disappointment, but also anger for some readers. The fact that these people are living as nomads was seen as a result of our country’s move away from its past, three-legged retirement planning model. articles.text: car·tog·ra·phy. noun. The science or practice of drawing maps. Recently I was perusing the Sunday New York Times Magazine and bumped into an article by Rachel del Valle titled Why Use a Dictionary in the Age of Internet Search. She defined dictionaries as field guides to the life of language. It was an analog that prompted me to read on. She went on to say that she owned a much-prized 1954 Webster’s New International Second Edition Dictionary, purchased some years ago on a street in New York City. It has 5,000 pages, the paper marbled India ink with a thumb index. Like a compelling sculpture, it has found a place on a table near her workspace, always opened, likely to the last word she looked up. I’ve owned countless dictionaries over the years, some dogeared paperbacks, others hard covered, the corners a bit frayed, often boxed up along with favored fiction when I moved, others lost or loaned. For a time, I owned the Oxford English Dictionary, which arrived in a two-volume set, accompanied by a magnifying glass; by the early 1800s the Oxford had some 400,000 entries, ever revised and added to. I confess that I love language, and relish coming across an esoteric word that appears like a stranger, unrecognizable, yet used with confidence in the context of a sentence. Often the meaning is elusive until the definition of that singular word is nailed down. An example would be the word “inchoate,” meaning “not fully formed or developed.” I doubt that I have ever used that word in conversation, or could pronounce it correctly. And for reasons that escape me, I can’t seem to hold its definition in memory. But there is something about inchoate that is interesting, even attractive in that category referred to as onomatopoeia – phonetically resembling the sound it describes (like oink or tick tock). If I still had my Oxford English Dictionary, I might even look up its derivation. An example offered by del Valle is “orrery,” which is defined as a mechanical model of our solar system used to represent relative positions and motions of our sun and planets. I can look at that word with admiration and try to quietly pronounce it, knowing I will never slip it into a sentence, written or spoken. But it stands at the ready, just in case. Del Valle compares finding such a word to prying open an oyster and finding a small pearl inside, or discovering a solvable mystery. Such words and their meaning do not exist in the realm of guesswork, for dictionaries are not arbiters of language nor do they create language – people do. And it’s people who swim in the stream of connotation and denotation, ever changing verbs into nouns, a most recent example being a simple word like “ask.” Still a verb, but now a favored noun, i.e. “that’s a big ask.” I’m tempted to say that encountering a newbie word is akin to a bird watcher spotting a rare species, one never seen before, requiring a field guide search, the excitement almost palpable. As a final note and in the interest of full disclosure: I first write all my copy by hand, (I favor ink on paper, in books and newspapers). And then, for the final edit, I turn to my MacBook Pro that possesses an image of a dictionary cum thesaurus with “Aa” on its cover, tucked into a long row of helpful guides, right next to Firefox. I use it repeatedly, on occasion glancing over at my opened dictionary with a sigh, trying to reject the idea that it is anachronistic, but still a useful cartography of our language. Chris Honore’ is the Post’s movie reviewer, and a member of its staff for more than 22 years.
articles.title: The Dictionary: A cartography of words and meaning

articles.text: Part 30 in a biweekly series One of the delights that comes from walking around town is discovering and actually reading the many commemorative plaques located in Piedmont. Apparently originating in the middle ages, historical interest groups at all levels of governments all over the world seem to have their own commemorative system of celebrating the connection of a location with a special event, person or structure. These range from a very coordinated, consistent aesthetic such as on the blue ceramic heritage plaques found throughout all of England, to the more common mixed styles found in the U.S. including Piedmont. Since the majority are quite often outside in the weather, what they all have in common is durability. Many are made of different long lasting materials such as bronze, marble, stone and zinc to name a few. Brass is however probably the most common material because of its shiny, gold-colored appearance, strength and low maintenance. Historical plaques are most often mounted to a wall, large stone or other vertical surface. However, like many things in our age of more information and resulting reevaluation, commemorating history can now be a contentious issue. When we find out more about the dark side of celebrated historical figures, what has resulted in some cases in the removal of older plaques We have discussed the beauty, function and importance of urban design in previous columns. A city that understands these concepts should indeed honor the people who support them and make them possible. These appropriate, well-designed and well deserved plaques themselves add interest and punctuation to the urban design of the city. Piedmont’s Centennial House plaques rest on 173 homes, all built before city incorporation in 1907 and judged to have maintained the architectural style and character of the original buildings. The Wetmore house, adjacent to City Hall, is on the National Register of Historic Places. A similar sub-category of historical plaques are “donor bricks” such as this nice installation honoring the supporters of Witter Field construction. Memorial benches, found throughout the parks of Piedmont, add interesting detail as well as a welcome place to relax.

articles.text: I’m a witch, or, to keep with the preferred terminology, I practice witchcraft. Witchiness does not define me. That said, I’ve been a practicing witch since the Middle Ages, making me, I suppose, a middle-aged witch. I know of what I speak when I say that many of you have unpleasant misconceptions about us. I address them herewith. Myth 1 - Witches are ugly. I’m really surprised to hear this in our supposedly woke era. Our faces have character. We have strong features. Personally, I wouldn’t trust a woman who doesn’t have a large wart on the tip of her nose. A pointy chin and missing teeth proclaim our refusal to accept traditional ideas of beauty. Admittedly, none of us own mirrors. Myth 2 - Witches have green skin. No, it just looks that way when we stand under fluorescent light. No one looks good under fluorescent light. Myth 3 - Witches cackle. Such an ugly way of saying we enjoy a good laugh. While not everyone shares our sense of humor –I crack up seeing our neighbor’s livestock break out in boils after my shadow crosses their path, for example – we’re not the type to titter demurely behind a dainty fan. Deal with it. Myth 4 - Witches live in castles. Don’t I wish! More like a third-floor walkup with no view. Some of us are fortunate enough to live in a cooperative housing community, but you have to join a coven. Myth 5 - There are good witches and wicked witches. Is anyone really all good or all evil? Even a “good” witch might omit a spell-casting fee on her tax return, and a “wicked” witch might spend a quiet afternoon grooming her flying monkeys. Let’s drop the labels please. Myth 6 - Witches eat children. False! We used to eat children. We removed children from our diet in the late 1950s, early 1960s, when – coincidentally, I emphasize – the childhood obesity epidemic began. For a variety of reasons, and not just for our own health concerns, we witches as a group decided to forego excessive consumption of adipose tissue. The many benefits of our abstemious approach include being able to stay aloft longer on our brooms. Myth 7 - Witches construct gingerbread houses to lure children. I’ve already addressed the child-eating canard, but it should be obvious that gingerbread does not weather well. You can still find some pre-war lofts made of the stuff, but hipsters have remodeled them and stripped much of the ornaments that once made them so attractive to youngsters – not that yummy icing was ever intended to lure the little ones. And if people associate gingerbread houses with eating kids, why bake them as a Christmas treat? Weird. Myth 8 - Male witches are called warlocks. To outsiders, yes, but we refer to them as the men’s auxiliary to the witch community. Myth 9 - Witches always wear black. in Manhattan. You see that more with witches Myth 10 - Witches concoct poisons. We have recipes, just like any culturally distinct people. We slowcook them in simmering cauldrons using traditional ingredients, such as eyes of organic newts, toes of local frogs, and tongues of dogs (pure-bred only). Right now, we’re in our test kitchens developing dishes suitable for the general public. Here, try the soup … just a spoonful … that’s all you’ll need … for a nice, long sleep. Phil Witte, a Piedmont resident, is a humorist and a weekly cartoonist in the Piedmont Post with the single-panel cartoon, FLIP.
articles.title: HUMOR I’m A Witch, And I’d Like To Dispel Some Unfortunate Myths

articles.text: Members of Walking on Wednesdays gather for a photo on Wednesday, October 8 at a home on La Salle Avenue. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group was surprised last Wednesday, October, to see a half dozen police officers at the Exedra, the starting location each Wednesday morning for the walkers. Was there a problem, they wondered? No. The Police Department was hosting another in their series of Coffee With a Cop events. Chief Jeremy Bowers welcomed the walkers and stressed the importance of community and how Piedmont benefits from it. A large group of 40 walkers were on hand for Part 2 of Hope Salzer’s tours of Healthy Landscapes Front Gardens sponsored by Piedmont Connect. Hope had taken the walkers to three gardens the prior Wednesday, and the walkers wanted to see more. Piedmont Connect is a community organization supporting efforts to build a sustainable future. The plan for the day was for Hope to take the walkers to four new gardens, starting at 250 La Salle Avenue, a unique, steep, natural garden, with every inch packed with “succession planting” vegetation that provides color throughout the year. Additionally, all these plants absorb rain better than grass would (if we ever get rain again), reducing excessive runoff down the steep yard to the house. Even the strip from the curb to the front of the garden is covered with plants. The yard supports birds, insects, and other wildlife, but has also survived the deer that roam throughout the neighborhood. The next stop was 131 La Salle with a different type of drought tolerant garden. It is more formally structured, and currently has vibrant, early fall red and yellow colors from bottle brush, firecracker, and other plants. It was noted that former Piedmont mayor and landscape designer Valerie Matzger designed the yard for the homeowner. There is a permeable walkway and other surfaces that allow rain to soak into the ground. The environmental mindset of the owner was further evidenced by solar panels on the roof. The home’s front steps provided tiers for the walkers to pose for the attached group photo. The group continued to 66 La Salle where a new garden was planted this past spring, and shows how quickly a lovely, drought tolerant garden can be created. This was another steeply sloped front garden of a home above the creek on St. James that also survives the foraging of local deer. The garden has many plants that attract bees for their pollen and nectar. Hope stressed the importance of all types of bees and the need to protect them. She told the group they are in real danger. In fact, the bumble bee has been recently named an endangered species. Birds are also being harmed by human actions, and their population is in decline. This garden uses drip irrigation and includes a colorful flower named Salvia “Hot Lips.” Asked about the ground covering, Hope explained her preference for using compost. She said the challenge is getting enough of it to cover a garden. Piedmont residents can get quantities of compost from Republic Services, the city’s trash removal and recycling service. The last garden was at 98 Sea View Avenue, another beautifully designed and lovingly maintained garden with a large variety of plants, flowers, and small trees. There are manzanita, citrus, climbing roses, native grasses, and many more. Succession planting provides color throughout the year and highly efficient drip irrigation minimizes water usage. While they were there, the owner came out and told the walkers how he has maintained the yard, and how much he enjoys it. Before the parade of walkers made their way back to the Exedra, they gave Hope a big round of applause. Everyone was impressed with her knowledge and passion for environmental sustainability. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov.

Personally, I wouldn’t trust a woman who doesn’t have a large wart on the tip of her nose. A pointy chin and missing teeth proclaim our refusal to accept traditional ideas of beauty. Admittedly, none of us own mirrors. Myth 2 - Witches have green skin. No, it just looks that way when we stand under fluorescent light. No one looks good under fluorescent light. Myth 3 - Witches cackle. Such an ugly way of saying we enjoy a good laugh. While not everyone shares our sense of humor –I crack up seeing our neighbor’s livestock break out in boils after my shadow crosses their path, for example – we’re not the type to titter demurely behind a dainty fan. Deal with it. Myth 4 - Witches live in castles. Don’t I wish! More like a third-floor walkup with no view. Some of us are fortunate enough to live in a cooperative housing community, but you have to join a coven. Myth 5 - There are good witches and wicked witches. Is anyone really all good or all evil? Even a “good” witch might omit a spell-casting fee on her tax return, and a “wicked” witch might spend a quiet afternoon grooming her flying monkeys. Let’s drop the labels please. Myth 6 - Witches eat children. False! We used to eat children. We removed children from our diet in the late 1950s, early 1960s, when – coincidentally, I emphasize – the childhood obesity epidemic began. For a variety of reasons, and not just for our own health concerns, we witches as a group decided to forego excessive consumption of adipose tissue. The many benefits of our abstemious approach include being able to stay aloft longer on our brooms. Myth 7 - Witches construct gingerbread houses to lure children. I’ve already addressed the child-eating canard, but it should be obvious that gingerbread does not weather well. You can still find some pre-war lofts made of the stuff, but hipsters have remodeled them and stripped much of the ornaments that once made them so attractive to youngsters – not that yummy icing was ever intended to lure the little ones. And if people associate gingerbread houses with eating kids, why bake them as a Christmas treat? Weird. Myth 8 - Male witches are called warlocks. To outsiders, yes, but we refer to them as the men’s auxiliary to the witch community. Myth 9 - Witches always wear black. in Manhattan. You see that more with witches Myth 10 - Witches concoct poisons. We have recipes, just like any culturally distinct people. We slowcook them in simmering cauldrons using traditional ingredients, such as eyes of organic newts, toes of local frogs, and tongues of dogs (pure-bred only). Right now, we’re in our test kitchens developing dishes suitable for the general public. Here, try the soup … just a spoonful … that’s all you’ll need … for a nice, long sleep. Phil Witte, a Piedmont resident, is a humorist and a weekly cartoonist in the Piedmont Post with the single-panel cartoon, FLIP. articles.text: • The Rhone River wine growing region in France is divided into two halves – the north and the south. They could not be more different. The South is huge and produces oceans of wine – a lot of it cheap Cotes du Rhone, yet it also has some heavyweight appellations like Chateauneuf du Pape, Gigondas and Vacqueras. The main red grape is Grenache with lots of Mourvedre, Carignanne and Syrah grown. By comparison the Northern Rhone region is tiny and it stars only one red grape – Syrah. For whites, Viognier is king. with some Marsanne and Roussanne grown. Being from California, my wine palate was developed on Zinfandel, Cabernet, Pinot Noir and Petite Sirah. As much as I still love those varietals, I must say I have fallen in love with the Northern Rhone. These days I rarely get more satisfaction than opening a bottle of Viognier from the Condrieu AVA or a Syrah from Cote Rotie, Hermitage or St. Joseph. While California makes some great Syrahs, too many of them become heavy and ponderous, lacking balance and acidity. And as for Viognier, I have had many California examples, but I have yet to find anything close to the magic of Condrieu. I was thrilled to have the opportunity recently to evaluate the wines of one of the Northern Rhone’s premier producer, Francois Villard. His wines have tremendous perfume and are exquisitely balanced and refreshing. I also appreciate that in a world where wine prices have gone absolutely crazy, Villard has held the line; his wines represent great values. The wines are imported in the U.S. by Jack Edwards Selections, a Napa based firm that specializes in small, high-quality producers from France. You can check out their other portfolio wines at www.jackedwardscollection.com. 2018 Francois Villard Les Contours de Deponcins Viognier, $19.99 (Great Value) This is a “baby Condrieu” made from Viognier vines planted outside the official boundaries of Condrieu. It comes close to its daddy and is a good value to boot. It has a lovely jasmine nose with tasty pear and apricot fruit Francois Villard Francois Villard is one of the up-and-coming bright lights in the Rhone Valley. After previous careers as a chef and sommelier, he ventured into wine growing in 1991 with a small parcel of vines in Condrieu, He has since expanded it into holdings in Cote Rotie. Villard’s style has evolved from the big, heavy oak-laden style of wines that were popular in the 90’s (and still are with Guigal) to more elegant finesse-style wines attained by short fermentations with mostly full clusters. Winemaker Francois Villard The vineyards of Condrieu and Cote Rotie are on the steep hillsides of the Rhone River.

articles.text: Swim Across America event a major fundraiser for cardiology, cancer Bob Tandler (left), Levy Gerzberg, Josh Bernstein, and Peter Gertler celebrate after completing the swim in the annual Golden Gate Invitational on October 2. Last weekend in San Francisco Bay, intrepid swimmers from all over the United States converged to raise money for UCSF. On Saturday, October 2, Dr. Josh Bernstein hosted his annual Golden Gate Invitational Swim to benefit the UCSF Cardiology Council. Chief of Cardiology, Dr. Carlin Long, spoke to the 28 swimmers beforehand about the importance of their fundraising efforts, which raised thousands of dollars. However, the infamous San Francisco fog didn’t cooperate, and Bernstein called for Plan B on the morning of the swim, changing the route to a swim from Alcatraz to Aquatic Park. The swimmers all took the change in stride. Then, on Sunday hundreds of swimmers gathered on the beach at St Francis Yacht Club to swim to Aquatic Park for UCSF Pediatric Cancer research and treatment. Bernstein swam again, this time as a member of the team of 3-time cancer survivor Susan Helmrich, “Team Susan Survives.” Team Susan raised over $135,000 of the more than half a million dollars raised on Sunday. “For those of us who love swimming, it’s a pleasure to raise money for such worthy causes, even when the water in the Bay is chilly,” he said. Josh Bernstein and Susan Helmrich in San Francisco Bay at the Golden Gate Invitational Swim. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03
articles.title: Open water swimmers raise $135,000 for UCSF

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: As an interior designer, finding clarity in my purpose for my design practice has helped me serve with meaning and intention. If you follow me on social media or read my columns here every month, you probably know by now how committed I am to creating interiors that nourish my firm’s clients on many levels. I invite you to listen to a brand-new podcast, “The Lavender Room,” all about the topic of creating nourishing spaces, hosted by Cheryl Janis. This link is for her recent interview with me: cherylrjanis.com/the-lavender-room-design-podcast/comehome-to-your-self Cheryl and I had so much fun talking about the “why” behind what we do as interior designers. I hope you will give it a listen! In today’s column, I am sharing a few highlights from the conversation. First, a note on the podcast’s title. “The Lavender Room” comes from how, in the design of restful break rooms for hospital nursing staff, these rooms are often painted in this color. Cheryl, whose background is in that design niche, founded this podcast to have conversations with female interior designers about creating nourishing, healing spaces in clients’ homes, especially in light of what the collective has been going through in this time of Covid. If you know me, you know I love to “go deep or go home.” Cheryl asked me some very compelling questions. I shared about my military family’s tumultuous history (“If you pull up a carrot every time it starts to grow, you don’t have a full carrot”), and how that inspired my desire to become an interior designer and have an impact on the experience of home for others. Ultimately, my life transformed exponentially when I realized that what matters is our connection to Self, higher power, Source, whatever you want to call it. If we aren’t connected to that, we will never feel at home, no matter how beautiful our spaces are. As a beauty maker, my primary desire is to facilitate, inspire, invite people to see this. Being connected to Self, soul, heart, is everything. It is the most important thing. When I’m sitting with a new client, I’m listening to and watching where their energy lifts, where they get excited, and where they retract from a story that causes them pain. I’m listening for how they spend their time, what they are wanting to grow into, what they need. I’m like a ninja when it comes to seeing how we can help somebody become their best self – not to fix them, but to draw out what makes their life richer. Upleveling their environment can be a starting place for supporting them in that process. I love it when I get feedback from a client saying, “I didn’t even know that a space like this was possible for me.” A bonus tip from our conversation: one client reported that she often found herself in conflict with her husband in the kitchen. We observed that the walls were red. I believe that too much red does not contribute to harmony. The shift that a new, more soothing and energetically-apt paint color wrought was profound. (See “Hillsborough Haven” in our portfolio for more images from that project.) Cheryl agreed that too many warm colors in a space can trigger irritability. Single-family only zoning inherently exclude individuals, she said, and housing elements should include robust zoning. “The level of what we need to solve is huge, and it means that every community needs to do its fair share,” she said. “There is no city insulated from the housing crisis.” Bruce pointed to the “Three P’s” housing framework: protecting people where they are, producing affordable homes of all types, and preserving existing affordable housing. Her organization works on all three of these fair housing elements. She also praised the city for not appealing its RHNA, despite the fact that many cities across the state have appealed or are in the process of appealing. articles.text: Reconciliation, the establishment and re-establishment of healthy relationships is not only good medicine, it is remarkable medicine, for it is both preventative and curative. In that healthy relationships keep us from hurting ourselves and others, they are preventative. In that they help us heal at the places we are broken, they are curative. More about Ceasefire You have heard me speak often about Ceasefire, the violence reduction strategy that, when practiced, can greatly reduce incidents of gun violence and the number of homicides in our city. You have heard me say that hosting the Cease-fire call-ins, at which the young men most likely to shoot, or be shot, are invited to come back into the community in Barnett Hall. It is among the most important things we have done in the 161-year history of our congregation. Reconciliation, the restoration of healthy relationships is at the heart of this strategy. Listen to what Dr. George Cummings the CEO of Faith In Action East Bay writes about Ceasefire. What is Ceasefire, and why was it successful, and what are our challenges now? Ceasefire is a data-driven violence reduction strategy designed to reduce homicides by gun violence by a laser-like focus on those who are the primary perpetrators of gun violence in the community. According to the data in 2012, the two key factors in urban gun violence were gangs and open drug markets. By working with data collected by law enforcement it was possible to identify the key players driving homicides and by mean of direct communication with them engage them about putting down their guns. By means of monthly call-ins and custom notifications, there was ongoing communication that emphasized that shooting had a major impact on the whole community, and that the community was concerned about them being ALIVE and FREE, and wanted to invite them to participate in creating solutions to the problem. Those who were most at risk of being either victims (who were killed) or perpetrators (who ended up incarcerated) were the primary targets of the Ceasefire message and those who chose to change their lives were offered resources

articles.text: In the first weekend of October, Cub Scouts and parents descended on Bort Meadows in Chabot Regional Park near Castro Valley for two nights and one day filled with activities. Families rolled into camp Friday evening, set up their tents, and enjoyed a spaghetti dinner. The Order of the Arrow lodge cooked dinner, and then Raulin Morales and Kevin McKillop led the Cubs in a campfire program by lantern light. It included skits by the older Scouts, a round of jokes from the younger Cubs, and a spooky ghost story presented by OA Lodge Advisor Kevin Fischer. For many of the younger Cubs, this was their first overnight adventure in the wilderness, and they relished the chance to sleep in tents and listen to the owls and coyotes after lights out. On Saturday morning, the Lodge prepared French toast for all the campers, and then McKillop and Enzo Kohler led the younger Cubs on a 1-mile hike. After they finished the hike, the tired younger cubs and their parents headed home. At the same time, the Webelos were just getting started. Fourth and fifth graders arrived with their families early Saturday morning to drop off their gear and begin their day with a 3-mile hike. Mollie King, a Life Scout from Troop 4 and member of the Piedmont Community Service Crew, helped the Webelos put together a basic First Noah Otto, a Tiger Cub from Pack 6, grins after the Saturday morning opening flag ceremony at Bort Meadow in Anthony Chabot Regional Park on October 2. articles.text: Piedmont’s City staff outlined the upcoming public engagement processes related to the housing element at a recent joint study session on September 29. Since 1969, California has required that all local governments plan to meet the housing needs of everyone in a community. Local governments throughout the state must meet this requirement by adopting housing plans as part of their general plans. California’s housing element law acknowledges that local governments must adopt plans for housing development, and drafts must be submitted to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for approval. According to HCD, Government Code 65583(c)(7) required that “local government make a diligent effort to achieve public participation of all economic segments of the community in the development of the housing element, and the program shall describe this effort.” A joint study session of the city’s Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee was held virtually last week to consider the basic requirements of housing elements in California. articles.text: On Monday, October 4, City Council determined that conducting meetings with the public attending in City Hall could present imminent risk to the health and safety of attendees. It issued a resolution proclaiming a continuing need to meet remotely. All five members of the council and City Administrator Sara Lillevand were present at the October 4 meeting, which residents were able to join virtually. The pandemic has resulted in changes to how local governments conduct business, and legislative bodies were freed from some Brown Act requirements in light of the COVID-19 public health crisis that continues to linger. Now, with vaccine availability, some legislative bodies have once again welcomed the public to in-person meetings; at the same time, state Legislature has stepped in to formally amend open meeting laws to account for a new reality. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 361 into law on September 15, which allows local legislative bodies to continue meeting by teleconference, or remotely, during a proclaimed state of emergency. The governor’s original executive order allowing for virtual meetings was set to expire on June 15, the day the statewide shutdown was set to end. Instead, Gov. Newsom announced an extension allowing local agencies to conduct public meetings virtually. The bill passed 66-4 in the Assembly and 28-7 in the Senate. The Piedmont City Council determined on Monday by a 5-0 vote that meeting in person presents imminent risks to the health and safety of attendees. Piedmont City Council met in person for the first time for its regularly scheduled meeting on Monday, October 4. The public is not yet invited to attend in-person, but may still participate virtually.
articles.title: Public not yet invited to attend City Council meetings

Since 1969, California has required that all local governments plan to meet the housing needs of everyone in a community. Local governments throughout the state must meet this requirement by adopting housing plans as part of their general plans. California’s housing element law acknowledges that local governments must adopt plans for housing development, and drafts must be submitted to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for approval. According to HCD, Government Code 65583(c)(7) required that “local government make a diligent effort to achieve public participation of all economic segments of the community in the development of the housing element, and the program shall describe this effort.” A joint study session of the city’s Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee was held virtually last week to consider the basic requirements of housing elements in California. It issued a resolution proclaiming a continuing need to meet remotely. All five members of the council and City Administrator Sara Lillevand were present at the October 4 meeting, which residents were able to join virtually. The pandemic has resulted in changes to how local governments conduct business, and legislative bodies were freed from some Brown Act requirements in light of the COVID-19 public health crisis that continues to linger. Now, with vaccine availability, some legislative bodies have once again welcomed the public to in-person meetings; at the same time, state Legislature has stepped in to formally amend open meeting laws to account for a new reality. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 361 into law on September 15, which allows local legislative bodies to continue meeting by teleconference, or remotely, during a proclaimed state of emergency. The governor’s original executive order allowing for virtual meetings was set to expire on June 15, the day the statewide shutdown was set to end. Instead, Gov. Newsom announced an extension allowing local agencies to conduct public meetings virtually. The bill passed 66-4 in the Assembly and 28-7 in the Senate. The Piedmont City Council determined on Monday by a 5-0 vote that meeting in person presents imminent risks to the health and safety of attendees. articles.text: What does the Bible say? One answer is: absolutely nothing. Maybe it’s the politics in the air and perhaps even in our drinking water, but whatever the source, it seems like there is a renewed desire to be on God’s side. The introductory phrase “the Bible says…” is back with a vengeance. But I can assure you that any sentence that begins with those words makes no sense whatsoever. That babbling Bible has told women to sit down and shut up, called science a tool of the devil and fueled anti-Semitism and racism. This theological ventriloquism has led people through valleys of guilt, shame and fear, no doubt to support the status quo and keep the powerful in power. This arrogant preface is defended with the argument that a true believer takes the word of God literally. But which word are we talking about? If we are talking about the actual words composed by the original authors of the books of the Bible then shouldn’t those who feel so strongly about the literal word only quote from the original language? Obviously the first thing to note is that the Bible is a translation in progress. For example, the Greek word for “sin” is the same word used in archery to describe an arrow that has simply missed its mark. In the original language the sense is that one might be just a little off from center and yet in many circles “sin” has come to be understood as a dark and gruesome plague that compels us to feel guilt, shame and self-loathing.
articles.title: Interpreting the Bible is hard work...and necessary

articles.text: Piedmont holds the distinction of being the most vaccinated city in Alameda County with over 90% of its eligible residents vaccinated. Residents are not immune, however, to “breakthrough” cases of COVID despite the high vaccination status among residents. According to the Center for Disease Control, vaccine “breakthrough” cases are expected, but rare. While vaccines are an “effective and critical tool to bring the pandemic under control…no vaccine is 100% effective at preventing illness,” the agency said. There is evidence that vaccination makes illness less severe, and that risk of infection, hospitalization, and death are all much lower in vaccinated people compared to unvaccinated. This was reiterated by Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF Epidiemiologist, at a League of Women Voters virtual forum in September. “Despite the fact that the vaccines work really well, we do have breakthrough cases where fully vaccinated people do get infected,” Dr. Rutherford said. “If you are unvaccinated you are 4.9 times more likely to be diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2, and 29.4 times more likely to be hospitalized [due to complications from the virus.]” Breakthrough cases On October 2, Piedmont Community Church issued an announcement alerting residents of a COVID incident. On September 28, church staff was informed that a volunteer who was in the Christian Education Building two days prior had tested positive for COVID-19. The person who was infected is fully vaccinated and was double-masked, Transitional Pastor Dr. Steve Schibsted said. “The individual was feeling fine on Sunday morning but started experiencing flu-like symptoms on Sunday evening. The individual was tested for COVID-19, received the test results on Tuesday and immediately informed Leslie Quantz, our Director of Children’s Ministries,” Dr. Schibsted said. The church then notified all people who were in contact with the individual, and those involved notified the Alameda County Public Health Department. County Health Department guidance The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) orders that all persons who are diagnosed with COVID-19 self-isolate for at least 10 days from their last exposure. This applies to both vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. “A close contact [exposure] is still defined as having spent 15 minutes within six feet of someone known to have COVID-19, either after they were diagnosed or up to two days before they started showing symptoms, or if you have had multiple brief exposures adding up to 15 minutes, especially if indoors, and even if you wore face coverings or masks,” said ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram. A person who is vaccinated and has been exposed does not need to quarantine if they don’t have symptoms, Balram added, but they are recommended to test for the virus three to five days after exposure. The County provided the following example: “if Alex received her second dose of the Moderna vaccine on January 1, and had close contact on March 31 with someone who later tested positive for COVID-19, Alex does not need to quarantine. However, she should continue to monitor for symptoms of infection until April 12. If she does develop symptoms during that time, she should immediately go into isolation and contact her health care provider.”

articles.text: The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and state officials released its latest report of statewide COVID-19 data on October 1. As of October 1, California has 4,496,717 confirmed cases to-date. The seven-day positivity rate is 2.8%. The vast majority of confirmed cases are among the age group 18-49, with 2,564,360 of cases occurring in that age range. To date, there have been 68,796 COVID-related fatalities in the state, according to the CDPH. The average case rate among unvaccinated Californians age 16 or older is 57 per 100,000 per day, and the average case rate among vaccinated Californians is significantly lower at 7 per 100,000 for the week of September 19 through 25. Cases are occurring largely among unvaccinated populations, according to the CDPH. The rate among the unvaccinated is eight times the rate among vaccinated individuals. As of October 1, according to the Centers for Disease Control, 84% of eligible Californians have received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. Medical providers reported to CDPH that a total of 49,486,002 vaccine doses have been administered statewide. In Piedmont, the number of residents who are considered fully vaccinated is now slightly over 90%, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Piedmont has had 267 COVID cases reported to-date.

articles.text: The Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) will hold a meeting tomorrow, October 7, to present the revised Piedmont Safer Streets plan. The public comment for the first draft of the Safer Streets Plan took place in July and August; during that period, the city received 46 emails and one phone call with comments from the public. The plan project team gave consideration to all comments and a revised initial draft plan incorporates them where appropriate. Comments are listed in the Safer Streets draft plan and were edited to remove personal-identification information. One respondent suggested “greater police effort to both stop and cite blatant stop sign violations by bicyclists.” Another respondent cited interest in “continuing to explore more ways to calm traffic in Wildwood from Grand Avenue to Nova.” Many comments were geared toward cycling routes and bicycle lanes, with suggestions for improvement or upgrades. “I must say I am disappointed in the solutions presented to address bicycle safety,” one respondent commented. “Road diets are good, and better than nothing. However, a skinny strip of white paint on the ground that is somehow supposed to keep cars away from bicycles, in reality do almost nothing.” The Piedmont Bicycle and Safety Advisory Committee held its first meeting a year ago, October 13, 2020, and is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Right-of-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan, and Complete Streets policy. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, October 6, 2021 Local Items Safer Streets plan discussed tomorrow By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) will hold a meeting tomorrow, October 7, to present the revised Piedmont Safer Streets plan. The public comment for the first draft of the Safer Streets Plan took place in July and August; during that period, the city received 46 emails and one phone call with comments from the public. The plan project team gave consideration to all comments and a revised initial draft plan incorporates them where appropriate. Comments are listed in the Safer Streets draft plan and were edited to remove personal-identification information. One respondent suggested “greater police effort to both stop and cite blatant stop sign violations by bicyclists.” Another respondent cited interest in “continuing to explore more ways to calm traffic in Wildwood from Grand Avenue to Nova.” Many comments were geared toward cycling routes and bicycle lanes, with suggestions for improvement or upgrades. “I must say I am disappointed in the solutions presented to address bicycle safety,” one respondent commented. “Road diets are good, and better than nothing. However, a skinny strip of white paint on the ground that is somehow supposed to keep cars away from bicycles, in reality do almost nothing.” The Piedmont Bicycle and Safety Advisory Committee held its first meeting a year ago, October 13, 2020, and is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Right-of-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan, and Complete Streets policy. Enhanced street crossings are considered a high-priority project for the committee. The meeting will be held virtually tomorrow, October 7, at 5:30 p.m. For questions about the Piedmont Safer Streets project or about the committee, contact Gopika Nair, acting staff liaison for the committee, at (510) 420- 3054, or by email at saferstreets@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works Department is working on the final design of a proposed pedestrian safety project at the corner of Oakland and El Cerrito avenues. The intersection was identified as a prominent pedestrian crossing for school children and was considered high-priority for pedestrian safety upgrades in the 2014 Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan and the 2021 Piedmont Safer Streets Plan. Currently a hand-operated flashing light exists at El Cerrito Avenue. In December 2018, City Council approved a contract with Coastland Engineers to design permanent bulb-outs and more safety improvements. Preliminary designs were considered at an April 2019 meeting, which included shortened crossing distances, high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, refreshed painting and new signage. These designs allow for the installation of landscaping. Since 2014, minor improvements such as painted crosswalks and stop signs have been made at numerous intersections identified as high-priority. The Public Works Department recommended moving forward with the project due to its high-priority status. The cost of improvements at El Cerrito and Oakland Ave., and Jerome and Oakland Ave., one block west, is estimated at $400,000. The city council will review a more detailed engineer’s estimate. The city was awarded a $19,000 Safe Route to Schools mini-grant for the design phase of this project. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation has indicated its interest in raising funds for the project with its holiday 2021 campaign, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said. Gail Lambert, President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, reiterated her support in public comment at an October 5 City Council meeting. “This is one of the projects [the Foundation] wanted to focus on, to move forward with and start a fundraising campaign,” said Lambert. housing and real estate professionals, and residents. articles.text: The Piedmont Center for the Arts’ popular annual Beer Festival rolls into town this Friday, October 8 from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The event is a celebration of a wide range of beers and beermakers, with the added attraction of an authentic German dinner prepared on the lawn in front of the Center. Dave Larson and his crew from Piedmont Grocery will provide grilled bratwurst, red cabbage, warm potato salad, and German mustard. Inside the Center guests will be able to taste a range of beers from some of Piedmont’s favorite home brewers. In the past five years, more than two dozen brewers have offered samples of their latest brew. Prizes will be provided to the beermakers voted as best in their specialty. A panel of celebrity judges will be on hand to encourage the crowd and reward the brewers with prizes best entries. This year’s judges include Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Piedmont Grocery’s Dave Larson, with Fire Chief Dave Brannigan overseeing their work. Guests will be able to purchase a signature PCA pilsner glass for $10 for tasting as many samples as they wish. For the very modest price of $5, guests can partake in the German food fest on the front lawn. In Piedmont, there’s nothing quite like the Brewers Competition in early October each year.
articles.title: Popular event features beer tasting, grilled dinner outside
